System Design
Detailed Study Guide

Long-form, end-to-end articles for 25 famous system design problems. Each problem is a complete deep-dive — requirements, capacity math, data model, APIs, architecture, component-level deep dives, failure modes, and expected interview cross-questions with full reasoning.

📋How to Use This Guide

This is not a cheat sheet. It is a textbook-style guide designed for deep learning. Read each problem cover-to-cover. Focus on the reasoning behind every design choice, not just the choice itself.

📖 Reading Order Recommendation

First-time: Interview Framework → Core Fundamentals → Cheat Sheet → Cross-Question Patterns. These four pages form your mental toolkit before touching any problem.

Beginner path: URL Shortener (P1) → Rate Limiter (P6) → Notification System (P8) → Distributed Cache (P9). Foundational patterns and clean trade-offs.

Intermediate path: Twitter (P2), Instagram (P13), WhatsApp (P3), YouTube (P4), Uber (P5). Fan-out, real-time, and media patterns.

Advanced path: Google Docs (P19), Payment Gateway (P21), UPI (P23), Job Scheduler (P16), Stock Broker (P17), Shazam (P12). Combine multiple advanced patterns.

🎯What Makes This Different

Most system design resources show you the "what" — the architecture diagram. This guide focuses on the "why". Every design choice is explained from first principles. Every alternative is discussed. Every number is calculated step-by-step so you can derive them yourself in an interview.

🔑 The Core Skill This Guide Teaches

The hardest interview skill is defending your decisions under pressure. When an interviewer asks "why not Cassandra?" or "won't that be too slow?", you need to respond with first-principles reasoning and concrete numbers — not buzzwords. Every problem in this guide includes a Cross-Questions section with the exact pushbacks interviewers use and how to defend properly.

The System Design Interview Framework

A repeatable, structured approach to any system design problem. Internalise this framework — every problem in this guide follows it.

1The 5-Phase Method

A typical interview lasts 45-60 minutes. Time allocation matters. Spending 30 minutes on requirements means you have 15 minutes for the actual design — you will fail. Conversely, jumping into the design without clarifying requirements means you'll design the wrong system.

PhaseTimeWhat You DoCommon Mistakes
1. Clarify Requirements5 minAsk functional & non-functional questions. Establish scale.Skipping this — designing the wrong thing
2. Capacity Estimation5 minCalculate RPS, storage, bandwidth. Identify bottlenecks early.Vague numbers — "lots of users"
3. High-Level Design10 minDefine APIs, data model, then draw the box-and-arrow diagram.Drawing boxes before defining APIs
4. Deep Dive15 minLead the conversation into the hardest component. Show depth.Waiting passively for interviewer to ask
5. Trade-offs & Failures10 minDiscuss bottlenecks, SPOFs, scaling path, failure recovery.Pretending there are no downsides

2Phase 1: Clarifying Requirements

Interviewers deliberately leave the problem vague. They want to see if you ask the right questions. The questions you ask reveal how you think.

Functional Requirements (what the system DOES)

Get the interviewer to commit to a specific feature set. Push back on ambiguous answers. Common questions:

  • "What are the core user actions?" — Force them to enumerate user-facing features.
  • "Is X in scope?" — For each potentially-large feature, explicitly check: "Should I include comments? Analytics? Search?" Out-of-scope is also a clear answer.
  • "Are we building the consumer-facing app or the admin tool too?" — These can be very different systems.
  • "What's the most important user journey?" — Helps you prioritize where to spend your design time.

Non-Functional Requirements (what the system PROMISES)

These drive your technology choices and architecture. The big ones:

  • Scale: "How many users? Daily active? Monthly active? Peak concurrent?" Get specific numbers.
  • Read/Write ratio: "Is this read-heavy or write-heavy?" — Twitter is 100:1 read:write; chat is closer to 1:1.
  • Latency: "P50 and P99 target?" — Stock trading needs <10ms; news feed can be 500ms.
  • Consistency: "Strong or eventual?" — Bank transfers need strong; social likes can be eventual.
  • Availability: "SLA target?" — Three 9s vs five 9s changes architecture significantly.
  • Durability: "Can we lose data? If so, how much?" — Chat messages can lose 1s of inflight; bank transactions cannot.
  • Geography: "Global or single region?" — Multi-region means CRDTs, latency-aware routing.
💡 Pro Tip — Always Quantify

"Many users" is useless. "300M DAU" is actionable. "Fast" is useless. "P99 < 200ms" drives technology decisions. If the interviewer is vague, propose specific numbers: "Let's assume 100M DAU with peak 5× traffic during sale events — does that sound right?"

3Phase 2: Capacity Estimation

Back-of-envelope math should take 5 minutes and produce 4-6 numbers that drive your design decisions. Show your work.

The 1M/day = 12 RPS Rule

Memorise this conversion. It's the foundation of all capacity estimation:

1 day ≈ 100,000 seconds (10⁵) ← use this, NEVER 86,400. Calculator-free wins. 1M requests/day = 1M / 100k = 10 QPS 100M/day = 1k QPS 1B/day = 10k QPS 10B/day = 100k QPS 100B/day = 1M QPS

What to Estimate

  1. RPS — Both reads and writes separately. Read RPS often dwarfs write RPS.
  2. Peak RPS — Usually 3-5× average. Driven by sales, time-of-day, viral content.
  3. Storage growth/day — Records/day × avg size. Multiply by retention period for total.
  4. Bandwidth — RPS × avg response size. Critical for video, large payloads.
  5. Cache memory — Hot data (20% of records typically serve 80% of traffic) × record size.
  6. Server count — Peak RPS ÷ RPS-per-server (use rough numbers: 2K RPS/server for general APIs, 50K for in-memory cache).
⚠ Beware Over-Engineering

If your math says "150 RPS", do NOT propose Cassandra-sharded-across-10-DCs. Match the solution to the problem. A single MySQL instance can handle thousands of RPS. Only invoke distributed systems when the numbers demand it.

4Phase 3: High-Level Design

Step 1: Define the APIs FIRST

Before drawing any boxes, define the 3-5 core APIs. This forces clarity about what the system actually does and prevents scope creep.

For a URL Shortener: POST /api/v1/urls → create short URL GET /{short_key} → redirect to long URL GET /api/v1/urls/{key}/analytics → get click stats DELETE /api/v1/urls/{key} → delete URL

Step 2: Sketch the Data Model

What are the entities? Their fields? Primary keys? What indexes are needed? This typically reveals storage choices (SQL vs NoSQL) before you commit to them on the diagram.

Step 3: Draw the Architecture

Now and only now, draw boxes and arrows. Standard components in order:

  1. Client → DNS → CDN (if static/media) → Load Balancer
  2. Load Balancer → Stateless Services
  3. Services → Caches → Databases
  4. Services → Message Queues → Async Workers
  5. Workers → Storage (S3) / External APIs

5Phase 4: Deep Dive — The Most Important Phase

This is where senior engineers shine. Don't wait for the interviewer to drive — lead the conversation into the most challenging component.

How to Lead the Deep Dive

After presenting the high-level design, say: "There are three interesting challenges in this system: A, B, and C. Let me start with A because it has the highest impact on scalability."

For each deep-dive component, cover:

  • The specific problem this component solves
  • Your proposed solution with a focused diagram
  • Alternative approaches and why you rejected them
  • Trade-offs of your choice
  • Failure modes and recovery

6Phase 5: Trade-offs & Failure Modes

Senior engineers proactively surface what could go wrong. Cover these dimensions:

  • Single Points of Failure: What happens if service X goes down? How quickly does the system recover?
  • Hot Spots: One celebrity, one viral post, one popular product — does the system handle 1000× normal load on a single key?
  • Network Partitions: If two data centers can't talk for 30 minutes, what breaks? What recovers automatically?
  • Cold Start: When a new server joins, how long until it can serve traffic? When cache is empty, can the system handle a thundering herd?
  • Data Loss Boundaries: In the worst case, how much data can be lost? Acknowledge this explicitly.
  • Cost: At scale, what's the dominant cost? Storage? Bandwidth? Compute?

7Handling Pushback — The Real Test

Interviewers will push back on EVERY decision you make, even correct ones. They want to see if you fold under pressure or defend with first principles.

🛡 The Pushback Protocol

Step 1: Listen fully. Don't interrupt. Acknowledge the concern.

Step 2: Quantify. "Let me check the numbers. We have N writes/sec, and PostgreSQL handles M — that's X% utilisation."

Step 3: If your original choice still holds, defend it with the cost of the alternative. "Switching to Cassandra would lose ACID transactions and SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED. We need both for correctness here."

Step 4: If the pushback is valid, acknowledge openly. "You're right, I missed that. Here's how I'd revise..." Honesty beats stubbornness.

8Common Anti-Patterns to Avoid

  1. Buzzword bingo: Saying "Kafka" and "Cassandra" without explaining why or how they work internally.
  2. Premature distributed systems: Proposing global sharding before establishing that single-machine solutions can't handle the load.
  3. Hand-waving the hard parts: "And then the load balancer routes appropriately" — this is where the interesting design lives.
  4. Ignoring failure: Designing only for the happy path. Real systems fail constantly.
  5. Defensive design: Adding 5 services and 3 caches "just in case". YAGNI applies.
  6. Silent design: Going quiet while you think. Narrate your reasoning out loud at all times.

System Design Cheat Sheet

The numbers and tables you fall back on when an interviewer says "give me a rough estimate." Memorise the bolded ones — derive the rest from them.

🔑 The Three Numbers That Save You

1. 1 day ≈ 100,000 seconds  (actually 86,400 — round up; makes all back-of-envelope math 10× cleaner)  ·  2. 1M requests/day ≈ 10 QPS  (direct from 1,000,000 ÷ 100,000)  ·  3. Peak load = 5× average  (10× for consumer social apps).

With these three numbers you can derive QPS, storage and bandwidth for any scale in your head. Always assume 1 day = 100k seconds in interviews — never pull out a calculator for 86,400.

From Jeff Dean's original list, updated. Order of magnitude is what matters — these are the deltas you use to argue "RAM vs disk" or "same DC vs cross-region."

📐 Two derived rules you'll use constantly

Rule of thumb 1: Anything on a different continent costs you ≥100 ms. Multi-region writes that need a round trip are always slower than 100 ms.

Rule of thumb 2: Cache miss to SSD is ~1000× a cache hit. If your cache hit rate drops from 99% to 90%, your average latency goes up ~100×, not 10%.

4QPS Quick Math

⚡ The Single Most-Used Calculation in Interviews

"How many QPS is X requests per day?" Just divide by 100,000. Don't bother with 86,400 — the rounding error is < 16% and it doesn't affect whether you need 1 server or 1,000.

So: 1M/day ÷ 100k = 10 QPS. 100M/day = 1k QPS. 10B/day = 100k QPS. Memorise that pattern — every order of magnitude in requests is one order of magnitude in QPS.

Requests/DayAvg QPS (÷100k)Peak QPS (5×)Peak QPS (10×)
100 K1510
1 M1050100
10 M1005001 k
100 M1 k5 k10 k
1 B10 k50 k100 k
10 B100 k500 k1 M
100 B1 M5 M10 M

The exact numbers using 86,400 sec/day are ~16% lower (e.g. 1M/day = 11.57 QPS), but you'll never need that precision in a system design interview. Calculator-free wins.

5Storage and Bandwidth Math Templates

// Daily storage growth storage_per_day = active_users × actions_per_user_per_day × bytes_per_action // 5-year storage need (with replication factor 3) total_storage = storage_per_day × 365 × 5 × replication_factor // Bandwidth (write) write_bw = QPS_write × payload_size_bytes // e.g. 10k writes/s × 1 KB = 10 MB/s = 80 Mbps // Bandwidth (read with cache) read_bw = QPS_read × payload_size × (1 − cache_hit_rate) // Cache size for 80/20 rule hot_data = total_data × 0.20 cache_size = hot_data × replication_factor (usually 1 if just cache)

7bPartitioning vs Sharding (Quick Recall)

People get these confused — and so do interviewers, sometimes. Crisp definitions:

PartitioningSharding
Where pieces liveSame machine, one DB instanceDifferent machines / DB instances
Why do itFaster scans, smaller indexes, cheap mass deletes (DROP PARTITION)Scale storage / throughput beyond one box
RoutingDB does it transparently (same SQL works)App / middleware (Vitess, Citus) routes to right shard
Cross-piece txnACID free (same DB)Hard (saga / 2PC)
ExamplesPostgres PARTITION BY RANGE/HASHCitus, Vitess, app-level shards, MongoDB shards
Cassandra / DynamoDB "partition"Confusingly, what these call a "partition" is what most people call a shard — it determines which node owns the row across a distributed cluster.

Mental model: "Partitioning = one table split into pieces on one machine. Sharding = one table split into pieces on many machines."

The natural progression: single Postgres → + read replicas → + partitioning → + sharding (Citus / Vitess / app-level). Don't skip step 3 — a partitioned Postgres handles workloads that people often unnecessarily shard for.

8Consistency Models (Cheat Card)

ModelGuaranteeExample system
LinearizableEvery read sees the latest committed write, globally orderedetcd, Zookeeper, single-leader Postgres
SequentialSame global order, but reads may lagSpanner with bounded staleness
CausalIf A happened-before B, every reader sees A before BCOPS, Bayou; many "session consistency" stores
Read-your-writesYou always see your own previous writesDynamoDB strongly consistent reads (per-key)
Monotonic readsSuccessive reads never go backwards in timeSticky-session designs
EventualIf writes stop, all replicas converge eventuallyS3, DynamoDB default, Cassandra QUORUM=1

Three Redis Patterns That Win Interviews

🔑 Redis Sorted Set — the swiss army inside the swiss army

Sorted Sets are O(log N) for inserts and range queries. You can use them for: leaderboards (score=points), top-K trending (score=count), news feeds (score=timestamp), priority queues (score=priority), sliding-window rate limiters (score=timestamp, ZREMRANGEBYSCORE to evict old entries, ZCARD to count), delayed-job schedulers (score=run-at-timestamp). When the interviewer says "I need X by Y," the answer is often "Redis Sorted Set."

🔑 Lua scripts for atomicity

Redis is single-threaded, and Lua scripts run atomically — no other command interleaves. Anywhere you'd need "check-then-set" (rate limiter token decrement, seat hold, inventory decrement), wrap the read + check + write in a Lua script. One round trip, zero races, no distributed lock needed. The pattern shows up in P6 (rate limiter), P10 (inventory), P20 (seat hold).

🔑 Pipelining vs MULTI/EXEC

Pipelining: send N commands without waiting for each reply; reduces round trips. Not atomic — other clients may interleave. MULTI/EXEC: queue N commands and execute atomically (no interleaving) but no conditional logic. Lua: atomic + can include conditionals + can read intermediate values. Pick by: latency need (pipeline), strict atomicity (MULTI), or conditional logic (Lua).

10HTTP Status and Idempotency Quick Card

CodeWhen to use
200 OKSuccessful GET / PUT / PATCH that returns body
201 CreatedSuccessful POST that created a resource
202 AcceptedAsync — accepted for processing, not yet done
204 No ContentSuccessful DELETE / PUT with no response body
301 vs 302301 = permanent (browser caches forever, kills your analytics). 302 = temporary (every click hits you — good for click counts)
400Bad request payload (validation failure)
401 vs 403401 = not authenticated. 403 = authenticated but not allowed
404Resource doesn't exist
409 ConflictDuplicate, version mismatch, optimistic-lock failure
410 GoneWas here, deleted permanently (use for expired short URLs)
429 Too Many RequestsRate limit hit — must include Retry-After header
500Unexpected server error — log and alert
502 / 503 / 504Bad gateway / unavailable / timeout — usually upstream issue

Idempotency rule of thumb: GET, PUT, DELETE are idempotent. POST and PATCH are not — protect with an Idempotency-Key header backed by a Redis SET (24-hour TTL) or a DB unique index.

Multi-leader replicationMulti-region writes, accept conflict resolution (CRDTs, LWW)
Leaderless (quorum) replicationCassandra, DynamoDB — tunable consistency via W+R>N
Range partitioningRange queries common (time-series, scheduled jobs by next_run_at)
Hash partitioningEven distribution, no range queries (user_id, tenant_id)
Composite partition + sort key"Latest N for a user" pattern (Cassandra, DynamoDB)
Geo-partitioningLatency-sensitive, data sovereignty (EU users stay in EU)

12Quick Capacity Templates (Copy-Paste in Interview)

// Template 1: Read-heavy with cache (1 day = 100k secs) DAU = 100M reads_per_user_per_day = 50 total_reads_per_day = DAU × 50 = 5B avg_QPS_read = 5B / 100k = 50k // vs 58k with 86400 — close enough peak_QPS_read = avg × 5 = 250k cache_hit_rate = 0.95 DB_QPS = 250k × 0.05 = 12.5k // well within Postgres // Template 2: Storage from daily writes writes_per_day = 100M actions avg_row_size = 500 B storage_per_day = 50 GB 5_yr_storage = 50 GB × 365 × 5 = ~90 TB with_3x_replication = ~270 TB // Template 3: Bandwidth from a feed feed_request_size = 50 KB // 25 items × 2 KB each peak_QPS = 50k egress_Gbps = 50k × 50 KB × 8 = 20 Gbps // → CDN absolutely required, or 20 × 10GbE NICs // Template 4: WebSocket fleet sizing concurrent_connections = 50M conns_per_node = 100k nodes_required = 500 // Template 5: Cron firings/sec at scale cron_jobs = 1M every 5 min fires_per_sec = 1M / (5 × 60) = 3,333/s // peak top-of-hour can spike 10× // → add deterministic jitter (hash(job_id) % 60s) to smear the spike

13Failure Modes Mental Checklist

Walk this list during any "what if it fails?" question:

  1. Single instance crash — health check, auto-restart, replica fail-over.
  2. Whole AZ down — multi-AZ deployment, replicas in other AZ.
  3. Whole region down — multi-region (active-active or active-passive), DNS fail-over.
  4. Network partition — CAP trade-off; what does the system choose (CP vs AP)?
  5. Cache stampede — request coalescing, soft TTL with background refresh.
  6. Thundering herd at startup — jittered TTL, exponential back-off, warm-up.
  7. Slow downstream — circuit breaker, bulkhead, timeout, fallback.
  8. Hot key / hot partition — secondary key sharding, request randomisation, in-memory hot cache.
  9. Message duplicate — idempotency keys, exactly-once at the consumer.
  10. Poison message — dead-letter queue, max-retry, alert.
  11. Schema migration — backwards-compatible, dual-write, expand-contract.
  12. Bad deploy — canary, blue/green, automated rollback on SLO breach.
  13. Data corruption — backups, point-in-time recovery, checksums.
  14. Clock skew — NTP everywhere; never use wall-clock for ordering (use HLC or Snowflake).

14What "Senior" Looks Like in a System Design Interview

✅ Signals That Move You Up a Level
  • Quantifying before reaching for a new technology.
  • Acknowledging trade-offs before the interviewer points them out.
  • Saying "I'd start with the simpler answer (X) and only move to (Y) when this number crosses (Z)."
  • Mentioning back-pressure, idempotency, and observability without prompting.
  • Asking about SLAs and consistency requirements early.
  • Drawing the failure path, not just the happy path.
  • Showing how the system evolves: 1k users → 1M → 100M.
⚠ Signals That Move You Down
  • Reaching for microservices on day one ("I'd use 12 services for this").
  • Saying "Cassandra is web-scale" without numbers.
  • Forgetting authentication, rate-limiting, monitoring.
  • Ignoring cost.
  • Going silent for >30 seconds — always narrate.
  • Defensive design — adding caches and queues "just in case."

Cross-Question Patterns

A meta-guide for handling interview pushback. Interviewers don't run out of follow-ups by accident — they have a small set of archetypes they cycle through. Learn the archetypes and you stop being surprised.

🔑 The Cardinal Rule

Defend with numbers, not buzzwords. When an interviewer pushes back, the wrong instinct is to swap technologies to appease them. The right instinct is to quantify the supposed problem and show whether it's real. This single discipline separates mid-level from senior.

1The Eight Archetypes of Interview Pushback

Every "but…" you'll hear in an interview is one of these. Recognise the archetype in the first three seconds and you've already won the exchange.

#ArchetypeWhat they're really testing
1"But what about scale X?"Can you do back-of-envelope math under pressure?
2"Why not Cassandra / DynamoDB / Mongo?"Can you articulate trade-offs without becoming defensive?
3"Won't that be too slow?"Do you know real benchmark numbers (latency, throughput)?
4"What if it fails?"Do you think about failure modes proactively?
5"How would you scale this 100×?"Can you describe the evolution path, not a redesign?
6"What's the bottleneck?"Do you know which component breaks first?
7"How do you handle hot keys / partitions?"Do you understand skew and how to absorb it?
8"What if two requests race?"Do you know concurrency primitives and their cost?

2Pattern 1 — "But What About Scale X?"

You said the system handles 1k QPS. The interviewer asks, "What about 100k QPS? Or 1M?"

The wrong move

Panic, switch your DB to something "web-scale", introduce three new caches, and start drawing arrows everywhere.

The right move — Quantify, then ladder

  1. Quantify the new load. "100k QPS reads × 50 KB payload = 5 GB/s egress. That's 40 Gbps."
  2. Find what breaks first. Walk through each component: API gateway? DB? Cache? Network? Identify the first thing that saturates.
  3. Apply the smallest fix. Not a redesign — the smallest change that addresses the specific bottleneck.
  4. Articulate the ladder explicitly. "At 100k QPS I'd add Redis with 95% hit rate, dropping DB QPS to 5k — still single-node. At 1M QPS I'd shard Postgres by user_id, and the cache fleet grows to N nodes. At 10M QPS I'd add a CDN for read-heavy responses."
📐 Stock phrase to memorise

"Let me work the numbers before changing the architecture. At {new_scale} the system would need {derived_load}. The first thing that breaks is {component} at {component_limit}. The minimal fix is {smallest_change}, which buys us {headroom}. If we need to go further, the next step is {next_change}."

3Pattern 2 — "Why Not Cassandra / DynamoDB / Mongo?"

You chose Postgres. The interviewer says, "Cassandra would be more scalable, no?"

The wrong move

Immediately switch to Cassandra to seem flexible. You just lost the exchange.

The right move — Defend, then articulate what you'd lose

Each NoSQL store has well-known limitations. State them as costs, not as opinions.

If they ask…You answer with the cost of switching
Why not Cassandra?No multi-table ACID, no SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, denormalisation forces read-modify-write on collection types. Great for write-heavy time-series, poor for relational workloads.
Why not DynamoDB?GSI queries are eventually consistent. Each partition caps at 1k writes/s. No multi-item transactions across partitions (only TransactWriteItems with 100-item limit and 2× cost).
Why not MongoDB?Single-document atomicity only (multi-doc transactions exist but are slow). Aggregation pipelines don't replace SQL joins at scale.
Why not Redis as the source of truth?Volatile. AOF persistence adds latency. No complex queries. No ACID across keys.
Why not Elasticsearch?Near-real-time, not real-time. Not a source of truth. Refresh interval (1 s default) means newly indexed docs aren't immediately searchable.
Why not Kafka as the database?Not queryable. Retention costs grow. Compaction loses history. Use it as the log, not the store.
📐 Stock phrase to memorise

"I considered {alternative}. We'd gain {benefit}, but lose {specific_capability}. For this workload {specific_capability} is more important because {requirement_from_problem}. If the workload were {hypothetical}, I'd switch."

4Pattern 3 — "Won't That Be Too Slow?"

Cite a benchmark. The Cheat Sheet exists for this exact moment.

  • "Won't reading from Postgres be slow at this rate?" → "Postgres does 50–100k cached reads/s per node. Our query is index-only on a partial index — it's a sub-millisecond lookup."
  • "Won't the cache be the bottleneck?" → "Redis handles 100k–1M ops/s on a single node. We're at 50k, well within capacity."
  • "Won't the network be the bottleneck?" → "A 10 GbE NIC carries 1.25 GB/s. Our peak egress is 200 MB/s — 16% utilisation."
  • "Won't WebSockets be slow?" → "A single Node.js server handles 50–100k concurrent WebSocket connections. For 1M concurrent users we need ~10–20 nodes."
⚠ Don't say "fast enough" — say a number

"It should be fine" loses you the exchange. "It's 50k QPS vs Redis's 200k QPS ceiling — 25% utilised" wins it.

5Pattern 4 — "What If It Fails?"

The interviewer points at any single component on your diagram and asks "what if this dies?" Have a structured answer.

  1. State the blast radius. "If this Redis node dies, all rate-limit checks in this AZ fail for ~5 seconds."
  2. State the detection. "Health checks every 1 s, and circuit breaker trips after 3 consecutive failures."
  3. State the mitigation. "We fail open on rate-limit decisions (allow the request) rather than fail closed — degraded service beats outage. For state-critical components like the DB we have a hot standby with automatic fail-over in ~30 s."
  4. State the recovery. "On recovery, Redis warms from a snapshot. We accept ~5 minutes of stale rate-limit data."

This four-step structure (blast radius → detection → mitigation → recovery) works for every "what if it fails" question.

6Pattern 5 — "How Would You Scale This 100×?"

This is asking for an evolution path, not a rewrite. The structure:

Current scale → 10× → 100× → 1000× │ │ │ │ Find bottleneck at each step: • CPU → horizontal scale-out • DB write → shard or move to LSM (Cassandra) • DB read → cache layer with high hit rate • Network → CDN, regional POPs • Storage → tiered (hot/warm/cold) • Latency cross-region → multi-region replicas

The trick is to not jump straight to the 1000× answer. The interviewer is testing whether you'd over-engineer. Acknowledge: "I wouldn't add Cassandra today — at our current scale Postgres is fine. I'd add it when write throughput crosses ~10k/s sustained, which is the right point given a single Postgres node tops out around there."

7Pattern 6 — "What's the Bottleneck?"

Have a confident answer ready for every design you draw. The candidate who can't name the bottleneck doesn't understand the system.

📐 Walk the request path

Mentally trace one request from client to response, naming the slowest hop. That's your bottleneck. Then trace one write from accept to durable storage — that's your write bottleneck. They're usually different.

Common bottlenecks by system type

SystemUsual bottleneck
Read-heavy feedCache miss → DB fan-out under load
Write-heavy log/chatDB write throughput, then partition skew
Real-time (chat, gaming)WebSocket node memory; cross-region latency
Media (video, image)CDN egress cost; transcoding compute
SearchIndex size in RAM; long-tail query latency
PaymentExternal processor latency; idempotency store contention
Order book / matchingSingle matching-engine thread CPU

8Pattern 7 — "How Do You Handle Hot Keys / Partitions?"

This is the most common "next level" question after the basic design. The answers cluster into four techniques:

  1. Read replicas for the hot key. Justin Bieber's tweet — replicate his timeline to 10 Redis nodes, route reads by user-hash-mod-10.
  2. Secondary key sharding. Append a random suffix on writes (key#0…key#9) and union on reads. Trades read complexity for write distribution.
  3. In-memory hot-key cache. Detect hot keys with a Count-Min Sketch; cache them in process memory of every application server (skip the cache entirely).
  4. Request coalescing. Multiple concurrent cache-misses for the same key — only one fetches the DB, others wait on the same promise. Prevents stampede.

9Pattern 8 — "What If Two Requests Race?"

Concurrency questions test whether you know which primitive to reach for.

Race scenarioPrimitive
Two workers claim the same jobSELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
Inventory decrement, two buyersOptimistic locking with version column, or atomic Redis DECR (Lua)
Two writes to same rowLast-write-wins (LWW), CRDT, or version conflict (409 to client)
Duplicate API call (network retry)Idempotency-Key header + Redis SET NX EX
Two messages with same paymentExactly-once via consumer dedup (Kafka offset commit + outbox)
Multiple writers in distributed systemSingle-leader (Raft) or quorum write (W+R>N)
Distributed counterSharded counter (N rows), aggregate on read; or CRDT G-Counter

10How To Concede Without Losing

Sometimes the interviewer is right. Conceding gracefully is a senior skill. The wrong way: "Oh you're right, let me change everything." The right way:

✅ Stock phrase

"Good point — I'd been thinking of {original_assumption}. If {their_constraint} is the priority then {their_suggestion} is the better choice because {specific_reason}. The trade-off I'd flag is {what_we_lose}, but for this requirement it's worth it."

You've conceded the point, validated their reasoning, but kept the trade-off conversation alive. That's the senior signal.

11The Phrase Library

Bank these. Drop them verbatim under pressure.

When you need to…Say this
Buy thinking time"Let me work the numbers on that before deciding."
Defend without sounding rigid"I'd push back on that — here's why."
Acknowledge a trade-off proactively"The trade-off here is X. For this requirement that's acceptable because…"
Show evolution awareness"I'd start with the simple answer and migrate to the complex one when {metric} crosses {threshold}."
Signal failure-thinking"What does this look like when it fails? When {component} dies we …"
Show cost-awareness"Cheaper alternative: …. The cost difference is roughly {$X/month}, justified because {reason}."
Stay structured when interrupted"Good question — I'll come back to {topic} after I finish the {current_topic} thread so I don't lose context."

12Anti-Patterns to Avoid

⚠ Things that make interviewers flinch
  • "It's web-scale" — meaningless phrase.
  • "We'd use microservices" as the answer to a scaling question.
  • "Eventually consistent" applied to anything financial.
  • "Just cache it" without discussing invalidation, hit rate, or stampede.
  • "Use Kubernetes" as an architectural answer.
  • "Throw more hardware at it" without saying what hardware or why it helps.
  • Designing for 1B users when interviewer said 10k.
  • Switching DBs the moment they say "but…".

🔑 The Compounding Habit

Every time you read a problem in this guide, mentally tag each cross-question with one of the 8 archetypes. After 25 problems × 10 questions each, you'll have seen each archetype ~30 times — and you'll recognise it in the first three seconds of a real interview.

Medium Foundational Hashing Caching KGS

Problem 1: Designing a URL Shortener (Bit.ly / TinyURL)

A foundational system design problem that exercises hashing, caching strategies, key generation, and high read-throughput design. Master this and you have the building blocks for many other systems.

📑 Article Contents
  1. Context and Why This Problem Matters
  2. Requirements Gathering
  3. Capacity Estimation
  4. API Design
  5. Data Model
  6. High-Level Architecture
  7. Deep Dive 1: Key Generation Service
  8. Deep Dive 2: Caching Strategy
  9. Deep Dive 3: Analytics Pipeline
  10. Deep Dive 4: The Redirect (301 vs 302)
  11. Deep Dive 5: URL Expiry and Cleanup

  13. Scaling Path: 1K → 100M Users

1Context and Why This Problem Matters

A URL shortener accepts a long URL (potentially hundreds of characters) and returns a compact alias of typically 6-8 characters. When someone visits the short URL, they get redirected to the original long URL. This seems trivial — why is it a famous system design problem?

The non-obvious reasons make URL shorteners interesting:

  • Extreme read-skew — A short URL is created once but may be clicked millions of times. The read:write ratio is typically 100:1 or higher. This forces aggressive caching.
  • Atomic uniqueness at scale — Two simultaneous "create" requests must never produce the same short key. With millions of requests/day across multiple servers, this is a coordination problem.
  • Latency-sensitive redirects — Every click is a redirect that the user is waiting for. A 100ms delay feels slow. This drives architecture toward edge caching and minimal database hits.
  • Analytics without blocking — Click counts and geographic analytics are valuable, but you cannot block the redirect to record them. This introduces async event streaming.
  • Storage growth over time — Years of accumulated URLs become petabytes. Sharding strategies matter.

URL shorteners are also foundational: the same patterns (KGS, cache-aside, async analytics) appear in Pastebin (Problem 18), Image hosting, and many other systems.

2Requirements Gathering

In the interview, the prompt is usually just "Design Bit.ly". Your first job is to ask the right questions and establish concrete requirements.

Functional Requirements

The core feature set, in priority order:

  • Shorten: Given a long URL, return a short alias (typically 7-8 chars). The mapping is permanent (or has a defined TTL).
  • Redirect: When someone visits the short URL, redirect to the original long URL. This must be fast (<100ms).
  • Custom aliases: Allow users to specify their own alias (e.g., bit.ly/mylink). Useful for branded links.
  • Expiration: URLs can have optional TTLs (10 min, 1 hr, 1 day, 1 month, never).
  • Analytics: Track total clicks, unique visitors, geographic distribution, referrer sources.
  • User accounts: Authenticated users can manage their URLs (list, edit, delete). Anonymous users can also create short URLs but cannot manage them later.

Non-Functional Requirements

The system's promises about scale, latency, and reliability:

  • Scale: 100M DAU. Only ~10% are creators (10M users × ~10 URLs/day each = 100M URLs/day); the other 90% just redirect to existing URLs. With 100:1 read:write ratio → 10B redirects/day.
  • Redirect latency: P99 < 100ms. Most users abandon if a link takes >3 seconds.
  • Availability: 99.99% (4-nines = ~52 min downtime/year). Redirect downtime is critical because every dead link hurts the brand.
  • Durability: Once a URL is created, it must not be lost. Users share these URLs publicly.
  • Unguessability: Short keys must be hard to guess (no sequential IDs in plaintext).
  • Retention: URLs live for at least 5 years after last access, unless explicitly deleted or expired.

Clarifying Questions to Ask the Interviewer

These questions show you understand the problem space and prevent design mistakes:

  • "Are custom aliases required, or are auto-generated keys sufficient?" — Custom aliases add complexity (collision check, profanity filter, reserved word list).
  • "Is analytics required at v1, or can it be added later?" — Analytics changes the architecture significantly (Kafka, ClickHouse).
  • "What's the short URL length budget?" — 7 chars in base62 = 3.5 trillion combinations. 8 chars = 218 trillion. Usually 7-8 chars is the standard.
  • "Should expired URLs return 410 Gone or just redirect to a 404?" — UX detail that affects API design.
  • "Is there a per-user rate limit?" — Free tier vs paid tier may have different limits. Drives the rate limiter design.
  • "Multi-region or single region?" — Global deployment means data replication and conflict resolution.
🔑 Key Insight from Requirements

The 100:1 read:write ratio is the most important number. It tells you that read path optimisation is paramount. Every architectural decision should prioritise making redirects fast and cheap, even at the cost of slower writes. This justifies aggressive caching, CDN, and read replicas.

3Capacity Estimation

Run the numbers. These will drive every architectural decision that follows.

Traffic

MetricCalculationValue
DAU (given)—100 M
Creators (10% of DAU)100M × 10%10 M
URLs created per creator per day—~10
URLs created per day10M × 10100 M
Writes per second (avg)100M / 100k~1 k/s
Reads per day (100:1 ratio)100M × 10010 B
Reads per second (avg)10B / 100k~100 k/s
Peak writes (5× avg)—~5 k/s
Peak reads (5× avg)—~500 k/s

What this tells us: 1k writes/sec is well within a single MySQL/Postgres instance (5–10k/sec ceiling). 100k reads/sec is far beyond a single DB — we must cache aggressively or use read replicas. The 90/10 creator/consumer split also means many DAU never trigger writes at all — keep this in mind for analytics.

Storage

MetricCalculationValue
Avg row sizeshort_key (8B) + long_url (~200B) + metadata (~200B)~500 bytes
Storage/day100M × 500 bytes~50 GB/day
Storage / 5 years50 GB × 365 × 5~91 TB
Storage / 10 years50 GB × 365 × 10~182 TB

What this tells us: Single-machine storage caps at ~10–20 TB SSD. At 91 TB we need sharding (~5–10 shards) or a managed solution like DynamoDB that handles sharding transparently.

Bandwidth

MetricCalculationValue
Read bandwidth100k/s × 500 bytes~50 MB/s
Write bandwidth1k/s × 500 bytes~500 KB/s

What this tells us: Bandwidth is modest. CDN edge caching of 301 redirects helps for popular URLs but isn't strictly required for these payload sizes.

Cache Memory

The 80/20 rule: 20% of URLs serve 80% of clicks. We should cache those 20%.

MetricCalculationValue
Daily unique active URLs10B clicks / 5 avg clicks per URL~2 B URLs/day
Hot 20% subset2B × 20%~400 M URLs
Cache memory400M × 500 bytes~200 GB

What this tells us: 200 GB is too large for a single Redis instance (typical max 64 GB). We need Redis Cluster (4–8 shards). At 95%+ cache hit rate, the DB sees only ~5,800 reads/sec — comfortable for read replicas.

Key Space

LengthCombinations (base62)Years of URLs at 100M/day
6 chars62⁶ = 56 billion~1.5 years
7 chars62⁷ = 3.5 trillion~96 years
8 chars62⁸ = 218 trillion~6,000 years

Decision: 7-character keys (base62 alphanumeric: a-z, A-Z, 0-9) give us a century of capacity. Bit.ly uses this length.

🔧 From Numbers to Architecture — what these estimates force

Every tech choice in the HLD below traces back to a number we just computed. Read these bullets as "number → constraint → tech choice".

  • 1k writes/sec avg, ~5k peak → a single MySQL/Postgres node (5–10k writes/sec ceiling) handles writes comfortably. No write-sharding needed for the first year; light 4-way shard if we ever 10×.
  • 100k reads/sec avg, ~500k peak → far beyond any single DB's read capacity. Redis cluster mandatory on the redirect path. At 95% cache hit rate the DB sees only ~5k reads/sec, handled by 3 read replicas.
  • ~200 GB hot cache (400M URLs × 500 B) → too big for one Redis node (typical 64 GB max). Redis Cluster of ~8 shards × 25 GB; with primary + replica per shard = 16 nodes.
  • 10B redirects/day with click-tracking → we cannot block the redirect on an analytics write (every ms hurts). Kafka introduced as the async bus for click events; ClickHouse downstream for analytical queries.
  • ~91 TB storage / 5 yr → exceeds a single SSD (10–20 TB ceiling). Shard MySQL ~4 ways by hash(short_key); each shard ~23 TB. Or use DynamoDB if we don't want to run shards.
  • P99 redirect < 200 ms target → cross-region calls (~80–150 ms) are too expensive on the hot path. CDN at the edge for top-N popular URLs + region-local Redis + read replicas. CDN can absorb 30–60% of redirects for viral links.
  • 1k+ writes/sec needing globally-unique 7-char keys → in-line collision-check on a 3.5T keyspace works in theory but adds DB round-trips on the write path. KGS with Redis LPOP from a pre-minted key pool eliminates the round-trip; pool is refilled by a background worker.
  • CAP: Availability ≫ Consistency → tolerate brief read-replica lag. Use async replication (MySQL row-based) rather than synchronous.
  • Unguessability requirement → keys must not be sequential. KGS generates random base62 strings; not derived from an incrementing counter.

4API Design

Before drawing any architecture, nail down the contracts. This forces clarity about what the system actually does.

POST /api/v1/urls — Create a Short URL

POST /api/v1/urls HTTP/1.1 Authorization: Bearer {api_key} Content-Type: application/json { "long_url": "https://example.com/very/long/path?with=params", "custom_alias": "myevent", // optional "ttl_hours": 168, // optional, null = never expires "user_id": "uuid" // optional, anonymous allowed } Response: 201 Created { "short_url": "https://bit.ly/abc1234", "short_key": "abc1234", "long_url": "https://example.com/very/long/path?with=params", "created_at": "2024-01-15T09:00:00Z", "expires_at": "2024-01-22T09:00:00Z" } Error responses: 400 Bad Request — invalid URL format 409 Conflict — custom_alias already taken 422 Unprocessable — URL contains malware (Safe Browsing check) 429 Too Many — rate limit exceeded

Design rationale:

  • POST not GET — creating state. Idempotent? No, each call creates a new short URL (unless custom_alias is given).
  • API key auth (not session cookie) — this is a backend API. Frontend has its own session layer.
  • TTL in hours — better unit than seconds for human readability; large enough to cover most cases.

GET /{short_key} — Redirect to Original URL

GET /abc1234 HTTP/1.1 Host: bit.ly Response: 302 Found Location: https://example.com/very/long/path?with=params Cache-Control: private, max-age=0 X-Short-Key: abc1234 Error responses: 404 Not Found — key doesn't exist 410 Gone — URL has expired or been deleted

Design rationale:

  • The redirect endpoint sits at the root path, not /api/v1/..., because the URL is what gets shared publicly.
  • 302 not 301: 302 is "temporary" — the browser will hit our server every time. 301 is "permanent" — the browser caches the redirect locally and never tells us again. We use 302 to capture analytics on every click. (See Deep Dive 4 for the full discussion.)
  • Cache-Control: private, max-age=0 ensures intermediate proxies don't cache the redirect.

GET /api/v1/urls/{key}/analytics — Click Analytics

GET /api/v1/urls/abc1234/analytics?from=2024-01-01&to=2024-01-31&granularity=day Authorization: Bearer {api_key} Response: 200 OK { "short_key": "abc1234", "total_clicks": 54200, "unique_visitors": 41000, "timeline": [ { "date": "2024-01-01", "clicks": 320, "unique": 280 }, { "date": "2024-01-02", "clicks": 412, "unique": 367 } ], "top_countries": [ { "country": "IN", "clicks": 30000 }, { "country": "US", "clicks": 18000 } ], "top_referrers": [ { "domain": "twitter.com", "clicks": 24000 }, { "domain": "facebook.com", "clicks": 12000 } ] }

DELETE /api/v1/urls/{short_key} — Delete a URL

DELETE /api/v1/urls/abc1234 Authorization: Bearer {api_key} Response: 200 OK { "deleted": true, "short_key": "abc1234" } Error responses: 403 Forbidden — caller is not the owner 404 Not Found — key doesn't exist

Soft delete vs hard delete: we soft-delete (set status=DELETED) and reclaim the key after a grace period. Hard-deleting immediately would prevent the click from returning 410 Gone with a helpful message.

5Data Model

Three core entities: urls, users, and the analytics events. The choice of database for each has different drivers.

Table: urls (MySQL or DynamoDB)

CREATE TABLE urls ( short_key VARCHAR(8) PRIMARY KEY, long_url TEXT NOT NULL, user_id UUID NULL, -- nullable for anonymous created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(), expires_at TIMESTAMPTZ NULL, -- null = never expires status SMALLINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 1, -- 1=ACTIVE, 2=EXPIRED, 3=DELETED click_count BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 -- snapshot updated from Redis ); -- Indexes CREATE INDEX idx_user ON urls(user_id, created_at DESC) WHERE user_id IS NOT NULL; CREATE INDEX idx_expiry ON urls(expires_at) WHERE status = 1 AND expires_at IS NOT NULL;

Why each field:

  • short_key as primary key (not auto-increment ID) — directly indexed for the most common query (lookup by key for redirect).
  • long_url as TEXT — URLs can be up to ~2000 chars. VARCHAR(2048) is also fine.
  • user_id nullable — allows anonymous creation.
  • status SMALLINT — soft delete pattern. Filtering by WHERE status=1 excludes expired/deleted.
  • click_count denormalised snapshot — the source of truth is Redis (live counts) and Kafka events (audit). This column is updated every 60s in batches.

Why this index strategy:

  • Primary key on short_key: serves the redirect query in O(1).
  • Partial index on (user_id, created_at): serves "list my URLs" for authenticated users. Partial (only WHERE user_id IS NOT NULL) saves space.
  • Partial index on expires_at: serves the background expiry sweep. Only indexes ACTIVE URLs that have an expiry — small subset, fast queries.

Why MySQL (or DynamoDB) and not Cassandra?

The access pattern is simple key-value lookup. Both MySQL and DynamoDB excel at this. Cassandra is overkill — its strength is high write throughput, and 1,160 writes/sec is trivial for MySQL.

Choice criteria:

  • MySQL: better for <10 TB. ACID transactions if we add features like atomic URL reassignment. Cheaper at moderate scale.
  • DynamoDB: better for >50 TB. Automatic sharding. Predictable latency. More expensive but zero ops.

Table: users

CREATE TABLE users ( user_id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(), email VARCHAR(255) UNIQUE NOT NULL, api_key_hash VARCHAR(64) UNIQUE NOT NULL, -- store HASH not plaintext rate_limit_tier SMALLINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 1, -- 1=free, 2=pro, 3=enterprise created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(), status SMALLINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 1 );

Why hash the API key? If the database is breached, attackers shouldn't get the API keys. We hash with bcrypt or argon2. On API request, we hash the incoming key and look it up.

Key Pool (Redis + MySQL — for KGS)

Pre-generated keys waiting to be assigned. Two-tier storage:

-- MySQL: durable source of truth for key pool CREATE TABLE key_pool ( key_value VARCHAR(8) PRIMARY KEY, status SMALLINT NOT NULL, -- 1=UNUSED, 2=ASSIGNED generated_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW() ); -- Redis: hot pool for fast LPOP LPUSH key_pool_ready "k1" "k2" "k3" ... -- list of unused keys LPOP key_pool_ready -- atomic, O(1), returns next key

Why two layers? Redis LPOP is atomic and fast (~0.1ms). MySQL ensures durability — if Redis crashes, we can rebuild the pool from MySQL. Details in the KGS deep dive below.

Analytics Events (Kafka + ClickHouse)

Click events are not stored in MySQL — they would overwhelm it. We use a streaming pipeline:

// Kafka message format ("clicks" topic) { "short_key": "abc1234", "timestamp_ms": 1705315200000, "ip_country": "IN", "user_agent": "Mozilla/5.0 ...", "referrer_domain": "twitter.com", "device_type": "mobile" } -- ClickHouse table (columnar, optimised for analytics queries) CREATE TABLE clicks ( short_key String, ts DateTime, ip_country LowCardinality(String), referrer_domain LowCardinality(String), device_type LowCardinality(String) ) ENGINE = MergeTree() PARTITION BY toYYYYMM(ts) ORDER BY (short_key, ts);

Why ClickHouse for analytics? Time-series analytical queries (GROUP BY day, country, etc.) are 100-1000× faster on a columnar database than on row-oriented MySQL. ClickHouse can scan billions of rows in seconds.

6High-Level Architecture

Now we draw the box-and-arrow diagram, with each component justified by what we established above.

CLIENT (browser / mobile app) │ ┌───────────────┼───────────────┐ │ CREATE URL │ REDIRECT │ ▼ │ ▼ ┌──────────────┐ │ ┌──────────────────┐ │ API Gateway │ │ │ CDN (CloudFront) │ ←─ optional, for popular URLs │ Rate Limit │ │ └────────┬──────────┘ │ Auth │ │ │ cache miss └──────┬───────┘ │ ▼ │ │ ┌──────────────────┐ ▼ │ │ Load Balancer │ ┌──────────────┐ │ └────────┬─────────┘ │ URL Service │ │ │ │ (write path) │ │ ▼ └──────┬───────┘ │ ┌──────────────────┐ │ │ │ Redirect Service │ │ │ │ (read path) │ ┌──────────┴────────┐ │ └────────┬─────────┘ │ Key Generator │ │ │ │ Service (KGS) │ │ ▼ │ Redis: LPOP │ │ ┌──────────────────┐ │ Source: MySQL │ │ │ Redis Cluster │ ← L1 cache └──────┬─────────────┘ │ │ short_key→long │ 95% hit rate │ │ └────────┬─────────┘ ▼ │ │ cache miss ┌──────────────┐ │ ▼ │ MySQL Primary │←───┘ ┌──────────────────┐ │ + 3 Replicas │ │ MySQL Replicas │ │ Sharded × 4 │ │ (read-only) │ └──────┬───────┘ └──────────────────┘ │ │ async (Kafka) ▼ ┌──────────────────────────────┐ │ Kafka "click-events" topic │ └──────────┬───────────────────┘ │ ┌──────────▼────────────────┐ │ Analytics Consumer │ │ → ClickHouse │ │ → Redis INCR (live count) │ └────────────────────────────┘

Why each component:

API Gateway

Sits in front of the create endpoint (not the redirect, since redirects must be ultra-fast). Handles:

  • Rate limiting: free tier = 100 URLs/min, paid = 10,000/min. Implemented via Redis (see Problem 6).
  • Authentication: validate API key by hash lookup.
  • Request logging: for security audit.

URL Service (Write Path)

Stateless service that handles URL creation. Steps:

  1. Validate the long URL (parse, check for malware via Google Safe Browsing API).
  2. If custom_alias provided: check uniqueness in DB. If clashes, return 409.
  3. If no custom alias: call KGS to get the next available key.
  4. INSERT into MySQL urls table.
  5. SET in Redis cache (write-through, populate immediately so first redirect hits cache).
  6. Return the short URL.

Key Generation Service (KGS)

The heart of avoiding collisions. Full discussion below.

Redirect Service (Read Path)

Stateless service optimised for sub-10ms latency. Steps:

  1. Extract short_key from path.
  2. GET from Redis. 95%+ hit rate.
  3. On miss: query MySQL replica, populate Redis, return.
  4. Issue HTTP 302 redirect.
  5. Asynchronously publish click event to Kafka (do NOT block on this — fire and forget).

Redis Cluster

Stores hot URL mappings. Key: url:{short_key}. Value: the long URL string. TTL: 24 hours (refresh on read).

Sharded across 8 nodes (16,384 hash slots distributed evenly). Total memory: ~200 GB. Each node 25 GB. Replication factor 2 (primary + replica per shard).

MySQL Cluster

Source of truth for the URL mappings. Sharded by short_key hash range across 4 shards. Each shard has 1 primary + 2 read replicas. Reads (cache misses) go to replicas; writes go to primaries.

Kafka + ClickHouse

Click events flow through Kafka to multiple consumers. ClickHouse stores them for analytics queries. Redis INCR keeps a live counter that's flushed back to MySQL every 60s.

7Deep Dive 1: Key Generation Service (KGS)

Generating unique 7-char keys at 1,160/sec across multiple servers without collisions is harder than it sounds. Let's evaluate the options.

Approach 1: Hash-Based (MD5 / SHA-256 truncated)

Hash the long URL and take the first 7 characters of the result.

key = base62_encode(md5(long_url))[:7]

Problems:

  • Same URL → same key. Could be a feature (deduplication) or bug (privacy: same URL from two users gets the same short key, leaking information).
  • Collision risk. With 7 chars (62⁷ = 3.5T space) and 100M URLs/year, birthday paradox kicks in around 1.8M URLs. We'd see ~1 collision/day at 100M/day. Manageable but requires collision retry logic.
  • Cannot guarantee unique keys for the same long URL from different users (or same user wanting two short URLs for the same destination).

Approach 2: Counter-Based (Auto-Increment + Base62)

Maintain a global counter. Each create increments it. Encode the counter value in base62.

counter = INCR global_counter // atomic key = base62_encode(counter) // 1 → "1", 100 → "1c", 10000000 → "1c5xS", 100000000000 → "L5g3sN3"

Problems:

  • Global counter = single point of failure and bottleneck. Centralised on Redis or DB.
  • Predictable keys leak information: anyone seeing key "abc1234" can guess "abc1235" exists. Crawlers can enumerate.
  • Sequential keys reveal volume: counter going from 1B to 2B in a month tells competitors how many URLs you create.

Approach 3: Random Generation with Collision Check

Generate a random 7-char base62 string. Check the DB. If it exists, regenerate.

Problems:

  • DB round-trip on every create. Doubles write latency.
  • As the keyspace fills up, collisions increase exponentially. Eventually you'd retry many times per write.

Approach 4: Key Generation Service (KGS) — The Winner

Pre-generate a pool of unique keys offline, store them in MySQL marked UNUSED, and load batches into Redis. The write path just LPOPs from Redis — O(1), guaranteed unique, no collision check needed.

BACKGROUND KGS WORKER (runs continuously): while true: // Step 1: generate 10K random unique base62 keys batch = [random_base62(7) for _ in 10000] // Step 2: insert as UNUSED into MySQL (DB enforces uniqueness) INSERT INTO key_pool(key_value, status) VALUES ... ON CONFLICT (key_value) DO NOTHING -- ignore rare collisions // Step 3: check current Redis pool size pool_size = LLEN key_pool_ready if pool_size > 1_000_000: // pool large enough, slow down sleep(60) continue // Step 4: pull 10K UNUSED keys from MySQL, mark ASSIGNED, push to Redis BEGIN TRANSACTION SELECT key_value FROM key_pool WHERE status=1 LIMIT 10000 FOR UPDATE UPDATE key_pool SET status=2 WHERE key_value IN (those keys) COMMIT RPUSH key_pool_ready k1 k2 ... k10000 WRITE PATH (URL creation): def create_short_url(long_url): key = LPOP key_pool_ready // O(1) atomic Redis op if key is None: trigger_emergency_refill() key = LPOP key_pool_ready // retry INSERT INTO urls(short_key, long_url, ...) VALUES (key, long_url, ...) SET url:{key} {long_url} EX 86400 // populate cache return key

Why KGS Wins

  • Zero collision at assignment time. Keys are unique by construction (DB enforces it during pre-generation).
  • O(1) atomic write path. Redis LPOP is atomic. Two concurrent creates always get different keys.
  • Decouples generation from assignment. Spike in URL creation? Just reload Redis from MySQL — keys are already generated.
  • Unguessable keys. Random generation prevents enumeration.

Handling KGS Failures

  • Redis pool depleted: rare if monitoring alerts on size < 100K. Emergency refill: KGS worker triggered immediately.
  • Redis crashes losing the in-memory list: keys are still in MySQL marked ASSIGNED but never reached a URL. They become orphaned. Acceptable — keyspace is huge. We can also re-mark them UNUSED on Redis recovery if we track which were ASSIGNED but not yet INSERTed.
  • Two URL services racing: impossible because LPOP is atomic.
  • KGS worker crashes during batch generation: partial batch in MySQL is fine. The unique constraint on key_value prevents duplicates.
🔑 Key Takeaway

The KGS pattern is widely applicable: any time you need to generate unique IDs at high throughput across distributed workers, pre-generating them offline and serving from a fast atomic queue (Redis LPOP) is faster and more reliable than online generation with collision retry.

8Deep Dive 2: Caching Strategy

The 100:1 read:write ratio means caching is the most impactful optimisation. Let's design it carefully.

Cache-Aside Pattern (Read-Through)

On read: try Redis first, fall back to DB, populate Redis.

def get_long_url(short_key): // Step 1: try cache cached = GET url:{short_key} if cached is not None: return cached // 95%+ hit rate // Step 2: cache miss → query DB replica row = SELECT long_url, expires_at, status FROM urls WHERE short_key=? if not row or row.status != ACTIVE: return None // 404 if row.expires_at and row.expires_at < now: return EXPIRED // 410 // Step 3: populate cache for next request SET url:{short_key} {row.long_url} EX 86400 // 24h TTL return row.long_url

Why TTL = 24 hours?

  • URLs rarely change once created (they're immutable in our system).
  • 24h gives auto-invalidation if data is somehow stale.
  • If a URL is deleted, we explicitly DEL the cache key. The TTL is a safety net.
  • Trades memory: every cached URL takes Redis memory for 24h whether actively read or not. Redis LRU eviction handles overflow.

Write-Through Population

When a URL is created, we populate Redis immediately (don't wait for the first read to populate). This avoids a cache miss for popular newly-created URLs:

def create_short_url(long_url): key = LPOP key_pool_ready INSERT INTO urls(short_key, long_url, ...) VALUES (...) SET url:{key} {long_url} EX 86400 ← populate at creation return key

Handling Cache Stampede

What if a viral URL has its cache entry expire, and 1000 requests hit the DB simultaneously?

Solution 1: Probabilistic Early Expiration

Before TTL fully expires, a small percentage of requests treat the cache as expired and refresh it. Spreads the refresh load.

Solution 2: Single-Flight Lock

def get_long_url(short_key): cached = GET url:{short_key} if cached: return cached // Try to acquire lock for refresh lock = SET lock:url:{short_key} 1 NX EX 5 if lock: // We got the lock, fetch from DB long_url = SELECT FROM urls WHERE short_key=? SET url:{short_key} {long_url} EX 86400 DEL lock:url:{short_key} return long_url else: // Someone else is fetching, wait and retry sleep(50ms) return GET url:{short_key} // should be populated by now

Trade-off: single-flight adds 50ms latency for the unlucky few requests during refresh, but prevents thundering herd on the DB.

Cache Sizing Math

From our estimation: hot set is ~400M URLs × 500 bytes ≈ 200 GB. Spread across 8 Redis shards = 25 GB/shard. Add 50% memory overhead for Redis internals → 38 GB instances. Use r6g.xlarge (32 GB) or similar.

What Gets Evicted

Configure Redis with maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru. When memory fills, Redis evicts the least recently used key. Rare URLs naturally evict; popular URLs stay hot.

9Deep Dive 3: Analytics Pipeline

Click analytics are valuable but must never block the redirect.

The Pipeline

REDIRECT SERVICE (hot path): Receive GET /{short_key} → Look up long_url in Redis → Issue 302 Location: {long_url} // SENT TO CLIENT IMMEDIATELY → Asynchronously fire-and-forget: Kafka.publish("clicks", {short_key, ts, ip, ua, ref}) → Return ANALYTICS CONSUMER (cold path): Consume Kafka "clicks" topic Batch every 1 second or 1000 events: For each event: ip_country = MaxMind.lookup(ip) // in-process device_type = parse_ua(ua) INSERT INTO ClickHouse(short_key, ts, country, ref, device) For each unique short_key in batch: INCR Redis live_clicks:{short_key} BATCH FLUSHER (every 60s): For each short_key with live_clicks counter > 0: delta = GETDEL Redis live_clicks:{short_key} UPDATE urls SET click_count = click_count + delta WHERE short_key=?

Why This Architecture

  • Kafka decouples the redirect path from the analytics path. The redirect is <10ms; analytics can take seconds.
  • Batching at the consumer reduces ClickHouse insertion overhead. 1000 events per INSERT instead of 1 INSERT per event.
  • ClickHouse is columnar — analytics queries that scan billions of rows run in seconds.
  • Redis INCR for live counters — needed for the "real-time click counter" display. Flushed to MySQL every 60s to persist.

Handling Loss

If the redirect service crashes after issuing the 302 but before publishing to Kafka, that click is lost. Accept this — clicks are analytics-grade data, not transactional. Loss tolerance: ~0.1% is acceptable.

To reduce loss: the Redirect Service can write to a local disk-backed buffer that drains to Kafka asynchronously. Bounded loss to whatever's in the buffer at crash time.

10Deep Dive 4: 301 vs 302 — The Eternal Debate

This question comes up in every URL shortener interview. The choice has real consequences.

HTTP 301 Moved Permanently

  • Browser caches the redirect target locally — sometimes forever, sometimes until cache clear.
  • Subsequent visits to the short URL never hit your server. The browser silently navigates to the long URL.
  • Pros: zero server load for repeat visitors. Faster perceived performance.
  • Cons: cannot track repeat clicks (the browser doesn't tell you). Cannot change the mapping later (browsers have already cached it).

HTTP 302 Found / Temporary Redirect

  • Browser does NOT cache the redirect. Every visit hits your server.
  • Pros: every click is logged for analytics. Mapping can be changed at any time.
  • Cons: every click costs a server round trip.

What Bit.ly Actually Uses

Bit.ly uses 301 for the public shortener (faster perceived performance, browser caching helps users) but with caveats:

  • They include Cache-Control: private, max-age=90 — a 90-second cache lifetime. Repeat clicks within 90s skip the server (perf benefit). Clicks beyond 90s hit the server (analytics benefit).
  • This is a compromise: ~80% analytics fidelity at significantly reduced server load.
🔑 Interview Answer

Say: "I'd use 302 by default to capture full analytics, but optimise high-traffic URLs with 301 + short Cache-Control to reduce server load. The choice depends on whether the business prioritises analytics fidelity or server cost reduction. Bit.ly does the latter; campaign trackers do the former."

11Deep Dive 5: URL Expiry and Cleanup

URLs with TTLs must be cleaned up. There are two layers of expiry handling.

Lazy Expiry (at read time)

When a URL is read, check if it's expired. If so, return 410 Gone and don't bother updating anything (let the cleanup job handle it).

def get_long_url(short_key): row = ... fetch ... if row.expires_at and row.expires_at < now(): return EXPIRED, 410 return row.long_url, 302

Eager Cleanup (background job)

A cron job runs daily to sweep expired URLs and reclaim resources:

-- Find expired ACTIVE URLs SELECT short_key FROM urls WHERE status = 1 AND expires_at < NOW() - INTERVAL '1 day' LIMIT 10000; -- For each: UPDATE urls SET status = 2 WHERE short_key = ? -- mark EXPIRED DEL url:{short_key} -- remove from cache RPUSH key_pool_ready {short_key} -- return to key pool

Why return keys to the pool? 7 chars = 3.5 trillion keys, but reclaiming saves storage. If 30% of URLs expire after 1 year, we save 30% of storage costs by reusing keys.

Why the 1-day grace period? Just in case any cache lookups are still serving stale data, give them a day to converge before recycling the key.

12Failure Modes & Recovery

Redis Cache Failure

If a Redis shard goes down, the read path falls back to MySQL replicas. Throughput drops 5-10× (since DB is slower than Redis), but the service stays up.

Mitigation: each Redis shard has a replica. Sentinel promotes the replica in <30 seconds. During promotion, cache misses spike — acceptable brief outage.

MySQL Primary Failure

Write path stops accepting new URLs. Reads continue from replicas. Once a replica is promoted to primary (~30s), writes resume.

Mitigation: synchronous replication to one replica ensures zero data loss on promotion. Slight write latency increase (5-10ms) is acceptable.

KGS Pool Depletion

If KGS worker is slow and Redis pool depletes, URL creation fails (LPOP returns nil).

Mitigation: alert when pool size < 100K. Automatic on-demand refill. Run KGS as multiple instances for HA.

Kafka Outage

If Kafka is down, click events are lost. Redirects continue working.

Mitigation: redirect service writes to local disk buffer if Kafka publish fails. Buffer is drained when Kafka recovers. Acceptable loss: whatever's in the buffer if the server crashes during Kafka outage.

Region-Wide Outage

If the entire region (us-east) goes down, traffic fails over to us-west via Route 53 health checks. Database has cross-region replication (async, ~5s lag).

Mitigation: warm standby. Multi-region active-active is also possible but adds write conflict resolution complexity.

13Scaling Path: 1K → 100M Users

Real systems evolve. Here's how the architecture grows.

Stage 1: 1K Users, 1K URLs/day

Single-machine deployment:

  • 1 server running the URL service + Redirect service (same process).
  • 1 PostgreSQL instance.
  • No Redis. No KGS. Just generate random 8-char keys and check for collision.
  • Cost: ~$50/month. Latency: 50ms. Plenty good.

Stage 2: 100K Users, 100K URLs/day

Read traffic grows. Cache becomes valuable:

  • Add Redis (single node, 8 GB).
  • Add a load balancer for HA (2 service instances).
  • Add a read replica for the DB.
  • Still using random keys + collision check — fine at this volume.

Stage 3: 10M Users, 10M URLs/day

Collision frequency increases. Time for KGS:

  • Introduce KGS (pre-generated keys in Redis list).
  • Scale Redis to 32 GB (single node still fits).
  • 4 service instances behind LB.
  • 3 read replicas.
  • Introduce Kafka + ClickHouse for analytics (was previously simple INSERT statements).

Stage 4: 100M Users, 100M URLs/day (target spec)

The full architecture from this article:

  • Redis Cluster (8 shards, 25 GB each).
  • MySQL sharded by short_key hash (4 shards × 1 primary + 2 replicas = 12 nodes).
  • 20 stateless service instances behind LB.
  • Kafka cluster (3 brokers).
  • ClickHouse cluster (3 nodes).
  • Multi-AZ deployment for HA.

Stage 5: 1B Users, Global

Multi-region:

  • Active-active deployment in 3 regions (us-east, eu-west, ap-south).
  • DynamoDB Global Tables or CockroachDB for cross-region replication.
  • GeoDNS routes users to nearest region.
  • CDN (CloudFront) caches popular redirects at edge.
  • Click events streamed to a central analytics warehouse (BigQuery / Snowflake).

14Trade-offs & Alternatives

SQL vs NoSQL for Primary Storage

ChoiceProsCons
MySQL/PostgresACID, cheap, well-understood, simple opsManual sharding needed beyond ~10 TB
DynamoDBAuto-sharding, predictable latency, zero opsVendor lock-in, expensive at high scale
CassandraLinear write scale, multi-region nativeOverkill for low write rate; complex ops

Our choice: MySQL until 50 TB, then evaluate DynamoDB.

Centralised KGS vs Distributed ID Generation

Alternative: Snowflake IDs (timestamp + machine ID + sequence) encoded in base62. No central KGS needed.

  • Pros: no Redis dependency for write path; truly distributed.
  • Cons: Snowflake IDs are 64-bit → 11 chars in base62. Doesn't fit our 7-char budget.
  • Pros: keys are sortable by creation time (sometimes useful).
  • Cons: leaks creation timestamp.

Our choice: KGS for the 7-char target; Snowflake if longer keys acceptable.

Redis vs Memcached for Cache

  • Redis: rich data structures, persistence options, atomic INCR for analytics.
  • Memcached: simpler, multi-threaded, slightly faster for pure string cache.

Our choice: Redis, because we use INCR for live click counters.

15Cross-Questions and Pushbacks

The questions interviewers ask after you've presented the design. These test depth.

How exactly do you handle hash collisions in your key generation?
Answer: We use the KGS approach which makes collisions impossible at assignment time. KGS pre-generates random 7-char base62 keys offline and inserts them into MySQL with a UNIQUE constraint on key_value. The DB rejects any collision during pre-generation (very rare due to the 3.5T keyspace). These unique keys are loaded into a Redis list. On URL creation, the URL Service does LPOP — an atomic Redis operation. Two concurrent creates always get different keys. If we used MD5-based generation, we'd need a collision check + retry loop, adding latency and complexity. KGS eliminates this entirely.
How do you scale the redirect service to 100K reads/sec?
Answer: Three layers handle the read load: (1) CDN at the edge caches popular 301 redirects — for top URLs, the browser never touches our server. (2) Redis Cluster (8 shards × 25 GB) holds the hot ~400M URLs with 95%+ hit rate. At 100K reads/sec with 95% hit rate, Redis handles 95K/sec — well within its capability. (3) DB sees only 5K reads/sec (cache misses) — comfortably handled by 3 read replicas. The redirect service itself is stateless and horizontally scaled — 20 instances at ~5K RPS each. The bottleneck is network bandwidth, not compute.
How do you prevent abuse — someone creating millions of spam URLs?
Answer: Four layers of defense: (1) Rate limiting per API key — free tier 100/min, paid 10K/min. Implemented in Redis with sliding window counter. (2) URL validation against Google Safe Browsing API — checks for malware/phishing URLs and blocks them. Asynchronous check after initial creation can also flag URLs for review. (3) Anomaly detection — sudden bursts of creation from a single user trigger a CAPTCHA challenge or temporary block. (4) For unauthenticated users, IP-based rate limiting + CAPTCHA on the create endpoint. Spam-classified short URLs are returned 451 Unavailable for Legal Reasons on redirect.
How would you implement custom aliases like bit.ly/mylink?
Answer: Before creating, check if the alias exists: SELECT 1 FROM urls WHERE short_key=? — if it returns a row, return 409 Conflict. If not, INSERT the URL with the custom alias as short_key. Two important details: (1) the alias must pass a profanity filter and reserved-word check (no "admin", "api", "www", etc.). (2) Set a minimum length of 4-6 characters to prevent users from squatting popular short combinations. We also bypass the KGS pool entirely for custom aliases — the custom alias goes directly into the urls table, not consuming a KGS-generated key.
How do you handle URL expiration at scale — millions of URLs expiring daily?
Answer: Two layers: (1) Lazy expiry at read time — on every redirect, check expires_at and return 410 if past. This catches expired URLs immediately for the user even if cleanup hasn't run yet. (2) Eager cleanup — a daily background job scans the partial index on expires_at: SELECT short_key FROM urls WHERE status=1 AND expires_at < NOW() LIMIT 10000. For each expired URL: mark status=EXPIRED, DEL from Redis cache, push the key back to KGS pool. Runs in batches with a 1-day grace period so cached lookups have time to drain. Index on expires_at makes the scan O(log N) — millions of rows take seconds to identify.
Why not just use MD5(long_url) and take first 7 chars?
Answer: Three reasons: (1) Same long URL from two different users would get the same short key — leaks information ("this user shortened the same URL I did"). Could be a feature (deduplication) but is usually undesired. (2) MD5 collisions on 7 chars (38 bits) occur at ~256K URLs by birthday paradox — we'd see frequent collisions requiring retry logic with random salting. (3) MD5 is deterministic — anyone with the long URL can predict the short key, which has security implications for "unlisted" URLs. KGS gives random, unguessable keys with zero collisions and supports multiple short URLs for the same long URL.
Why are you using MySQL? Won't it become a bottleneck at 100M URLs/day?
Answer: Let me run the numbers. 100M URLs/day = 1,160 writes/sec average. MySQL handles 5,000-10,000 writes/sec on a standard instance — we're at 12-23% utilisation. Not a bottleneck. For storage: 91 TB over 5 years, sharded across 4 MySQL instances = 23 TB each — still manageable. Where MySQL could fail is reads, but we're not reading from MySQL on the hot path — Redis serves 95%+ of read traffic. MySQL only sees ~5,800 read/sec on cache misses, easily handled by read replicas. If we ever needed more, we'd shard further or migrate to DynamoDB, but at 100M/day MySQL is the right choice — cheaper, simpler ops, more flexibility.
Cassandra would handle the writes better. Why not use it?
Answer: Cassandra's strength is high write throughput (100K+/sec per node) via LSM-Tree. We have 1,160 writes/sec — Cassandra is wildly overkill. What we'd LOSE by switching: (1) ACID transactions — important if we ever want to atomically reassign a URL or transfer ownership. (2) Read consistency — Cassandra's eventual consistency means a freshly created URL might not be readable for milliseconds. With MySQL, the URL is immediately available. (3) Simpler ops — Cassandra requires careful capacity planning, repair processes, tombstone management. MySQL just works. (4) Cost — Cassandra needs a cluster (3+ nodes minimum); MySQL works on a single instance until we outgrow it. Match the tool to the problem. Cassandra would be appropriate at 100K+ writes/sec, which is 100× our actual load.
Your analytics pipeline can lose data — how is that acceptable?
Answer: Acknowledged trade-off. Click analytics are not transactional — we're measuring a noisy metric (clicks), and 0.1% loss doesn't materially change the analytics or business decisions. The alternative — synchronously persisting every click before issuing the 302 — would add 20-50ms to every redirect, degrading user experience for billions of clicks to prevent the loss of 0.1%. To mitigate further: the redirect service can buffer events to a local disk-backed queue (chronicle queue, RocksDB) and drain to Kafka asynchronously — bounded loss to whatever's in the buffer at crash time, typically < 1 second of events. For genuinely transactional analytics (e.g., billing on per-click pricing), we'd use a different pipeline with synchronous writes — but the latency cost would be acknowledged upfront.
How would you implement a "preview" feature that shows the destination URL without redirecting?
Answer: Add an endpoint GET /api/v1/urls/{key}/preview that returns the destination metadata (title, favicon, content type) without redirecting. To implement: on URL creation, asynchronously crawl the destination URL with a headless browser, extract OG tags (og:title, og:image, og:description), and store the preview data. The preview endpoint just returns this stored data. For frequently changing destinations, refresh the preview every 24h. This is also how Slack, Twitter, etc. show link previews. The preview metadata can be cached aggressively (24h+) since destination pages don't change often.

End of Problem 1. Next: Twitter / News Feed (P2) — fan-out at scale.

Hard Social Fan-Out Timeline Generation Hybrid Strategy

Problem 2: Designing Twitter / News Feed System

The canonical "social feed" problem. The core challenge is generating a personalised, time-ordered feed for hundreds of millions of users from billions of posts — fast enough that timelines load in 200ms. This problem introduces the fan-out pattern, which appears everywhere in social systems.
