1Context and Why This Problem Matters

Imagine 300 million people, each following an average of 200 others, each potentially posting at any moment. When you open Twitter, the app must display the most recent (or most relevant) posts from those 200 accounts within 200 milliseconds. How?

The naive approach — at read time, query "SELECT * FROM tweets WHERE user_id IN (...your followees...) ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20" — fails catastrophically:

  • It would scan billions of tweets every time someone opens the app.
  • Users following celebrities (millions of followers) would trigger massive scans.
  • The DB would melt under the load.

This problem teaches you the most important pattern in social systems: precomputation via fan-out. Instead of computing the feed at read time, we precompute it at write time. When you post, we push your tweet to all your followers' precomputed timelines. Reads become trivial: just fetch the pre-built timeline.

But this seemingly simple solution has a critical edge case: celebrities. Beyoncé with 200 million followers posting a single tweet would trigger 200 million writes. So we evolve to a hybrid approach: push for normal users, pull for celebrities. This is one of the most elegant trade-offs in system design.

Related problems that share patterns: Instagram (P13), Facebook News Feed, LinkedIn feed, TikTok feed.

2Requirements Gathering

Functional Requirements

  • Post a tweet: up to 280 characters of text, optionally with images, videos, or polls. Once posted, immutable (no editing in classic Twitter; current Twitter has a 30-min edit window for paid users).
  • Follow / unfollow users: maintain a social graph of who follows whom.
  • Home timeline: the personalised feed shown when a user opens the app. Time-ordered or ranked by ML.
  • User profile timeline: list of tweets by a specific user, in reverse chronological order.
  • Like, retweet, reply: engagement on tweets. Counters update in near real-time.
  • Hashtags and trending topics: discover what's popular right now.
  • Search: find tweets by keyword, hashtag, or user.
  • Mentions and notifications: @username triggers notifications to the mentioned user.

Non-Functional Requirements

  • Scale: 300M monthly active users, ~50% daily active (150M DAU), 100M tweets/day.
  • Read:write ratio: 100:1 — far more people read feeds than post tweets.
  • Latency: home timeline load <200ms P99; tweet posting <500ms.
  • Consistency: eventual consistency is acceptable. If a tweet shows up in someone's feed 1 second late, no one cares.
  • Availability: 99.9% — Twitter outage is a news event. Down for 30 min/month is the absolute maximum.
  • Durability: tweets are public records. Loss is unacceptable.

Clarifying Questions to Ask the Interviewer

  • "What's the maximum number of followers a single user can have?" — Determines if we need celebrity-handling logic.
  • "Is the feed chronological or ML-ranked?" — ML ranking adds another whole pipeline.
  • "Are deleted tweets removed from already-fanned-out timelines?" — Has implications for the timeline data structure.
  • "Are images/videos in scope for v1?" — Media storage doubles the complexity (S3, transcoding for video, CDN).
  • "Should we support real-time mentions or batch?" — Real-time means a notification subsystem; batch is simpler.
  • "Multi-region or single region?" — Affects how we replicate the social graph.
🔑 Key Insight from Requirements

The 100:1 read:write ratio combined with the celebrity problem are the two driving forces of the design. The read-heavy nature pushes us toward precomputed timelines (fan-out on write). The celebrity problem prevents us from naively pushing everywhere. Together, they force the hybrid approach.

3Capacity Estimation

Tweet Volume

MetricCalculationValue
Tweets/sec (avg)100M / 100k~1k/s
Tweets/sec (peak, major event)5× avg~5,800/s
Timeline reads/sec150M × 5 / 100k~7.5k/s
Timeline read peak3× avg~26,000/s

Fan-Out Math (The Critical Number)

Average user has ~200 followers. So each tweet must be written to 200 followers' timelines.

MetricCalculationValue
Total fan-out writes/sec1,160 tweets/sec × 200 followers~232,000/s
If a celebrity (10M followers) posts10,000,00010M writes for ONE tweet
If Beyoncé (200M followers) posts200,000,000200M writes for ONE tweet

This is the killer. 232K writes/sec is achievable. 200M writes for a single tweet is not (it would take 200M / 232K = ~860 seconds to fan out, meaning followers wouldn't see Beyoncé's tweet for 14 minutes). Hence the celebrity bypass.

Storage

MetricCalculationValue
Tweet record sizetweet_id (8B) + user_id (16B) + content (~280B) + meta (~100B)~400 bytes
Tweet storage/day100M × 400B~40 GB/day
Tweet storage / 5 years40 GB × 365 × 5~73 TB
Social graph (follows)300M users × 200 follows × 32B~1.9 TB
Timeline cache (all users)300M users × 800 tweet IDs × 8B~1.9 TB

What this tells us: 73 TB for tweets requires sharding. Social graph fits comfortably on a few machines. Timeline cache (1.9 TB) is too large for a single Redis instance — needs Redis Cluster.

Media (out of v1 scope, but worth estimating)

If we add media: 100M tweets × 30% with media × 500KB average = 15 TB/day = 27 PB / 5 years. This goes to S3 with CDN.

🔧 From Numbers to Architecture — what these estimates force

Every tech choice in the HLD below traces back to a number we just computed. Read these bullets as "number → constraint → tech choice".

  • 1k tweets/sec avg, ~5k peak → a sharded MySQL/Postgres (by tweet_id via Snowflake range) handles writes easily. No single-node bottleneck.
  • ~7.5k timeline reads/sec → don't compute timelines on read. Pre-computed Redis ZSet per user, score = tweet timestamp. ZREVRANGE = sub-ms feed page.
  • ~200k fanout writes/sec (1k tweets × ~200 avg followers) → cannot block tweet POST on this. Kafka introduced; async fanout workers write to per-follower timelines.
  • Bieber problem — 100M+ follower users → fanning 100M writes/post is wasteful. Hybrid model: PUSH for <1M followers, PULL at read for celebs (merge celeb tweets into feed on the fly).
  • 73 TB tweet storage / 5 yr → exceeds single-node capacity. Shard MySQL ~4–8 ways by tweet_id, or move to Cassandra if write rate ever 10×.
  • 1.9 TB timeline cache (300M users × 800 entries × 8 B) → too large for a single Redis instance. Redis Cluster ~30 nodes × 64 GB, sharded by user_id.
  • Social graph fits in < 100 GB → keep follower edges in a separate graph-friendly store (Postgres / Neo4j / FlockDB-style). Cache hot users in Redis Sets.
  • Trending topics in near-real-time → cannot scan all tweets. Kafka → Flink / Spark Streaming → Count-Min Sketch for top-K hashtags, refresh per minute.
  • Tweet search → MySQL LIKE won't scale. Elasticsearch mirror via CDC from MySQL.
  • Media (27 PB / 5 yr if enabled) → S3 + CDN; metadata stays in MySQL.

4API Design

POST /api/v1/tweets — Post a Tweet

POST /api/v1/tweets HTTP/1.1 Authorization: Bearer {jwt} Content-Type: application/json { "content": "Just shipped a new feature! 🚀 #engineering", "media_ids": ["media_uuid_1"], // optional, pre-uploaded "reply_to_tweet_id": null, // optional "client_uuid": "..." // idempotency key } Response: 201 Created { "tweet_id": "1234567890123456", // Snowflake ID "author": { "user_id": "uuid", "username": "alice" }, "content": "Just shipped a new feature! ...", "created_at": "2024-01-15T09:00:00Z", "metrics": { "likes": 0, "retweets": 0, "replies": 0 } }

GET /api/v1/timeline/home — Get Home Timeline

GET /api/v1/timeline/home?cursor=1234567890&limit=20 Authorization: Bearer {jwt} Response: 200 OK { "tweets": [ { "tweet_id": "...", "author": { "user_id": "...", "username": "...", "avatar_url": "..." }, "content": "...", "media_urls": [], "created_at": "...", "metrics": { "likes": 230, "retweets": 45, "replies": 12 }, "is_liked_by_me": false, "is_retweeted_by_me": false }, ... 19 more tweets ... ], "next_cursor": "1234567880", "has_more": true }

Pagination via cursor: next_cursor is the tweet_id of the last item in the current batch. The next request passes it as ?cursor=.... We then return tweets older than this cursor. This is more efficient than offset-based pagination because Snowflake IDs are sorted.

POST /api/v1/users/{user_id}/follow — Follow a User

POST /api/v1/users/celebrity_uuid/follow Authorization: Bearer {jwt} Response: 200 OK { "following": true, "follower_count": 12345678 }

POST /api/v1/tweets/{tweet_id}/like — Like a Tweet

POST /api/v1/tweets/1234567890/like Authorization: Bearer {jwt} Response: 200 OK { "liked": true, "like_count": 231 }

GET /api/v1/search — Search Tweets

GET /api/v1/search?q=systemdesign&type=tweets&sort=recent&cursor=... Authorization: Bearer {jwt} Response: 200 OK { "tweets": [...], "users": [...], // user accounts matching the query "hashtags": [...], "next_cursor": "..." }

GET /api/v1/trending — Trending Topics

GET /api/v1/trending?location=IN Response: 200 OK { "trends": [ { "hashtag": "#GoodMorning", "tweet_count": 124000, "is_promoted": false }, { "hashtag": "#India", "tweet_count": 89000, "is_promoted": false } ] }

5Data Model

Table: tweets (sharded MySQL or Cassandra)

CREATE TABLE tweets ( tweet_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, -- Snowflake (time-ordered, distributed) user_id UUID NOT NULL, -- author content VARCHAR(280) NOT NULL, media_ids JSONB, reply_to_tweet_id BIGINT NULL, is_retweet_of BIGINT NULL, like_count INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0, -- denormalised retweet_count INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0, reply_count INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0, created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW() ); -- Sharding: by tweet_id range (Snowflake includes timestamp, so this also gives time-based sharding) -- Indexes CREATE INDEX idx_user_tweets ON tweets(user_id, tweet_id DESC);

Why Snowflake IDs: 64-bit IDs encoded as: 41 bits timestamp + 10 bits machine_id + 12 bits sequence. Generated locally on each app server without coordination. Sortable by time (newer ID = larger value). No central counter bottleneck.

Table: follows (Cassandra)

Bi-directional indexes for the two main queries: "who do I follow?" and "who follows me?"

-- Table 1: who do I follow (partition by follower) CREATE TABLE follows_by_follower ( follower_id UUID, followee_id UUID, created_at TIMESTAMP, PRIMARY KEY (follower_id, followee_id) ); -- Table 2: who follows me (partition by followee — celebrity lookup) CREATE TABLE follows_by_followee ( followee_id UUID, follower_id UUID, created_at TIMESTAMP, PRIMARY KEY (followee_id, follower_id) );

Why two tables? Cassandra queries by partition key only. To answer "who follows celebrity X?" efficiently, we need partition_key = X — that's the second table. Denormalisation is fine; follow events update both tables.

Timeline Cache (Redis Sorted Set per user)

Key: user:timeline:{user_id} Type: Sorted Set (ZSET) Score: tweet_id (Snowflake, so naturally time-ordered) Member: tweet_id (we store IDs, not full tweet content) Operations: ZADD user:timeline:{uid} {tweet_id} {tweet_id} // add new tweet to timeline ZREVRANGE user:timeline:{uid} 0 19 // fetch latest 20 ZREVRANGEBYSCORE user:timeline:{uid} cursor 0 LIMIT 0 20 // paginate ZREMRANGEBYRANK user:timeline:{uid} 0 -801 // trim to last 800 tweets

Why store only IDs in timeline cache? Tweet content changes (likes increase). If we stored full content, we'd need to update every copy. Storing just IDs and "hydrating" the full content at read time keeps the cache compact and consistent.

Why max 800 tweets? Users scroll back occasionally but rarely beyond 800 items. Beyond that, we can fall back to DB query (slow but rare path).

Tweet Object Cache

Key: tweet:{tweet_id} Type: Hash (HSET) Fields: content, author_id, created_at, like_count, retweet_count, ... Operations: HSET tweet:{id} content "..." author_id "..." like_count 0 ... HGETALL tweet:{id} HINCRBY tweet:{id} like_count 1

Social Graph Cache

For each user, cache their follower count and (for celebrities) the followers list:

user:{id}:follower_count → INT // updated on every follow user:{id}:followee_count → INT user:{id}:followers → ZSET (only for users with < 1M followers — celebrities don't fit)

6High-Level Architecture

CLIENT (mobile app / web) │ ┌────────▼────────┐ │ API Gateway │ └─┬────────┬──────┘ │ │ ┌──────────┴──┐ ┌──┴──────────────┐ │ Tweet │ │ Timeline │ │ Service │ │ Service │ │ (write) │ │ (read) │ └──────┬──────┘ └──────┬──────────┘ │ │ ┌────────────┴───┐ ▼ │ │ ┌──────────────────┐ ▼ ▼ │ Redis Timeline │ ┌────────────┐ ┌──────────┐ │ Cache (ZSET/user)│ │ Tweets DB │ │ Kafka │ └────────┬─────────┘ │ (Cassandra)│ │ "tweets" │ │ miss / pull │ Sharded │ └─────┬────┘ ▼ └────────────┘ │ ┌──────────────────┐ ▼ │ Tweet Service │ ┌──────────────┐ │ (fetch tweets │ │ Fan-Out │ │ from DB) │ │ Service │ └──────────────────┘ │ (Kafka │ │ consumer) │ └──────┬───────┘ │ Get follower list from Social Graph │ ▼ For NORMAL users: ZADD timeline:{uid} for each follower For CELEBRITY users: SKIP — Timeline Service pulls at read

Walking through a tweet post:

  1. User submits POST /tweets.
  2. Tweet Service generates a Snowflake ID, validates content, persists to Cassandra (or sharded MySQL).
  3. Tweet Service publishes the new tweet event to Kafka "tweets" topic. Returns 201 to user.
  4. Fan-Out Service (Kafka consumer) reads the event. Queries social graph for the author's followers.
  5. If the author has < 10K followers: iterate followers, ZADD the tweet_id to each follower's user:timeline:{uid} sorted set. Trim to last 800.
  6. If the author has >= 10K followers (celebrity): SKIP fan-out entirely. The tweet stays in the celebrity's own timeline only.

Walking through a home timeline read:

  1. User opens app, app calls GET /timeline/home.
  2. Timeline Service: ZREVRANGE user:timeline:{my_id} 0 19 → list of tweet IDs from pushed feed.
  3. Get the list of celebrities I follow (from social graph cache).
  4. For each celebrity, ZREVRANGE user:tweets:{celeb_id} 0 4 → their last 5 tweets.
  5. Merge: combine pushed tweets + celebrity tweets, sort by tweet_id desc.
  6. Hydrate: for the top 20, HMGET tweet:{id} to get full tweet content.
  7. Return to user.

7Deep Dive 1: The Fan-Out Problem — Push vs Pull vs Hybrid

This is THE topic for Twitter design interviews. Let me lay out all three approaches and the trade-offs.

Approach 1: Pull (Fan-Out on Read)

No precomputation. On every timeline read, query the DB for the latest tweets from followees.

def get_home_timeline(user_id): followees = get_follows(user_id) // e.g., 200 user IDs tweets = SELECT * FROM tweets WHERE user_id IN (followees) ORDER BY tweet_id DESC LIMIT 20 return tweets

Pros:

  • No write amplification — one tweet = one DB write.
  • Always fresh — newly posted tweets appear immediately.
  • Simple to reason about.

Cons:

  • Catastrophic read load: 8,680 timeline reads/sec × 200 followees per read = ~1.7M follower-tweet lookups/sec. DB melts.
  • Worst-case query: a user follows 5,000 people → IN clause with 5,000 IDs → query plan disaster.
  • High read latency: even with indexes, joining across 200 user partitions is slow.

Verdict: Unworkable at scale.

Approach 2: Push (Fan-Out on Write)

At write time, push the tweet to every follower's precomputed timeline.

def post_tweet(user_id, content): tweet_id = generate_snowflake() INSERT INTO tweets ... followers = get_followers(user_id) // could be 200 or 200M for follower_id in followers: ZADD user:timeline:{follower_id} {tweet_id} {tweet_id} def get_home_timeline(user_id): return ZREVRANGE user:timeline:{user_id} 0 19 // O(log N)

Pros:

  • Trivial reads: O(log N) sorted set lookup. Sub-millisecond.
  • Predictable read latency: doesn't depend on how many people you follow.
  • Cacheable: timelines are precomputed; reads serve from cache.

Cons (the killer):

  • Celebrity fan-out: Beyoncé posts → 200M writes for ONE tweet. At 232K writes/sec capacity, this takes 14 minutes to fan out. Followers don't see the tweet for 14 minutes.
  • Wasted writes: many followers won't open the app today. We wrote their timeline for nothing.
  • Inactive user storage: a user who hasn't logged in for 6 months still gets all their followees' tweets pushed to their timeline. Memory wasted.

Verdict: Works for normal users but breaks at the celebrity tail.

Approach 3: Hybrid (Push + Pull) — The Solution

Decide per-author whether to push or skip based on follower count. Combine at read time.

// WRITE PATH def post_tweet(user_id, content): tweet_id = generate_snowflake() INSERT INTO tweets ... ZADD user:tweets:{user_id} {tweet_id} {tweet_id} // always cache author's own timeline follower_count = HGET user:{user_id} follower_count if follower_count < CELEBRITY_THRESHOLD: // e.g., 10,000 Kafka.publish("fanout", {tweet_id, user_id}) // fan-out worker pushes to followers else: // celebrity: skip fan-out, will be pulled at read time pass // READ PATH def get_home_timeline(user_id): // 1. Get pushed tweets (from normal followees) pushed_tweet_ids = ZREVRANGE user:timeline:{user_id} 0 99 // 2. Get celebrities I follow celebrities = get_celebrity_followees(user_id) // usually ~10 // 3. Pull last 5 tweets from each celebrity celebrity_tweet_ids = [] for celeb_id in celebrities: ids = ZREVRANGE user:tweets:{celeb_id} 0 4 celebrity_tweet_ids.extend(ids) // 4. Merge, sort by tweet_id, take top 20 all_ids = pushed_tweet_ids + celebrity_tweet_ids all_ids.sort(reverse=True) // Snowflake IDs sort by time top_20 = all_ids[:20] // 5. Hydrate return hydrate_tweets(top_20)

How to Pick the Celebrity Threshold

The threshold trades off fan-out cost vs read complexity:

  • Low threshold (e.g., 1,000): more users classified as celebrities → less fan-out write work → but more pull queries at read time.
  • High threshold (e.g., 100,000): fewer celebrities → more fan-out work but simpler reads.

The sweet spot in practice is around 10,000 followers. Above that, the fan-out cost is high enough that pull-at-read is cheaper.

Re-classifying When a User Crosses the Threshold

If a user grows from 9,999 followers to 10,001, do we change strategy?

Yes, but lazily:

  1. From now on (their next tweet), they're treated as a celebrity — no fan-out.
  2. Tweets they already posted (before crossing threshold) remain in followers' pushed timelines. No retroactive cleanup needed.
  3. Their tweets continue to be cached in user:tweets:{id} for pull-at-read.

Conversely, if a celebrity loses followers and drops below 10K, future tweets get fanned out normally.

Edge Case: Backfill on Follow

Alice follows Bob (a normal user with 500 followers). What about Bob's recent tweets — should they appear in Alice's timeline?

Yes. After the follow event, async worker:

  1. Read Bob's last 20 tweets from user:tweets:{bob_id}.
  2. ZADD them to user:timeline:{alice_id}.

Alice's next timeline load includes Bob's recent posts. Takes 100-500ms async — feels instant.

Edge Case: Cleanup on Unfollow

Alice unfollows Bob. Should Bob's tweets be removed from Alice's timeline?

Yes, also async. But it's expensive: scan Alice's timeline ZSET, find entries authored by Bob (we'd need to track author in the timeline entry — currently we just store tweet_id).

Practical approach: at read time, check the author of each tweet against Alice's current follow list. Filter out tweets from people she no longer follows. Acceptable extra work because (a) timelines are small (top 20), (b) unfollows are rare relative to reads.

8Deep Dive 2: Timeline Storage and Retrieval

Why Redis Sorted Sets?

The timeline access pattern: "give me the latest N items, with optional pagination." This maps perfectly to Redis sorted sets:

  • ZADD: O(log N) insert. We add ~232K times/sec across all timelines.
  • ZREVRANGE: O(log N + M) where M is items returned. Sub-millisecond for fetching top 20.
  • ZREMRANGEBYRANK: O(log N + M). Used to trim old entries beyond 800.
  • ZREVRANGEBYSCORE: cursor-based pagination. O(log N + M).

Hydration: Resolving Tweet IDs to Full Tweets

After fetching tweet IDs from the timeline, we need the full tweet objects. Two-level cache:

  1. L1: Tweet object cache in Redis: tweet:{id} Hash. 95%+ hit rate for hot tweets.
  2. L2: DB: on cache miss, fetch from Cassandra and populate cache.

Bulk Hydration with Pipelining

For 20 tweets, we need 20 cache lookups. Don't issue them serially — use Redis pipelining:

pipeline = redis.pipeline() for tweet_id in tweet_ids: pipeline.hgetall(f"tweet:{tweet_id}") results = pipeline.execute() // 1 round-trip, 20 lookups

Latency: 1 RTT instead of 20. Critical for the <200ms timeline SLA.

Handling Inactive Users — Memory Optimisation

If a user hasn't logged in for 30 days, their timeline cache occupies memory pointlessly. Cleanup:

  • Track last_active timestamp per user.
  • Background sweep: for users inactive > 30 days, DEL user:timeline:{uid}.
  • When the user logs in again, regenerate their timeline by pulling from each followee's user:tweets:{id}. Takes 500ms-2s for the first load — acceptable for a returning user.

9Deep Dive 3: Feed Ranking — Chronological vs ML

Chronological Feed

Sort by tweet_id (which contains a timestamp). Simple, deterministic. Used by:

  • Twitter's "Latest" tab.
  • Users who toggle off algorithmic ranking.

ML-Ranked Feed (Twitter's "For You" tab)

Rank tweets by predicted engagement (likes, retweets, replies, time spent) for this specific user. The algorithm:

  1. Candidate generation: same as before — fetch pushed timeline + celebrity pulls + suggested users' tweets + replies you're tagged in.
  2. Feature extraction: for each candidate tweet, extract ~100 features (author affinity, recency, engagement velocity, content type, embedding similarity to user's interest profile).
  3. Scoring: pass features through an ML model (gradient boosted tree or neural net). Output: probability that the user will engage.
  4. Re-ranking: sort candidates by score. Apply diversity rules (don't show 5 tweets from same author in a row).

Where ML Inference Happens

Inline at read time: adds 50-100ms latency. Worth it for engagement uplift.

Model served by a dedicated ML inference service (TensorFlow Serving, Triton, or in-process if model is small).

Features are partly pre-computed (user embeddings, author embeddings) and partly real-time (engagement velocity in last hour).

10Deep Dive 4: Trending Topics in Real-Time

"#WorldCup" trending across India requires counting hashtag occurrences across millions of tweets per minute — and updating the top-N list every 30 seconds.

The Pipeline

TWEET POSTED: Tweet Service → INSERT tweet → publish to Kafka "tweets" topic │ ▼ Hashtag Extractor (Kafka consumer): Extract hashtags from tweet text via regex For each hashtag: Publish to Kafka "hashtag-events" topic FLINK STREAM PROCESSOR (sliding window): Window: 1 hour, slide every 30 seconds GroupBy: hashtag Aggregation: count(tweet_id) Output: stream of (hashtag, count_in_last_hour, country) EVERY 30 SECONDS: Top-N selector: sort all hashtags by count, take top 100 per country Write to Redis: ZADD trending:{country} {count} {hashtag} EXPIRE: trending:{country} 60 // only keep recent data USER REQUESTS TRENDING: GET /api/v1/trending?location=IN → ZREVRANGE trending:IN 0 9 WITHSCORES → Return top 10 trends

Why Flink Sliding Window?

  • The sliding window means "what's been popular in the last hour" — fresher than tumbling daily windows.
  • Flink maintains state in distributed RocksDB, surviving crashes.
  • 30-second slide rate balances freshness vs compute cost.

Geo-Specific Trending

Tweet → derive country from author's profile or IP geolocation → emit (hashtag, country) tuple to Flink. Flink groups by (country, hashtag).

Result: "#WorldCup" is #1 in India but #5 in the US. Different per-country trends.

Filtering Promoted / Spammy Hashtags

A blocklist (curated) excludes spam, profanity, or sensitive topics from public trending. Implemented as a filter in the Top-N selector. Updated dynamically.

11Deep Dive 5: Tweet Search

Searching billions of tweets by keyword requires a full-text search engine.

Pipeline

Tweet posted → Kafka "tweets" topic │ ▼ Elasticsearch Indexer (Kafka consumer) → Tokenize tweet text → POST to Elasticsearch: { tweet_id, content, author_id, hashtags, created_at } → Index by tweet content (with stemming, stopwords) → Index also by user mention, hashtag User searches: "system design" → API Gateway → Search Service → Elasticsearch query (BM25 ranking) → Returns matching tweet_ids sorted by relevance → Hydrate via tweet object cache → Return

Why Elasticsearch?

  • Inverted index: fast keyword lookup.
  • BM25 ranking: better than simple TF-IDF for short documents like tweets.
  • Horizontal scaling: shard by tweet_id range.
  • Built-in geo, time-range, faceted search.

Index Sharding for Old Tweets

10B tweets is a lot. Strategy: monthly indices.

  • Active index: tweets-2024-01 (current month). Heavy write traffic.
  • Past indices: tweets-2023-12, tweets-2023-11, ... read-only, optimised for query.
  • Search across all indices via Elasticsearch alias.
  • Indices > 1 year old can move to cold storage with slower query time.

12Failure Modes & Recovery

Fan-Out Service Backlog

If the Fan-Out Service falls behind (Kafka consumer lag grows), new tweets take longer to reach followers' timelines.

Mitigation: monitor Kafka lag. Auto-scale Fan-Out Service workers based on lag. Backpressure: if lag > 1 minute, alert on-call.

User experience: a 1-minute delay in tweets appearing is acceptable for social media.

Redis Cluster Node Failure

If one Redis shard goes down, the timelines on that shard are unavailable. Users with timelines on other shards are unaffected.

Mitigation: Redis Cluster automatic failover to replica (~30s downtime for affected users). Users see "loading..." until replica is promoted.

Celebrity Tweet Pull at Read Becomes Slow

If a user follows 50 celebrities, the read path makes 50 Redis pulls (parallelizable). At ~1ms each, 50ms total (if pipelined). For users following 500 celebrities, this becomes slow.

Mitigation: cap "celebrity follows" pulled per read at 20 most active. Less active celebrity timelines are merged from a cached snapshot updated every 10 seconds.

Tweet DB (Cassandra) Partial Failure

Cassandra replication factor 3, quorum reads. Survives 1 node failure transparently. 2 node failures = stale reads possible.

13Scaling Path: 100K → 300M Users

Stage 1: 100K Users, 100 tweets/sec

Simple pull architecture. Single PostgreSQL. No precomputation. Works fine until ~5M users.

Stage 2: 10M Users, 10K tweets/sec

Read load becomes painful. Introduce timeline cache (Redis). Push fan-out via async worker. Still no celebrity handling (everyone has < 100K followers).

Stage 3: 100M Users, 50K tweets/sec

Celebrities emerge. Add hybrid push/pull logic. Shard tweet DB. Move to Cassandra for write throughput.

Stage 4: 300M Users (target spec)

Full architecture from this article. Multi-AZ deployment. Elasticsearch for search. Flink for trending.

Stage 5: Global, multi-region

Active-active across regions. Social graph replicated globally. Timeline caches local to region (cross-region cache invalidation is expensive — accept eventual consistency).

14Trade-offs & Alternatives

Cassandra vs MySQL for Tweets

Cassandra wins at this scale because:

  • Write throughput: 1,160 writes/sec with peaks of 6K. Cassandra handles per node; MySQL needs sharding effort.
  • Schema flexibility: tweets evolve (new fields like polls, threads).
  • Multi-region native: Cassandra replicates across DCs without much config.

MySQL would also work but with more sharding management overhead.

Snowflake IDs vs UUIDs

Snowflake (64-bit, time-ordered):

  • Sortable by time without an extra timestamp field.
  • Smaller than UUIDs (8 bytes vs 16).
  • Requires a service to mint them OR per-machine generation logic with machine_id allocation.

UUIDs (random):

  • Generated anywhere with no coordination.
  • Not time-ordered — bad for time-based pagination, bad for B-Tree index performance (random insertion = page splits).

Twitter chose Snowflake for these reasons.

15Cross-Questions and Pushbacks

How exactly does the hybrid approach decide between push and pull?
Answer: The decision is per-author, based on their current follower count. We store follower_count as a denormalised field in the user profile, updated transactionally on every follow/unfollow. When a user posts: lookup their follower_count → if < 10,000 → publish to Kafka for fan-out worker to push → if ≥ 10,000 → skip fan-out (they're a celebrity, will be pulled at read time). The threshold (10K) is tunable based on observed write/read load. Users near the threshold may oscillate; that's fine because timelines self-heal: at read time, we always merge pushed cache + celebrity pulls, so transitions are seamless.
What happens when a celebrity loses followers and drops below the threshold?
Answer: Their future tweets get fanned out normally (because the threshold check is per-tweet, at post time). Tweets they posted while a celebrity remain pull-only — followers who view their timeline still pull from celebrity_cache. No retroactive migration is needed; the system naturally handles the mix. The next time those followers reload, the new (post-threshold-drop) tweets are in their pushed timeline; older tweets need to come from the celebrity cache. Eventually, as new tweets are posted and the timeline scroll horizon recedes, the celebrity-period tweets fall off the visible window.
How do you handle a user who follows 5,000 celebrities — that's 5,000 pull queries at read time?
Answer: Three mitigations: (1) Cap pulls per read at 20 — pick the 20 celebrities whose tweets are most likely to score high in this user's ranking (based on past engagement). (2) Cache an aggregated celebrity feed: a background job every 30 seconds merges the latest tweets from all celebrities into a "global celebrity feed" cached in Redis. Each user picks from this pre-merged feed instead of pulling individually. (3) For ML-ranked feeds, candidate generation can be more aggressive — pull from 50 celebrities, but only 5 tweets each, then re-rank. With pipelining, even 50 parallel Redis pulls take ~5ms.
How do you ensure a user sees their own tweet immediately after posting?
Answer: Read-your-own-writes consistency is handled by: (1) The Tweet Service ZADDs the new tweet to the author's own timeline (user:tweets:{author_id}) synchronously, before returning. (2) For the home feed: the client optimistically prepends the new tweet locally for 30 seconds, before reload. (3) The fan-out worker eventually pushes the tweet to followers' timelines, but the AUTHOR's view doesn't need to wait — their own timeline is always read by pulling from user:tweets:{author_id} which is immediately updated.
How do you handle a deleted tweet that's already in millions of timelines?
Answer: Two strategies: (1) Tombstone marker: mark the tweet as DELETED in the tweet DB and tweet cache. When timelines are hydrated, deleted tweets are filtered out at read time. The timeline entry (tweet_id) remains in Redis ZSETs, but it returns nothing on hydration. Over time, as timelines are trimmed (max 800 items), the stale entries fall off naturally. (2) Active cleanup (for serious content removals — DMCA, CSAM): publish DELETE event to Kafka. A consumer iterates the author's recent tweets and removes the entry from each follower's timeline ZSET. This is expensive but rarely needed. Default is tombstone; active cleanup for legal/safety cases.
Why fan-out on write? The write amplification (232K writes/sec) seems wasteful.
Answer: The trade-off is intentional. We're optimising for read latency, which matters more than write cost. 232K Redis ZADDs/sec is achievable on a modest Redis Cluster (3-4 nodes). The alternative — pull at read time — would require 8,680 reads/sec × 200 followee tweet lookups each = ~1.7M follower-tweet queries/sec on the tweet DB. Even with caching, this is much harder to scale than ZADDs. Redis writes are ~10× cheaper than DB reads. Plus, fan-out is async (via Kafka) — it doesn't block the user's post. Reads are user-facing and synchronous, so they get the optimisation budget.
Why not just use Cassandra for everything and skip Redis?
Answer: Cassandra is great for writes but slower for reads (10-20ms read latency vs Redis's 1ms). At 8,680 timeline reads/sec, each with 20 tweet hydrations = 173K Cassandra reads/sec. Achievable but expensive. Redis at 1ms latency gives us much better user experience and is cheaper per-op. The architecture has Cassandra as the durable source of truth (tweet objects) and Redis as the hot-path serving layer (timelines + tweet object cache). Both have their role; using one for both compromises one axis.
Your design loses tweets if the fan-out worker fails between Kafka consume and Redis ZADD.
Answer: Acknowledged — but it's recoverable. The tweet itself is durably stored in Cassandra (the worker doesn't fail before the tweet is persisted; only the fan-out step can fail). If the Fan-Out Service crashes mid-batch, Kafka doesn't commit the offset → on restart, the consumer re-reads the same tweet event and re-processes the fan-out. ZADD is idempotent (adding the same tweet_id to the same sorted set is a no-op). So at-least-once delivery + idempotent operation = effectively exactly-once outcome. The tweet will reach every follower's timeline, even if slightly delayed.
How would you implement "users you might know" recommendations?
Answer: Compute offline (daily) for each user: candidates = friends_of_friends ∩ NOT(already_following). Score each candidate by overlap_count (mutual friends), engagement signals (do you interact with this person's content?), and topic affinity (do you follow similar people?). Use Spark on the social graph. Store top 50 candidates per user in Redis: user:{id}:recommendations. Refresh weekly. When the user opens "Who to follow", serve from this cache. For real-time signals (new followee), trigger a fresh recommendation in background and update.
How does the system handle a viral tweet that gets 10M likes in an hour?
Answer: Likes are tracked in the tweet object's like_count, which is incremented per like. At 10M likes/hour = 2,800 likes/sec on one tweet. Directly UPDATE-ing MySQL/Cassandra is fine at this rate. BUT: if we also wanted to maintain "who liked this tweet" for the activity feed, the writes per tweet skyrocket. Strategy: asynchronous counter aggregation. Each like event goes to Kafka. A consumer aggregates per-tweet counts in Redis (HINCRBY tweet:{id} like_count 1) and periodically flushes to the persistent store. The "who liked" list is paginated and stored separately, fetched only when a user clicks to see the like list.

End of Problem 2. Next: WhatsApp / Chat (P3) — real-time messaging at scale.

Core Fundamentals — Under the Hood

The foundational technologies and patterns that appear in every problem. Understand HOW each one works internally, not just WHAT it does. Interviewers will ask.

1How Redis Achieves Sub-Millisecond Latency

Redis serves 100K-1M ops/sec from a single node with sub-millisecond latency. The mechanisms:

  • Everything in RAM: data lives in memory, never disk. RAM access is ~100ns; SSD is ~100μs (1000× slower). No I/O wait.
  • Single-threaded event loop: one thread handles all commands using epoll (Linux) or kqueue (BSD). No context switches, no mutex locks. Each command runs to completion before the next starts → atomic by default, no race conditions.
  • Optimised data structures: hash tables for O(1) GET/SET, skip lists for sorted sets (O(log N)), Simple Dynamic Strings (SDS) for O(1) length queries on binary data.
  • Non-blocking I/O: thousands of client connections multiplexed by a single thread using epoll. No thread-per-connection overhead.
  • Pipelining: clients can send multiple commands without waiting for replies, then read all replies — amortises network round-trips.

Trade-off: single-threaded means a slow command (e.g., KEYS on a large DB) blocks everyone. Use SCAN, never KEYS. Use BLOCKING commands cautiously.

2How Cassandra Achieves High Write Throughput

Cassandra writes 100K+ ops/sec per node. Why? LSM-Tree architecture.

  1. Step 1 — Commit Log: every write is first appended to the Commit Log on disk. Sequential disk writes are ~500 MB/s on modern SSDs — comparable to RAM throughput. No seeks.
  2. Step 2 — MemTable: the write is also placed in an in-memory sorted structure. Subsequent reads see the new write immediately from memory.
  3. Step 3 — SSTable flush: when the MemTable fills (~64 MB), it's flushed to disk as an immutable SSTable. Sequential write, very fast.
  4. Step 4 — Compaction: background process merges older SSTables, removing overwritten values. Pays the "cost" of LSM-Tree's write speed asynchronously.

Compare to MySQL B-Tree: writes find a leaf node (random I/O), may split nodes (more random I/O), update indexes (more random I/O). 10× slower for write-heavy workloads.

Trade-off: Cassandra reads can be slower (multiple SSTables to check), and you need to plan your partition keys carefully because Cassandra doesn't support arbitrary queries.

3How Kafka Handles 1M+ Messages/Sec

Kafka achieves throughput that traditional message brokers can't:

  • Append-only log: every message is appended to a partition log file. Sequential disk writes, no random I/O.
  • Zero-copy sendfile(): when a consumer reads, Kafka uses the Linux sendfile() syscall to send data directly from disk cache to the network socket, skipping user space. Saves 2 memory copies and 2 context switches per message batch.
  • OS page cache: Kafka deliberately doesn't maintain its own RAM cache — it relies on the OS page cache. Recent messages are served from RAM. Free RAM caching.
  • Batching: producers batch messages before sending. Consumers receive in batches. Amortises per-message overhead (network frames, syscalls).
  • Partition parallelism: a topic is split into N partitions, each on a different broker. Linear throughput scaling.

Trade-off: Kafka is optimised for high throughput sequential consumption. Random access (read message at offset X) is fast, but seeking by message content is not — that's what databases are for.

4The Power of Partial Indexes (PostgreSQL)

From the Job Scheduler problem: a partial index dramatically reduces index size.

CREATE INDEX idx_pending ON jobs(next_run_at) WHERE status = 'PENDING';

Without WHERE: index has 100M rows. With WHERE: index has only ~3,500 rows (the PENDING ones). Index fits in CPU cache. Queries that match the WHERE clause use this tiny index. Queries that don't match it use a different index (or full scan).

Use whenever you have a small subset of rows that's queried far more often than the rest.

5SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED — The Distributed Job Pattern

The classic pattern for multi-worker job queues:

BEGIN; SELECT job_id FROM jobs WHERE status = 'PENDING' AND next_run_at <= NOW() ORDER BY next_run_at LIMIT 10 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED; UPDATE jobs SET status = 'RUNNING' WHERE job_id IN (...); COMMIT;

How it works:

  • FOR UPDATE: acquires a row lock on each returned row.
  • SKIP LOCKED: if another transaction holds the lock on a row, skip it (don't block). Return the next eligible row.
  • Result: 50 workers running the query concurrently each get a different set of 10 rows. No coordination needed. No external lock manager (Redis, Zookeeper) needed.

Used by: Sidekiq Pro, GoodJob, Que, Oban — battle-tested at scale.

6Consistent Hashing — Adding/Removing Nodes Without Mass Reshuffling

Problem: with N servers, naive sharding is hash(key) % N. Add a server (N+1) and almost every key remaps. Disaster.

Consistent hashing: imagine a circular ring with positions 0 to 2³². Each server gets a position. Each key is hashed to a position. The key is "owned" by the next server clockwise.

Adding a server: it takes over the keys between its position and the previous server's position. Only 1/N keys remap. Other servers untouched.

Virtual nodes: each physical server has 150 positions (vnodes) on the ring. Distributes load evenly even with non-uniform server capacity.

Used by: Cassandra, DynamoDB, Akamai CDN, Riak, Memcached client libraries.

7Bloom Filters — Probabilistic Set Membership in Tiny Memory

A Bloom filter answers: "Is this element maybe in the set, or definitely not in the set?" Zero false negatives. ~1% false positives. Storage: ~10 bits per element.

How: bit array of M bits, all initialised to 0. K hash functions. To add element X: hash with K functions, set the corresponding K bits to 1. To check: hash with K functions, see if all K bits are 1. If any is 0 → definitely not in set. If all are 1 → maybe in set (need to verify another way).

Use cases:

  • Malicious URL detection: 500M URLs in 600 MB instead of 25 GB.
  • Cassandra: checks if a row exists in an SSTable before reading from disk.
  • Google Bigtable: same purpose.
  • Web crawler dedup: have we seen this URL?

8The CAP Theorem in Practice

In a distributed system, you can have at most 2 of: Consistency, Availability, Partition tolerance. Since network partitions DO happen, the real choice is CP vs AP.

SystemCAP ChoiceWhy
PostgreSQL primary-replicaCPIf primary partitioned from replicas, primary refuses writes until quorum
CassandraAP (tunable)Available during partitions; you choose consistency level per operation
DynamoDBAPAlways available; eventual consistency default; optional strong consistency
HBaseCPIf region server fails, region unavailable until reassigned
etcd / ZookeeperCPQuorum required for any write — coordination service must be consistent

When choosing: financial data → CP. Social feed, DNS, CDN → AP. Inventory → CP. Analytics → AP.

9Idempotency — The Multi-Layer Defense

Network calls fail. Clients retry. Without idempotency, retries cause duplicates. Standard defense:

  1. Client-supplied idempotency key (UUID per request).
  2. Redis SETNX (atomic): if key exists → return cached result.
  3. DB UNIQUE constraint on idempotency_key: backup if Redis fails.
  4. Downstream gateway idempotency: pass the key to Stripe/Razorpay/etc. — they also dedupe.
  5. Reconciliation: nightly job compares records across systems to catch any missed.

4 layers seem like overkill until you've seen a single missed dedup cause a double-charge in production.

10Why Snowflake IDs Beat UUIDs (When You Need Time Ordering)

Snowflake = 64 bits = 41 timestamp + 10 machine ID + 12 sequence. Generated per-machine without coordination.

  • Time-ordered: newer = larger. Sortable. Great for cursor-based pagination ("give me items older than this ID").
  • Compact: 8 bytes vs UUID's 16 bytes. Better B-Tree index performance.
  • Insertion order: sequential IDs cluster at the right side of B-Tree. UUIDs are random, causing page splits.
  • Trade-off: requires machine_id allocation (Zookeeper, manual) and clock-skew handling.

11Cache Strategies — The Four Read/Write Patterns

Pick the right pattern based on (a) is the workload read-heavy or write-heavy, (b) how stale can the cache be, and (c) what happens if the cache or DB fails mid-write.

1. Cache-Aside (Lazy Loading) — the default

READ: app → cache? ┌── hit → return value └── miss → DB → write into cache → return value WRITE: app → DB app → cache.DEL(key) // invalidate; next read re-populates
  • Pros: simple; cache only holds what's actually read; cache failure doesn't break writes.
  • Cons: cache miss = slow (one DB round-trip + one cache write); stale data possible if writer forgets to invalidate; stampede risk on hot-key expiry.
  • Use when: read-heavy workload, can tolerate brief staleness (URL shortener, product catalog, user profiles).

2. Read-Through — cache fronts the DB transparently

READ: app → cache ┌── hit → return └── miss → cache loads from DB → returns to app WRITE: app → cache → cache writes to DB // combined with write-through usually
  • Pros: app code is simpler — no DB code on the miss path; cache and DB are coupled by configuration, not code.
  • Cons: requires a cache layer or library that "knows" the DB schema; harder to override per-query.
  • Use when: managed caches that proxy a DB (DAX for DynamoDB, Hibernate L2 cache, NGINX caching proxy).

3. Write-Through — cache and DB updated together, synchronously

WRITE: app → cache.SET(key, val) cache → DB.write(key, val) // synchronous; both must succeed return success to app READ: app → cache → hit (always; even fresh writes are cached)
  • Pros: cache and DB always consistent; readers never see stale data; read-after-write is guaranteed.
  • Cons: write latency = max(cache, DB); pollutes the cache with data that may never be read; cache failure can block writes (unless you fail-open).
  • Use when: read-after-write consistency is critical and write rate is moderate (e.g., user profile updates that the user immediately re-reads on next page).

4. Write-Back (Write-Behind) — cache absorbs writes, flushes to DB async

WRITE: app → cache.SET(key, val) // returns immediately cache → buffers writes cache → DB.batchWrite(...) // asynchronously, e.g. every 100 ms or 1000 entries READ: app → cache → hit (cache is source of truth between flushes)
  • Pros: extremely high write throughput; absorbs spikes; batched DB writes are 10–100× more efficient.
  • Cons: data loss if cache crashes before flush; cache becomes temporary source of truth; complicated recovery semantics.
  • Use when: write-heavy, tolerable durability loss — view counters, click events, leaderboard scores, like counts. For money or auth data: never use write-back.

Bonus pattern: Write-Around

Writes go directly to the DB, bypassing the cache. Reads use cache-aside. Useful for write-once-read-rarely data so the cache isn't polluted by writes that won't be read soon (e.g., audit logs, archival writes).

Bonus pattern: Refresh-Ahead

Cache proactively refreshes hot keys before their TTL expires. Eliminates cold-miss latency cliffs on popular keys. Trade-off: wasted refreshes for keys that aren't actually re-accessed. Use when you have a predictable hot-key access pattern.

Decision matrix

WorkloadStrategyExample
Read-heavy, stale OKCache-AsideURL shortener, product catalog
Read-after-write must be freshWrite-ThroughUser profile, cart contents
Write-heavy, durability tolerantWrite-BackView counts, like counts, analytics
Managed cache fronting DBRead-ThroughDAX, ORM L2 cache, CDN
Write-once, read-rarelyWrite-AroundAudit logs, cold archives
Predictable hot keysRefresh-AheadTop-N lists, leaderboards

12Eviction Policies — Choosing What to Throw Out

When the cache hits its memory limit, something must go. The policy decides which key. Get this wrong and your hit rate tanks.

PolicyRuleStrengthsWeaknesses
LRU (Least Recently Used)Evict the key not accessed for the longest timeO(1) with doubly-linked list + hash map; matches typical temporal-locality workloadsScan pollution: a full-table scan evicts every hot key in one shot
LFU (Least Frequently Used)Evict the key with the lowest hit-countResists scan pollution; stable popular keys stay hotOld hot keys that stop being accessed linger forever (mitigated by aging variants)
FIFOEvict the oldest-inserted, regardless of accessSimplest; cheap O(1)Ignores actual access patterns; usually worst hit rate
RandomEvict a random keyTrivially simple; surprisingly OK for many workloads; no metadata to trackCan evict the hottest key by bad luck
TTL-basedEach key auto-expires after a set timePredictable memory pressure; great for time-bounded data (sessions, rate-limit windows)Not a true eviction; you still need a fallback policy if you fill up before TTLs hit
ARC (Adaptive Replacement Cache)Two lists (recency + frequency); balance shifts based on workloadBetter hit rate than LRU on mixed workloadsMore complex; was patent-encumbered by IBM (now expired)
W-TinyLFUWindow-LRU front + Count-Min Sketch frequency estimator; admit new key only if estimated freq > victim'sBest hit rate in published benchmarks; resists scan pollutionMore complex; small CMS memory overhead

Picking a policy (quick guide)

  • LRU — safe default for typical app workloads with temporal locality.
  • LFU — when you have analytical scans that mustn't pollute the working set.
  • TTL-based — when data is naturally time-bound (sessions, OTPs, rate-limit windows). Combine with another policy as fallback.
  • W-TinyLFU — when you need the best possible hit rate and can afford the complexity (Caffeine library is the reference).
  • Random — when you genuinely don't care or you're aiming for minimum metadata overhead.

Redis eviction policies (specific commands)

Redis's maxmemory-policy setting controls behaviour when maxmemory is reached:

PolicyWhat it does
noeviction (default)Reject new writes with an error. Reads keep working.
allkeys-lruLRU across all keys, whether they have a TTL or not. The most common choice for a pure cache.
allkeys-lfuLFU across all keys (added in Redis 4.0; uses a probabilistic counter).
volatile-lruLRU but only on keys that have a TTL set. Keys without TTL are protected.
volatile-lfuLFU but only on keys with TTL.
volatile-ttlEvict keys closest to expiry first. Useful when TTLs encode "freshness need."
allkeys-random / volatile-randomRandom eviction.
🔑 Two practical Redis defaults

If Redis is a pure cache (you can lose any key any time): use allkeys-lru and don't bother setting TTLs unless you want them for staleness reasons.

If Redis holds some "must keep" state mixed with cache (e.g., sessions you can't lose alongside cached data you can): use volatile-lru and set TTLs only on the cache keys; the session keys without TTL are safe from eviction.

13Elasticsearch — How It Works and When to Use It

Elasticsearch is built on Apache Lucene; it's a distributed search and analytics engine. Think of it as "Postgres for text and aggregations" — but never as a primary source of truth.

How an inverted index works (the heart of Elasticsearch)

Instead of storing rows and scanning them, the index stores a mapping from term → list of documents containing that term:

Documents: doc1 = "The quick brown fox" doc2 = "The lazy brown dog" doc3 = "A quick fox jumped" Inverted index (after tokenize + lowercase + stemming): "the" → [doc1, doc2] "quick" → [doc1, doc3] "brown" → [doc1, doc2] "fox" → [doc1, doc3] "lazy" → [doc2] "dog" → [doc2] "jump" → [doc3] "a" → [doc3] Query: "quick fox" → intersect postings: [doc1, doc3] ∩ [doc1, doc3] = [doc1, doc3] → score each with BM25 → return ranked

Pipeline per query (the path of a search request)

  1. Tokenize — split the query into terms ("quick fox" → ["quick", "fox"]).
  2. Analyze — lowercase, stem ("running" → "run"), remove stop-words ("the", "a"), apply synonyms.
  3. Lookup — for each term, fetch its posting list from the inverted index (sub-ms; lists are sorted and compressed).
  4. Intersect / union — AND query intersects lists; OR unions.
  5. Score — each matching doc gets a BM25 score (term-frequency × inverse-document-frequency, length-normalised).
  6. Sort and return top-K — usually top-10 with highlights.

Distributed architecture

  • Index = collection of documents (think: a logical "table").
  • Shard = a Lucene index file; each index is split into N shards distributed across nodes.
  • Replica = a copy of a shard on another node; provides failover and parallel read throughput.
  • Refresh interval = how often new documents become searchable. Default 1 s — this is what people mean by Elasticsearch being "near real-time."
  • Coordinator node = receives the query, fans it out to all shards, gathers responses, merges top-K, returns to client.

Strengths

  • Full-text search with relevance scoring (BM25), out of the box.
  • Faceted search and aggregations — "how many products in this filter combination?" computed at index time.
  • Fuzzy matching, synonyms, autocomplete (edge n-grams), phonetic search.
  • Geo-spatial queries (bounding box, distance, polygons).
  • Log/metric analytics — the "E" in ELK stack; analysts run ad-hoc queries on billions of log lines in seconds.

Weaknesses (the reasons you don't make it your primary DB)

  • Not a source of truth — refresh interval, eventual consistency, no real transactions. Always feed it from your real DB via CDC.
  • Memory-hungry — JVM-heavy; ~50% of RAM for heap, the rest for OS page cache. A 1 TB index needs ~250 GB+ RAM across the cluster.
  • Writes are amplified — every doc update is a delete+insert in Lucene segments; high write rate causes segment merging pressure.
  • Cluster ops are operationally heavy — yellow/red status, shard rebalancing, mapping conflicts. Most teams use managed offerings (Elastic Cloud, AWS OpenSearch).

When to use Elasticsearch

Use caseWhy Elasticsearch wins
Search box (product, document, articles)BM25, fuzzy match, synonyms, highlighting — built-in
Log analytics (ELK / EFK stack)Aggregations over billions of lines in seconds; Kibana dashboards
Faceted filters (e.g. e-commerce filters)Fast counts per facet via pre-computed bucket aggregations
AutocompleteEdge n-gram analyser; prefix search at the edge
Geo-spatial queriesR-tree indexes; "within 5 km of point" in milliseconds

When NOT to use Elasticsearch

  • Primary key-value lookups (use Redis / DynamoDB; far cheaper and faster).
  • Transactional updates (use Postgres / MySQL).
  • Source of truth for business data (use a real OLTP DB + CDC-mirror to ES).
  • Tiny datasets (Postgres full-text search is enough up to ~10M rows).

14Database Selection Guide — When to Use Which

The most common interview pushback: "why did you pick this database?" Memorise the table below so you can answer with one sentence per option.

The shortlist

Decision tree (when in doubt, follow this)

Q: Do you need ACID transactions across multiple rows / tables? ├── Yes → relational (Postgres / MySQL). │ ├── Need to scale beyond ~10 TB? → shard MySQL OR use NewSQL (Spanner / CockroachDB). │ └── Otherwise → single Postgres + read replicas. Move on. │ └── No, eventual consistency is fine. Then ask: │ ├── Is it search / faceting / full-text? → Elasticsearch (mirror from primary). │ ├── Is it analytics / aggregations? → ClickHouse / BigQuery (mirror via CDC). │ ├── Is it cache / session / rate-limit? → Redis. │ ├── Is it blobs / files / videos? → S3. │ ├── Is it time-series metrics? → InfluxDB / TimescaleDB. │ ├── Is it heavy graph traversal? → Neo4j. │ ├── Are you write-heavy with simple per-row access? → Cassandra. │ └── Need managed key-value with auto-scale? → DynamoDB.

Trade-off matrix (the famous 4 dimensions)

DatabaseConsistencyScale shapeQuery flexibilityOperational cost
Postgres / MySQLStrong (single-leader)Vertical (then sharded)Very high — full SQL, joinsLow — mature ops
CassandraTunable (eventual default)Linear horizontalLow — must design tables per queryHigh — repair, compaction

🔑 The Universal Pattern: One Source of Truth + Many Specialised Views

Almost every real system has:

  • One OLTP DB (Postgres / MySQL / Cassandra) as the source of truth.
  • Multiple specialised views kept in sync via CDC: Elasticsearch for search, ClickHouse for analytics, Redis for cache, S3 for archive.

Don't try to make one DB do everything — that's the route to a stack you can't operate. Specialise per workload; sync via CDC.

15CDN — How It Reduces Latency (With Actual Numbers)

A Content Delivery Network is a globally distributed cache of HTTP responses (static assets, API responses, video segments). The user connects to the nearest CDN POP (Point of Presence) instead of your origin server. This single optimisation can speed up page loads 10× and cut your bandwidth bill by 90%.

The latency arithmetic

Real numbers for a typical "user in Mumbai, origin server in Virginia, USA":

StepWithout CDNWith CDN (cache hit)
TCP / TLS handshake3 round trips × ~200 ms = ~600 ms3 round trips × ~15 ms = ~45 ms
HTTP request → response (1 byte)1 round trip × 200 ms = 200 ms1 round trip × 15 ms = 15 ms
Download 200 KB asset~250 ms (long-distance throughput)~50 ms (POP throughput)
Total time-to-display~1,050 ms~110 ms

That's ~10× faster on first access, and after the TLS handshake is reused, subsequent requests are sub-50 ms vs ~300 ms direct.

Compound effect on a typical page

A modern web page loads ~50–100 assets (JS, CSS, images, fonts). Without HTTP/2 multiplexing or CDN:

Without CDN, sequential connections: 50 assets × 200 ms RTT ≈ 10 s page load With CDN + HTTP/2: 50 assets × 15 ms RTT ≈ 0.75 s page load (Multi-connection HTTP/1.1 gets you ~5× concurrency, so without CDN you actually see ~2 s — still 3× worse than with CDN.)

How a CDN reduces latency, mechanically

  1. Anycast routing: same IP address advertised from every POP; BGP routes user to the nearest one (network-shortest, not geographic-shortest, but usually close).
  2. TCP / TLS termination at edge: handshakes happen between user and POP (low RTT) instead of user and origin (high RTT). Major win for HTTPS pages.
  3. Cache hit at edge: 90–99% of requests for popular static content are served from POP RAM/SSD without ever touching origin. Total RTT = single edge round trip.
  4. HTTP/2 / HTTP/3 multiplexing: one connection, many concurrent streams. CDNs upgrade clients to HTTP/2 even if your origin only speaks 1.1.
  5. Connection pooling to origin: CDN keeps long-lived persistent connections to your origin → cache miss adds only one RTT origin→POP, plus the regular POP→user RTT.

What CDNs are great for

  • Static assets: images, CSS, JS bundles, fonts, downloadable files. Trivially cacheable.
  • Video segments: HLS / DASH chunks with long TTL (hours). One PUT to origin → distributed worldwide automatically.
  • Frequently-read API responses: with appropriate Cache-Control headers and CDN-side cache keys, even dynamic responses can hit edge (e.g. weather API, product catalogue).
  • HTTPS termination: TLS handshake at edge is dramatically faster than at origin for far-away users.
  • DDoS absorption: CDNs (Cloudflare, Akamai) have terabits-per-second of edge capacity; attack traffic dies at the edge.

What CDNs are NOT great for

  • Personalised / per-user content — cache key would have to include user_id, so hit rate is near zero. (Edge compute like Cloudflare Workers can help.)
  • Strict consistency reads — a CDN's cache can be ~minutes stale. If you need "what's my balance right now", bypass CDN.
  • POST/PUT (write) traffic — CDNs don't cache writes; only saves the TLS-handshake latency.
  • One-off content — first request always misses; if your asset is only requested once globally, CDN doesn't help.

Cost numbers (so you can defend "yes we need a CDN")

ItemOrder-of-magnitude
CDN egress (CloudFront, India zone)~$85 / TB
CDN egress (CloudFront, US/EU zones)~$50–60 / TB
Origin egress (EC2 to internet)~$90 / TB
Typical cache hit rate (well-configured)90–99% for static, 50–80% for dynamic
Net bandwidth savings vs origin-only~70–90% lower bill plus much faster page loads

16CDC Pipelines — When and Why

Change Data Capture streams every insert / update / delete from a database into downstream consumers in near real time. The killer use case: keep your search index / cache / analytics warehouse / downstream services in sync with your OLTP DB without the dual-write problem.

The dual-write problem (the reason CDC exists)

The naïve approach: when your app writes to the DB, it also publishes a message to Kafka.

app → DB.write() ✓ succeeded app → Kafka.publish() ✗ network error, retry? Result: DB has the new state, but downstream consumers never learn. Or worse — Kafka.publish() succeeds and DB.write() fails after.

Solutions: 2-phase commit (too slow), the Outbox pattern (write to DB + outbox table in one transaction; separate process publishes outbox), or — best — just read the DB's own log.

How CDC works

The DB already maintains a durable, ordered log of every change for its own crash recovery — the Postgres WAL, the MySQL binlog, the MongoDB oplog. CDC tools read that log and publish each event to Kafka.

Source DB (Postgres / MySQL / Mongo) │ │ WAL / binlog / oplog (append-only, ordered) ▼ CDC connector (Debezium / AWS DMS / Maxwell) │ - decodes binary log entries │ - resolves schema │ - emits one event per row change ▼ Kafka topic per table (e.g. `db.users`, `db.orders`) │ ┌──┴────────┬───────────────┬────────────────┐ ▼ ▼ ▼ ▼ Search Cache Data Warehouse Microservice index invalidator loader consumer (ES) (Redis) (Snowflake) (Service B reacts)

When to use CDC

Use caseWhy CDC
Search index syncPostgres → Elasticsearch via CDC. Whenever a row changes, ES is updated within seconds. No dual-write.
Cache invalidationPostgres → consumer → DEL on Redis. Frees the writer from remembering to invalidate.
Data warehouse / analyticsOLTP → Kafka → Snowflake / BigQuery / ClickHouse. Analysts query a near-live copy without touching production DB.
Microservices integrationService B reacts to Service A's data changes without coupling code. A new payment row → Service B sends receipt email.
Cross-region replicationStream changes from primary region to read replicas in other regions; bring up DR in minutes.
Outbox patternService writes a domain event to an `outbox` table in the same DB transaction; CDC publishes from the outbox. Solves "I must publish after DB commit but before another change."
Audit logsEvery row change captured immutably to S3 / data lake. Compliance loves this.

When NOT to use CDC

  • You don't have access to the source DB's transaction log (some managed services don't expose it — though most do now).
  • You need application-level events (e.g. "the user did a checkout") rather than row-level changes; let the app publish those events explicitly.
  • Latency requirements < 100 ms end-to-end — CDC typically adds 1–10 s of lag. For real-time, use synchronous fan-out.
  • Your throughput is tiny (< 100 writes/s) — Outbox pattern + cron polling can be simpler.

What you get for "free" by using CDC

  • Replay: re-process all history when downstream logic has a bug.
  • Multiple consumers: same event stream feeds N independent consumers (Kafka strength).
  • Decoupling: source DB owner doesn't need to know which services consume; new consumers added without touching the source.
  • Ordering guarantees: Kafka per-partition ordering = per-row ordering if partitioned by primary key.
🔑 The Mental Model

Think of CDC as turning your database into an event stream. Every row change becomes a Kafka message; every downstream system subscribes. One source of truth, many consistent copies — without the dual-write bug.

This pattern (Database → CDC → Kafka → many consumers) is the backbone of Netflix, LinkedIn, Uber, and most modern data architectures.

Hard Real-Time WebSocket E2EE Cassandra

Problem 3: Designing WhatsApp / Real-Time Chat System

A real-time messaging system serving 2 billion users requires solving four hard problems simultaneously: maintaining 200M persistent connections, delivering messages in under 500ms, supporting end-to-end encryption, and never losing a message. This article walks through how each piece fits together.

1Context and Why This Problem Matters

Real-time messaging is fundamentally different from request-response systems like Twitter or e-commerce. The server pushes data to clients, not the other way around. This inverts most of the architecture you'd build for a typical web app.

The hard parts of chat:

  • Persistent connections: 200M users online at peak means 200M open WebSocket connections — far beyond what traditional HTTP servers handle.
  • Stateful routing: when Alice sends to Bob, the server must know which physical machine Bob is currently connected to.
  • Offline delivery: if Bob is offline, the message must be queued and delivered the moment he reconnects.
  • Ordering guarantees: messages in a chat must appear in order across all participants, even when the system is distributed across data centers.
  • End-to-end encryption: the server should not be able to read the messages it's routing. This drives a specific cryptographic protocol design.
  • Write throughput: 100B messages/day = 1.16M writes/sec. Few databases handle this.

Patterns from this problem reappear in: Slack, Discord, Microsoft Teams, multiplayer games, live trading systems (Problem 17), real-time collaborative editing (Problem 19).

2Requirements Gathering

Functional Requirements

  • 1:1 messaging: send/receive text messages between two users in real-time.
  • Group chat: up to 1024 members (WhatsApp's current limit).
  • Delivery receipts: Sent ✓ / Delivered ✓✓ / Read ✓✓ (blue).
  • Offline delivery: messages queued and delivered when recipient reconnects.
  • Media sharing: images, videos, audio, documents — uploaded once, referenced by URL.
  • Presence: online status, last-seen timestamp.
  • Reply/quote: reference a specific previous message.
  • End-to-end encryption: server cannot read messages.

Non-Functional Requirements

  • Scale: 2B total users, 200M concurrent (~10% online at peak), 100B messages/day.
  • Latency: messages delivered in <500ms when both users online.
  • At-least-once delivery: no message lost. Duplicates must be handled at the client.
  • Ordering: messages in a chat preserve send order.
  • E2EE: forward secrecy + future secrecy via Signal Protocol.
  • Availability: 99.9% — chat downtime is a major event.

Clarifying Questions to Ask

  • "What's the max group size?" — Changes fan-out strategy significantly. 256 vs 1024 vs 10000.
  • "Is E2EE mandatory or can server see plaintext?" — Affects whether server can do search, message preview, etc.
  • "How long are messages retained on server?" — WhatsApp: stored until delivered, then deleted. Telegram: stored permanently. Big architectural difference.
  • "Is voice/video calling in scope?" — Adds WebRTC signalling, TURN/STUN servers — different architecture.
  • "Is web client / multi-device sync in scope?" — Multi-device E2EE is genuinely hard (separate keys per device).
🔑 Key Insight

The WhatsApp model: messages are stored on the server only until delivered to all recipients, then deleted from the server. The client devices are the long-term storage. This reduces server storage by orders of magnitude vs storing messages forever.

3Capacity Estimation

Traffic

MetricCalculationValue
Messages/sec (avg)100B / 100k~1M/sec
Concurrent connections2B × 10%200M
WS servers @ 100K conns each200M / 100K~2,000 servers
Messages per user per day100B / 2B~50/day
Peak msgs/sec (3× avg)—~3.5M/sec

Storage (Short-Term Buffer)

Since WhatsApp deletes server-side after delivery, storage is much smaller than you'd expect.

MetricCalculationValue
Avg message size (text)content (~100 bytes) + metadata (~100 bytes)~200 bytes
Undelivered queue (1-week buffer)1M/sec × 100k × 7 × 5% × 200B~7 TB
Media storage (1yr)30% × 1MB × 1M/sec × 100k × 365~11 PB
Group metadata500M groups × 1KB~500 GB

MetricCalculationValue
Outbound message traffic1.16M × 200B × 2 (sent+delivered)~460 MB/sec
