Insight: Keep-alive overhead is comparable to message traffic. Heartbeat frequency matters at this scale.

🔧 From Numbers to Architecture — what these estimates force

Every tech choice in the HLD below traces back to a number we just computed. Read these bullets as "number → constraint → tech choice".

  • 200 M concurrent WebSocket connections → HTTP polling is impossible (200M × 1 poll/s = 200M req/s). WebSocket fleet ~2000 nodes @ 100k conns each; consistent-hash routing by user_id so the same user always lands on the same WS terminator.
  • ~1 M messages/sec sustained → far beyond MySQL/Postgres (5–10k writes/s ceiling). Cassandra mandatory — LSM tree, 100k+ writes/s/node, partition by user_id, cluster by timestamp.
  • 10 TB/day text storage → multi-PB at 5-yr retention. Cassandra scales linearly by adding nodes; ring grows organically.
  • Online presence + last_seen for 200M users → ephemeral, sub-ms reads. Redis with TTL on each presence key; losing state on restart is acceptable.
  • Online vs offline message routing → recipient online = direct WS push; offline = store-and-forward. Need a fast "is this user online and on which WS node?" lookup → Redis Hash presence:{user_id} → {ws_node, last_seen}.
  • Group chat fanout (100-member groups) → one message can fan to 100 recipients. Kafka as the async fanout bus; consumer writes to each recipient's Cassandra partition and pushes to their WS terminator.
  • E2E encryption requirement → server CANNOT read message payloads. Only metadata routing: who sent to whom, when. Cassandra stores ciphertext blobs; no analytics on content.
  • Media (130 PB / 5 yr at 30% media rate) → S3 + CDN; messages reference media URLs, not blobs.
  • Message ordering matters per conversation, not globally → Cassandra clustering key by (conversation_id, timestamp); ordering free within a partition.
  • 460 MB/sec outbound + 330 MB/sec heartbeats → ~800 MB/sec network egress. Scales with fleet size; multi-region with regional WS terminators reduces cross-DC traffic.

4API Design (WebSocket Protocol)

WhatsApp doesn't use REST for messages — it uses a custom protocol over WebSocket. Here's a simplified version.

Connection Setup

Client → WebSocket Handshake → wss://chat.example.com/v1 Headers: Authorization: Bearer {jwt} Device-ID: {device_uuid} Server responds: HTTP 101 Switching Protocols Subsequent messages are JSON frames over the WS:

Send Message

// Client → Server { "type": "send_message", "client_msg_id": "uuid-v4", // idempotency key "chat_id": "uuid", "recipient_id": "uuid", // for 1:1; not needed for groups "content": "", // encrypted on device "msg_type": "TEXT", // TEXT, IMAGE, VIDEO, etc. "media_url": null } // Server → Sender (ack) { "type": "ack", "client_msg_id": "uuid-v4", "server_msg_id": "TIMEUUID", "timestamp_ms": 1705315200000, "status": "SENT" // SENT → DELIVERED → READ } // Server → Recipient (delivery) { "type": "incoming_message", "server_msg_id": "TIMEUUID", "chat_id": "uuid", "sender_id": "uuid", "content": "", "msg_type": "TEXT", "timestamp_ms": 1705315200000 } // Recipient → Server (delivery receipt) { "type": "delivery_receipt", "server_msg_id": "TIMEUUID", "received_ts": 1705315200200 } // Recipient → Server (read receipt) { "type": "read_receipt", "server_msg_id": "TIMEUUID", "read_ts": 1705315230000 }

Why WebSocket and Not HTTP Polling?

  • Server push: the server initiates messages to the client; HTTP polling can't do this without long-polling hacks.
  • Bi-directional: single connection handles send + receive; no separate request channels.
  • Lower overhead: 2-byte WS frame vs ~800-byte HTTP headers per message. At 50 msgs/day × 2B users = significant savings.
  • Persistent: connection stays open, no per-request TCP handshake or TLS negotiation.

5Data Model

Messages (Cassandra)

The most critical schema decision. Optimised for "give me the latest N messages in this chat":

CREATE TABLE messages ( chat_id UUID, -- partition key msg_id TIMEUUID, -- clustering key (time-ordered, unique) sender_id UUID, content BLOB, -- E2EE ciphertext msg_type TINYINT, -- TEXT=0, IMAGE=1, ... media_url TEXT, -- nullable, S3 URL reply_to_id TIMEUUID, -- quote/reply status TINYINT, -- 0=SENT, 1=DELIVERED, 2=READ PRIMARY KEY (chat_id, msg_id) ) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (msg_id DESC);

Why this schema works:

  • Partition key = chat_id: all messages for a single chat live on the same node. Retrieving chat history is one partition lookup.
  • Clustering by msg_id DESC: newest messages first. LIMIT 50 gives you the latest 50 in O(1) — no sorting needed.
  • TIMEUUID: time-ordered UUID. Generated by Snowflake service. Naturally sortable. Unique even across servers.
  • BLOB content: stores E2EE ciphertext. Server cannot read it.

User Devices (PostgreSQL)

Tracks all devices (phone, web, desktop) for each user. Needed for E2EE multi-device.

CREATE TABLE user_devices ( device_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, user_id UUID NOT NULL, device_type VARCHAR(20), -- 'PHONE', 'WEB', 'DESKTOP' identity_pub_key BYTEA NOT NULL, -- Curve25519, ~32 bytes signed_prekey_pub BYTEA NOT NULL, -- rotated periodically registered_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW(), last_active TIMESTAMPTZ ); CREATE INDEX idx_user_devices ON user_devices(user_id);

One-Time Prekeys (PostgreSQL)

Used by Signal Protocol for asynchronous key exchange. Each device uploads ~100 of these. Consumed on first message from another user.

CREATE TABLE one_time_prekeys ( device_id UUID, prekey_id INT, pub_key BYTEA NOT NULL, used BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE, PRIMARY KEY (device_id, prekey_id) );

Groups (PostgreSQL)

CREATE TABLE groups ( group_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(100), created_by UUID, created_at TIMESTAMPTZ, avatar_url TEXT ); CREATE TABLE group_members ( group_id UUID, user_id UUID, role VARCHAR(20), -- 'ADMIN', 'MEMBER' joined_at TIMESTAMPTZ, PRIMARY KEY (group_id, user_id) ); CREATE INDEX idx_user_groups ON group_members(user_id); -- "what groups am I in?"

Routing Table (Redis)

Critical for delivering to online users — maps user_id → which chat server they're connected to.

Key: online:{user_id} Value: Hash { server_id: "chat-server-42", connected_at: 1705315200, device_id: "uuid" } TTL: 60 seconds (refreshed every 30s by heartbeat)

Offline Message Queue (Cassandra)

When a user is offline, messages destined for them are buffered:

CREATE TABLE undelivered ( user_id UUID, -- partition key msg_id TIMEUUID, -- clustering key chat_id UUID, sender_id UUID, content BLOB, msg_type TINYINT, enqueued_at TIMESTAMP, PRIMARY KEY (user_id, msg_id) ) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (msg_id ASC) AND default_time_to_live = 2592000; -- 30-day TTL, then deleted

6High-Level Architecture

CLIENT (Mobile / Web) │ WebSocket (TLS, persistent) │ ┌────────▼────────┐ │ Load Balancer │ — consistent hash by user_id │ (L4, TLS pass) │ (sticky routing) └────────┬────────┘ │ ┌───────────────┼───────────────┐ │ │ │ ┌────▼─────┐ ┌────▼─────┐ ┌────▼─────┐ │ Chat Server│ │ Chat Server│ │ Chat Server│ │ #1 │ │ #2 │ │ #N │ ... 2000 servers │ holds 100K │ │ 100K conns │ │ 100K conns │ │ WS conns │ │ │ │ │ └────┬───────┘ └─────┬──────┘ └────────────┘ │ │ │ ┌──────────┴────────────┐ │ ▼ ▼ │ ┌──────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ │ │ Redis: route │ │ Kafka: │ │ │ user_id → │ │ msg events │ │ │ server_id │ │ │ │ └──────────────┘ └──────┬───────┘ │ │ │ ┌──────▼──────────┐ │ │ Message Worker │ │ │ (persist + push) │ │ └──────┬──────────┘ │ │ │ ┌─────────────────────────┤ │ ▼ ▼ │ ┌────────────┐ ┌────────────────┐ │ │ Cassandra: │ │ Cassandra: │ │ │ messages │ │ undelivered │ │ │ (by chat) │ │ (offline buf) │ │ └────────────┘ └────────────────┘ │ └─→ For groups: fan-out service queries group_members and emits per-recipient delivery

Message Path (1:1, both online)

  1. Alice's phone has a persistent WebSocket to Chat Server A (assigned via consistent hash on Alice's user_id).
  2. Alice's app encrypts the message and sends it over the WS.
  3. Chat Server A:
    • Looks up Bob's location: HGET online:{bob_id} server_id → "Chat Server B".
    • Persists to Cassandra messages table.
    • Publishes the event to Kafka.
  4. Chat Server A's Kafka consumer delivers to Bob via Chat Server B (gRPC internal call).
  5. Chat Server B pushes the message to Bob's WebSocket.
  6. Bob's app sends back a delivery_receipt → Server B → Kafka → updates message status to DELIVERED.
  7. Alice's Chat Server A receives the delivery_receipt event → pushes ✓✓ to Alice over her WS.

Message Path (Bob offline)

  1. Steps 1-3 same as above.
  2. Chat Server A looks up Bob: online:{bob_id} returns nothing → Bob is offline.
  3. Server A writes the message into the undelivered Cassandra table partitioned by Bob's user_id.
  4. Server A also sends a push notification via APNs/FCM to wake Bob's phone.
  5. When Bob's app eventually reconnects (Chat Server C, perhaps a different one), it sends {last_received_msg_id: ...}.
  6. Chat Server C queries the undelivered table for messages newer than last_received_msg_id, pushes them all over WS, and deletes them from undelivered.

7Deep Dive 1: Connection Management at 200M Scale

Maintaining 200 million simultaneous TCP connections is one of the hardest infrastructure problems in the design. Let's break it down.

Per-Server Connection Limit

How many WebSocket connections can one server hold?

  • OS-level: file descriptors. Default 1024 (laughable). Tune ulimit -n to 1M+.
  • Per-connection memory: ~10 KB OS-level buffers + ~30 KB application state (user_id, session keys, queued ops) → ~40 KB.
  • 100K connections × 40 KB = 4 GB RAM. Easily fits in a 32 GB server.
  • Network bandwidth: 100K conns × 50 msgs/day = ~6 msgs/sec per server outbound. Tiny.

Realistic limit: 100K-500K connections per server. Need 400-2000 chat servers for 200M total.

Routing a User to a Specific Server

When Alice's phone connects, the load balancer chooses one of 2000 servers. Two questions:

  1. Should Alice land on the same server every time (sticky), or any available server?
  2. How does Server A find Server B (where Bob is connected)?

Sticky Routing via Consistent Hashing

The L4 load balancer hashes the user_id (from a header set by the client) and routes to the corresponding server:

target_server = consistent_hash(user_id) % N_servers

Why sticky:

  • Alice's session state (encryption keys, last received msg_id) lives on her assigned server. Bouncing between servers would require external session storage.
  • The routing lookup (online:{bob_id}) becomes simpler: each user has a deterministic "home" server.

Why consistent hashing specifically: if a server fails or is added, only 1/N users are reassigned (vs all users with simple modulo hashing).

The Routing Registry (Redis)

Even with sticky routing, we need to dynamically know where each user is connected, because:

  • Users disconnect/reconnect (different server if their assigned one is down).
  • Multiple devices: same user can be connected from phone AND web simultaneously.
  • Failover: if Chat Server 5 dies, its 100K users reconnect to other servers temporarily.

The Redis online:{user_id} registry handles this:

// On connect, Chat Server 42 writes: HSET online:{user_id} server_id "chat-server-42" device_id "phone-uuid" connected_at 1705315200 EXPIRE online:{user_id} 60 // Heartbeat every 30 seconds refreshes the TTL: EXPIRE online:{user_id} 60 // On disconnect: DEL online:{user_id} // When delivering a message, Server A queries: HGET online:{recipient_id} server_id → "chat-server-87" → call that server's internal API to push

If Redis returns nil → user offline → write to undelivered queue + send push notification.

Server-to-Server Message Routing

When Server A needs to deliver to Bob on Server B, two options:

  1. Direct gRPC call: Server A calls Server B's internal "deliver_to_user" API. Lowest latency (~1ms within data center). Requires every server to know every other server.
  2. Via Kafka: Server A publishes to Kafka; Server B's consumer picks it up. Decouples servers. Adds ~10ms latency but better resilience.

WhatsApp uses direct gRPC for online users (low latency matters) and Kafka for offline message persistence (durability matters more than latency).

8Deep Dive 2: Message Delivery Pipeline

The 4-State Status Machine

StatusWhen SetUI Indicator
SENTServer received and persisted the messageSingle ✓
DELIVEREDRecipient's device received it (any device)Double ✓✓
READRecipient opened the chat and saw the messageBlue ✓✓
FAILEDCould not deliver after retriesRed ⚠️

Status updates flow back to the sender via the same WS infrastructure, in the opposite direction.

Idempotency and Deduplication

The client generates a client_msg_id (UUID v4) for each message. The server uses this to deduplicate:

  • If the client sends the same message twice (e.g., it didn't receive the ack and retried), the server detects the duplicate via the client_msg_id and returns the original ack.
  • If the recipient receives the same message twice (e.g., due to internal retry), the client deduplicates by client_msg_id and shows it only once.
// Server-side dedup (lightweight, in Redis) key = "msg_seen:" + client_msg_id if SETNX key "" EX 86400: // First time, process the message persist + deliver else: // Duplicate, return the stored response return cached_ack

Ordering Within a Chat

Messages in a chat must appear in the same order on all clients. Achieved via TIMEUUID:

  • The Chat Server generates a TIMEUUID when persisting the message.
  • TIMEUUIDs include a high-resolution timestamp + node ID + counter. They sort lexicographically by time.
  • Cassandra clusters by TIMEUUID DESC, so messages are stored in time order.
  • All clients see the same TIMEUUID per message, so the order is consistent.

Wait — what about cross-server ordering? If Alice (on Server A) and Charlie (on Server C) both send to the same group chat at the "same time", who comes first?

Answer: TIMEUUID resolves it. The server that processes the message first gets the earlier timestamp. Race conditions can produce slight ordering differences (microseconds), but every client sees the SAME order (the order Cassandra stored). Consistent ordering is the guarantee, not strictly send-time ordering.

9Deep Dive 3: Cassandra Schema Design

Why Cassandra, and how does the schema map to access patterns?

Why Cassandra (Not MySQL)

  1. Write throughput: 1.16M writes/sec. MySQL caps at ~10K/sec per node. Cassandra: 50-100K writes/sec per node, scales linearly with nodes. We'd need ~20 Cassandra nodes vs hundreds of sharded MySQL nodes.
  2. Time-series workload: messages are append-only, never updated. LSM-Tree (Cassandra's storage) excels here.
  3. Partition-key access pattern: "give me all messages for chat X" maps perfectly to Cassandra's partition model.
  4. Replication built-in: Cassandra automatically replicates to N nodes (typically 3) for durability. No external setup.

Partition Key Choice

Partition by chat_id means all messages for one chat live on the same node (and its replicas). Trade-offs:

  • Pro: single-partition reads are fast (one node hit, sequential scan).
  • Pro: a chat with 100K messages = a single ~50 MB partition. Comfortable size for Cassandra.
  • Con: if one chat is extraordinarily active (e.g., a global broadcast chat with millions of messages), the partition can grow unbounded → "hot partition" problem.

Avoiding Hot Partitions for Mega-Chats

Solution: composite partition key including a time bucket:

CREATE TABLE messages ( chat_id UUID, time_bucket DATE, -- daily bucket msg_id TIMEUUID, ... PRIMARY KEY ((chat_id, time_bucket), msg_id) );

Each day's messages for a chat are a separate partition. Reads for "today's messages" hit one partition; reads for "this week" hit 7. Bounds partition size.

Time-To-Live (TTL) for Server Storage

Server stores messages only until delivered to all recipients. Once delivered, the row can be deleted. Cassandra TTL handles this:

// On insert, set TTL = 30 days as safety net INSERT INTO messages (...) USING TTL 2592000; // When all recipients have DELIVERED status, explicit delete: DELETE FROM messages WHERE chat_id=? AND msg_id=?;

This keeps server storage minimal. Client devices retain messages indefinitely (their problem, not the server's).

10Deep Dive 4: End-to-End Encryption (Signal Protocol)

WhatsApp uses the Signal Protocol — the same one used by Signal and Facebook Messenger's "Secret Conversations". The server CANNOT read messages, even if compromised.

Key Distribution: X3DH (Extended Triple Diffie-Hellman)

The challenge: Alice wants to send to Bob, but Bob is offline. How does Alice get Bob's keys without involving Bob right now?

Bob's app does this at registration:

  1. Generates an identity key (long-term, never changes).
  2. Generates a signed prekey (medium-term, rotated weekly).
  3. Generates 100 one-time prekeys (single-use).
  4. Uploads all public keys to the WhatsApp server.

When Alice wants to message Bob:

  1. Alice's app downloads Bob's identity_pub + signed_prekey_pub + 1 one-time_prekey_pub from the server.
  2. Alice's app generates an ephemeral key pair.
  3. Alice computes a shared secret using ALL these keys via Diffie-Hellman:
    • DH1 = alice_identity_priv × bob_signed_prekey_pub
    • DH2 = alice_ephemeral_priv × bob_identity_pub
    • DH3 = alice_ephemeral_priv × bob_signed_prekey_pub
    • DH4 = alice_ephemeral_priv × bob_one_time_prekey_pub
    • shared_secret = KDF(DH1 || DH2 || DH3 || DH4)
  4. Alice's first message includes her ephemeral_pub + which one-time_prekey she used. Bob can derive the same shared_secret from his side.

The server only sees:

  • Public keys (useless without private keys).
  • The encrypted message (cannot decrypt).

Forward Secrecy: Double Ratchet

Once Alice and Bob have a shared secret, they don't use it directly. They use it to seed a "Double Ratchet" — a key derivation chain that produces a fresh key for every message.

Forward secrecy: if an attacker steals today's key, they cannot decrypt yesterday's messages. The old keys have been deleted.

Future secrecy: if an attacker steals today's key, they cannot decrypt future messages (Alice and Bob rotate keys via the ratchet).

Each message uses a unique encryption key derived from the ratchet. Even if a single message's key is leaked, only that one message is exposed.

Multi-Device E2EE

If Alice has phone + web + desktop, all 3 devices must be able to decrypt incoming messages. The server cannot help (it can't decrypt!).

Approach 1 (WhatsApp's original): only phone has keys. Web client is a "view" of phone — phone decrypts and sends to web over a separate encrypted channel.

Approach 2 (WhatsApp's newer multi-device): each device has its own key pair. The sender encrypts the same message N times, once for each of the recipient's devices. More bandwidth but each device is independent.

What Bob's Phone Sees

  1. Server pushes {server_msg_id, sender_id, ciphertext, ratchet_metadata}.
  2. Bob's app derives the message-specific key from his ratchet state.
  3. Decrypts the ciphertext.
  4. Stores the plaintext locally.
  5. Sends delivery_receipt back to the server.

11Deep Dive 5: Group Chat Fan-Out

1:1 messages are easy: one recipient, one delivery. Groups multiply the work by N members.

Fan-Out Strategy

When Alice sends to a 100-member group:

  1. The Chat Server receives the message.
  2. Persists it to messages table partitioned by group_id.
  3. Looks up the group's member list (cached in Redis: group:{group_id}:members).
  4. For each of the 99 other members:
    • Look up their location: online:{user_id}.
    • If online: push via internal RPC to their Chat Server.
    • If offline: write to their undelivered table.

For a 100-member group: 99 deliveries × ~5ms each, but parallelized → total ~50ms (parallel batches of 20).

Fan-Out Limits

WhatsApp's group limit (1024 members) was deliberately chosen to bound fan-out cost. Telegram's groups (200K members) require a different design — they use a "channel" model where messages broadcast to read-only subscribers, not full peer-to-peer.

E2EE in Groups (Sender Keys)

The Signal Protocol's pairwise model doesn't scale to large groups — Alice would have to encrypt the message N times. Instead:

  1. Alice generates a sender key for this group.
  2. Alice sends the sender_key (encrypted) once to each member via pairwise Signal sessions.
  3. Subsequent messages: Alice encrypts ONCE with sender_key, sends the same ciphertext to all members. Each member already has the sender_key, so they decrypt.

When membership changes: sender_key rotates (so removed members can't decrypt future messages). Rejoining requires re-establishing.

12Deep Dive 6: Presence and Last-Seen

Online Status

"Online" = currently has an active WebSocket. The Redis online:{user_id} registry already tracks this. Last-seen = the timestamp of when the user was last online.

The 30-Second Heartbeat Pattern

  • Every 30 seconds, the client sends a heartbeat over the WS.
  • Chat Server: EXPIRE online:{user_id} 60 — refreshes TTL.
  • If the client disconnects (TCP RST or just dies), heartbeats stop. After 60 seconds, the Redis key expires automatically.
  • A background job watches for expirations and updates last_seen in PostgreSQL.

"Last Seen" Privacy

Many users hide last-seen from non-contacts. Privacy model:

  • Three settings: Everyone / Contacts Only / Nobody.
  • API: GET /user/{id}/presence respects the target user's privacy setting.
  • If hidden: return null (not "lying" — explicit "not visible").

Typing Indicator

"Bob is typing..." When Bob starts typing, his app sends a typing_event over the WS. The server forwards to Alice's WS. Auto-expires after 5 seconds if no further keystrokes.

Not persisted anywhere — it's an in-flight notification only. Bandwidth is significant (one typing event per keystroke) so typically rate-limited to 1 event per 2 seconds.

13Failure Modes & Recovery

Chat Server Crashes

One server holds 100K WS connections. If it dies:

  • All 100K clients detect disconnection (TCP RST or connection timeout).
  • Clients reconnect with exponential backoff (1s, 2s, 4s, 8s, max 30s).
  • Consistent hashing reassigns them to a different server.
  • Redis routing entries for the failed server's users expire after 60s — new entries are created as clients reconnect.
  • Any messages in-flight (received by the failed server but not yet processed) might be lost. Idempotency at the client (client_msg_id) ensures retries don't cause duplicates.

Redis Routing Registry Down

Without Redis, the server doesn't know where to route messages. Fallback:

  • Treat every message as if the recipient is offline → write to undelivered queue.
  • Recipient gets message on next reconnect (still works, just slightly delayed).
  • Push notification (APNs/FCM) ensures clients reconnect quickly.

Use Redis Sentinel for HA — primary failure promotes replica in <30 seconds.

Cassandra Node Failure

Cassandra has replication factor 3 by default. Single node failure = transparent. Two-node failure = stale reads possible (depends on consistency level).

For chat, we use:

  • Write: CL=QUORUM (need 2 of 3 acknowledgements). Tolerates 1 node down.
  • Read: CL=ONE (any node responds). Fast, slightly stale OK for chat history.

Cross-Region Outage

If a whole data center goes down:

  • DNS failover (Route 53 health checks) sends clients to a different region.
  • Cassandra has cross-DC replication (async). Data is available in the other region within ~1 second.
  • Users may briefly see "connecting..." but resume within 30 seconds.

14Scaling Path

Stage 1: 1M users

Single Chat Server (100K conns is fine for an avg-DAU of 100K). PostgreSQL for everything. Redis for routing. No need for Kafka or Cassandra yet.

Stage 2: 10M users

10-20 Chat Servers. Introduce Cassandra (messages outgrow PostgreSQL). Add Kafka for async event processing.

Stage 3: 100M users

100-500 Chat Servers. Cassandra cluster ~30 nodes. Multi-AZ for HA. Media storage on S3 + CDN.

Stage 4: 2B users (target)

Full architecture. 2000 Chat Servers across multiple regions. Cassandra ~200 nodes globally. Active-active multi-region.

15Cross-Questions and Pushbacks

How exactly is message ordering preserved across distributed servers?
Answer: TIMEUUIDs are assigned by the Chat Server that processes the message. Cassandra clusters by TIMEUUID DESC, so messages are physically stored in time order within a chat's partition. All clients reading the chat see the same order. Cross-server "race conditions" (two servers processing concurrent sends at the same millisecond) are resolved by the TIMEUUID's node ID and counter components — the orderings are deterministic per-server, and Cassandra accepts whichever arrives first. Users in the chat see SOME consistent order, even if it's not strictly real-time send order (the difference is microseconds and invisible to users).
What happens if a Chat Server dies in the middle of processing a message?
Answer: The client's send_message ack hasn't been received → client retries with the same client_msg_id (idempotency key). The retry lands on a different server (consistent hash reassigns). The new server processes it normally. If the original server had partially persisted to Cassandra before crashing, the dedup check (SETNX msg_seen:{client_msg_id}) catches the duplicate. The user sees their message once, not twice.
How do you scale to 2B users with 200M concurrent connections?
Answer: Connection handling is the bottleneck. Each chat server holds ~100K WebSocket connections (limited by RAM ~ 40 KB per conn). For 200M concurrent = ~2000 servers. These are stateless beyond the conn state — adding/removing servers is just a config change in the load balancer + consistent hash ring. The bottlenecks become Redis (for routing) and Cassandra (for messages) — Redis Cluster sharded by user_id range, Cassandra cluster 100+ nodes. Bandwidth: 200M users × 50 msgs/day = 100B msgs/day = 1.16M/sec; multiplied by ~200 bytes = 230 MB/sec total — well within capacity.
How does E2EE work when WhatsApp has billions of users with multiple devices each?
Answer: Each device has its own identity key pair. When Alice (phone + web) sends to Bob (phone + desktop), Alice's phone encrypts the message N times — once for each of Bob's devices' key bundles (fetched from server). Server stores public keys + ciphertexts; it cannot decrypt anything. For Alice's own web client to also see her sent message, she encrypts a copy for her own web's key too. Yes, this means ~4× encryption work and bandwidth for typical multi-device users; but messages are small and CPUs are fast enough that it's invisible to users. For groups, the "sender keys" optimization reduces O(N) encryption to O(1) for steady-state messaging.
Why use WebSocket instead of just doing HTTP long-polling or Server-Sent Events?
Answer: Two reasons: bandwidth and bidirectionality. (1) Bandwidth: HTTP requests carry 500-800 bytes of headers per message. WebSocket frames are 2-6 bytes overhead. At 2B users × 50 msgs/day, that's a 100× bandwidth difference — terabytes saved daily. (2) Bidirectional: messages flow both ways (send AND receive AND receipts AND typing indicators) on a single TCP connection. SSE is unidirectional; we'd need a separate HTTP channel for sending, doubling TCP connections. (3) Latency: long-polling adds 1-2 RTTs per message vs WS's 0 RTTs for already-established connection. The only "downside" is more complex infrastructure (must hold persistent connections), but at this scale the bandwidth/latency win is non-negotiable.
Cassandra is overkill. Why not just shard MySQL?
Answer: Run the numbers. 1.16M writes/sec average, 3.5M/sec at peak. MySQL handles ~10K writes/sec per node optimally. We'd need ~350 MySQL shards minimum, with manual rebalancing on hot shards and complex cross-shard queries when chats span shards. Cassandra handles 100K writes/sec per node natively, so ~30 nodes for the same throughput. Plus: Cassandra's data model maps perfectly to "messages by chat" (partition key = chat_id, clustering = TIMEUUID DESC) — single-partition reads for chat history are O(1). The same query in sharded MySQL requires routing logic, no in-DB sorting at that scale, and complex backup/restore. Cassandra was designed for this exact workload (time-series, write-heavy, partitioned). MySQL is the wrong tool here.
What about message search? E2EE means server can't search.
Answer: Correct — full-text search must happen client-side. The client builds a local search index (SQLite FTS5 on iOS/Android) over decrypted messages as they arrive. Searches run locally. This is exactly how WhatsApp implements search: it's on-device only. A server-side search would require either breaking E2EE or implementing searchable encryption (theoretically possible but adds complexity and weakens security guarantees). The trade-off is privacy over feature richness.
How do you handle media (images, video) at WhatsApp scale?
Answer: Media is never sent over WebSocket. Flow: (1) Sender's app encrypts the file locally with a random AES key. (2) Uploads ciphertext directly to S3 via pre-signed URL. (3) Sends the S3 URL + AES key over E2EE messaging channel. (4) Recipient downloads ciphertext from S3, decrypts with the key from the message. CDN serves popular media (forwarded viral images). Media TTL on S3: 30 days for general media, 365 days for "Status" stories. Encrypted at rest, only sender's & recipient's apps have the AES key.
How do you handle a group with 1024 members where 500 are online — fan-out latency?
Answer: Fan-out happens in parallel batches. Server queries the 500 online members' locations (one Redis MGET = 1ms). Then in batches of 50, delivers via internal RPC (50 parallel gRPC calls = 5ms). Total fan-out: ~50ms for 500 recipients. Offline members (500) are batch-written to the undelivered table (single Cassandra batch insert = 10ms). Total: ~60ms from send to all recipients having either received or queued. Sender sees their own ack within ~20ms. The 60ms is acceptable for group chat — users don't perceive this delay.

End of Problem 3. Next: YouTube / Video Streaming (P4) — media transcoding and CDN at petabyte scale.

Hard Media Transcoding CDN HLS/DASH Adaptive Bitrate

Problem 4: Designing YouTube / Video Streaming Platform

Storing and streaming petabytes of video to billions of viewers worldwide is an exercise in massive-scale data engineering. The interesting technical work isn't in the database — it's in the video processing pipeline, the CDN strategy, and the streaming protocol that makes a 4K video play smoothly on a 3G connection.

1Context and Why This Problem Matters

Video streaming is the largest single user of internet bandwidth. YouTube alone serves 1+ billion hours of video daily. Storing 13 exabytes and serving 57 Gbps continuously is hard. But the engineering depth in this problem is less about scale and more about the pipeline that turns a raw upload into something that can play on any device, any network.

The hard parts:

  • Upload reliability: a 10 GB upload over flaky mobile internet can't fail at 9.9 GB and start over. Resumable uploads required.
  • Transcoding throughput: 5 million uploads per day, each must be transcoded into 5+ quality variants. Need massive parallelism to complete in minutes, not days.
  • Adaptive Bitrate Streaming: the player must seamlessly switch between 360p and 1080p as bandwidth changes — without buffering.
  • CDN economics: the top 5% of videos drive 80% of traffic. Cache them aggressively. Long-tail content can't all live on every edge node.
  • View counting: 5 billion views/day is 57,870/sec. Naive UPDATE to the videos table would melt the database.

Patterns from this problem reappear in: Instagram Reels (P13), Netflix, Twitch (live streaming), TikTok, audio platforms (Spotify, Audible).

2Requirements Gathering

Functional Requirements

  • Upload: creators upload video files (up to ~256GB, up to 12 hours).
  • Transcode: convert uploaded video to multiple quality tiers (240p, 360p, 480p, 720p, 1080p, 4K).
  • Stream: viewers watch videos with adaptive bitrate selection based on network conditions.
  • Search: full-text search over title, description, tags, transcripts.
  • Engagement: views, likes, dislikes, comments, subscribes.
  • Recommendations: "up next" videos, home page suggestions.
  • Channel pages: list of all videos by a creator.

Non-Functional Requirements

  • Scale: 5M uploads/day, 5B views/day → 1000:1 read:write ratio.
  • Latency: video starts playing within 2 seconds of click ("startup latency").
  • Rebuffer rate: <0.5% of playback time spent buffering.
  • Upload availability: 99% — brief upload failures acceptable if user can retry.
  • Streaming availability: 99.99% — streaming downtime is highly visible.
  • Storage: indefinite retention by default. Cost optimisation via tiered storage.

Clarifying Questions to Ask

  • "Is live streaming in scope?" — Live is a different architecture (sub-second latency, real-time transcoding).
  • "Max video length / file size?" — Determines upload pipeline (single PUT vs multipart vs TUS).
  • "Which codecs to support?" — H.264 (universal), VP9 (web-optimised), AV1 (best compression but slow encode). Affects transcoding costs significantly.
  • "DRM / paid content?" — Adds encryption layer + license server.
  • "Captions / transcription?" — Adds ASR (automatic speech recognition) pipeline.
  • "Geographic restrictions?" — Geo-blocking adds complexity to CDN delivery logic.

Traffic and Throughput

Views/sec5B / 100k~50k/s

Concurrent viewers (peak)~5% of DAU watching simultaneously~50M concurrent

Storage

MetricCalculationValue

Raw upload daily5M × 600 MB~3 PB/day
Transcoded variants per video5 quality tiers + thumbnails~5×

Reality check: 27 exabytes over 5 years. This is a real engineering challenge — even at $20/TB/month for S3, that's $500M/month JUST for storage. Tiered storage (S3 → S3 IA → Glacier) for long-tail content reduces this 5-10×.

Bandwidth

MetricCalculationValue
Avg stream bitrateMix of 360p / 720p / 1080p~2 Mbps avg
Streaming bandwidth (peak)50M concurrent × 2 Mbps~100 Tbps
Upload bandwidth (peak)58/s × 600 MB~280 Gbps

Insight: 100 Tbps of streaming bandwidth is impossible from a single origin. CDN absorbs ~95% of this; origin egress is "only" ~5 Tbps.

Transcoding Compute

Transcoding is CPU-heavy. Rough estimates: 1 minute of 1080p video → 30 seconds of CPU on a modern server. To transcode 5 variants of 600 MB videos at 58 uploads/sec, we need significant compute capacity.

🔧 From Numbers to Architecture — what these estimates force

Every tech choice in the HLD below traces back to a number we just computed. Read these bullets as "number → constraint → tech choice".

  • 58 uploads/sec × 600 MB each (~17 GB/s ingress) → app servers cannot proxy this traffic. Resumable multipart upload direct-to-S3 (TUS or S3 presigned URLs); origin servers only see metadata.
  • Transcoding is CPU-heavy (5 variants × 600 MB) → cannot run synchronously on the upload server. Kafka video.uploaded topic → auto-scaled transcoding worker fleet; parallel chunked transcoding per variant.
  • 50k views/sec sustained, 100 Tbps peak streaming bandwidth → impossible from one origin. CDN absorbs ~95–99%; multi-CDN (CloudFront + Akamai + Fastly) for resilience and per-region cost optimisation.
  • 13 EB storage over 5 yr (5 variants × 600 MB × 5M/day × 1825 days) → only blob stores can handle this. S3 with lifecycle policies: hot (Standard) → warm (IA, 30+ days no views) → cold (Glacier IR, 1 yr+ no views) → archive (Deep Archive). ~70% cost reduction vs all-Standard.
  • Adaptive bitrate streaming on mobile + desktop → 5 quality variants (240p, 360p, 720p, 1080p, 4K) pre-rendered. HLS / DASH manifest served from CDN; client picks bitrate based on bandwidth.
  • View counts at 50k/s (peak 250k/s) → MySQL UPDATE view_count = view_count+1 on hot videos = lock contention disaster. Redis INCR for live counter + Kafka stream → ClickHouse for durable analytics; counter flushed to MySQL every ~60 s.
  • Video metadata small (5M × 2 KB = ~10 GB) → fits a single MySQL cluster easily. Sharded by video_id range; replicated for read scaling.
  • Search by title / tags / category → MySQL LIKE doesn't scale. Elasticsearch mirror via CDC from MySQL.
  • DMCA / content moderation on every upload → cannot block the upload path. ContentID fingerprinting (audio + perceptual hash) async after upload; matched videos enter a review queue or are auto-blocked.
  • Recommendation feed at scale → can't compute on-demand. Two-tower neural net + ANN search (FAISS) for candidates; LambdaMART re-rank on top-N; online signals from Kafka watch-events.

4API Design

Initiate Upload

POST /api/v1/uploads Authorization: Bearer {jwt} { "filename": "my_video.mp4", "size_bytes": 642380288, "content_type": "video/mp4" } Response: 200 OK { "upload_id": "uuid", "upload_url": "https://upload.example.com/v1/uploads/{upload_id}", "chunk_size_bytes": 5242880, // 5 MB chunks "expires_at": "2024-01-15T10:00:00Z" }

Upload a Chunk (TUS-like Resumable Protocol)

PATCH /v1/uploads/{upload_id} Upload-Offset: 5242880 // bytes already uploaded Content-Type: application/offset+octet-stream Content-Length: 5242880 [binary chunk data] Response: 204 No Content Upload-Offset: 10485760 // server confirms cumulative offset To resume after disconnect: HEAD /v1/uploads/{upload_id} Response: 200 OK Upload-Offset: 5242880 // server tells client where to resume

Publish Video (after upload complete)

POST /api/v1/videos Authorization: Bearer {jwt} { "upload_id": "uuid", "title": "Tutorial: System Design", "description": "Learn how to design Twitter", "tags": ["systemdesign", "tutorial"], "category": "EDUCATION", "visibility": "PUBLIC" } Response: 201 Created { "video_id": "uuid", "status": "PROCESSING", "estimated_ready_at": "2024-01-15T09:15:00Z" }

Get Stream Manifest

GET /api/v1/videos/{video_id}/manifest Accept: application/dash+xml or application/vnd.apple.mpegurl (for HLS) Response: 200 OK Content-Type: application/vnd.apple.mpegurl #EXTM3U #EXT-X-VERSION:3 #EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=400000,RESOLUTION=640x360 360p/playlist.m3u8 #EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=1500000,RESOLUTION=1280x720 720p/playlist.m3u8 #EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=4500000,RESOLUTION=1920x1080 1080p/playlist.m3u8

Video Details

GET /api/v1/videos/{video_id} Response: 200 OK { "video_id": "uuid", "title": "...", "channel": { "id": "uuid", "name": "Author" }, "duration_sec": 845, "thumbnail_url": "https://cdn.example.com/thumbs/{video_id}.jpg", "metrics": { "view_count": 1234567, "like_count": 45000, "comment_count": 3200 }, "manifest_url": "https://cdn.example.com/manifests/{video_id}.m3u8", "created_at": "..." }

5Data Model

videos (PostgreSQL with sharding by video_id range)

CREATE TABLE videos ( video_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, channel_id UUID NOT NULL, title VARCHAR(200), description TEXT, category VARCHAR(50), status VARCHAR(20), -- PROCESSING | READY | FAILED | TAKEN_DOWN visibility VARCHAR(20), -- PUBLIC | UNLISTED | PRIVATE duration_sec INT, upload_size BIGINT, thumbnail_url TEXT, manifest_url TEXT, -- CDN URL of master m3u8 view_count BIGINT DEFAULT 0, -- denormalised, eventually consistent like_count BIGINT DEFAULT 0, created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW(), published_at TIMESTAMPTZ ); CREATE INDEX idx_channel ON videos(channel_id, published_at DESC); CREATE INDEX idx_status ON videos(status) WHERE status='PROCESSING';

video_variants (PostgreSQL)

CREATE TABLE video_variants ( video_id UUID, quality VARCHAR(10), -- 240p | 360p | 720p | 1080p | 4k codec VARCHAR(20), -- h264 | vp9 | av1 bitrate_kbps INT, s3_path TEXT, -- path to .m3u8 of this variant file_size BIGINT, PRIMARY KEY (video_id, quality, codec) );

upload_chunks (Redis, ephemeral)

Tracks which chunks of a multipart upload have arrived:

Key: upload:{upload_id} Type: Hash Fields: status, total_size, received_bytes, last_chunk_at TTL: 24 hours (abandoned uploads auto-expire)

views (Cassandra) and aggregated counts

Individual view events are stored in Cassandra for analytics. Aggregated counts live in Redis (with periodic flush to PostgreSQL).

// Cassandra (raw events) CREATE TABLE views ( video_id UUID, ts TIMEUUID, user_id UUID, country VARCHAR(2), duration_watched_sec INT, PRIMARY KEY (video_id, ts) ); // Redis (aggregated, hot path) Key: video:{video_id}:views Value: counter (INCR on each view) Key: video:{video_id}:viewers Value: HyperLogLog (PFADD for unique users)

7Deep Dive 1: Resumable Upload Pipeline

Uploading 10 GB over a flaky mobile connection: a single TCP socket may break dozens of times. We need a protocol that can resume.

The TUS Protocol (Resumable Upload)

  1. Client requests an upload session: POST /uploads with total size → server returns upload_id and chunk_size (e.g., 5 MB).
  2. Client splits the file into chunks. For each chunk, PATCH /uploads/{upload_id} with Upload-Offset header indicating where this chunk starts.
  3. Server validates Upload-Offset matches its expectation, streams the bytes to S3 (multipart upload), returns the new offset.
  4. If a chunk fails: client retries the same chunk. Server is idempotent on chunk-level (same offset, same content).
  5. If the entire connection drops: client does HEAD /uploads/{upload_id} on reconnect to find where to resume.
  6. When the last chunk is received and Upload-Offset == total_size, server marks the upload complete.

Why S3 Multipart Under the Hood

The Upload Service doesn't store chunks itself — it forwards each chunk to S3 as an UploadPart in a multipart upload:

  • S3 Multipart Upload allows up to 10,000 parts (5 MB to 5 GB each).
  • Each part is uploaded independently and acknowledged separately.
  • After all parts uploaded, a CompleteMultipartUpload call assembles them into a single S3 object.
  • S3 handles durability, parallel uploads, and most edge cases.

Direct-to-S3 Uploads (Optimization)

To avoid bandwidth costs at the Upload Service, generate pre-signed S3 URLs and let the client upload chunks directly to S3:

  • Server generates a pre-signed PUT URL for each chunk.
  • Client uploads chunks directly to S3 using those URLs.
  • Server only orchestrates (creates the multipart upload, assigns part numbers, completes the upload).
  • Saves egress costs and reduces Upload Service compute footprint.

What Happens on Successful Upload

  1. Upload Service confirms all chunks received → calls S3 CompleteMultipartUpload.
  2. Stores upload record in PostgreSQL with status=UPLOADED.
  3. Publishes "video.uploaded" event to Kafka with S3 path and upload metadata.
  4. Returns 200 to client (now they can publish/edit metadata).

8Deep Dive 2: Parallel Transcoding

Transcoding a 10-minute 4K video into 5 quality variants might take 30 minutes on a single CPU. At 5M uploads/day, that's 2.5M CPU-hours daily. Need massive parallelism.

The Chunk-Level Parallelism Trick

Don't transcode the whole video on one machine. Split it into 10-second chunks, transcode each chunk on a different machine in parallel:

Raw 10-min video (uploaded to S3) │ ▼ Splitter Worker (ffmpeg -ss / -t, no re-encoding) │ ┌──────────┼──────────┐ │ │ │ ... 60 chunks of 10s each ▼ ▼ ▼ chunk_0.ts chunk_1.ts ... chunk_59.ts (in S3) (in S3) (in S3) │ │ │ // 60 messages published to Kafka "transcode-chunks" │ │ │ ▼ ▼ ▼ Worker 1 Worker 2 ... Worker 60 (transcodes (transcodes (transcodes chunk 0 to chunk 1 to chunk 59 to 5 qualities)5 qualities) 5 qualities) │ │ │ │ │ │ each writes 5 quality variants ▼ ▼ ▼ S3: chunk_N_360p.ts S3: chunk_N_720p.ts ... │ ▼ Assembler Worker Concatenates chunks per quality: chunk_0_360p.ts + chunk_1_360p.ts + ... = 360p.ts chunk_0_720p.ts + ... = 720p.ts Generates HLS manifests (.m3u8 files) │ ▼ Marks video as READY in PostgreSQL Publishes to "video.published" Kafka topic

Throughput Calculation

  • Each chunk is 10 seconds of video → ~5 seconds of CPU on a modern server (×5 qualities × 30% efficiency = ~7.5 seconds total).
  • 60 workers in parallel finish a 10-minute video in ~10 seconds (limited by slowest chunk).
  • End-to-end: 1-2 minutes from upload complete to publishable video.

Why This Works for HLS/DASH

Both HLS and DASH are designed around video chunks (called "segments" in the spec). The manifest is just a list of segment URLs. So transcoding chunks independently and stitching their URLs into a manifest is natively supported by the streaming format.

Quality Tiers (Bitrate Ladder)

QualityResolutionTarget BitrateCodec
240p426×240400 KbpsH.264
360p640×360800 KbpsH.264
480p854×4801.5 MbpsH.264
720p1280×7202.5 MbpsH.264 + VP9
1080p1920×10805 MbpsH.264 + VP9 + AV1
1440p2560×14409 MbpsVP9 + AV1
2160p (4K)3840×216018 MbpsVP9 + AV1

Why multiple codecs? Browser/device compatibility:

  • H.264: universal, decoded in hardware on every device. Largest files.
  • VP9: ~30% better compression, supported on Chrome, Firefox, Edge.
  • AV1: ~50% better than H.264 but slow to encode and limited hardware support. Used for high-quality variants where bandwidth savings outweigh encode cost.

9Deep Dive 3: Adaptive Bitrate Streaming (HLS / DASH)

The video player picks a quality based on current network bandwidth, switching seamlessly mid-playback as conditions change.

HLS Manifest Structure

// master.m3u8 — top-level manifest with quality variants #EXTM3U #EXT-X-VERSION:3 #EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=400000,RESOLUTION=640x360,CODECS="avc1.42c00d" 360p/playlist.m3u8 #EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=1500000,RESOLUTION=1280x720,CODECS="avc1.4d401f" 720p/playlist.m3u8 #EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=4500000,RESOLUTION=1920x1080,CODECS="avc1.640028" 1080p/playlist.m3u8 // 720p/playlist.m3u8 — list of segments for the 720p variant #EXTM3U #EXT-X-TARGETDURATION:10 #EXTINF:10.0, segment_0.ts #EXTINF:10.0, segment_1.ts #EXTINF:10.0, segment_2.ts ... #EXT-X-ENDLIST

How the Player Selects Quality

  1. Player downloads master.m3u8.
  2. Picks the highest bitrate variant that fits the current bandwidth (e.g., 720p at 2.5 Mbps if connection is 3 Mbps).
  3. Downloads the variant's playlist + first segment.
  4. Plays the segment. Measures how long the download took.
  5. If download was faster than playback (good bandwidth): consider upgrading to higher quality.
  6. If download was slower than playback (buffering risk): downgrade quality.
  7. Maintains a buffer of 30+ seconds ahead of playback position.

Why 10-Second Segments?

  • Shorter (e.g., 2s): faster quality switching, but more HTTP requests overhead, more files to manage.
  • Longer (e.g., 60s): fewer files, but slower quality switching, choppy when bandwidth drops mid-segment.
  • 10 seconds: industry-standard balance. Quality decisions can happen 6× per minute.

HLS vs DASH

HLSDASH (MPEG-DASH)
OwnerApple (proprietary, now spec)ISO standard
Container.ts segments.m4s segments
Manifest.m3u8 (text).mpd (XML)
iOS supportNativeLimited (needs player library)
Android/WebVia player libraryNative (Shaka Player)

Most platforms generate BOTH for maximum compatibility — same segments, two manifest formats.

10Deep Dive 4: CDN Strategy — Hot vs Long-Tail Content

The CDN serves 95%+ of streaming bandwidth. But you can't cache everything at every edge node — that's exabytes of data per location.

The Pareto Distribution of Views

Empirical observation: ~5% of videos drive ~80% of views. The rest is long-tail content watched rarely.

Strategy:

  • Hot content: pre-warm at all CDN edge locations. Cache for days.
  • Warm content: pull-through caching — first viewer in a region pulls from origin, populates regional cache. Cache for hours.
  • Cold content: pull from origin every time. Acceptable because cold content has few viewers.

How to Classify Content

An ML model predicts whether a new video will go viral, based on:

  • Channel size and historical view distribution.
  • Topic / category (some categories trend faster).
  • Time of day / day of week.
  • Real-time engagement signals (view velocity in the first hour).

High predicted-virality videos are pre-warmed across CDN before they go viral.

Geographic Pre-Warming

A video popular in India should be pre-warmed at Mumbai/Singapore edges, not necessarily at North American edges. Region-aware caching:

  • Track view distribution by country.
  • Auto-promote to "hot" status only in regions exceeding a threshold.
  • Cold regions pull on-demand.

Storage Tiering (Origin)

TierUse CaseCostRetrieval Time
S3 StandardRecently uploaded, hot$23/TB/moMilliseconds
S3 Standard-IA30+ days old, occasional$12/TB/moMilliseconds
S3 Glacier IR90+ days old, rare$4/TB/moMilliseconds
S3 Glacier DeepYears old, archive$1/TB/mo12-48 hours

Auto-tiering rules: videos with no views in 30 days → IA. No views in 90 days → Glacier IR. The savings on long-tail content are massive.

11Deep Dive 5: View Counting at Scale

57,870 views/second. Naive UPDATE statements would melt the DB. Here's the pipeline.

The Write-Back Pattern

  1. Player sends a "view" event after the user has watched ≥30 seconds (filters spam/preview clicks).
  2. Event published to Kafka "view-events" topic.
  3. Consumer aggregates: INCR video:{video_id}:views in Redis.
  4. Every 60 seconds, a batch flusher reads counter deltas from Redis and UPDATEs PostgreSQL.

Redis takes the 57K writes/sec hit (trivial for Redis). PostgreSQL gets ~1 update per video per minute — easily handled.

Unique Viewer Counts

"5M unique viewers" is more valuable than "12M total views". Counting unique users naively requires storing every viewer's ID = expensive.

HyperLogLog solves this:

PFADD video:{video_id}:uniq_viewers {user_id} PFCOUNT video:{video_id}:uniq_viewers // returns estimated count
  • Uses ~12 KB of memory regardless of how many users.
  • ±0.8% accuracy at scale.
  • For "billions of unique viewers" estimates, this is the standard tool.

Spam Filtering

"Views" must be real. Filters:

  • Min watch time (≥30 seconds).
  • Rate limit per IP (no 1000 views/min from one IP).
  • Drop bot-detected user agents.
  • De-dupe per user_id per video per day (the same user watching multiple times doesn't 10× the count beyond a threshold).

12Deep Dive 6: Recommendation Pipeline

The home page "for you" feed is YouTube's most engaging feature. High-level architecture:

  1. Candidate generation: produce a candidate pool of ~500 videos that might interest this user. Two-tower neural network embeds users and videos into a shared space; ANN (approximate nearest neighbor) search retrieves close matches.
  2. Ranking: a heavier model scores each candidate for predicted watch time. Returns top 20.
  3. Re-ranking: apply diversity rules (don't show 5 videos from the same channel), freshness boosts, business logic (subscribed channels get a boost).

Compute is heavy. Cached per-user for 5-15 minutes. Refreshes in background.

13Failure Modes & Recovery

Upload Service Crash Mid-Upload

Client receives a connection error → retries after exponential backoff. The TUS HEAD request tells client where to resume. S3 multipart uploads survive — chunks already in S3 remain.

Transcoding Worker Failure

Kafka doesn't commit the offset until the worker confirms successful transcoding. If a worker crashes, the message is redelivered to another worker. Idempotent: each chunk has a deterministic output path; re-transcoding produces the same output. Result: at-least-once delivery, with idempotent processing = exactly-once outcome.

CDN Edge Failure

Multiple CDN providers (CloudFront + Akamai + Fastly). DNS routes to a different provider on failure. Origin serves directly in worst case (with latency penalty).

Origin S3 Region Outage

S3 has 99.99% SLA per region. Cross-region replication ensures another region has a copy. CDN failover to alternate origin.

14Scaling Path

  • Stage 1 (1M views/day): single transcoding server, one CDN, single-region S3.
  • Stage 2 (100M views/day): auto-scaling transcoding fleet, regional CDN, multi-region S3 replication.
  • Stage 3 (5B views/day, target): full pipeline as described. Hundreds of transcoding workers. Global CDN with predictive pre-warming. Tiered S3 storage.
  • Stage 4 (live streaming): separate real-time transcoding pipeline (sub-second latency, WebRTC for ultra-low latency, HLS-LL for moderate latency).

15Cross-Questions and Pushbacks

How does ABR decide which quality to switch to in real-time?
Answer: The player uses a "buffer-based" algorithm. Goal: maintain a buffer of ~30 seconds of playback ahead. If buffer is shrinking (downloads slower than playback), downgrade quality. If buffer is full and stable (downloads faster than playback), try upgrading. Algorithms like BOLA (Buffer Occupancy-based Lyapunov Algorithm) make optimal decisions. Quality switches happen on segment boundaries (every 10s), so they're seamless to the viewer. Modern players also predict short-term bandwidth using rolling averages of recent segment download speeds.
Why split video into chunks for transcoding instead of using a fast GPU?
Answer: GPUs are faster per-video but limited supply. Chunk-based parallelism uses cheap commodity CPUs distributed across thousands of machines, achieving the same throughput at lower cost. A 4K 1-hour video transcoded with 360 parallel CPU workers (10s chunks) finishes in seconds, comparable to GPU performance, at 1/10th the per-frame cost. Also: chunks fit Kafka's message model and HLS/DASH's segment model natively. GPUs are still used for AV1 encoding (CPU-prohibitive at scale).
How does the CDN decide what to cache where?
Answer: Multi-tier: (1) Tier-1 pre-warming: ML predicts which videos will trend; those are pushed to all regional edges before traffic arrives. (2) Tier-2 pull-through: when a viewer in Mumbai requests a video, Mumbai edge fetches from origin, caches it, serves to subsequent viewers. (3) Tier-3 popularity decay: cached content's TTL is extended when accessed, expired when not. Long-tail content fetched on-demand. CDN providers (CloudFront, Akamai) implement these strategies internally; we just need to set good Cache-Control headers and provide trending signals via API.
How do you handle a single video going viral — 10M views in 1 hour?
Answer: The CDN handles it. Once cached at edge nodes, each edge can serve thousands of viewers concurrently. 10M views/hour = 2,800/sec spread globally = ~50/sec per edge node = trivial. The bottleneck would be view-count writes, not bandwidth. Redis INCR handles 100K/sec easily. PostgreSQL writes are batched every 60s. Recommendation engine notices the velocity and amplifies the video on the home page, which is the desired feedback loop.
Aren't 5 transcoding variants per video wasteful? Why not just stream the original?
Answer: Streaming the original would mean a 4K source uploaded as 8 Mbps would force every viewer to download 8 Mbps. Most viewers (especially mobile) don't have that bandwidth. They'd see endless buffering. By transcoding to multiple tiers, viewers on a 1 Mbps connection get 360p smoothly. Bandwidth waste vs storage cost: serving 100M users at 5 Mbps when 4 Mbps would suffice would cost orders of magnitude more in CDN bandwidth. The 5× storage cost saves 50× bandwidth cost. Also: device support — old TVs can't decode 4K, but they can decode 720p. ABR is fundamentally about meeting users where they are.
Storing 27 exabytes over 5 years sounds infeasible. How do you actually do this?
Answer: The actual figure for hot storage is far lower. Tiered storage: ~5% of content in S3 Standard ($23/TB), ~15% in IA ($12/TB), ~30% in Glacier IR ($4/TB), ~50% in Glacier Deep Archive ($1/TB). Effective avg cost: ~$5/TB/month for "all storage". 27 EB × $5/TB = $135M/month, not $500M. Still significant but feasible at YouTube's revenue. Additional savings: video deduplication (the same upload from different users stored once), compression improvements over time (AV1 reduces storage 50%), and aggressive deletion of low-engagement private uploads.
How do you handle DMCA / copyright takedowns at scale?
Answer: ContentID system. On upload: extract audio + video fingerprints (Shazam-like for audio, perceptual hash for video keyframes). Compare against a database of copyrighted content fingerprints. Match → automated action: block in jurisdictions where rights holder requests it, monetize (revenue shared with rights holder), or track (analytics only). For 90%+ of cases, no human review needed. Formal DMCA takedown requests trigger immediate removal followed by counter-notice process. Removed videos: status=TAKEN_DOWN, manifest URL returns 410 Gone.

Real-time geo-indexing, supply/demand matching, multi-party trip state, and surge pricing — all of it has to happen in under five seconds on a flaky mobile network.

1Context and Why This Problem Matters

Uber is a load-bearing interview problem because it forces you to combine five disciplines that look separate on a whiteboard but interact violently in production:

  • Geo-indexing — finding the nearest five drivers out of a million across a city, every few seconds.
  • Real-time bidirectional communication — drivers ping their location every 4 s; riders need live updates of their car.
  • Distributed state machine — every trip moves through ~10 states; both rider and driver must always agree on the current state.
  • Two-sided matching — riders compete for scarce drivers, drivers compete for fares. The system has to break ties fairly and quickly.
  • Money + people — the trip ends with payment and a rating. Mistakes here aren't just bugs, they're refunds and PR.

The cliché "use a queue" doesn't work here — match latency is the product. If matching takes 30 s instead of 3 s, drivers go to Lyft. The whole architecture is structured around keeping the hot path (request → match → first push to driver) under ~500 ms.

2Requirements Gathering

Functional

  • Rider opens app → app shows nearby drivers (visual only, no commitment) → rider requests a ride from origin to destination → system finds best driver.
  • Driver accepts within ~15 s, otherwise the request rolls to the next driver.
  • Both parties see each other's real-time location until the trip ends.
  • Rider can cancel; driver can cancel (with penalty after threshold).
  • Trip ends → payment auto-charged → both parties rate each other.
  • Pricing: base fare + per-km + per-minute, scaled by a per-zone surge multiplier when demand outstrips supply.

Non-functional

  • Match latency: P99 < 5 s.
  • Location accuracy: ~10 m (GPS-bounded).
  • Location update lag rider-sees-driver: P99 < 4 s.
  • Global multi-region with regional sticky routing (an Indian rider should match against Indian drivers, served from Indian data centres).
  • Availability: 99.95% (downtime measured in hundreds of dollars per second of revenue).
  • Survive AZ failure with no rider impact; survive region failure with degraded service.

Explicitly out of scope

  • Routing / map rendering (we'd buy from a maps provider — Mapbox, Google, or OSRM).
  • Fraud detection deep dive (mentioned as a service, not designed).
  • Driver onboarding and document verification.

3Capacity Estimation

We'll size for a "real Uber" scale: ~100M total users globally, ~5M DAU riders, ~3M total drivers, ~1M concurrent online drivers at peak, ~18M trips/day.

MetricDerivationNumber
Driver location pings/sec (avg)1M online × 1 ping / 4 s250 k/s
Driver location pings/sec (peak)2× rush hour multiplier500 k/s
Ride requests/day18M trips/day18 M
Ride requests/sec (avg)18M / 100k~180/s
Ride requests/sec (peak, 10×)Friday 6 pm + Saturday 11 pm~2,000/s
Trip metadata storage/day18M × 2 KB36 GB/day
Trip storage / 7 yrs (with 3× repl)36 GB × 365 × 7 × 3~275 TB
Location ping bandwidth (peak)500k/s × 60 B~30 MB/s
WebSocket concurrent conns1M drivers + 1M riders in-app~2 M
WS terminator fleet2M / 100k per node~20 nodes
🔑 From Numbers to Architecture
  • 500 k/s peak location pings → Postgres can't take this. Pings go to a sharded in-memory geo-grid (Redis GEO or self-managed S2/H3 cell store) — never durably persisted.
  • 2 k/s peak ride requests + needing ACID for trip lifecycle → sharded Postgres for trips (per-region shards for locality + data residency).
  • ~5 s P99 match SLA → matching service reads geo-grid in memory only (no DB on the hot path); driver accept timeout dominates the budget.
  • 2 M concurrent WebSocket connections (drivers + riders) → dedicated WS gateway fleet (~20 nodes, each holding ~100k connections), sharded by user_id.
  • Per-city localisation → service mesh routes trips by region; cross-region calls only for analytics, never on the hot path.
  • Audit / billing trail → trip events streamed to Kafka, archived to S3 + warehouse (offline analytics, not on the hot path).

4API Design

Rider Flow (HTTP REST)

POST /v1/rides Authorization: Bearer {rider_jwt} { "origin": { "lat": 37.7749, "lng": -122.4194 }, "destination": { "lat": 37.7849, "lng": -122.4094 }, "vehicle_type":"UBER_X", "payment_method_id": "pm_abc123" } Response: 201 Created { "ride_id": "uuid", "state": "MATCHING", "fare_estimate": { "min_cents": 1200, "max_cents": 1500, "currency": "USD" }, "surge_multiplier": 1.2, "expires_at": "2026-05-16T16:25:30Z" // request invalidates after 60 s }
GET /v1/rides/{ride_id} Response: 200 OK { "ride_id": "uuid", "state": "EN_ROUTE_TO_RIDER", // see state machine below "driver": { "id": "...", "name": "...", "vehicle": "Toyota Camry · ABC 123", "rating": 4.9, "location": { "lat": ..., "lng": ... } }, "eta_sec": 240, "fare_so_far_cents": 0 }
POST /v1/rides/{ride_id}/cancel { "reason": "RIDER_NO_LONGER_NEEDED" } Response: 200 OK { "state": "CANCELLED", "cancellation_fee_cents": 0 } // cancellation_fee > 0 if driver was already EN_ROUTE for >2 min

Driver Flow (HTTP REST + WebSocket)

POST /v1/drivers/availability { "status": "ONLINE" | "OFFLINE", "vehicle_id": "uuid" } // ONLINE → driver becomes matchable
POST /v1/rides/{ride_id}/accept // Driver received offer, has ~15 s to accept Response: 200 OK { "state": "EN_ROUTE_TO_RIDER", "rider": { ... } }
POST /v1/rides/{ride_id}/arrive // driver at pickup POST /v1/rides/{ride_id}/start // rider boarded, trip begins POST /v1/rides/{ride_id}/complete // dropped off, final fare computed

Real-Time Location Channel (WebSocket)

WS /v1/location → Server expects per-frame: { "type": "PING", "lat": ..., "lng": ..., "heading": 87, "speed_kmh": 32, "ts": 1747396523123 } // Driver sends every 4 s (every 2 s during a trip). // Server validates ts (no future / no >30 s past), upserts in Redis GEO. ← Server pushes: { "type": "RIDE_OFFER", "ride_id": "...", "pickup": {...}, "expires_in_s": 15 } { "type": "RIDER_LOC", "ride_id": "...", "lat": ..., "lng": ... } { "type": "STATE_CHANGE", "ride_id": "...", "state": "EN_ROUTE_TO_RIDER" }

5Data Model

trips (PostgreSQL, sharded by trip_id hash)

CREATE TABLE trips ( trip_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, rider_id UUID NOT NULL, driver_id UUID, -- NULL until matched state VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL, -- see state machine origin_lat DOUBLE PRECISION NOT NULL, origin_lng DOUBLE PRECISION NOT NULL, dest_lat DOUBLE PRECISION NOT NULL, dest_lng DOUBLE PRECISION NOT NULL, vehicle_type VARCHAR(20), requested_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL, matched_at TIMESTAMPTZ, started_at TIMESTAMPTZ, ended_at TIMESTAMPTZ, fare_cents INT, surge_mult NUMERIC(3,2), -- 1.00 / 1.50 / 2.50 distance_m INT, duration_s INT, cancel_reason VARCHAR(50), payment_id UUID, rider_rating SMALLINT, -- 1..5 driver_rating SMALLINT ); CREATE INDEX idx_trips_rider ON trips(rider_id, requested_at DESC); CREATE INDEX idx_trips_driver ON trips(driver_id, requested_at DESC); CREATE INDEX idx_trips_active ON trips(state) WHERE state IN ('MATCHING','EN_ROUTE_TO_RIDER','IN_TRIP');

driver_state (Redis Hash + GEO, ephemeral)

This is the hot path. Every driver's current location is in Redis, never Postgres:

// Redis Hash per driver (driver-level metadata) HSET driver:{driver_id} status "ONLINE" // ONLINE | OFFLINE | OFFERED | ON_TRIP vehicle "UBER_X" last_ping "1747396523" current_ride "" or "uuid" // Redis GEO index per city / shard GEOADD drivers:sf:available -122.4194 37.7749 "driver:abc" // Only drivers with status=ONLINE are present here. // When a driver gets OFFERED a ride → ZREM removes them so they can't be double-matched. // TTL: driver_state expires after 60 s of no ping → auto-cleanup of dead sessions.

ride_offers (Redis Sorted Set, ephemeral)

When matching service offers a ride to a driver, an entry lives here to track timeouts:

ZADD ride_offers:{driver_id} {expires_at_unix} {ride_id} // Scanner sweeps expired offers and re-matches.

surge_zones (Redis, refreshed every 60 s)

// Per H3 cell (resolution 7 ≈ 5 km²), latest demand/supply ratio HSET surge:zone:{h3_index} demand_5min 42 // ride requests in the last 5 minutes supply_5min 18 // online drivers in the cell multiplier 1.5 // computed
