7Deep Dive 1: Geo-Indexing — H3 vs Geohash vs S2

The single most important data structure in this system is the index that answers "give me the K nearest drivers to (lat, lng)." Three serious options exist.

Geohash

Encodes (lat, lng) into a Base32 string. Prefix length controls precision: 7 chars ≈ 150 m × 150 m cell. Easy and supported by Redis natively (GEOADD).

⚠ The Geohash Edge-Case Problem

Rectangular cells with non-uniform area near the poles. Worse: two points 10 m apart can sit in different cells whose prefixes diverge in the first character — a naive "match prefix" query misses them. Production geohash queries always need to check the cell and its 8 neighbours.

S2 (Google)

Projects the Earth onto a cube, recursively subdivides each face into cells via a Hilbert curve. Cell IDs are 64-bit integers and spatially close points have spatially close IDs. Used by Google Maps, Pokémon Go, Foursquare.

H3 (Uber)

Hexagonal grid with 16 resolutions. Hexagons have uniform neighbour distances (a square cell has different distances to side-neighbours vs corner-neighbours; hexagons don't). Uber built and open-sourced H3 specifically for this problem.

ResolutionEdge lengthAreaUse case
5~9 km~250 km²City
7~1.2 km~5 km²Surge zones
9~175 m~100 k m²Driver matching
11~25 m~2 k m²Pickup precision

How matching uses H3

Store each driver in a Redis Set keyed by the H3 cell at resolution 9. To find K nearest drivers to a rider:

  1. Compute rider's H3 cell.
  2. SUNION the cell + its 6 hexagonal neighbours (= ~7 sets).
  3. If union size < K, expand to the next ring (k-ring 2, ~19 cells).
  4. Compute precise distance for each candidate using the haversine formula; sort; return top K.
🔑 Why this beats Redis GEO directly

Redis's native GEOSEARCH works fine for <100k entries in a key, but degrades for millions. Hex-cell bucketing partitions the space into ~1M independent small sets per city, each of which fits in cache and scans in microseconds.

8Deep Dive 2: The Location Ping Pipeline

500k pings per second is the system's highest write rate. Hitting Postgres with this would melt it. The pipeline is built for fire-and-forget speed.

Driver app │ WS frame every 4 s (every 2 s during a trip) ▼ WS Terminator │ // stateless: validate JWT, parse, drop if >30 s stale ▼ Kafka topic: location.ping (1024 partitions, hashed by driver_id) │ ├─▶ Redis GEO writer (consumer group A) │ // GEOADD into city shard at H3-cell key │ // throughput ~50k upserts/s/node, easy │ ├─▶ Real-time push fanout (consumer group B) │ // if driver has an active trip, push driver loc to rider WS │ └─▶ S3 cold archive (consumer group C) // keep for analytics, fraud, post-trip replay (7 days hot, 90 d cold)

Why Kafka in front of Redis

  • Back-pressure — if Redis is briefly slow, pings queue up; they don't get dropped silently.
  • Replay — analytics and fraud teams need historical pings; reading from Kafka or S3 is cheap; reading from Redis is impossible (no history).
  • Multi-consumer fanout — three different consumer groups eat the same stream for different purposes without burdening Redis.

Skipping Kafka for very hot paths

For drivers currently in a trip, latency from driver to rider must be sub-2-second. Going driver → WS → Kafka → consumer → WS adds ~200–400 ms. So we run a shortcut: while a trip is active, the WS terminator pushes the ping directly to the rider's WS connection (via in-memory pub/sub like Redis Pub/Sub) and emits to Kafka in parallel. Riders see the car move smoothly; Kafka remains the durable audit log.

9Deep Dive 3: Matching Algorithm

A naive "give me the closest driver" approach fails for several reasons. Production matching has to consider:

  1. ETA, not distance — 200 m on a freeway is 30 s; 200 m through a market is 5 min.
  2. Vehicle type — only UberX cars match an UberX request.
  3. Rating — riders with a 4.9 rating preferred by drivers; drivers with <4.7 deprioritised.
  4. Driver acceptance rate — drivers who reject often pushed back in queue.
  5. Cool-down — driver just finished a trip, give them 30 s to breathe.
  6. Reposition incentives — driver heading toward a high-demand zone gets preference for trips into that zone.

The pipeline

function findDriver(request): candidates = H3_nearby_drivers(request.origin, k=20) // 20 closest by cell-ring candidates = filter(c => c.vehicle_type == request.vehicle_type) candidates = filter(c => c.status == 'ONLINE') // exclude OFFERED, ON_TRIP for c in candidates: c.eta_sec = compute_eta(c.location, request.origin) // map-provider call c.score = composite_score( eta: c.eta_sec, rating: c.rating, accept_rate: c.accept_rate, cool_down: c.seconds_since_last_trip ) candidates = sort_by(score asc) offer(candidates[0], timeout=15s) if rejected/timeout: offer(candidates[1]) ... up to top-5 sequentially, then top-5 in parallel as "any-takes-it"

The score formula is tuned offline using historical data. In an interview, just outline the inputs — they don't expect a derivation.

Preventing the same driver from being offered two rides

This is the classic concurrency trap. Solution: when matching service makes an offer, it does SREM drivers:available {driver_id} (atomic), preventing another match thread from seeing this driver. On accept → stays out, transitions to ON_TRIP. On reject / timeout → SADD back to available.

Why offer to one driver at a time (mostly)

If you broadcast a request to 5 drivers and 3 accept, you have to anger 2 of them. Sequential offers preserve trust. The exception: peak surge time where waiting 15s × 5 attempts = 75s — too long; the system switches to "first-to-tap-accept" parallel mode and refunds drivers who lose the race with a small bonus.

10Deep Dive 4: Trip State Machine and Invariants

REQUESTED │ rider posts /rides ▼ MATCHING ──────── 60s no driver ───▶ CANCELLED_NO_DRIVER │ driver offered + accepted ▼ EN_ROUTE_TO_RIDER │ driver hits "arrived" ▼ ARRIVED │ rider taps "I'm here" or auto on geo-fence ▼ IN_TRIP │ driver hits "complete" ▼ COMPLETED │ payment captured ▼ PAID │ ▼ RATED (rider rates driver, driver rates rider) Anytime before IN_TRIP: rider cancel → CANCELLED_BY_RIDER (fee if >2 min) driver cancel → CANCELLED_BY_DRIVER (penalty to driver) Anytime during IN_TRIP: SOS button → EMERGENCY (alerts ops, keeps trip live)

Invariants enforced by the DB

  • At any time, a driver is in at most one non-terminal trip (UNIQUE (driver_id) WHERE state IN active states).
  • State transitions are linear (no skipping ARRIVED → COMPLETED). Enforced by a CHECK constraint in a trigger.
  • matched_at <= started_at <= ended_at (CHECK constraint).

Writing transitions atomically

Every state transition is one transaction: read current state with SELECT … FOR UPDATE, validate the transition is legal, write new state, emit Kafka event in the same transaction (use Outbox pattern). This avoids the classic bug where two state-change events arrive out of order and the trip "regresses."

11Deep Dive 5: Surge Pricing

When demand exceeds supply in a zone, prices rise to (a) ration scarce supply to highest-willingness-to-pay riders and (b) attract drivers from adjacent zones.

Computation

Every 60 s, per H3 cell at resolution 7 (~5 km²):

demand_5min = COUNT of ride requests in last 5 min in this cell supply_5min = COUNT of ONLINE drivers currently in this cell unfulfilled = demand_5min − matched_in_same_window ratio = unfulfilled / max(supply_5min, 1) multiplier = 1.0 if ratio < 0.2 1.2 if ratio < 0.5 1.5 if ratio < 1.0 2.0 if ratio < 2.0 2.5 if ratio >= 2.0 (capped)

Stored in Redis with TTL 90 s (so a stale multiplier auto-expires). Surfaced to rider apps via push. When a rider commits to a fare estimate, the multiplier in effect at commit time is the one used, regardless of how it moves during the trip.

Avoiding "surge whack-a-mole"

If surge in Zone A spikes, drivers stream in from Zone B → Zone B's surge spikes → drivers leave A → A surge spikes again. Solution: smooth the multiplier with exponential moving average (α=0.3), and use a 60 s cool-down on multiplier downgrades.

12Deep Dive 6: ETA Computation

Three precision tiers, all needed:

Use caseApproachLatency
"How long to nearest 5 drivers?" (matching)Haversine distance × city-avg speed<1 ms
"How long for my driver to arrive?" (rider sees in app)Map provider routing API, cached 60 s per (origin, dest, time-of-day) bucket~50 ms uncached
"How long is my whole trip?" (fare estimate)Full routing, traffic-aware, with confidence interval~100 ms

The cheap tier (haversine) is used inside the matching loop because we don't have time to call the map provider for 20 candidates per request. The expensive tiers run only once a match is made.

13Failure Modes & Recovery

FailureBlast radiusMitigation
Redis GEO cluster down for a cityNo matches possible in that cityMulti-AZ Redis with failover; degraded mode falls back to Postgres geo-table (slow but functional) for a few minutes.
WS terminator crashes50–100k drivers disconnectDrivers auto-reconnect with exponential backoff. Sticky session via JWT, not connection identity, so any terminator can take over.
Match service overloadedRequests queue; latency spikesShed load by zone — surge auto-rises in busy zones, throttling demand naturally. Auto-scale on QPS.
Trip stuck in MATCHING for 60 sRider waitingAuto-cancel → refund any hold → suggest larger search radius / different vehicle type.
Driver app crashes mid-tripRider sees no location updatesLast-known location shown with "connection lost" badge. If >90 s with no ping during a trip, ops notified and rider gets safety call option.
Postgres primary failsNo new state transitions, no new tripsStandby promoted within 30 s (Patroni). Existing trips continue from cache; new requests briefly fail. Total impact < 1 min.
Map provider outage (Mapbox / Google)No ETAs, no routesCached ETAs for 5 min; degrade to haversine estimates with a warning in the UI. Most users tolerate this briefly.

14Scaling Path

StageArchitecture
1k DAU (single city MVP)Monolith. Postgres + one Redis. Polling for location (HTTP every 5 s).
100k DAUSplit into Ride Service + Location Service. Move to WebSocket for driver pings. Redis GEO for matching.
1M DAU (national)Per-region Postgres (e.g. East, West). Kafka introduced for location pings. Surge service.
10M DAU (multi-country)Per-city Redis cluster. H3 cell-based sharding. Multi-region active-active for the driver-state plane.
100M DAU (global)Trip data sharded by trip_id hash. Cold trip archive in S3 + Glacier. Streaming analytics on Kafka → Flink → ClickHouse.
🔑 What does NOT scale by adding boxes

The matching service's mental load (knowing where every driver is in this city) is fundamentally a per-city problem. You can't shard "the driver pool of San Francisco" across two regions without ugly cross-region calls. The geographic boundary is the natural shard key.

15Cross-Questions and Pushbacks

"Why H3 instead of just using Redis's built-in GEOSEARCH?"
Answer: Redis GEOSEARCH is fine up to ~100k entries per key, but it scans linearly over the whole sorted set per query. At 1M drivers per city × 200 ride requests/s, that's 200M location-comparisons per second on a single key — Redis becomes the bottleneck. H3 cell-based bucketing partitions the space: each cell is a small Redis Set with hundreds of drivers, not millions. K-nearest queries scan 7–19 cells = thousands of candidates, not millions. Same correctness, 1000× cheaper. Secondary benefit: hexagonal neighbours have uniform distance (squares don't), which makes k-ring expansion deterministic.
"500k location pings/second to Redis — won't that throttle it?"
Answer: A single Redis node handles ~100k ops/s; we shard the GEO index by city (a city is ~10–50k online drivers, well within a node). Across ~50 cities globally, 500k pings/s spreads to ~10k/s per node — 10% utilisation. Reads (GEOSEARCH-equivalent k-ring on H3 cells) are even cheaper. If a single city outgrows a node, we split further by H3 resolution-5 cells (sub-city shards). The architecture scales by city count, not by total system load.
"What if two riders request a ride to the same driver at the same instant?"
Answer: The match service removes the offered driver from the available pool atomically before sending the offer: SREM drivers:available {driver_id}. Redis SREM is atomic, so exactly one of the two match attempts succeeds. The other thread sees the driver missing from the SUNION result and picks the next-best candidate. This pattern is essentially SELECT FOR UPDATE in Redis-shape, and it prevents the double-booking race entirely without a distributed lock manager.
How do you handle a driver whose phone has 30 s of dead GPS but they're actively driving a passenger?
Last known location is held in Redis with the timestamp. If ts_now - last_ping > 30 s during an active trip, the rider's UI shows a "connection lost" badge and the car icon stops moving (rather than teleporting). Driver app retries with exponential back-off up to 5 min before declaring offline. If still offline at trip end, the trip is auto-completed using the driver's last-known location and flagged for ops review. Crucially, we never extrapolate location — showing the car at the wrong place is worse than showing it not moving.
How do you compute fares when GPS drifts and the recorded distance is wrong?
Two independent signals: (a) odometer-style sum of haversine distances between pings, (b) map-routing distance between start/end with traffic-aware path inference. We charge the smaller of the two to avoid penalising the rider for GPS jitter. Significant discrepancies (>20%) flag the trip for manual review. Time-based fare is unaffected (timestamps are reliable). The actual fare = base + per-km×distance + per-min×duration, scaled by surge_mult at request time.
"Why not just push every ride request to all nearby drivers and let them race to accept?"
Answer: Three problems. (1) Driver experience: 5 drivers accept, 4 are told "too late" — repeated rejection sours them and they go to a competitor. (2) Rider experience: if the closest driver is 200 m away but a 1 km driver taps faster, the rider waits 5 min instead of 1 min. (3) Latency variance: drivers with worse network connections never win races — systematically excluded from earnings. Uber actually tried this in early years and reverted. The sequential offer pattern with 15 s timeout balances fairness and speed; we only switch to parallel-offer in extreme surge when every second matters more than rider-optimal pickup.
How does the rider's app show real-time driver location with low latency across continents?
During an active trip we don't go through Kafka. Driver pings hit the WS terminator, which writes to Redis and also pushes directly to the rider's WS connection via in-memory pub/sub (Redis Pub/Sub or NATS) keyed by the active ride_id. Both rider and driver WS connections are pinned to the same regional cluster for the trip's lifetime. So the data path is: driver phone → WS node A → Redis pub/sub → WS node B → rider phone — typically ~200 ms regional, never cross-region.
How do you prevent surge multiplier from being gamed (a driver going offline to inflate surge, then accepting)?
Three defences. (1) The supply count uses online OR currently completing a trip in this zone, not just "online right now" — going offline doesn't reduce the count instantly. (2) Surge multiplier is smoothed with EMA(α=0.3) over a 5-min window, so a single driver flipping offline barely moves the number. (3) Fraud detection flags drivers whose acceptance rate drops sharply during high-surge periods; repeat offenders are deactivated. The math alone defeats single-driver gaming; coordinated gaming requires the fraud system.
When a driver finishes a trip at the airport (a high-demand zone), how does the system decide their next match?
After completion, the driver enters a 30 s cool-down (no offers) and the app shows the current heat-map. The driver is added back to drivers:available with their final drop-off location. Because the airport's H3 cell typically has high demand and they're already in it, they usually get offered a new trip within seconds. For airport queues specifically, many cities use FIFO queuing: drivers join an electronic queue on arrival and are matched in order — implemented as a per-airport Redis Sorted Set scored by arrival timestamp.
"Postgres for trips at 18M/day — that's 200 writes/s average, 2000 peak. Won't it crumble?"
Answer: Quantify first. 2000 writes/s × ~6 state transitions per trip = ~12k row-writes/s. Postgres handles 5–10k writes/s comfortably on a single node, with batching and connection pooling closer to 20k. We're at 60% utilisation on a single primary — well within bounds. If we need more headroom: shard by trip_id hash across 4 instances (3k writes/s each, trivial). Sharding is also natural geographically — North American trips on a US shard, European on EU. We do not move to Cassandra because (a) we need ACID across the trip + driver_state + payment_intent atomicity, (b) we need SELECT FOR UPDATE for state transitions, (c) trips form a row of structured fields with a finite state machine — relational is the right model.

Problem 6: Designing a Distributed Rate Limiter

The most common follow-up to "design API gateway" — and a problem where the wrong algorithm choice can silently let traffic through or hammer legitimate users with 429s.

1Context and Why This Problem Matters

Every API at scale needs a rate limiter — to defend against abuse, isolate noisy neighbours, enforce paid tiers, and protect downstream services. The interview is rarely "design a rate limiter" in isolation; it's usually "you've designed Twitter, now show me how login is rate-limited" or "here's your API gateway, walk me through the limit pipeline." The reason it's a great interview problem:

  • Five well-known algorithms with non-obvious trade-offs — picking the right one is the whole point.
  • Forces you to think about where the state lives: locally per-node, in Redis, in a shared store?
  • Concurrency: many requests hit the same counter at the same time → you must reason about atomicity.
  • Fail-open vs fail-closed: a senior engineer always has a position on this.

2Requirements Gathering

Functional

  • Allow at most N requests per identity per window.
  • Identity is configurable: user ID, API key, IP, tenant, endpoint+user.
  • Return 429 Too Many Requests when exceeded, with Retry-After header.
  • Support tiered limits (free: 100 req/min, paid: 10k req/min, enterprise: custom).
  • Support multi-tier composition: "free user can do 100/min AND globally 10M/min across all free users."
  • Limits configurable at runtime without redeploying the gateway.

Non-functional

  • Add <5 ms P99 to every request (this runs on the hot path of every API call).
  • Handle 1M+ QPS across the API gateway fleet.
  • Accuracy: aim for "approximately correct" — being off by a few requests at the boundary is acceptable; letting through 10× the limit is not.
  • Fail-open by default — if the limiter is down, allow the request and alert. Outage of the limiter must not outage the API.
  • Multi-region: each region enforces its own limits with eventually-consistent global aggregation.

Out of scope

  • WAF / DDoS protection (different layer, usually CloudFlare/AWS Shield in front).
  • Per-request cost weighting (we'll touch this lightly in cross-questions).

3Capacity Estimation

Assume the API gateway sees 1M QPS sustained, 5M QPS peak. Every request hits the rate limiter exactly once.

MetricNumber
Rate-limit checks/sec (peak)5M/s
State per identity (token bucket)~50 B (tokens + last_refill_ts)
Active identities (users + IPs + keys)~100M
Total state size~5 GB — fits one Redis node
Redis cluster, 6 nodes (5M ops/s ÷ 1M/node)6
Per-request latency budget<5 ms P99
Network round-trip to Redis (intra-AZ)~0.5 ms
🔑 From Numbers to Architecture
  • 5 M check ops/sec at < 5 ms budget → in-memory store with constant-time decisions; Redis Cluster (6 nodes × 1 M ops/s/node) sized for QPS, not RAM.
  • Read-modify-write must be atomic (else races overshoot the limit) → Redis Lua script bundles "fetch counter + decide + write" into one round-trip; ~1 ms.
  • Multiple limits per request (per-user + per-IP + per-tenant) at 5 ms total → all three checked in one Lua call (or partly via local in-memory bucket cached by gateway).
  • 100 M+ identities → key-space sharded across Redis cluster by hash(identity); virtual nodes for graceful resharding.
  • Redis outage / partition → fail-open (allow traffic) for user-facing APIs to preserve UX; fail-closed for billing-grade endpoints. Decision is per-policy.
  • Limits change without restart → config service pushes JSON limits to gateways via streaming; no Redis schema changes.

4The Five Algorithms — A Trade-Off Tour

Almost every system design rate-limiter question is really asking: "Do you know these five and the trade-offs?"

1. Fixed Window Counter

Increment a counter keyed by "{user}:{minute_bucket}". If counter > N, reject.

  • Pros: Trivially simple. One INCR per request. Constant memory.
  • Cons: Edge bursting — a user can fire N requests at 11:59:59 and another N at 12:00:00, achieving 2N in two seconds. Catastrophic for tight limits.

2. Sliding Window Log

Store every request's timestamp in a list (e.g., Redis Sorted Set). On each request, evict entries older than window, count, accept-or-reject.

  • Pros: Mathematically exact — no edge bursting.
  • Cons: Memory cost = O(N) per identity. For N=10,000 and 1M users → 10 GB just for logs. Per-request cost includes ZREMRANGEBYSCORE + ZCARD.

3. Sliding Window Counter (Approximate)

Keep two fixed-window counters: current and previous. Compute weighted sum:

count_in_window = current_count + previous_count × (1 − (time_into_current_window / window))
  • Pros: Constant memory (2 counters). No edge bursting.
  • Cons: Approximation — assumes previous-window requests were uniform.
  • This is what most production systems use. Cloudflare published the same approach.

4. Token Bucket

Each identity has a bucket of capacity B; tokens refill at rate R/sec. Each request consumes 1 token. Empty bucket → reject.

  • Pros: Allows controlled bursting (up to bucket capacity). Smooth long-run rate. Natural model for "rate" and "burst" separately.
  • Cons: Slightly more state (last_refill_ts + tokens). Refill calculation on each request.
  • The default choice for user-facing APIs.

5. Leaky Bucket

FIFO queue with fixed leak rate. Requests join the queue; if queue is full, reject.

  • Pros: Output rate is perfectly constant — good for protecting fragile downstreams.
  • Cons: Adds latency (queueing). Doesn't permit bursting at all. Less popular than token bucket for API limiting; common for outbound traffic shaping.
🔑 Pick One Sentence to Memorise

"For user-facing APIs I pick token bucket — it allows controlled bursts (better UX) and has constant memory per identity. For protecting fragile downstreams (like a payment processor that crashes above X RPS) I pick leaky bucket — guaranteed output rate. For tight precision without storing full logs I pick sliding window counter — Cloudflare's choice and a good default for global limits."

5API Design

The decision API (internal, called by every gateway)

POST /v1/check Content-Type: application/json { "identity": "user:abc123", // user, ip, key, tenant "action": "POST:/v1/tweets", // optional endpoint scoping "cost": 1 // some calls are heavier (1=default) } Response (200 always — never 4xx on the check itself): { "allowed": true, "limit": 100, "remaining": 47, "reset_at": 1747397200, // unix seconds when window resets "retry_after_s": 0 // 0 if allowed; >0 if rejected }

In practice this isn't a separate microservice — it's a library call from the gateway into a co-located Redis cluster. The "API" exists for testing and for systems that prefer a service boundary.

Headers the gateway sets on every response

X-RateLimit-Limit: 100 X-RateLimit-Remaining: 47 X-RateLimit-Reset: 1747397200 // On 429 only: Retry-After: 32

6Data Model

Token bucket state (Redis Hash)

Key: rl:tb:{identity} // e.g. rl:tb:user:abc123 Type: Hash Fields: tokens → 47.3 (float; fractional tokens during refill) last_refill_ts → 1747397123.456 (unix seconds with millis) TTL: max(window × 2, 1 hour) // auto-cleanup of dormant identities

Limit configuration (PostgreSQL, cached in-memory)

CREATE TABLE rate_limit_rules ( rule_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, scope VARCHAR(20), -- USER | IP | TENANT | GLOBAL identity VARCHAR(255), -- user_id, ip, tenant_id; '*' for tier-default tier VARCHAR(20), -- FREE | PRO | ENTERPRISE endpoint VARCHAR(255), -- '*' for any algorithm VARCHAR(20), -- TOKEN_BUCKET | SLIDING_WINDOW | LEAKY capacity INT, -- bucket size / window N refill_rate NUMERIC(10,4), -- tokens per second (only for TB) window_sec INT, -- only for SW enabled BOOLEAN DEFAULT TRUE, updated_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW() ); CREATE INDEX idx_rl_scope ON rate_limit_rules(scope, identity, endpoint);

Rules are pulled into every gateway node every 30 s into a local LRU cache. Per-request lookup is O(1) in process memory; no DB hit.

7High-Level Architecture

Client request │ ▼ ┌────────────────────────────┐ │ API Gateway │ ← horizontally scaled │ ┌────────────────────────┐ │ │ │ Rate Limiter Middleware │ │ │ │ ┌────────────────────┐│ │ │ │ │ 1. Load rule (cache)│ │ │ │ │ 2. Lua to Redis ││ │ │ │ │ 3. Decide allow/429││ │ │ │ └────────────────────┘│ │ │ └────────────────────────┘ │ └──────────┬─────────────────┘ │ allowed ▼ Upstream service ┌──────────────────────────────┐ │ Redis Cluster (sharded) │ ← state for ~100M identities │ - keys hashed by identity │ │ - Lua scripts for atomicity│ └──────────────────────────────┘ ┌──────────────────────────────┐ │ Config DB (Postgres) │ ← rule definitions │ refresh into gateways every 30s └──────────────────────────────┘ ┌──────────────────────────────┐ │ Metrics + Audit (Prom) │ ← every 429 emitted │ Alerting on 429 spikes │ └──────────────────────────────┘

8Deep Dive 1: Atomic Token Bucket in Redis (with Lua)

A naïve implementation reads tokens, computes the refill, writes back — three round trips and a race condition. The right implementation is one round trip, atomic, using a Lua script.

Why naïve is broken

# Pseudocode — DO NOT USE state = redis.HGETALL("rl:tb:user:abc") tokens = state.tokens + (now - state.last_refill_ts) * refill_rate tokens = min(tokens, capacity) if tokens >= cost: tokens -= cost redis.HSET("rl:tb:user:abc", tokens=tokens, last_refill_ts=now) return ALLOWED else: return REJECTED

Race: two requests read the same state simultaneously, both compute "allowed", both write — bucket only decremented once. User effectively gets 2× their limit at peak load.

The atomic Lua script

-- KEYS[1]: rl:tb:{identity} -- ARGV[1]: capacity, ARGV[2]: refill_rate, ARGV[3]: cost, ARGV[4]: now_ms local key = KEYS[1] local capacity = tonumber(ARGV[1]) local rate = tonumber(ARGV[2]) local cost = tonumber(ARGV[3]) local now_ms = tonumber(ARGV[4]) local state = redis.call('HMGET', key, 'tokens', 'last_refill_ms') local tokens = tonumber(state[1]) or capacity local last_ms = tonumber(state[2]) or now_ms local elapsed_s = (now_ms - last_ms) / 1000 tokens = math.min(capacity, tokens + elapsed_s * rate) local allowed = 0 if tokens >= cost then tokens = tokens - cost allowed = 1 end redis.call('HMSET', key, 'tokens', tokens, 'last_refill_ms', now_ms) redis.call('PEXPIRE', key, 3600000) -- 1 hr TTL local retry_after_s = 0 if allowed == 0 then retry_after_s = math.ceil((cost - tokens) / rate) end return { allowed, math.floor(tokens), retry_after_s }

Redis executes Lua scripts atomically — no other command runs in between. One round trip, no race. Cost is ~50 μs of Redis CPU + ~0.5 ms network.

📐 Use EVALSHA

Load the script once with SCRIPT LOAD, then call EVALSHA with just the hash + args. Saves ~200 bytes of network per request × millions of requests = significant bandwidth.

9Deep Dive 2: True Distributed Counters at Scale

A single Redis cluster can handle ~1M ops/s per node. With sharding by identity hash, we can scale to many millions/s. But two patterns get trickier:

Problem: Global limit across the whole fleet

"All Free-tier users combined cannot exceed 10M req/min." Every API gateway must agree on this global count. Hammering a single Redis key with 5M ops/s = hot-key disaster.

Solution: Sharded counter with periodic aggregation

N shards (e.g. 100). Each gateway picks a shard by node_id: shard = hash(node_id) % 100 key = "rl:global:free:{minute}:shard:{shard}" On request: INCR that single shard's key (just 1 ops to one Redis node). Every 1 second: a separate aggregator process reads all 100 shards, sums them, and writes the total to "rl:global:free:{minute}:total". Each gateway every 1s reads the total and uses it for "global cap" decisions. The local decision can be 1 second stale → fine for soft caps.

Trade-off: global cap enforcement is now ~1 s stale, so a brief overshoot is possible (millions of extra requests in the second after the cap is hit). For soft business limits this is fine. For hard limits (e.g. anti-DDoS), use a smaller stale window or a stricter algorithm at the edge.

Problem: Hot key — one user is being attacked

A single user_id receiving 100k req/s would saturate one Redis shard. Two defences:

  • Hash bucketing: a single hot identity is split into rl:tb:user:abc#shard_{0..9} automatically when traffic exceeds threshold. Lua script picks a random shard on write; reads sum all shards (10 GET pipeline). Trade: slightly lossy because each shard is independent, but at scale it averages out.
  • Local-first defence: when a hot identity is detected (per-node counter exceeds local threshold), each gateway node reject locally for the next 1 s without talking to Redis at all. This is the only way to handle "1 user firing 1M req/s" — the network capacity to even ping Redis exceeds the request budget.

10Deep Dive 3: Multi-Tier Limits

A real request has to satisfy several limits simultaneously:

  1. Per-user (user's tier quota)
  2. Per-tenant (organisation's umbrella quota)
  3. Per-IP (anti-abuse)
  4. Per-endpoint (write endpoints are limited more tightly than reads)
  5. Global (free-tier cap, anti-DDoS aggregate)

Five limits × one Redis call each = 5 ms of network latency = unacceptable.

Solution: Pipeline or merge into one Lua

Redis pipelining batches all 5 commands into one round trip (~1.2 ms total, not 5 × 1 ms). Even better: a single Lua script that takes all 5 keys + their parameters and returns 5 decisions atomically. One round trip total.

The composition rule

If any limit rejects, return 429 with the smallest retry_after of the rejections. If all allow, only then decrement all 5 (atomic in Lua). Never decrement first then check — that's broken when limit 3 rejects after 1 and 2 were already consumed.

⚠ Common Bug

Decrementing before all-allow check leaks tokens. Always do: check-all → if all-pass, then decrement-all in the same Lua block.

11Deep Dive 4: Dynamic Config — Changing Limits Without Restart

Sometimes during an incident you need to drop a customer's limit from 10k to 100 RPS instantly. The architecture supports this without redeploying:

  1. Operator updates the rule via admin API: PATCH /v1/rules/{rule_id} with new capacity.
  2. Postgres row updated; a Kafka event is emitted on config.rate_limit.updated.
  3. Every API gateway subscribes to this topic; on receipt, it invalidates its local rule cache for that identity.
  4. Next request from that identity re-loads the rule from Postgres (or from a config-cache service); the new limit takes effect.
  5. Total propagation time: ~200 ms across a fleet.

For broader sweeps (e.g. "tighten ALL free-tier limits"), the operator updates the FREE tier default rule and all FREE identities pick up the change on their next 30 s cache refresh.

12Failure Modes & Recovery

FailureBlast radiusMitigation
Redis cluster downNo rate limiting at allFail-open: gateway allows requests, alerts operators, falls back to per-node local limits as a coarse backup. Better to risk overload than to deny all customers.
Redis split-brain after partitionTwo halves have divergent stateUse Redis Sentinel / Cluster with quorum-based leader election. On reconcile, last-write-wins is acceptable for rate-limit state.
Lua script bug crashes RedisLimiter goes downTest scripts under load before deploy. Use canary deploy: 1% of traffic on new script for 10 min before full roll-out.
Hot identity floods one shardThat shard saturatesHash-bucket the hot identity into N sub-keys; local-first rejection at the gateway.
Config DB unreachableCan't load new rulesGateway uses its last-known cached rules indefinitely. New customers added during the outage default to the FREE tier.
Clock skew between gatewaysSlightly wrong refill calculationsNTP everywhere. Use Redis's clock (TIME command) as the source of truth inside Lua scripts, not the gateway's clock.
🔑 Fail-Open vs Fail-Closed

For customer-facing APIs: fail-open. A broken limiter taking down the whole API is worse than briefly allowing too many requests.
For protecting downstream from collapse (e.g. a payment processor): fail-closed. Better to reject than to topple the downstream.
For anti-abuse / fraud: fail-closed. The whole point is to block bad actors; if the limiter is down, bad actors get through.

13Scaling Path

StageArchitecture
10k QPSIn-process token bucket per node. No external state.
100k QPSOne Redis node, Lua-based token bucket. Local cache of rules.
1M QPSRedis Cluster with 4–6 shards, hashed by identity. Pipelined multi-tier checks.
10M QPSPer-region Redis Cluster. Global aggregations via the sharded-counter pattern. Hot-key auto-detection.
100M QPSEdge rate-limiting (CloudFlare/Akamai workers) handles the coarse layer; backend handles fine-grained per-user. Hierarchical limits — coarse rejection saves Redis bandwidth.

14Cross-Questions and Pushbacks

"Just use Nginx's built-in limit_req module — why build anything?"
Answer: Nginx limit_req is per-node, not distributed. With 50 Nginx nodes in front of the API and limit_req=100/min per IP, a single attacker spreading their traffic across nodes effectively gets 50×100 = 5000/min. For meaningful protection you need shared state. limit_req is fine as a coarse first defence at the edge, but real per-user limits need a shared store.
"Redis is single-threaded — won't 5M ops/s overload one core?"
Answer: A single Redis node handles 100k–1M ops/s on one core depending on command complexity. At 5M ops/s we shard across 6+ nodes (~830k each, well within bounds). Identity is the natural shard key — keys are hashed and distributed automatically by Redis Cluster. The hot-key problem (one identity overwhelming one shard) is solved separately via local-first rejection and key-hash-bucketing as described above.
"Sliding-window log is the only mathematically correct algorithm — why approximate with sliding-window counter?"
Answer: Sliding-window log requires storing every request timestamp per identity. For 100M active identities × average 100 stored requests = 10B entries = ~80 GB just for state. That's a Redis cluster on its own. Sliding-window counter uses 2 numbers per identity — total ~10 GB — with error bounded by <1% under typical traffic distributions. Cloudflare published their analysis: the approximation lets through at most 0.003% more than the limit in realistic traffic. For typical use cases, that's a great trade.
How do you handle requests that have variable cost — a search query vs a simple GET?
Each request has a cost parameter (default 1). The Lua script consumes cost tokens instead of 1. Cost is configured per endpoint: simple GETs are 1, full-text searches are 10, heavy report generations are 100. This lets a single bucket represent "compute load" rather than "request count" — far more meaningful for protecting backends. The user-facing API documents the cost weights so customers can plan.
What happens when a customer pays for an upgrade — how fast does their new limit kick in?
Payment service publishes customer.upgraded event → config service updates the user's tier in Postgres → emits config.rate_limit.updated on Kafka → every gateway invalidates the cached rule for that user. Next request loads the fresh rule. Total propagation: ~200 ms. The user's existing token bucket state is not reset — they keep their current tokens. The new (larger) capacity just means future refills can accumulate more.
"Latency budget is 5 ms but a Redis call is 1 ms. Multi-tier needs 3 calls = 3 ms = 60% of budget. What if we add more tiers?"
Answer: Two options. (1) Merge all tiers into a single Lua script that takes all the keys+params and returns a single allow/reject decision atomically — one round trip regardless of tier count. (2) Move the most-coarse limits (per-IP, global) to in-process counters synced from Redis every 1s; these are inherently fuzzy but cheap. The fine-grained per-user limit hits Redis; the coarse ones don't. Combining both keeps the per-request budget at ~1.5 ms for any number of tiers.
How do you give 429 responses a useful Retry-After header?
The Lua script computes it during rejection: retry_after = ceil((cost - current_tokens) / refill_rate). This is the number of seconds until enough tokens accumulate for one more request. The gateway returns it in the Retry-After header (HTTP standard, RFC 7231). Well-behaved clients respect it; bad clients that retry immediately at least don't make things worse because they keep getting rejected. SDKs we publish include automatic backoff using this header.
How do you rate-limit unauthenticated requests (no user_id)?
Fall back to IP-based limits, with stricter caps. The IP key is rl:tb:ip:{ip} with maybe 60 req/min default. For dual-stack v4/v6, hash IPv6 to its /64 prefix (since a single end-user typically owns a full /64). For shared NATs (corporate networks), legitimate users sometimes get caught — we expose an unauthenticated POST /v1/captcha endpoint that, on completion, grants a short-lived signed token with a higher limit. The token is also rate-limited by IP to prevent unlimited captcha-farming.
How do you observe and tune limits without breaking customers?
Two pillars. (1) Shadow mode: when introducing a new limit, run it in "evaluate but don't enforce" mode for 1–2 weeks. Log "would have rejected" decisions with full context. Tune capacity based on actual data. (2) Per-customer 429 dashboards: alert on any single customer hitting >5% 429s — usually means their integration has a bug or the limit is wrong for their use case. Account team reaches out before they file a complaint.
"Tokens are floats — won't floating-point drift cause inconsistencies?"
Answer: Excellent catch. Two safeguards. (1) The bucket is clamped on every write: tokens = min(capacity, tokens + refill) — it can't drift above capacity. (2) The refill is computed from now - last_refill_ms in milliseconds (integer arithmetic) multiplied by rate; only the final result is float. For most use cases, ε-level drift on the unused-token count is invisible to users. If absolute precision matters (e.g. paid API quotas billed by token), use integers and an explicit "millitoken" scale (capacity = 100,000 millitokens = 100 tokens with 3 decimal places of precision). I'd default to floats and only switch if a customer complaint reveals the drift.

Crawl ~50 billion documents, index them so any query returns ten results in 200 ms, and rank by relevance — at a scale where every component you'd reach for off-the-shelf melts.

1Context and Why This Problem Matters

"Design Google" is the apex system-design question. It looks impossible — Google's been built by tens of thousands of engineers over 25 years. The trick is that the interviewer doesn't expect you to reproduce Google; they expect you to:

  • Decompose the problem into three independent subsystems: crawl, index, query.
  • Explain the canonical data structure (inverted index) and its scaling story.
  • Reason about ranking signals and admit you'd combine handcrafted with neural.
  • Push back gracefully when they say "design the whole thing" — scope down to "I'll cover the architecture and one deep-dive into ranking; we can pick another deep-dive next if we have time."

2Requirements Gathering

Functional

  • Continuously crawl the web — discover new pages, refresh existing ones.
  • Index pages for keyword search; support phrase queries ("system design") and basic operators (-word, site:).
  • Return top-10 ranked results in <200 ms.
  • Freshness: news-style pages indexed within minutes; long-tail pages within days.
  • Personalisation (user history, location) — keep this out of v1; mention in scaling.

Non-functional

  • Index ~50 billion documents (≈ visible Web).
  • P99 query latency < 200 ms.
  • ~100k queries/second globally.
  • Availability 99.99% — search outages make headlines.
  • Multi-region serving for global latency.

Explicitly out of scope

  • Ad serving (separate system entirely; just expose hooks).
  • Image / video search (huge separate verticals).
  • Knowledge Graph / direct answers (boxes above the ten blue links).

🔑 From Numbers to Architecture
  • ~500 TB inverted index → 500 shards × ~1 TB each (practical Lucene shard size); shards partitioned by term-hash for even load.
  • ~300 k peak QPS with each shard doing ~1 k QPS → 10× replication of each shard → ~5 000 index servers.
  • Every query fans out to all 500 shards in parallel → scatter-gather; aggregator picks top-10 from each shard's top-10. Tail-latency dominates → hedged requests + tight RPC budgets.
  • ~10 B queries/day → most query strings recur; CDN / edge cache + Redis cache absorb 50%+ before reaching the index.
  • Crawl + index build offline (separate pipeline) → query path never blocks on indexing; Kafka decouples crawler from index builder.
  • Ranking is a separate concern (ML model + signals) layered on top of retrieval — kept out of the hot index for separability.

4API Design

Public search API

GET /search?q=system+design+interview&page=0&hl=en Authorization: optional (anon search supported) Response: 200 OK { "query": "system design interview", "results_total": 184000, "took_ms": 132, "results": [ { "url": "https://example.com/sd-guide", "title": "System Design Interview Guide", "snippet": "...A comprehensive guide covering URL shorteners, ...", "displayed_url": "example.com › sd-guide", "cached_url": "/cached?id=abc" }, ... 9 more ], "did_you_mean": null, "related": ["system design fundamentals", "...questions"] }

5Data Model

The crawl frontier (priority queue across cluster)

// Stored in distributed KV (e.g. Bigtable / RocksDB) // Key: hash of URL → row url : full URL host : example.com last_crawl : timestamp next_crawl : timestamp // scheduled by adaptive policy priority : 0..100 // higher → crawl sooner fetch_status: OK | 404 | 5xx | timeout robots_allowed: bool content_hash : sha1(body) // for dedup links_out : [url, url, ...] // for graph computation

The page store (raw + parsed content)

// Bigtable-like, sharded by hash(url) url : key raw_html_zst : compressed body extracted_text : plain text title, meta : ... fetched_at : ... http_headers : ... parsed_lang : "en" content_type : "text/html" seo_signals : { canonical: ..., schema_org: ..., open_graph: ... }

The inverted index (the heart of search)

// Posting list per term term: "system" postings: [ { doc_id: 12, tf: 5, positions: [3, 47, 102, ...] }, { doc_id: 17, tf: 2, positions: [18, 220] }, ... ] total_docs: 4,200,000,000 idf: log(N / total_docs) // Stored on disk as compressed sequential block per term. // Doc IDs delta-encoded + variable-byte; positions delta + variable-byte. // Compression ratio ~5–10× on natural-language text.

Per-document features (for ranking)

// One row per doc, joined at ranking time doc_id : 64-bit url : ... title : ... length_tokens : 1840 pagerank : 0.0021 // precomputed periodically language : "en" spam_score : 0.01 last_modified : ... clickthrough_history: { query_hash: ctr, ... } // from logs

[Shard 500] ← each returns its top-10 │ gather ▼ Aggregator (merge, re-rank with ML) │ ▼ Snippet generator (fetch & highlight from page store) │ ▼ Response cache (Redis, keyed by query+location) for 60 s │ ▼ User

7Deep Dive 1: The Distributed Crawler

Crawling sounds simple ("fetch URL, store HTML") and is in reality the hardest of the three subsystems. The challenges are politeness, freshness, dedup, and infinite traps.

The frontier queue

A distributed priority queue keyed by URL hash. Workers pop URLs in priority order. Each URL is also constrained by host-level rate limiting: at most 1 fetch per second per host (configurable in robots.txt's Crawl-delay). This is enforced by a per-host token bucket co-located with the worker; workers don't take URLs from a host whose bucket is empty.

Politeness

  • Respect robots.txt — cache for 24 h per host.
  • User-Agent identifies as the crawler with contact info.
  • Back off aggressively on 429 / 503 — exponential back-off, up to 24 h per host.
  • Skip hosts that have repeatedly served errors (poison-list).

Freshness — adaptive recrawl

Not all pages change at the same rate. The crawler learns:

  • News sites: recrawl every 5–10 min.
  • Wikipedia: every few hours.
  • Static reference docs: every 30 days.
  • Pages that haven't changed in months → recrawl every 90 days, lower priority.

Mechanism: store last_modified and content_hash per page; track the rate of change. The next-crawl time is a function of historical change rate.

Dedup

Two layers:

  • URL-level dedup: canonicalise URLs (remove tracking params, normalise trailing slash, lower-case host). Two URLs with the same canonical form → store as one.
  • Content-level dedup: SHA-1 of the extracted text. If a different URL has the same hash, mark as duplicate and pick the canonical one (highest PageRank, oldest first-seen).
  • Near-duplicate dedup: SimHash with a 64-bit fingerprint and Hamming distance ≤3 considered "near-dup." Useful for boilerplate-heavy template pages.

Spider traps

Some sites generate infinite URLs (calendar pages with "next month" forever, faceted-search permutations). Defences:

  • Per-host page cap (~10M pages per host).
  • Detect URL patterns with high cardinality and low content variation → demote priority.
  • Maximum URL depth (~20 segments).

8Deep Dive 2: Building the Inverted Index

An inverted index maps each term → list of documents containing it. For a corpus of 50B docs × 500 terms each, the index has ~25T entries. Building it requires MapReduce-scale jobs.

Index build pipeline

  1. Tokenize: split on whitespace, strip punctuation, lowercase. Handle CJK with proper segmenters.
  2. Normalise: stem (running → run), expand common abbreviations, optional language-specific Unicode normalisation (NFKC).
  3. Stop-word handling: keep stop words in the index (so phrase queries work) but down-weight them in ranking.
  4. Per-document local index: for each doc, emit (term, doc_id, tf, [positions]) tuples.
  5. Shuffle and merge: group by term across the cluster; each shard gets a range of terms (or a hash partition).
  6. Posting list construction: per term, sort by doc_id; delta-encode and variable-byte compress; write to disk as a sequential block.
  7. Index serving: each shard loads its terms into memory (or memory-mapped) and serves queries.

Compression

Delta encoding makes consecutive doc_ids small numbers. Variable-byte encoding (VByte) uses 1 byte for small numbers and grows as needed. Real production indexes use more advanced schemes (PFOR-Delta, Simple9) but VByte is a fine interview answer.

Index updates — incremental indexing

Rebuilding 500 TB from scratch is a weeks-long job. Production uses a "main + delta" pattern:

  • Main index: rebuilt nightly or weekly from the full corpus.
  • Delta index: real-time, holds the last few hours of updates. Much smaller.
  • Query searches BOTH; results merged. After the next main rebuild, delta is cleared.

9Deep Dive 3: Query Path — From Keywords to Ten Blue Links

q = "system design interview" │ ▼ ┌─────────────────────────────┐ │ Query Parser │ │ - tokenize, lowercase │ │ - spelling correction │ ← "systen" → "system" (confidence) │ - synonym expansion │ ← "sd"→{"system design"} (cautious) │ - intent classification │ ← informational | navigational | local └────────┬─────────────────────┘ │ ▼ ┌─────────────────────────────┐ │ Query Coordinator │ ← <1 ms work │ - decide shards to hit │ │ - scatter parallel RPCs │ └────────┬─────────────────────┘ │ scatter ▼ ┌──────┐ ┌──────┐ ┌──────┐ ... 500 shards │ S1 │ │ S2 │ │ S500 │ │ - intersect posting lists │ ← bitmap or skiplist intersection │ - score: BM25 × PageRank... │ │ - return local top-10 │ └──┬───┘ └──┬───┘ └──┬───┘ │ │ │ gather ▼ ▼ ▼ ┌─────────────────────────────┐ │ Aggregator │ │ - merge 500 × 10 = 5000 cands│ │ - re-rank with global features│ ← per-shard scores normalised │ - apply business rules │ │ - dedup near-identical URLs │ └────────┬─────────────────────┘ │ ▼ ┌─────────────────────────────┐ │ Snippet Generator │ │ - fetch page text for top-10│ │ - highlight query terms │ └────────┬─────────────────────┘ ▼ User

The two-phase ranking

Per-shard ranking uses fast features (BM25, PageRank, language match). It's cheap because each shard only sees its own subset. The aggregator gets the union of all shards' top-10 (5000 candidates) and runs expensive ranking — features that require global statistics, ML inference (BERT-style relevance), user-personalisation signals.

This two-phase split keeps per-shard cost low (millisecond) and lets expensive computation run on a small candidate set.

10Deep Dive 4: Ranking — TF-IDF, BM25, PageRank, Neural

TF-IDF (the foundation, not used directly anymore)

tfidf(term, doc) = tf(term, doc) × log(N / df(term))

Higher term-frequency in this doc = more relevant; higher rarity overall (low document-frequency) = more discriminating. Sum over query terms gives the doc's score.

BM25 (the workhorse since the 90s)

An improvement on TF-IDF that handles document length and TF saturation:

BM25(doc, query) = Σ over terms t in query: IDF(t) × tf(t, doc) × (k+1) / ( tf(t, doc) + k × (1 − b + b × |doc|/avgdl) ) Typical k = 1.2, b = 0.75

BM25 is still the bedrock of modern search engines. Elasticsearch and Solr ship it by default.

PageRank

"A page is important if other important pages link to it." Recursive definition solved by power iteration on the link graph:

PR(p) = (1 − d)/N + d × Σ over pages q linking to p: PR(q) / out_degree(q) Typical d = 0.85

Computed offline (Spark or BigQuery job) over the whole link graph; results joined into per-doc features for ranking. Recomputed weekly.

Neural ranking

The modern stack adds learned models on top of classical signals:

  • Cross-encoder re-rankers: BERT-style models that take (query, doc) and predict relevance. Too expensive to run on millions of candidates; run on the top 1000 from BM25.
  • Dense retrieval: encode queries and docs as embeddings; ANN search (FAISS, ScaNN) finds candidates by embedding similarity. Complements keyword search for semantic queries ("how do birds fly" finding pages about avian aerodynamics).
  • Learning-to-rank: LambdaMART / GBDT models that combine ~100 features (BM25, PageRank, freshness, click-history, language match, …) into a single relevance score. The "real" final ranker in most production engines.
🔑 The Ranking Pyramid

Cheap features (BM25, PageRank lookup) prune billions to thousands. Medium features (LambdaMART) prune thousands to hundreds. Expensive features (BERT cross-encoder, personalisation) re-rank the final hundred. This pyramid is universal across all serious search engines.

11Deep Dive 5: Freshness — Real-Time Index for News

The main index is rebuilt nightly. For "breaking news" queries (an earthquake just happened), nightly is way too slow. The trick is two parallel indexes:

  • Main index: 500 TB, rebuilt every 24 h. Holds the long-tail web.
  • Real-time index: ~100 GB, updated within seconds of a page being crawled. Holds only the last 24–48 h of content. Memory-resident on a separate fleet.

Every query is sent to both. The aggregator merges results, with the real-time index getting a freshness boost for queries classified as "news intent."

How a news page goes from publication to indexed in <5 minutes

  1. Crawler picks up the page (from a high-priority list or a publisher's sitemap ping).
  2. Text extracted and pushed to a real-time indexing pipeline (Kafka-backed).
  3. Real-time index updates in-place (CRDT-style or "small-index swap" every 30 s).
  4. Query coordinators consult both indexes for every query.

12Deep Dive 6: Index Sharding and Replication

Two sharding choices

Document-sharded: each shard holds all terms for a subset of docs. To answer a query, every shard's posting lists must be consulted (scatter to all 500 shards).

Term-sharded: each shard holds posting lists for a subset of terms. To answer a query, only the shards holding the query terms need to be consulted (typically just 2–4 shards).

Why Google chose document-sharded

Term-sharded sounds more efficient per query, but it has a fatal flaw: hot terms create hot shards. The shard holding "the", "a", and "of" gets every query, while shards holding rare terms sit idle. Document sharding load-balances naturally because every query hits every shard equally.

The cost is fan-out: every query becomes 500 RPCs. But with replication, each shard's hardware is cheap; the bottleneck shifts from per-shard load to network fan-out, which is well-engineered at Google scale (gRPC + custom RPC libraries).

Replication

Each shard has ~10 replicas. The coordinator picks one replica per shard for each query (least-loaded, lowest-latency, closest region). Replicas are identical static snapshots — no consistency problem. Updates are pushed by replicating the new index segment to all replicas atomically.

13Failure Modes & Recovery

FailureMitigation
Single index replica downCoordinator routes to another replica. ~10 replicas, single failure invisible.
Entire shard down (all replicas)Query returns "incomplete" results — the missing shard's documents are simply absent. Better than failing the query. A short banner notifies of degraded results.
Crawl pipeline behindIndex freshness suffers; main results unaffected for hours. Auto-scale crawler workers.
Region downTraffic shifted to other regions via global LB. Latency increases for affected users but search remains functional.
Bad index pushCanary deploy: new index goes to 1% of replicas; A/B compared on relevance metrics before full roll-out. Automatic rollback on quality regression.
Spam/manipulation attack on PageRankSeparate spam classifier; manual reviews for top-N domains; dynamic penalties.

14Scaling Path

StageArchitecture
1M docs (toy)Elasticsearch single-node, off-the-shelf BM25, no PageRank.
100M docsElasticsearch cluster with 10 shards. Custom ranking plugin. Periodic crawl from sitemaps.
1B docsMove off Elasticsearch — build custom inverted index on commodity disks (or RocksDB). Distributed crawler. PageRank computed monthly.
10B docs500 shards × 5 replicas. MapReduce-based index build. Real-time delta index for freshness. ML re-ranking layer.
50B docs (full web)Document-sharded with thousands of shards. Multi-region serving. Per-region replicas. Custom hardware (Google's TPUs for inference).

15Cross-Questions and Pushbacks

"Why not just use Elasticsearch? It does inverted index + BM25 out of the box."
Answer: Elasticsearch is excellent up to ~10s of TB. Beyond that, several constraints bite. (1) Memory: ES holds significant index structures in JVM heap; 500 TB across an ES cluster would need petabytes of RAM. (2) Ranking flexibility: ES's pluggable ranking is constrained — running LambdaMART or BERT re-rankers requires bolt-ons. (3) Crawl scale: ES doesn't crawl; you'd need a separate pipeline anyway. (4) Cost: at 50 B docs the licensing or self-hosted cost dwarfs custom-built. For 100M-1B docs, ES is the right answer. For Google-scale, you build your own — which is exactly the path Google took (they started on commodity boxes, then designed custom storage).
"500 shards scatter-gather per query — what about the 99th percentile tail latency?"
Answer: This is the classic tail-latency problem in fan-out systems. The probability that all 500 shards respond in <50 ms is (P(one shard responds in 50ms))^500 — even 99.9% per-shard becomes 60% overall. Three mitigations: (1) Hedged requests — coordinator sends the query to 2 replicas of each shard after a small delay (~5 ms); first response wins. (2) "Good enough" results — if 95% of shards respond in 100 ms, return those results; the missing 5% might miss a few docs but rarely changes the top-10. (3) Per-shard timeout — anything past 200 ms is dropped. Hedging alone typically cuts P99 from 500 ms to ~150 ms in 500-way fan-out, as Jeff Dean's "Tail at Scale" paper documented.
"Term-sharded would be way more efficient. Why fan-out to 500 shards when you could hit only 2–3?"
Answer: Term-sharded systems suffer hot-shard collapse: the shard holding stop words ("the", "a") receives nearly every query, while shards of rare terms sit idle. Load balancing requires constant key rebalancing. Document-sharded distributes load uniformly: every query hits every shard ≈ once, so capacity planning is trivial. Hybrid systems exist (split by language, then doc-shard within each), but at the top level, doc-sharded wins for predictable load distribution. The fan-out cost is real but well-mitigated by gRPC and hedging.
How do you handle a query like "system design" -interview site:medium.com with operators?
The parser tokenises operators into a query AST. The phrase "system design" becomes a phrase node — at index time, we stored positions, so phrase matching requires that the two terms appear in adjacent positions. -interview becomes a negation node (exclude any doc containing "interview"). site:medium.com is a metadata filter applied before scoring. The shard intersects the postings for "system" AND "design" (with adjacency), filters out postings present in "interview", and filters down to docs whose host metadata matches medium.com. Each shard returns its top-K, then merge.
How do you spell-correct queries like "systen desigm" → "system design"?
Edit-distance lookup against a dictionary built from the corpus. For each query token: (1) check if it's a known term; (2) if not, find all dictionary words within edit distance 2 (typo) using a Levenshtein automaton or a BK-tree; (3) score candidates by (term frequency in corpus) × (1 / edit distance) × (co-occurrence with surrounding query terms); (4) if confidence is high, replace; if medium, show "Did you mean...?"; if low, leave as-is. Modern engines use language-model approaches (n-gram or neural) for higher accuracy, but Levenshtein + frequency-weighting gets you 80% there.
How does the system avoid being gamed by SEO spam farms?
Multi-layer. (1) Spam classifier: ML model trained on labelled examples; features include keyword stuffing, hidden text, link-farming patterns. Docs above a threshold get a penalty multiplier on their score. (2) PageRank intrinsically resists keyword-density spam — a single page can't fake incoming links from reputable domains. (3) TrustRank: propagate trust from a hand-curated seed set of trustworthy domains. (4) Manual review: human-curated penalties for known offenders. (5) User behaviour signals: low click-through and high bounce rate hurt rankings. The full system is an arms race; the design is to make it expensive to game.
"PageRank requires the full web graph — how do you compute it on 50B docs?"
Answer: The link graph at 50B docs × 100 links each = 5T edges. Stored as adjacency lists, ~80 TB. PageRank is computed via Spark or BigQuery iteratively — each iteration is a join of (dst_node, contributions) and a reduce. Convergence takes ~30–50 iterations. Running on ~10k cores, it completes in a few hours. We don't recompute from scratch — incremental PageRank only re-converges from the changed nodes. Production: run weekly, push results to per-doc features in the index. Inside ranking, PageRank is just a lookup: O(1) per doc. Computing isn't on the query path.
How do you handle non-English queries — Hindi, Chinese, Arabic?
Language-specific tokenisation is essential. (1) CJK: word boundaries are not whitespace — use ICU segmenter or model-based segmenters. (2) Arabic / Hebrew: right-to-left, vowel diacritics often missing → normalise. (3) Indic languages: complex compounding; per-language stemmers (sandhi splitter for Sanskrit-influenced languages). The index is partitioned by language; queries are language-detected (often via the user's UI language or n-gram detector), then dispatched to the matching index shards. Cross-lingual queries (search Hindi pages in English) use translated query expansion as a separate feature.
How do you measure ranking quality?
Two layers. (1) Offline evaluation: relevance judgements (humans rate query-doc pairs); metrics like NDCG@10, MAP, MRR. Rerank models are first evaluated this way. (2) Online A/B testing: real traffic split between control (current ranker) and treatment (new ranker). User-behaviour metrics: clickthrough rate, dwell time, abandonment rate, time-to-first-click, query reformulation rate. Statistical significance over millions of queries. Any change must move at least one core metric without regressing others.
How do you balance freshness and authority?
It's per-query and learned. For navigational queries ("CNN homepage") and fresh-intent queries ("earthquake just now"), recent results win. For evergreen queries ("how does TCP work"), older, well-linked results win. This is encoded as a feature in the learned ranker: days_since_pub × query_freshness_weight, where the weight is learned from labelled data per query class. Real-time index gets a boost for queries classified as news intent; the main index dominates for everything else.

End of Problem 7. Next: Notification System (P8) — multi-channel delivery, dedup, dunning.

Problem 8: Designing a Multi-Channel Notification System

"Send X to N users via push/email/SMS/in-app" sounds trivial — until you face dedup, retries, third-party failures, user preferences, rate limits, dunning, and the chance of paging 10M users with the same wrong alert.

1Context and Why This Problem Matters

Every product needs to send notifications: "your order shipped," "someone commented on your post," "your card was declined." Building this looks deceptively simple — call FCM, call SendGrid, done. Production reality:

  • One business event → many notifications: an "order shipped" event triggers push, email, in-app, maybe SMS, in 60 languages, for 100k orders/day.
  • Third-party providers fail: APNs has outages; SendGrid throttles; carriers drop SMS silently. The system must retry without spamming.
  • Dedup is harder than it looks: the same logical event can arrive twice (Kafka rebalance, retry storm). You must not send the same email twice.
  • User preferences are first-class: marketing vs transactional, quiet hours, channel preferences, unsubscribes. Forgetting these is a GDPR / CCPA / TCPA legal violation.
  • One bad template = global blast: a templating bug once sent millions of "Hello {first_name}" emails. The pipeline must protect against this.

2Requirements Gathering

Functional

  • Accept a notification request from any internal service (with template ID + data + recipient + channel).
  • Deliver via push (FCM/APNs), email (SendGrid/SES), SMS (Twilio/MSG91), in-app inbox, webhook.
  • Honour user preferences: opt-outs, channel choice, quiet hours, language.
  • Dedup: same event sent twice → delivered once.
  • Retries on transient failures; permanent failures recorded and surfaced.
  • Audit log: who sent what to whom, when, with what result.
  • Scheduled and recurring sends ("send tomorrow 9 am").

Non-functional

  • Throughput: ~10k notifications/sec sustained, 100k/sec during marketing burst.
  • Transactional notification P99 delivery latency: <5 s end-to-end.
  • Marketing burst: 100M emails in <2 h.
  • Durability: never drop a transactional notification on a single component failure.
  • Cost per notification: fractions of a cent (push) to ~$0.01 (SMS).

Out of scope

  • The product UIs that build templates and target audiences (those would call this system).
  • Deep ML personalisation / send-time optimisation — touched in cross-questions.

3Capacity Estimation

MetricDerivationNumber
Users—100 M
Avg transactional notifs/user/day—~3
Avg marketing notifs/user/week—~5
Total notifs/day (avg)100M × 3 + 100M × 5/7~370 M
Notifs/sec (avg)370M / 100k~3.7 k/s
Notifs/sec (peak, 10×)Marketing burst at 10 am~50 k/s
Channel mix50% push, 30% email, 5% SMS, 15% in-app—
SMS spend/day (worst case)5% × 370M × $0.01$185 k/day
Notification record size—~1 KB
Storage/day370M × 1 KB~370 GB/day
Storage/year hot30 days × 370 GB~11 TB hot
Storage/year cold11 mo × 370 GB × 30~120 TB cold
🔑 From Numbers to Architecture
  • ~50 k/sec peak (10× marketing bursts) → Kafka as a write buffer; topic per channel (push / email / SMS / in-app) → channel-specific consumer pools auto-scale.
  • Push 50% / Email 30% / SMS 5% / In-app 15% → separate workers per channel; SMS guarded by per-second cost cap (~$185 k/day worst case).
  • 100 M users × 5 device types → device registry in Cassandra/DynamoDB (partition by user_id); user prefs cached in Redis (~95% hit rate).
  • Per-user dedup + frequency caps → Redis SETNX with TTL (e.g. "this campaign once/24h per user"); avoids spamming.
  • ~370 GB/day notification log → hot tier in Postgres for 30 days, then S3 cold for 1 year (compliance).
  • Idempotency on send → idempotency_key per request; retries are safe; SMS-providers' webhooks reconcile delivery state.

4API Design

Internal API — Send a Notification

POST /v1/notifications Authorization: Bearer {service_jwt} Idempotency-Key: order-shipped-{order_id} // dedup key { "template_id": "order_shipped_v3", "recipient": { "user_id": "u_abc", "lang_override": "hi-IN" }, "channels": ["PUSH", "EMAIL"], // multi-channel "data": { "order_id":"o_123", "tracking_url":"https://..." }, "priority": "TRANSACTIONAL", // TRANSACTIONAL | MARKETING "scheduled_at": null, // null = send now "ttl_seconds": 3600 // drop if not delivered in 1 h } Response: 202 Accepted { "notification_id": "n_uuid", "status": "QUEUED", "channels": [ { "channel": "PUSH", "status": "QUEUED" }, { "channel": "EMAIL", "status": "SUPPRESSED_BY_PREFERENCE" } ] }

Bulk send (campaign)

POST /v1/notifications/bulk { "template_id": "weekly_digest_v7", "audience_id": "aud_premium_users_us", // pre-computed audience "channels": ["EMAIL"], "schedule_at": "2026-05-17T09:00:00Z" } Response: 202 Accepted { "campaign_id": "c_uuid", "estimated_recipients": 2_400_000 }

Status, audit, callbacks

GET /v1/notifications/{id} // current status + channel results POST /v1/webhooks/provider/{name} // SendGrid/Twilio status callbacks GET /v1/audit?user_id=...&from=... // for support / compliance

User preferences API

GET /v1/users/{id}/preferences PUT /v1/users/{id}/preferences { "email": { "transactional": true, "marketing": false }, "push": { "transactional": true, "marketing": true }, "sms": { "transactional": true, "marketing": false }, "quiet_hours": { "tz": "Asia/Kolkata", "from": "22:00", "to": "08:00" }, "language": "hi-IN" }

5Data Model

notifications (PostgreSQL, partitioned by month)

CREATE TABLE notifications ( notification_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, idempotency_key VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL, user_id UUID NOT NULL, template_id VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL, priority VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL, -- TRANSACTIONAL | MARKETING data_json JSONB NOT NULL, scheduled_at TIMESTAMPTZ, ttl_at TIMESTAMPTZ, created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW(), UNIQUE (idempotency_key, user_id) -- dedup at write time ); CREATE INDEX idx_user_created ON notifications(user_id, created_at DESC); CREATE INDEX idx_scheduled ON notifications(scheduled_at) WHERE scheduled_at IS NOT NULL;

notification_channels (one row per channel-attempt)

CREATE TABLE notification_channels ( channel_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, notification_id UUID REFERENCES notifications, channel VARCHAR(20), -- PUSH | EMAIL | SMS | IN_APP | WEBHOOK state VARCHAR(20), -- QUEUED|SENT|DELIVERED|FAILED|SUPPRESSED|BOUNCED provider VARCHAR(50), -- 'fcm', 'apns', 'sendgrid', 'twilio' provider_message_id VARCHAR(255), rendered_subject TEXT, rendered_body TEXT, attempts INT DEFAULT 0, last_error TEXT, sent_at TIMESTAMPTZ, delivered_at TIMESTAMPTZ, failed_at TIMESTAMPTZ );

user_devices (push tokens, Redis-cached)

CREATE TABLE user_devices ( device_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, user_id UUID, platform VARCHAR(20), -- IOS | ANDROID | WEB push_token VARCHAR(500), -- FCM token or APNs token last_seen TIMESTAMPTZ, active BOOLEAN DEFAULT TRUE ); CREATE INDEX idx_devices_user ON user_devices(user_id) WHERE active = true;

user_preferences (PostgreSQL + Redis cache)

CREATE TABLE user_preferences ( user_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, channel_prefs JSONB NOT NULL, -- nested {email:{txn:true,mkt:false}, ...} quiet_hours JSONB, language VARCHAR(10), unsubscribe_token VARCHAR(64) UNIQUE, updated_at TIMESTAMPTZ );
