7Deep Dive 1: Fanout — One Event to Millions of Devices

A marketing campaign targets 10M users. Each user has 1–3 active devices. Total push targets: ~25M. We must complete in <2 h.

The fanout pipeline

  1. Campaign API receives the request → writes campaign row → emits one Kafka message per audience segment chunk (e.g. 100k user_ids each).
  2. Audience segmenter expands each chunk into individual notification records (writes to notifications with idempotency key campaign:{id}:user:{id}).
  3. Channel dispatcher reads from Kafka, parallelises into per-provider worker pools.
  4. Per-device, per-provider rate-limit respected (FCM caps at 600k QPS per project; SendGrid at ~10k/s per account).

Why we don't pre-expand to all 25M push records up front

Pre-expanding makes the API call's transaction huge (25M row inserts = minutes). Better: stream-expand by reading the audience query in chunks and inserting one chunk at a time. Each chunk is independent; partial failures only re-run their chunk.

Token expiration / unregistered devices

Push tokens expire silently. When FCM returns NotRegistered, the dispatcher marks the device inactive in user_devices. Saves money and respects users who uninstalled.

8Deep Dive 2: Idempotency and Deduplication

The same business event can hit our API multiple times: producer retry on network blip, Kafka consumer rebalance reprocessing, manual retry by ops. We must send exactly once.

Idempotency at the API layer

Every POST /notifications requires an Idempotency-Key. The DB enforces uniqueness:

INSERT INTO notifications(notification_id, idempotency_key, user_id, ...) VALUES (...) ON CONFLICT (idempotency_key, user_id) DO NOTHING RETURNING notification_id;

If no row was returned, the same notification was already created. The API returns the existing notification_id with its current state. Producer sees a successful response either way.

Idempotency at the consumer layer

Kafka guarantees at-least-once. Consumer may process the same message twice. Defence:

  • Each channel dispatcher inserts a row in notification_channels with state=QUEUED before calling the provider. The row's primary key (notification_id + channel) prevents duplicate inserts.
  • If the row already exists with state ≠ QUEUED, skip (already processed).
  • If state=QUEUED and last_attempt < some threshold, skip (in-flight retry).
  • If state=QUEUED and the row is "stuck" past threshold, take ownership and retry.

Provider-level dedup as a backstop

Most providers accept a client-side message ID. FCM has message_id, SendGrid has unique_args.dedup_key. We pass our channel_id. Even if our consumer-side dedup fails, the provider drops the duplicate.

9Deep Dive 3: Retries, Dunning and Provider Failures

Providers fail in three ways and each needs a different response:

Failure typeExamplesStrategy
Transient5xx, timeout, 429 rate-limitExponential backoff, retry up to 5 attempts, then DLQ
Permanent invalid input4xx malformed email, bad phone numberDon't retry; mark FAILED; alert (likely user-data issue)
Permanent recipient-sideNotRegistered (uninstalled), bounce, spam-trapMark device/email inactive; suppress future sends

Exponential backoff with jitter

backoff_ms = min(MAX, BASE × 2^attempt × (0.5 + random())) e.g. BASE=1000, MAX=60_000 → 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s, 16s, capped at 60s

Dunning (the unloved cousin)

Dunning means "retry over time with diminishing aggressiveness." For payment failures: try at +1d, +3d, +5d, +7d, then dunning ends. Notifications inherit this for "your payment failed, please update card" → at most 4 sends in 7 days, all on different channels.

Circuit breakers per provider

If SendGrid is returning 500s for 30% of requests in 5 min, break the circuit — stop sending email entirely for 2 minutes. New requests are queued. Re-enable after a healthcheck succeeds. Prevents a flaky provider from clogging the entire pipeline.

Provider failover

Critical-path channels (SMS for 2FA, transactional email for password resets) configure secondary providers. If Twilio errors persist, automatically route to MSG91 / AWS SNS. The cost-per-send differs, so this only applies to high-priority TRANSACTIONAL traffic.

10Deep Dive 4: User Preferences and Quiet Hours

Preference matrix

Two axes: channel × purpose. Channels: PUSH, EMAIL, SMS, IN_APP. Purposes: TRANSACTIONAL (delivery confirmations), MARKETING (promotions), DIGEST (weekly summaries). The system pre-filters every notification against this matrix.

Transactional always wins

Users can never disable transactional emails — they're legally required (order confirmations, refund notices). Marketing/Digest is opt-out at any time. Some jurisdictions require granular opt-out (CASL, CAN-SPAM). The unsubscribe URL embeds a signed token so we can verify the unsubscribe.

Quiet hours

If a marketing push would land at 11 pm in the user's tz, we defer it to the next morning. Transactional is exempt (your card was charged — you need to know now).

Implementation: the eligibility filter checks local_time_in(user.tz) against quiet_hours. If in quiet hours, re-enqueue the notification with scheduled_at = next_morning_start.

Frequency capping

Even with all opt-ins, no user should get more than ~3 marketing notifications a day or ~10 a week. Frequency caps tracked in Redis: freq:{user_id}:day incremented per send; if > cap, drop. Resets daily.

11Deep Dive 5: Template Rendering and Localisation

Templates as code

Templates are versioned in a content service, written in a safe templating DSL (Liquid or Mustache — never raw Jinja or {% exec %} primitives). Each template ID has variants per language and channel:

order_shipped_v3: email: en-US: "Hi {first_name}, your order #{order_id} has shipped..." hi-IN: "Hi {first_name}, आपका ऑर्डर #{order_id} ..." push: en-US: "Your order is on the way!" hi-IN: "..." sms: en-US: "Order #{order_id} shipped: {tracking_url}"

The two-stage safety

  1. Template lint at upload: required variables present, no unsupported syntax, max length per channel, no HTML in SMS templates.
  2. Canary at send: a new template version sends to 0.1% of recipients first; bounce/spam rate compared to v(N-1). Only promotes to 100% if metrics are healthy.

Personalisation data merge

The producer service sends a small JSON blob with the notification ({order_id, tracking_url}). The renderer merges with user profile data (name, language) fetched from a profile service, then runs the template. Failures (missing variable) raise a render error rather than sending "Hello {first_name}".

⚠ The famous "Hello {first_name}" bug

Several big companies (Airbnb, GitHub) have publicly sent millions of emails that read literally "Hello {first_name}". The template engine silently substituted nothing instead of failing loud. Fix: configure the engine to error on missing variables, then have the renderer fall back to a safe alternative ("Hello there!") and log a critical-priority alert.

12Failure Modes & Recovery

FailureMitigation
Kafka lag spike during marketing burstAuto-scale channel dispatchers on consumer lag. Marketing is low-priority — transactional has a separate higher-priority topic + dedicated consumer pool.
Provider outage (FCM down)Circuit breaker opens. Push messages queued in Kafka (durable). When FCM recovers, queued messages drain. If FCM down >1 h, ttl_at-expired ones are dropped to avoid sending hours-stale alerts.
Bad template promoted globallyCanary catches it. Manual kill-switch: POST /admin/templates/{id}/disable stops sends immediately; queued ones use previous version.
Database failurePostgres primary fails over to standby; Kafka continues queuing. Worst case: ~30 s of new requests fail; consumers resume after failover.
Duplicate consumer processingChannel-level uniqueness + provider-level dedup keys eliminate double sends.
SMS provider charges spikingCost alert thresholds; auto-throttle marketing SMS when daily spend exceeds budget. Transactional SMS uninterrupted.
Mass user-data corruption (e.g. wrong email mapping)Pre-flight check on bulk campaigns: sample 100 recipients, manually verify rendering, require ops approval to launch >100k-recipient campaigns.

13Scaling Path

StageArchitecture
100 notifs/daySynchronous calls from producer service direct to provider. No queue.
10k/dayAdd Redis-backed queue (BullMQ / Sidekiq) for retries. Single worker pool.
1M/dayMigrate to Kafka. Split workers by channel. Add idempotency table.
100M/dayThis article's design. Per-channel rate limiting. Circuit breakers. Multi-provider failover.
1B/dayMulti-region Kafka clusters. Per-region channel dispatchers. Edge-side preference enforcement.

14Cross-Questions and Pushbacks

"Why Kafka instead of a simpler queue like SQS or RabbitMQ?"
Answer: Three reasons. (1) Throughput: 50k/s peak exceeds RabbitMQ's comfortable ~50k/s ceiling per node; Kafka handles 1M+/s/broker. (2) Multiple consumers per event: an event triggers push + email + audit log + analytics. Kafka's consumer groups let each subscribe independently to the same topic; SQS doesn't fan out to multiple consumers natively (you'd need SNS + multiple SQS queues, which is more moving parts). (3) Replay: when a bug is found, we replay last hour's notif.delivered events to fix downstream tables. Kafka retains; SQS deletes after consumption. SQS is fine up to ~10M/day; Kafka is the right tool above that.
"Why dedup in the DB instead of just in Redis?"
Answer: Redis dedup is fine for short windows (last 24 h), and we do use Redis for the idempotency-key lookup hot-path. But DB-level uniqueness is the safety net: even if Redis loses data on restart, the unique index in Postgres prevents the duplicate send forever. The combined cost is one Redis GET + one DB INSERT-ON-CONFLICT, both sub-millisecond. The DB row is also our audit log — the same record that proves "yes we sent this." For transactional notifications (especially payment failures), losing dedup is far worse than the few ms of cost.
How do you handle "send to 10M users at exactly 9 am IST"?
Three patterns. (1) Pre-expand the audience into notifications rows with scheduled_at=9am IST, indexed for the scheduler. A scheduler service polls jobs due within the next 30 s and emits to Kafka. (2) Smear over a window — if the campaign tolerates ±5 min, deterministic jitter (hash(user_id) % 300 seconds) spreads load uniformly. We default to smearing to protect downstream providers. (3) For "exactly synchronous" use cases (rare), all dispatchers wait until 9:00:00 then drain — this is hostile to providers (FCM throttles you) so we add an exception per campaign.
How do you measure delivery quality?
Per-channel metrics from provider webhooks. Email: delivered, opened, clicked, bounced, complained (spam-marked). Push: delivered, opened, dismissed; FCM provides only delivered confirmations, not opens (privacy). SMS: delivered, failed, no-callback-for-opens. We compute per-template/per-channel bounce rate, open rate, complaint rate, and alert on regressions. A bounce rate >5% gets a template flagged for review; a complaint rate >0.1% can get your SendGrid IP blocklisted.
"How do you handle a producer accidentally calling /notifications a million times for the same event?"
Answer: Three layers of defence. (1) Idempotency key uniqueness: the DB silently dedups; only one notification is created. (2) Producer-level rate limit: each producing service has a per-second budget at the gateway; a runaway loop gets 429'd. (3) Anomaly detection: notif requests per service are monitored; sudden 1000× spike triggers an automated alert and a manual ops circuit. (1) protects from correctness; (2) and (3) protect from cost (each call costs CPU, and downstream SMS costs real money).
How do unsubscribe links work without requiring login?
Embedded in every email: https://example.com/u/{token}, where the token is HMAC-signed and contains user_id + channel + purpose. Click → server verifies HMAC, applies the opt-out to that user's preferences, shows confirmation page. No login. Critical: signed tokens prevent enumeration attacks (you can't trivially unsubscribe other users). Tokens are scoped — an "unsubscribe from marketing email" token can't disable transactional. For one-click unsubscribe (GMail's list-unsubscribe header), the same token works via the List-Unsubscribe-Post mechanism.
How do you keep marketing pushes from disabling notifications for the whole product?
Two safeguards. (1) Frequency capping: max 3 marketing pushes per user per day. (2) Per-user complaint feedback loop: if a user repeatedly mutes notifications (FCM provides this signal), reduce their marketing-push frequency further. The product surfaces "you've been seeing fewer marketing notifications because of your engagement signals — would you like to re-enable?" — restoring user control. Goal: marketing pushes never become why the user disables push notifications entirely (which would break transactional).
"100k notifs/sec to Postgres — won't the writes overwhelm it?"
Answer: Quantify. At 100k notifs/s peak, with two writes each (notifications + notification_channels), that's 200k writes/s — above single-node Postgres limits. Two fixes. (1) Batch inserts: the channel dispatcher batches 100 inserts into one statement; ~20× reduction in IOPS, drops actual write rate to ~10k/s — comfortable. (2) Shard by user_id: 8-way shard across Postgres instances gives 12.5k/s each, well within capacity. Marketing-only events that don't need a Postgres row at all can fast-path through Kafka → directly to dispatcher without DB persistence (audit log written async).
How do you A/B test a notification template?
Variants are first-class. A template can declare variants v3.A and v3.B. The campaign config specifies the split (50/50). Renderer hashes user_id + template_id to pick a variant deterministically (so the same user always sees the same variant). Provider webhooks carry the variant ID; downstream analytics compare open/click rates. Winner promoted to 100% next campaign. Statistical sig over ~10k recipients per variant.
How does the in-app inbox channel differ from the others?
In-app inbox isn't push — it's pulled by the client on app open. We don't go through FCM/SendGrid. Instead, the dispatcher writes a row in an in_app_messages table with TTL and read state. The client fetches GET /v1/inbox?since=... on app open and again periodically. Crucially: we deliver in-app notifications even for users who disabled push (they didn't opt out of in-app), so it's a reliable backstop. Read/dismiss events are POSTed back; we track read rates as a delivery signal.

Medium Infrastructure Consistent Hashing LRU / LFU Replication

Problem 9: Designing a Distributed In-Memory Cache

Build the thing that sits between your app and your database. The trick: 1ms latency on 10M QPS without losing keys when a node dies.

1Context and Why This Problem Matters

Caching is the single most common scaling technique in system design. Every interview that touches a read-heavy system asks "where's the cache?" Asking you to design the cache itself is a deeper test — it forces you to engage with consistent hashing, eviction theory, replication trade-offs, and stampede prevention. The reference implementations (Memcached, Redis Cluster, Hazelcast) embody decades of hard-won decisions; the interview is checking if you can articulate why they made them.

2Requirements Gathering

Functional

  • GET(key), SET(key, value, ttl), DELETE(key).
  • Optional: atomic INCR, CAS (Check-And-Set), MGET for batching.
  • TTL support: keys auto-expire after N seconds.
  • Eviction: when memory full, evict by policy (LRU default).
  • Replication: every key on N nodes for durability against single-node failure.
  • Add/remove nodes without downtime; minimal key remapping.

Non-functional

  • P99 GET latency < 1 ms in same-DC.
  • Throughput: 10M ops/s aggregate.
  • Capacity: 1 TB total in-memory.
  • Availability: 99.99% (cache outage cascades to DB).
  • Eventual consistency across replicas is acceptable for most cache uses.

Out of scope

  • Durable storage / persistence (it's a cache — durability is a non-goal).
  • Complex queries / secondary indexes (this is a key-value store).

3Capacity Estimation

MetricDerivationNumber
Total cache size—1 TB
Avg value sizeApp-dependent; assume~1 KB
Number of keys1 TB / 1 KB~1 B keys
Ops/sec (aggregate)—10 M/s
Per-node capacity (RAM)r6g.16xlarge ≈ 512 GB~256 GB usable
Per-node throughputSingle Redis-style server~200 k ops/s
Nodes for capacity1 TB / 256 GB × 2 (replication)~8
Nodes for throughput10M / 200k~50
Cluster sizemax(8, 50)~50 nodes
🔑 From Numbers to Architecture
  • 10 M ops/sec peak ÷ 200 k ops/sec/node = ~50 nodes for QPS — this dominates capacity sizing (only 8 nodes needed for memory).
  • Cluster is QPS-bound, not RAM-bound → each node is intentionally over-provisioned on memory; the alternative (fewer fatter nodes) saturates CPU first.
  • 50 nodes + frequent membership churn → consistent hashing with virtual nodes (~150 vnodes/node) so adding/removing 1 node remaps only ~1/50 of keys.
  • Replication factor 2 (one primary + one async replica) → reads served by either; small write amplification; failure of one replica still keeps 100% data availability.
  • ~1 ms P99 latency budget → no DB fallback on the hot path; clients route directly via the hash ring (no proxy hop).
  • Gossip-based membership → handles node up/down within seconds without a central coordinator; eventual consistency on cluster view is fine for a cache.

4API Design

Client protocol (text or binary)

// Memcached-style binary protocol example GET key123\r\n → VALUE key123 0 1024\r\n [1024 bytes of value]\r\n END\r\n SET key123 0 600 1024\r\n // flags=0, ttl=600s, length=1024 [1024 bytes of value]\r\n → STORED\r\n DELETE key123\r\n → DELETED\r\n or NOT_FOUND\r\n INCR counter:abc 5\r\n → 47\r\n // new value after +5 GETS key123\r\n // get + cas-token → VALUE key123 0 1024 cas=4711\r\n [data]\r\n END\r\n CAS key123 0 600 1024 4711\r\n [data] // CAS write, fails if token mismatch → STORED or EXISTS

Management

STATS // hit/miss, mem, evictions, etc. FLUSH_ALL // wipe a node (rare, ops only) SLABS / MEMORY // memory allocator stats

5Data Model

Per-node in-memory structures

// Main store: hash table from key → entry HashTable<Key, Entry> Entry { value: bytes expires_at: uint64 // unix ms; 0 = no TTL flags: uint32 cas_token: uint64 size: uint32 // for accounting } // LRU list (doubly-linked) for eviction LRUList = head ⇄ entry ⇄ entry ⇄ ... ⇄ tail On GET → move entry to head On evict → remove from tail // Slab allocator (memcached approach): // Pre-allocate chunks of size 64, 128, 256, 512 B, 1 KB, ... // Reduces fragmentation; each slab has a free-list

Cluster metadata (in cluster manager, e.g. ZooKeeper or built-in gossip)

- ring_version: int // bumped on topology change - nodes: [ { id, addr, status, ranges_owned } ] - virtual_node_count: 200 per real node // for consistent hash spread - replica_factor: 3 // copies per key

6High-Level Architecture

App servers (1000s) — each holds Smart Client │ hashes key → picks node(s) ▼ ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Cache Cluster (50 nodes) │ │ ┌──────┐ ┌──────┐ ┌──────┐ ... │ │ │ Node │ │ Node │ │ Node │ │ │ │ A │ │ B │ │ C │ │ │ │ keys │ │ keys │ │ keys │ │ │ │ rep │ │ rep │ │ rep │ │ │ └──┬───┘ └──┬───┘ └──┬───┘ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ └─ gossip + heartbeat ─┘ │ └─────────────────────────────────────┘ │ ▼ Cluster manager (e.g. Sentinel / Cluster Bus) - membership, failure detection - re-balancing on add/remove - replica promotion on failure

7Deep Dive 1: Consistent Hashing

The naive approach is node = hash(key) mod N. Problem: if N changes from 50 to 51 (one node added), nearly every key remaps to a different node — cache becomes useless. Consistent hashing solves this.

The ring

  1. Hash each node to one or more positions on a 2^32 ring.
  2. Hash each key to a position on the same ring.
  3. The key belongs to the next node clockwise.

When a node is added at position P, only the keys between P and the previous node clockwise move — at most 1/N of the keys, not all N-1/N as in mod-N.

Virtual nodes

With one position per real node, key distribution is uneven (some nodes hold 5%, some 0.5%). Solution: each real node owns 100–200 virtual positions on the ring (random hashes of node_id|i). This smooths the distribution and makes failure impact uniform.

Replication via the ring

For RF=3, the key lives on the next 3 distinct real nodes clockwise. On reads, the smart client picks any one of the 3 (lowest latency, random, or sticky-by-key). On writes, it sends to all 3 (or to the primary, which then replicates).

🔑 What "Minimal Remapping" Buys You

Adding a node to a 50-node cluster only moves ~2% of keys; the other 98% stay in their slot, retaining their cache value. Without consistent hashing, you'd lose 98% of your cache hits during scale-out — a guaranteed self-DDoS on the DB.

8Deep Dive 2: Eviction Policies

When memory is full and a new write arrives, something must be evicted. The choice determines hit rate. Four policies worth knowing:

PolicyRuleStrengthWeakness
LRUEvict least recently usedSimple, O(1), good for typical workloads with temporal localityScan pollution: a full-table scan evicts hot keys
LFUEvict least frequently usedResists scan pollution; better for stable hot setsOld hot keys never evicted even after they cool off
FIFOEvict oldest writtenTrivially cheapIgnores actual access — bad for caching
W-TinyLFUHybrid: LRU + count-min sketch counts; admit a new key only if its sketch frequency > victim'sBest hit rate in published benchmarksMore complex; small CMS overhead

The TTL exception

Expired keys are evicted regardless of policy. Two implementations:

  • Active expiration: a background thread scans a sample of keys every 100 ms, deletes expired.
  • Passive expiration: on GET, check expiry; if expired, delete and return MISS. Required to handle keys never touched.

Most caches use both — Redis does.

9Deep Dive 3: Replication and Anti-Entropy

Synchronous vs asynchronous replication

Synchronous: writes wait for all replicas to ack. Slower (P99 ≈ slowest replica), but no data loss on primary failure. For a cache where stale-by-a-few-ms is fine, asynchronous is the right call. The smart client can request SET … WAIT 2 for synchronous behaviour when it matters (counter increments, leader-elected keys).

Hinted handoff

If a replica is down when a write arrives, the primary stores a "hint" for that replica. When the replica returns, hints are replayed. Standard in Cassandra and DynamoDB; works the same way in cache clusters.

Read repair

On a GET that returns from multiple replicas (high-consistency read), if values disagree, the freshest is propagated to the laggers. Cheap and bounded — only triggers when divergence is observed.

Anti-entropy (Merkle trees)

Periodic background sync between replicas. Each shard's keyspace is a Merkle tree; the root hash is compared between replicas; mismatching subtrees are recursively compared and reconciled. O(log N) bandwidth to detect divergence. Cassandra's repair process; not always needed for short-TTL cache data.

10Deep Dive 4: Access Patterns

Cache-aside (lazy loading) — the default

function get(key): v = cache.get(key) if v != null: return v v = db.read(key) cache.set(key, v, ttl=600) return v

Used everywhere. Trade-off: on cache miss, latency = DB latency (1–10 ms). And stale values can sit in cache if the DB is updated without invalidating the cache — explicit invalidation is the responsibility of the writer.

Write-through

function update(key, v): db.write(key, v) cache.set(key, v, ttl=600) // synchronous write to both

Keeps cache consistent. Trade-off: every write is now slower (cache write adds latency).

Write-back (write-behind)

Write to cache immediately; the cache lazily flushes to DB. Higher write throughput, but risk of data loss if cache fails before flush. Used when DB write throughput is the bottleneck (e.g. counters). Risky for transactional data.

Refresh-ahead

For hot keys with predictable expiry, asynchronously refresh before TTL expires (e.g. at 80% of TTL). Avoids the "first reader after expiry pays full DB cost" cliff.

11Deep Dive 5: Stampede, Hot Keys, Thundering Herd

Cache stampede (dog-pile)

A hot key expires at T=0. Between T=0 and T=ε, a thousand concurrent requests all see MISS, all hit the DB. The DB melts. Three defences:

  • Request coalescing (singleflight): in each app server, when a MISS triggers a DB read, mark the key as "in flight"; subsequent concurrent MISSes for the same key wait on the in-flight promise. Only one DB read per server per key.
  • Probabilistic early refresh (XFetch): as TTL nears expiry, each requester probabilistically refreshes the cache asynchronously even while the cached value is still valid. The probability rises as TTL approaches 0. Empirically eliminates synchronised expiry storms.
  • TTL jitter: set TTL to base + random(-base/10, +base/10) so synchronised sets don't expire synchronously.

Hot key (one key gets disproportionate load)

  • One celebrity's profile is GET'd 100k times/s — saturates the single node holding it.
  • Replica reads: if RF=3, the smart client randomises between the 3 replicas — 33k QPS each, manageable.
  • Client-side caching: hot keys cached in process memory of app servers (with short TTL ~1s). Bypasses the cache cluster entirely for the hottest 0.01% of keys.
  • Hot-key sharding: detect a hot key, write it to key#0..key#9; readers pick randomly. Trade some consistency for distribution.

12Failure Modes & Recovery

FailureMitigation
Single node crashCluster manager detects via missed heartbeats; reads fail over to replicas. Failed node's keys are still served from RF=3 redundancy.
Network partitionCache prefers AP (availability + partition-tolerance) — both sides keep serving; reconcile on heal via anti-entropy. Cache staleness is acceptable.
Cluster restart (cold start)All keys lost (in-memory). DB suddenly sees 100% of read traffic — must survive. Warm-up: rolling restart instead of total. If total restart is necessary, queue reads through an admission control gate.
Bad client floods one nodePer-node connection limit; per-client rate limit; circuit breaker in the smart client.
Adding 10 nodes at onceRe-balance is rate-limited; new node accepts traffic only after its keyspace is preloaded from replicas or sourced from DB on misses (graceful warm-up).
Memory exhaustion edge caseEviction handles it under normal conditions. If a single set is bigger than the slab supports, reject the write (don't OOM).

13Scaling Path

StageArchitecture
Single app serverIn-process cache (Caffeine, Guava). No network.
Multi-app, single cache nodeOne Redis/Memcached node. Cache-aside pattern. Smart client.
Multi-DCPer-region cache clusters. Replication for inter-region — usually async via Redis CRDTs / write-replicate to remote.
Global scaleHierarchical caching: in-process tier (1 ms) → regional cluster (5 ms) → cross-region replica (50 ms) → DB (100 ms+). Each layer absorbs 99% of misses below.

14Cross-Questions and Pushbacks

"Why not just use Redis Cluster off the shelf?"
Answer: In production we absolutely do. The interview question is testing whether you understand what's inside Redis Cluster — consistent hashing, virtual slots, async replication, gossip-based membership, master failover via sentinel. If you can articulate those, you've answered the question. The "build it yourself" mode is for the rare case where you need behaviour Redis doesn't have (e.g. cell-based geographic partitioning, custom eviction informed by query cost, embedded with the app for sub-microsecond access).
"Memcached is even simpler — why not just use that?"
Answer: Memcached is great for pure GET/SET with TTL. The reason to choose Redis (or build something similar) is when you need richer data types (lists, sorted sets, hashes), pub/sub, Lua scripts, persistence, or replication built-in. Memcached has no replication — losing a node loses its keys; DB load spikes proportionally. For caches where uptime > raw throughput, Redis is better. For pure read-through with no replication need (e.g. CDN-style edge caching), Memcached is fine.
How does the cache handle write-heavy keys (e.g. counters)?
Atomic ops like INCR/DECR live in the cache; the DB is only updated periodically (write-back). For correctness on persistence: periodically flush counter values to DB with a watermark. On crash, lose up to one flush interval of increments — acceptable for view counts, unacceptable for billing counters (use the DB directly with a sharded counter table instead).
How do you ensure cache consistency with the source-of-truth DB?
Three patterns. (1) Write-through: writer updates both atomically (or as best-effort). (2) Invalidate on write: writer deletes the cache key; next reader fetches fresh and re-populates. Most common. (3) Pub/sub invalidation: when the DB changes (via CDC or app event), publish on a channel; all cache nodes evict the affected key. None of these are perfectly consistent — a race window of a few ms always exists. For applications that need strong consistency, don't cache (or cache with very short TTL and pay the staleness cost).
"How do you avoid the "split-brain" where two replicas both think they're primary?"
Answer: Quorum-based leader election via a coordination service (etcd, ZooKeeper, or Raft built into the cluster manager). A new primary must collect votes from a majority of cluster nodes; the deposed primary, even if still running, cannot serve writes because clients only accept writes from the elected leader. For a 50-node cache cluster, write availability requires >25 nodes online. If you can't form a quorum, fail closed for writes. Reads can continue from replicas — for a cache, this is the right trade-off.
When you add 10 nodes to scale out, how do you avoid stampeding the DB?
Three measures. (1) Sequential addition: add nodes one at a time, let re-balance complete before the next. (2) Slot pre-loading: when slots are reassigned to a new node, source replicas copy their data to the new owner before traffic shifts — the new node serves from this preload, not from DB. (3) Cold-cache admission control: requests from the new node to the DB go through a rate limiter; misses queue rather than concurrently hitting the DB. Together: scale-out is invisible to the DB.
How do you handle very large values (e.g. a 10 MB serialized object)?
Three options. (1) Compress: zstd or lz4 typical 4× savings. Decompression cost is tiny vs network. (2) Chunk into smaller keys: split into 1 MB chunks, store as key:chunk_0, etc.; MGET to reassemble. (3) Cache the index, not the blob: cache a pointer to S3; fetch S3 on miss. Generally avoid storing very large values directly — they pollute the cache (LRU evicts many small valuable keys to make room for one huge one), and they slow down the single-threaded cache node.
"For a 1 ms P99, network latency alone is 0.5 ms. Where does the rest go?"
Answer: Excellent. Budget: 0.5 ms network + 0.1 ms TCP framing + 0.2 ms server processing (hashtable lookup + LRU update + serialization) + 0.2 ms client-side parsing. The server side is the part we control most. Single-threaded Redis-style servers achieve ~50 μs server processing per op. To stay within budget: pipeline multiple ops, use binary protocol over text, run client and cache in the same AZ (sub-0.5 ms RTT), and pin connections to avoid TLS handshake on every request. Sub-ms is achievable but every ms component matters.
How would you implement multi-region writes?
Two models. (1) Active-active with conflict resolution: each region accepts writes, replicates to others. Conflicts resolved via LWW (last-write-wins) using globally synchronised timestamps (HLC). Suitable for cache-style data where staleness is fine. (2) Active-passive: one region is the writer; others are read-only replicas. Lower complexity but write traffic crosses regions. For a pure cache, active-active with LWW is usually right — the cache's job is read latency, and a brief LWW conflict is invisible compared to the consistency Cost.

Problem 10: Designing an E-Commerce Platform

Amazon-style: catalog, cart, checkout, payment, inventory, with flash-sale spikes that can sell 100k units in a minute without overselling a single one.

1Context and Why This Problem Matters

E-commerce is a "system design biggie" because it combines several hard problems in one box:

  • Inventory correctness: overselling 1 phone is a refund + apology. Overselling 1000 is the news.
  • Hot products / flash sales: 100k requests/s for a single SKU is a hot-key problem at the scale of "you cannot use Postgres alone."
  • Money: payments must be exactly-once, refundable, auditable.
  • Two consistency regimes side by side: catalog browsing is eventually-consistent and cheap; inventory + checkout is strongly-consistent and expensive.
  • The most common interview tangent: "now make it work during a flash sale" — separates juniors from seniors.

2Requirements Gathering

Functional

  • Browse / search catalog; product detail pages with reviews.
  • Add to cart; cart persists across sessions and devices.
  • Checkout: shipping address, payment method, place order.
  • Inventory: never sell more than available.
  • Order tracking: see status (placed / packed / shipped / delivered / returned).
  • Flash sales: announce a deal; permit a fixed number of buyers in a fixed window.
  • Returns / refunds (touched in cross-questions).

Non-functional

  • Catalog read latency: P99 < 100 ms.
  • Checkout latency: P99 < 2 s (includes payment provider call).
  • Throughput baseline: 100k QPS reads, 10k QPS writes.
  • Flash sale peak: 1M QPS for ~5 min on hot SKUs.
  • Inventory consistency: linearizable for the decrement step. No oversell.
  • Availability: 99.95% (commerce outages are $/second).

Out of scope

  • Recommendation engine (out of scope but reference it).
  • Returns / refunds full workflow (mention briefly).
  • Warehouse / fulfilment (assume an external WMS exists).

3Capacity Estimation

MetricDerivationNumber
Users—100 M
DAU—10 M
Catalog browses/day10M × 20 pages200 M
Browse QPS (avg)200M / 100k~2 k/s
Browse QPS (peak)10× burst~23 k/s
Orders/day10M × 1% conversion~100 k
Checkouts/sec (avg)—~1.2/s
Checkouts/sec (peak flash)10k orders in 5 min~33/s
Reads on hot product page (flash)—1 M/s
SKUs—~50 M
Average product record—~2 KB
Catalog DB size50M × 2 KB~100 GB
🔑 From Numbers to Architecture
  • ~23 k peak browse QPS spread across 50 M SKUs (long-tail) → single Postgres + Redis cache + Elasticsearch for search; comfortable.
  • 1 M QPS on ONE product page during a flash sale → totally different code path: CDN edge cache (HTML + JSON) + edge compute for inventory hint; origin only sees 1% of traffic.
  • ~100 GB catalog → fits in a single Postgres; CDC → Elasticsearch keeps search index in sync.
  • Cart per session → Redis hash with TTL (no DB write per add-to-cart); abandoned carts purged automatically.
  • Inventory contention at flash-sale time → Redis-backed reservation with TTL; fall back to optimistic SQL on long-tail SKUs.
  • Checkout = multi-step (payment + inventory + shipping + email) → saga pattern with compensating actions; idempotency keys on every external call.

4API Design

Catalog

GET /v1/products?q=...&category=...&page=0 GET /v1/products/{sku} // detail page GET /v1/products/{sku}/reviews

Cart

GET /v1/cart // current user's cart POST /v1/cart/items { sku, qty } // add PATCH /v1/cart/items/{sku} { qty } // change qty DELETE /v1/cart/items/{sku}

Checkout

POST /v1/checkout Idempotency-Key: ck_uuid { "items": [{sku, qty}, ...], // copy from cart at this moment "shipping_address": {...}, "payment_method_id":"pm_abc", "expected_total_cents": 12340 // anti-tamper check } Response 201: { "order_id": "o_uuid", "state": "PAYMENT_PENDING", "total_cents": 12340, "estimated_delivery_date": "2026-05-22" } GET /v1/orders/{id} // status polling POST /v1/orders/{id}/cancel // if not shipped

Flash sale (admin)

POST /v1/admin/flashsales { "sku": "iphone-17-pro", "starts_at": "2026-05-20T09:00:00Z", "ends_at": "2026-05-20T09:05:00Z", "stock_units": 10000, "max_per_user": 1 }

5Data Model

Catalog (PostgreSQL + Elasticsearch mirror)

CREATE TABLE products ( sku VARCHAR(64) PRIMARY KEY, title VARCHAR(255), description TEXT, category_id UUID, brand_id UUID, price_cents INT, attributes JSONB, -- color, size, etc. images JSONB, active BOOLEAN DEFAULT TRUE, created_at TIMESTAMPTZ, updated_at TIMESTAMPTZ ); CREATE INDEX idx_category ON products(category_id) WHERE active; CREATE INDEX idx_brand ON products(brand_id) WHERE active; -- Elasticsearch: indexed on title, description, attributes for full-text + faceting

Inventory (PostgreSQL — source of truth + Redis hot copy)

CREATE TABLE inventory ( sku VARCHAR(64) PRIMARY KEY, available_qty INT NOT NULL, -- units that can be sold reserved_qty INT NOT NULL, -- holds during checkout warehouse_qty INT NOT NULL, -- physical stock version BIGINT NOT NULL, -- optimistic-lock token updated_at TIMESTAMPTZ ); -- Redis: HSET inv:{sku} qty {available_qty} (eventual mirror, atomic DECR)

Cart (Redis primary + Postgres archival)

// Redis Hash per user HSET cart:{user_id} sku_a "qty:2" sku_b "qty:1" TTL: 30 days // Async write-back to Postgres for analytics & cross-device sync

Orders (PostgreSQL, partitioned by month)

CREATE TABLE orders ( order_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, user_id UUID, state VARCHAR(30), -- PAYMENT_PENDING, CONFIRMED, PACKED, SHIPPED, DELIVERED, CANCELLED, RETURNED total_cents BIGINT, shipping_addr JSONB, payment_id UUID, idempotency_key VARCHAR(255) UNIQUE, placed_at TIMESTAMPTZ, confirmed_at TIMESTAMPTZ ); CREATE TABLE order_items ( order_id UUID, sku VARCHAR(64), qty INT, price_cents_each INT, PRIMARY KEY(order_id, sku) );

6High-Level Architecture

Browser / Mobile │ HTTPS ▼ ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐ │ CDN (CloudFront) │ ← product pages cached 60 s └────────────┬────────────────────────┘ │ misses ▼ ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐ │ API Gateway (auth, rate-limit) │ └─┬──────┬────────┬──────────┬────────┘ │ │ │ │ ▼ ▼ ▼ ▼ Catalog Cart Checkout Order Svc Svc Svc Svc │ │ │ │ ▼ ▼ ▼ ▼ Postgres Redis Postgres+Redis Postgres (catalog) (cart) (inventory + idemp) (orders) Checkout flow side calls: ▶ Pricing Svc (taxes, promos) ▶ Payment Svc (Stripe / Razorpay) ▶ Fulfilment WMS (warehouse pick) ▶ Kafka events (order.placed)

7Deep Dive 1: Inventory Atomicity

The hardest correctness problem in this system. Two buyers click "Buy" on the last unit simultaneously — exactly one wins.

Approach 1: Database-level optimistic locking

UPDATE inventory SET available_qty = available_qty - 1, version = version + 1 WHERE sku = $1 AND available_qty >= 1 AND version = $2 -- expected version from read RETURNING version;

If 0 rows updated, the read was stale (or no stock) — retry with fresh read. Works at ~5k checkout/s comfortably; collapses for flash sales (~33k checkouts/s on a single row = lock contention).

Approach 2: Redis atomic DECR for hot SKUs

// Pre-load hot SKU stock into Redis SET inv:iphone-17-pro 10000 // On purchase attempt (Lua script for atomicity) local q = redis.call('DECR', KEYS[1]) if q < 0 then redis.call('INCR', KEYS[1]) return 0 // sold out end return 1 // got one

Redis handles ~200k DECRs/s on a single hot key. Persisting back to Postgres is async (write-behind, every 1 s). On Redis crash, replay from Postgres + the recorded order events to reconcile.

Approach 3: Reservation pattern (two-phase)

  1. Reserve: at checkout start, decrement available_qty, increment reserved_qty. Reservation expires in 15 min.
  2. Commit: on payment success, decrement reserved_qty (it's now sold).
  3. Release: on payment failure or timeout, return reserved → available.

This makes the rare "payment took 12 minutes" case correct. Standard pattern in Amazon, Flipkart, BookMyShow. We use Approach 1 for low-traffic SKUs and Approach 2+3 for flash-sale SKUs.

⚠ The Oversell Anti-Pattern

Reading available_qty, checking >= 1 in app code, then issuing UPDATE without the WHERE available_qty >= 1 condition. Two requests can both read 1, both think they can buy, both decrement to 0 and -1. Always include the inventory predicate in the WHERE clause so the atomic decrement can fail.

8Deep Dive 2: Flash Sales — Surviving 100× Traffic

An iPhone launch at 9:00 IST: 1M users mash F5. 10k units available. The system must:

  1. Serve 1M product-page reads in the buildup without melting.
  2. Atomically allocate 10k units to the fastest 10k clickers.
  3. Reject the other 990k cleanly with a friendly "sold out" page.

Layer 1: CDN absorbs reads

The product page (HTML, images, JS) is cacheable for 60 s. CDN serves 99% of reads from edge. Origin sees ~10k QPS, manageable.

Layer 2: Virtual queue for "Buy" clicks

Clicking "Buy" doesn't directly try to decrement inventory. Instead:

  1. Client gets a queue token (signed JWT with position).
  2. Position is determined at the gateway by Redis INCR queue:iphone.
  3. Client polls or holds an SSE connection waiting for "you're up."
  4. Server admits batches (e.g. 100 tokens every 100 ms) into the actual checkout path.

Backpressure is built-in: the inventory subsystem only sees admitted traffic, never the raw firehose.

Layer 3: Atomic Redis DECR

Admitted requests hit the Lua DECR script above. First 10k succeed; rest are told "sold out" and redirected to similar products.

Layer 4: Async write to Postgres

Successful purchases are immediately committed in Redis (inventory) and Kafka (order.placed). A consumer durably writes to Postgres within seconds. The user sees confirmation from the Redis path; durability is achieved via Kafka.

Layer 5: Anti-bot

Captcha before queue entry; per-user / per-IP rate limit; behavioural scoring (mouse movement, typing rhythm). Bot purchases are reversed within minutes via fraud rules; the seat returns to inventory.

9Deep Dive 3: Checkout Idempotency & Order State Machine

Idempotency end-to-end

Network blips cause the client to retry. We must not create two orders. The client generates an Idempotency-Key (UUID); the server inserts orders with that key as a unique constraint. The second request sees the same order_id and the same state — duplicates collapse into one.

Order state machine

CART → CHECKOUT_INITIATED → PAYMENT_PENDING │ ┌────────────────────────┤ ▼ ▼ PAYMENT_FAILED CONFIRMED │ │ ▼ ▼ CANCELLED PICKED → PACKED → SHIPPED │ ▼ DELIVERED │ ┌─────────────────────────┤ ▼ ▼ RETURNED (final)

The reservation lifecycle

At CHECKOUT_INITIATED: reserve inventory (15-min TTL). At CONFIRMED: convert reservation to sale (decrement reserved_qty). At PAYMENT_FAILED / timeout: release reservation back to available. This dance is the most common source of subtle bugs — always test reservation-expiry edge cases.

10Deep Dive 4: Cart — Server-Side vs Client-Side

Why server-side wins

  • Cross-device sync (cart on phone visible on laptop).
  • Marketing analytics (cart abandonment is a $$ metric).
  • Price recalculation (promo expired since you added the item).
  • Recovery emails ("you left these in your cart").

Storage

Redis Hash per user (sub-ms reads). Async-mirrored to Postgres every minute for durability and cross-device sync. On Redis miss (cold), reconstruct from Postgres.

Cart correctness, not order correctness

Adding to cart does not reserve inventory. The cart is just a list of intentions; only checkout reserves. This means the cart can contain SKUs that have since sold out — surfaced at checkout, not on cart add.

11Deep Dive 5: Catalog Search & Product Pages

The CDC-fed Elasticsearch mirror

Catalog Postgres is the source of truth. CDC (Debezium) streams updates to Kafka → consumer indexes into Elasticsearch. ES handles full-text search, faceted filters (price/brand/rating), and category browse.

Product detail pages

Pre-rendered HTML at deploy time for stable info; dynamic blocks (price, inventory status, reviews) hydrated client-side. Each block has its own caching policy (price cached 30 s, inventory cached 5 s).

12Failure Modes & Recovery

FailureMitigation
Payment provider downCheckout returns "try again in a few minutes." Reservation persists for 15 min so cart isn't lost. Failover to secondary provider for high-priority traffic.
Redis hot-key crashPostgres has the source of truth. Reconstruct Redis from last snapshot + replay order events. Brief flash-sale outage (~30 s) recoverable; we surface "demand spike, please retry" rather than 500.
Inventory undersold (cron mismatch)Daily reconciliation job compares Postgres inventory with Redis snapshot + sum(order_items where state=CONFIRMED). Discrepancies flagged for ops.
Bot army drains stockAnti-bot defences before queue entry. Suspicious orders quarantined > 1 hour; if fraud confirmed, cancel and re-release inventory.
Postgres failover during flash saleRead replicas continue serving catalog. Writes paused for ~30 s during failover; pending checkouts retry. Reservation TTL extended for affected window.

13Scaling Path

StageArchitecture
1k usersMonolith. Single Postgres. No cart service; just a session.
1M usersCatalog cache in Redis. Cart service. Async order events to a queue for emails.
10M usersMicroservices split. CDN. Inventory in dedicated Postgres. Optimistic locking everywhere.
100M usersMulti-region. Hot-SKU Redis sharded by SKU. Virtual queue for flash sales. Event-driven order pipeline.
1B usersGeographic data residency. Edge-side personalised pricing. ML demand forecasting integrated with inventory pre-positioning.

14Cross-Questions and Pushbacks

"Postgres for inventory at 1M QPS flash sale — won't it die?"
Answer: Postgres absolutely cannot take 1M QPS on a single row. That's why hot SKUs route through Redis with atomic DECR (200k+/s on a single key, comfortably). Postgres becomes the durable mirror. The architecture is "Postgres for correctness, Redis for hot-path speed." The reconciliation runs every few seconds; on Redis failure, we replay from Postgres. For the long tail of cold SKUs, Postgres with optimistic locking is perfectly fine (less than 1 update/s/SKU typically).
"What happens if Redis crashes mid-flash-sale? Did we just oversell?"
Answer: Three layers of defence. (1) Redis AOF persistence with fsync-every-second — at most 1 s of orders lost on crash. (2) Order events via Kafka are durable independently — even if Redis loses 0.5 s, Kafka has the order list. (3) Reconciliation: on Redis recovery, we count orders in Kafka and rebuild the Redis counter as initial_stock − orders_in_kafka. If the recovered counter is negative, we have oversold — alert ops, cancel the latest N orders (refunds), apologise. The frequency of this in practice is <1 in 10,000 flash sales.
How do you handle "buy 5 items in one checkout where one is sold out"?
Atomicity at checkout: reserve all 5 in a single transaction. If any of the reserves fails (insufficient stock), roll back all. The user is told which item failed; can edit cart and retry. This is one transaction in Postgres — easy. For multi-SKU with mixed Redis-hot + Postgres-cold, we acquire Redis reservations first (one Lua script per SKU); on any failure, rollback Redis (INCR back) and roll back Postgres in the same transaction.
How does cancellation work after the order is placed?
State machine guards it. Cancellable if state ∈ {CONFIRMED, PICKED, PACKED}. Once SHIPPED, must be a return flow instead. Cancel returns inventory atomically (Redis INCR + Postgres UPDATE in a tx). Refund triggers a payment-reverse event. After SHIPPED, the user must use returns: package recovery + warehouse intake + condition check before refund. Different workflow, both share the order state machine.
"Why not Cassandra for orders? It scales better."
Answer: Orders require ACID for state transitions (CONFIRMED → SHIPPED can't lose), joins for analytics, and the order/order_items relationship. Cassandra would force denormalisation (items as a list inside the order row); updating one item's status would require read-modify-write on the entire list — slow and race-prone. Postgres sharded by user_id handles our 10k writes/s easily, and we get strong consistency + joins. We do use Cassandra-style stores for high-volume eventually-consistent things (session, view-event logs); orders aren't that.
How do you handle promo codes / discount stacking?
A separate Pricing Service computes the final total at checkout: base price + tax + shipping − promotions. Promos have rules (one per cart, stackable types, expiry, user-eligibility). The result is locked at expected_total_cents in the checkout request — if the recalculated server-side total differs, reject (anti-tamper). Per-user-per-promo redemption tracked in Postgres with a unique constraint to prevent double-use. For high-traffic promos (Black Friday code), pre-mint redemption tokens in Redis instead of a global counter to avoid contention.
How do you avoid showing a "10 in stock" badge that is wrong?
The displayed stock count is intentionally fuzzy: "in stock", "low stock", "out of stock" — not a precise count. Hard count would require constant cache invalidation. Fuzzy levels are cached for 30 s. For checkout, we use real-time atomic decrement; the user sees the precise outcome at the checkout moment, not before. Showing "1 left" leads to fake-urgency complaints; showing "in stock" is honest and stays cacheable.
"Virtual queue means users wait. Won't they churn to competitors?"
Answer: The alternative for a real flash sale is server collapse — they don't get to buy anyway, and they see a 500 error. Compared to that, "you're #4,217 in line, estimated 90 s" is the better UX. Apple, Sony, Nike all use virtual queues for hyped launches. We also make the wait useful: show stock status, similar products, related accessories. Conversion on "you didn't get the limited unit but here's a similar one in stock" is ~10–15%.
How do you handle abandoned carts?
Carts have TTL 30 days but don't reserve inventory. An async job runs hourly: any cart unchanged for >1 h triggers a recovery flow (email at 1 h, push at 4 h, discount offer at 24 h). Tracked as a funnel metric: which step in checkout led to abandonment. Abandoned cart recovery typically recaptures 5–10% of would-be lost orders — large business value.

End of Problem 10. Next: Search Autocomplete (P11) — trie, top-K, trending.

Medium Information Retrieval Trie Top-K Real-Time

Problem 11: Designing Search Autocomplete

User types two characters, you have 50 ms to return the ten most-likely completions out of billions of possibilities — and the popularity list should be fresh enough to surface "Taylor Swift Eras Tour" the same evening it starts trending.

Article Contents

  2. Requirements Gathering
  3. Capacity Estimation
  4. API Design
  5. Data Model
  6. High-Level Architecture
  7. Deep Dive 1: Trie with Top-K Caching
  8. Deep Dive 2: Offline Trie Build Pipeline
  9. Deep Dive 3: Real-Time Trending Updates
  10. Deep Dive 4: Personalisation and Locale
  11. Deep Dive 5: Typo-Tolerance and Fuzzy Match
  12. Failure Modes & Recovery
  13. Scaling Path
  14. Cross-Questions and Pushbacks

1Context and Why This Problem Matters

Autocomplete sits in front of every search box on the web. It looks trivial ("just match prefix → top results") and is in fact a tight optimisation problem in three dimensions simultaneously: latency (sub-50 ms), freshness (trending in minutes), and personalisation (your history matters). The interview question tests if you understand the trie data structure and how to extend it with caching, real-time updates, and personalisation without falling into the obvious traps.

2Requirements Gathering

Functional

  • Given a prefix (1–32 chars), return top-10 completions ordered by popularity.
  • Support hot-trending queries within minutes.
  • Per-locale results (en-US vs en-IN differ in popularity).
  • Per-user personalisation (history bias).
  • Spelling tolerance — minor typos still return useful suggestions.

Non-functional

  • P99 latency < 50 ms end-to-end (typing feel).
  • QPS: ~30k autocomplete calls/sec aggregated (3× the user's actual search QPS — every search produces multiple autocomplete calls).
  • Unique queries indexed: ~100M.
  • Availability: 99.95% (broken autocomplete looks broken to users).

Out of scope

  • The actual search engine (autocomplete is a separate, lighter system).
  • Voice / image autocomplete.

3Capacity Estimation

MetricNumber
Searches/day~1 B
Autocomplete calls/day~3 B (3× searches)
Avg QPS~35 k/s
Peak QPS~100 k/s
Distinct queries seen~1 B (long tail)
Queries with popularity > 100/day (worth indexing)~100 M
Avg query length~20 B
Trie size (raw)~5 GB
Trie + top-K caches per node~15 GB — fits a single big-RAM node
🔑 From Numbers to Architecture
  • ~100 k peak QPS at < 100 ms (perceived as instant) → in-memory trie servers; no DB on the hot path.
  • ~15 GB trie + top-K caches per language → fits in RAM on one large node (~64 GB box); horizontally replicated for QPS, not partitioned (trie shape is too small to shard usefully).
  • Each trie replica owns a language / locale → router picks the right node by locale header; ~5 replicas per locale for 100 k QPS handles peak.
  • Long-tail (~1 B distinct queries) → only ~100 M queries with popularity > 100/day are worth indexing; rest fall through to plain search.
  • Popularity scores derived from clickstream → offline batch job (Kafka → Spark) rebuilds the trie hourly; hot reload via blue-green swap.
  • Personalisation (user history) → small per-user re-ranker applied on top of trie's top-K; user history cached in Redis.

4API Design

GET /v1/suggest?q=sys&locale=en-US&user_id=u_abc&limit=10 Response 200: { "query": "sys", "took_ms": 23, "suggestions": [ { "text": "system design", "score": 0.97 }, { "text": "systeme international", "score": 0.41 }, ... ] }

Cache headers: Cache-Control: private, max-age=10 — short, since trending changes.

5Data Model

Trie node

struct TrieNode { children: Map<char, TrieNode*>, top_k: Array<(query, score)> // pre-computed cached list of top-10 from this prefix is_term: bool // marks an end of word }

Query popularity store (the offline-build input)

// Daily aggregated query → count CREATE TABLE query_counts ( query VARCHAR(255), locale VARCHAR(10), day DATE, count BIGINT, PRIMARY KEY (query, locale, day) ); -- Aggregation source: search logs in Kafka → BigQuery / ClickHouse

Real-time trending counts (Redis)

// Count-Min Sketch in Redis, updated per search event PFADD trending:1min:cms:{shard} query_string (probabilistic) ZADD trending:1min:topk score query (top-K leaderboard)

6High-Level Architecture

Client │ GET /suggest?q=sys ▼ ┌─────────────────────────────┐ │ Edge Cache (CDN) │ ← cache hits served at edge, 10 s TTL └────────┬─────────────────────┘ │ miss ▼ ┌─────────────────────────────┐ │ Suggest Service │ │ - look up trie shard │ │ - read top-K from prefix │ │ - blend with trending Redis │ │ - blend with user history │ │ - return top-10 │ └────┬──────────────┬─────────-┘ │ │ ▼ ▼ Trie shards Redis trending (in-memory) (recent queries) Async pipelines: • Search events (Kafka) → ClickHouse (daily aggregation) → Trie build (nightly) • Search events → Streaming aggregation → trending Redis (every minute)

7Deep Dive 1: Trie with Top-K Caching

A vanilla trie supports prefix search but to find top-10 completions, you'd traverse the entire subtree below the prefix node. With millions of words, that's slow. Optimisation: store top-K at every node.

Trie for queries: "sys", "system", "system design", "system call" root │ s │ y │ s ── top_k = [(system design, 0.97), (systems, 0.5), ...] / | \ _ t ... │ e ── top_k = [(system design, 0.97), (systems, 0.5), ...] │ m ── top_k = [(system design, 0.97), (system call, 0.3), ...]

Lookup is now O(prefix length). For "sys", walk 3 nodes, return their cached top_k. Sub-millisecond inside the node; the bulk of the latency is network.

Memory cost

Storing 10 entries per node × ~10 chars per entry × millions of nodes = a few GB extra. Worth it.

8Deep Dive 2: Offline Trie Build Pipeline

Computed nightly from yesterday's data:

  1. Aggregate raw search logs (Kafka) into (query, locale, count) in ClickHouse / BigQuery.
  2. Apply a popularity decay: score = sum_over_days_d ( count_d × 0.9^d ). Older days count less, so trending naturally surfaces.
  3. Per locale, take the top 10M queries.
  4. Build trie in batch (MapReduce): map each query → emit at every prefix length; reduce → at each prefix, keep top-K by score.
  5. Serialise to binary trie format; publish to S3.
  6. Suggest service nodes pull the new trie file, swap in-memory pointer atomically (no read downtime).

The build runs in ~30 minutes on a modest Spark cluster. Daily refresh keeps the corpus current; intraday freshness comes from the Redis trending layer below.

9Deep Dive 3: Real-Time Trending Updates

"Taylor Swift announces tour" needs to be in autocomplete results within minutes, not 24 hours.

The streaming pipeline

  1. Search events flow to Kafka topic search.queries.
  2. A Flink job consumes, maintains rolling 1-minute and 1-hour counters per (query, locale) using Count-Min Sketch (~bounded memory).
  3. Top-K per minute (~10k entries) written to Redis sorted set.
  4. Suggest service blends: take the trie's top-K and Redis trending top-K, re-rank by combined score (weighted, e.g. 0.8 × static + 0.2 × trending).

Tuneable: more weight on trending during news events, less during stable times. Some systems detect "burst" patterns (acceleration in count) and dynamically up-weight.

10Deep Dive 4: Personalisation and Locale

Locale

One trie per locale. "Cricket" is huge in en-IN, niche in en-US. The locale parameter routes to the right trie. Per-locale tries are independent — trivially scaled.

Per-user history bias

Maintain a small per-user Redis hash of their last ~50 queries with frequencies. At suggest time:

  • Get top-K from the trie (global popularity).
  • Get user's history matching the prefix (small list).
  • Combine: final_score = global_score + α × user_history_score; α tuned offline.

Result: a user who searches "system" often sees "system design" higher than a random user.

11Deep Dive 5: Typo-Tolerance and Fuzzy Match

User types "sysetm" — we want "system" to come up. Approaches:

Levenshtein automaton (BK-tree)

Build a BK-tree of all indexed queries. Query: find all words within edit distance 2 of the input. Combined with prefix matching, this works for short typos. Computational cost is higher than pure trie traversal.

N-gram index

Each query is decomposed into character n-grams (3-grams: "system" → "sys", "yst", "ste", "tem"). The input is decomposed similarly; matching queries share many n-grams. Tolerant to non-prefix typos. Used by Elasticsearch's edge-n-gram analyser.

Pragmatic compromise

Pure trie for the on-prefix case (99% of queries). On a low-confidence trie result (top result's score is low), fall back to a fuzzy match path against the popularity table. Adds latency for the rare case but doesn't penalise the common.

12Failure Modes & Recovery

FailureMitigation
Trie shard downSuggest service routes to replicas. ≥2 replicas per shard; behind health-check load balancer.
Bad trie build deployedBuild pipeline runs offline test against held-out queries; if relevance drops, halt deploy. Manual roll-back is one S3 pointer change.
Redis trending lagStale by minutes is fine — autocomplete works against trie only. Trending boost just doesn't fire.
Hot trending event overwhelms RedisPer-shard sketches; aggregation step picks union top-K. No single hot key.
Personalisation Redis missFall back to global results. User sees standard autocomplete (acceptable).

13Scaling Path

StageArchitecture
1k queriesIn-memory trie in app process. Local cache.
1M queriesStandalone autocomplete service. Trie loaded from S3 on startup. Nightly refresh.
100M queriesSharded trie (by prefix range). Redis trending overlay. CDN cache for top prefixes.
Multi-regionPer-region trie replicas. Locale-routed. Edge caching aggressive.

14Cross-Questions and Pushbacks

"Elasticsearch has edge-n-gram out of the box. Why not just use that?"
Answer: Elasticsearch with edge-n-grams works fine up to ~1M queries indexed and ~5k QPS. Beyond that: index size explodes (every query stored as 20 n-grams), latency rises (P99 starts hitting 100 ms+), and tuning popularity ordering becomes painful (BM25 isn't designed for ranking by frequency). A purpose-built trie with cached top-K is 10× faster at our scale. We do use ES for typo-fallback and rare-query cases, hybrid model.
"Storing top-K at every node — that's 100× memory blowup, no?"
Answer: Per node we store ~10 entries × ~15 bytes = ~150 B overhead. Tries typically have ~10 nodes per query × 100M queries = 1B nodes; total ~150 GB. We shard tries by alphabet prefix across 10 nodes: ~15 GB per node, fits in RAM (256 GB instance). Without the top-K cache, every suggest call would walk thousands of subtree nodes — 100× slower. The memory cost is the price of latency, and it's bounded.
How does popularity decay handle the "old hit song" problem (was popular in 2008, indexed forever)?
Time-decayed score: score = Σ count_d × 0.9^d. A song popular only in 2008 (~6,000 days ago) decays to ~0. Recent popularity dominates. The trade-off: a slow-burn meme that gains attention over months ranks competitively because recent counts matter more. Decay rate α=0.9 is tuned; some queries (evergreen — "weather", "calculator") get α=1 (no decay) by classifier.
How do you avoid surfacing offensive autocomplete suggestions?
Blocklist of phrases. Two-layer: (1) exact-match blocklist of known offensive queries — never indexed. (2) Classifier model run at build time on candidate top-Ks; predicted offensive entries dropped. Some terms are contextual ("knife" is fine, "how to … with knife" isn't); the classifier handles n-grams not single tokens. False positives are reviewed quarterly. Critical: prefix matching doesn't propagate — typing "how to" doesn't surface anything offensive even if a longer offensive query exists in raw logs.
When does the suggested list get refreshed during a typing session?
Every keystroke after the first triggers a request, with a 100 ms debounce. So typing "sys" fires after the "s" pause, then another for "y", then "s". The HTTP response includes the prefix used; the client only renders if the response's prefix matches the current input (race protection). Cancellation via AbortController for in-flight requests when a new key is pressed.
How would you handle non-Latin scripts (Hindi, Chinese)?
Per-language trie because character-level structure differs. For Chinese, indexing pinyin (Romanised) alongside characters lets users type "beijing" and find "北京". For Indic, transliteration map "kal" → "कल" expands prefixes. Each language has its own trie + transliteration adapter. The locale param picks the right combination.
"50 ms latency budget — but you mentioned CDN cache + service + Redis. That's three hops at least."
Answer: Most requests are served at CDN (95% hit rate on common prefixes like "th", "the", "sys") — ~10 ms total. The misses go through one service call (10 ms) which reads in-memory trie (<1 ms) plus a Redis trending check (1 ms parallel) — total ~15 ms. Add 10–15 ms client-to-edge network. 50 ms budget is comfortable. The personalisation Redis call is also parallel, not serial.

Hard Audio / Pattern Match Fingerprinting FFT Inverted Index

Problem 12: Designing Shazam — Audio Fingerprinting at Scale

"Identify a song from a 5-second noisy snippet against 50M tracks." Looks like signal processing magic; underneath it's a particularly clever inverted-index lookup.

Article Contents

  2. Requirements Gathering
  3. Capacity Estimation
  4. API Design
  5. Data Model
  6. High-Level Architecture
  7. Deep Dive 1: The Fingerprinting Algorithm
  8. Deep Dive 2: The Hash Database
  9. Deep Dive 3: Time-Offset Voting
  10. Deep Dive 4: Noise Tolerance and False Positives
  11. Deep Dive 5: Ingesting Music — Building the Index
  12. Failure Modes & Recovery
  13. Scaling Path
  14. Cross-Questions and Pushbacks

1Context and Why This Problem Matters

Shazam is one of the few system-design questions where the algorithm matters as much as the architecture. The 2003 Wang paper describes a "constellation map" fingerprinting scheme that's been the industry baseline since. The interview tests whether you understand:

  • Why naive approaches (waveform matching, FFT-only) don't work in noisy environments.
  • How to turn a continuous signal into discrete hashes for inverted-index lookup.
  • How voting on time offsets discriminates one true match from millions of coincidental hash hits.

2Requirements Gathering

Functional

  • Upload a 5–15 s audio clip recorded on a phone (noisy bar / car / kitchen).
  • Return the matched song's metadata: title, artist, album, links to streaming.
  • Return "no match" when there's no high-confidence identification.
  • Support ad-hoc index updates (label releases new singles daily).

Non-functional

  • End-to-end match latency < 3 s (the clip is 5–10 s; users tolerate a moment after).
  • Throughput: ~10M queries/day at peak hour ~1k QPS.
  • Index: ~50M songs × ~2,000 hashes each = ~100B index entries.
  • Accuracy: >95% true positive on clean recordings; >80% in moderate noise.
  • False positives strictly < 0.1%.

3Capacity Estimation

MetricDerivationNumber
Songs indexed—50 M
Hashes per song~2 per 100 ms × 3-min avg~3,600
Total hashes50M × 3,600~180 B
Index entry size (hash → (song_id, time_offset))~16 B—
Total index size180B × 16 B~3 TB
Query: hashes generated per 10s clip—~200
Index lookups per query~200 hash lookups → fan into list of (song,offset)—
Average matches per hashfingerprint hash collision rate~50–200
Candidates per query (raw)200 × ~100~20,000
After voting consolidation—~10 plausible
🔑 From Numbers to Architecture
  • ~3 TB fingerprint index + 200 hash lookups/query at < 2 s → must be in RAM (disk would be ~2 s alone); shard the hash → postings index across ~50 RAM-rich nodes.
  • Each query = 200 hashes → fan out to multiple shards in parallel; aggregator votes by song-offset alignment; sub-second.
  • Music catalog ~30 M songs × ~10 KB metadata → fits in a single Postgres (no contention with the heavy index path).
  • Hash collision rate ~50–200 entries/hash → ~20 k raw candidates per query; offset-voting consolidates to ~10 plausible matches; threshold for high-confidence.
  • Audio clip upload from mobile → client computes the fingerprint locally; only ~200 hashes (small) sent to server, not the audio bytes. Bandwidth savings.
  • Index build (offline) → ingest pipeline computes constellation map and writes shards; new songs visible within hours.

4API Design

POST /v1/identify Content-Type: audio/aac (or .wav, .m4a) Body: ~10 seconds of audio Response 200: { "match": { "song_id": "s_abc", "title": "Bohemian Rhapsody", "artist": "Queen", "album": "A Night at the Opera", "confidence": 0.97, "matched_time_in_song_sec": 142 // where in the song we matched }, "alternatives": [ { "song_id": "s_xyz", "confidence": 0.21 }, ... ] } Response 200 (no match): { "match": null, "alternatives": [] }

Optionally the client extracts fingerprints locally and sends only hashes (lower bandwidth, more CPU on phone). Shazam supports both modes.

5Data Model

Songs metadata (PostgreSQL)

CREATE TABLE songs ( song_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, title VARCHAR(255), artist VARCHAR(255), album VARCHAR(255), duration_s INT, isrc VARCHAR(20), release_dt DATE, cover_url TEXT, links_jsonb JSONB -- Spotify, Apple Music, YouTube );

Fingerprint index (the heart — distributed inverted index)

// Conceptual schema (real impl: sharded RocksDB or in-memory custom) hash_key: uint32 (32-bit fingerprint hash) postings: [ (song_id: uint32, time_offset_ms: uint32), ... ] // Across cluster: shards by hash_key prefix // Each shard: in-memory hashmap or LSM-tree backed

6High-Level Architecture

Phone records 10 s audio │ ▼ Optionally: client-side fingerprint extraction (lower upload) │ ▼ HTTPS POST /identify (audio or hashes) ┌─────────────────────────────┐ │ Match API Gateway │ └────────┬─────────────────────┘ │ ▼ ┌─────────────────────────────┐ │ Fingerprint Extractor │ ← if server got raw audio │ - FFT, peaks, hashes │ └────────┬─────────────────────┘ │ ~200 hashes ▼ ┌─────────────────────────────┐ │ Match Service │ │ - scatter to N index shards│ │ - vote on time offsets │ │ - pick winner by confidence│ └────────┬─────────────────────┘ │ song_id ▼ ┌─────────────────────────────┐ │ Songs metadata (Postgres) │ └─────────────────────────────┘ Async pipelines: • Label releases → Ingest pipeline → Add fingerprints • Match logs (Kafka) → Analytics (popularity, trends)

7Deep Dive 1: The Fingerprinting Algorithm

The "constellation map" approach (Wang 2003) is the canonical interview answer:

  1. Window the audio: slide a 100 ms window every 20 ms.
  2. FFT each window: produce a frequency-vs-time spectrogram.
  3. Find peaks: in each frequency band, locate strong amplitude peaks. These are "anchor points" — frequency-time coordinates where the song has a distinctive feature.
  4. Form pairs: pair each anchor point with several nearby peaks within a "target zone" (next 1–2 s, fan-out factor ~5). Each pair becomes a hash.
  5. Compute hash: hash = (freq1, freq2, delta_t) → 32-bit integer.
  6. Store: (hash) → (song_id, anchor_time_offset) in the index.
Spectrogram of a song: frequency │ * * │ * * * * │ * * * │ * * * │_________________________________ time Peaks (asterisks) are the "constellations." Hash = pair of two peaks: (f1, f2, Δt) This combination is robust: • Background noise adds non-peak energy — peaks survive. • Volume changes don't matter — only the peak locations are used. • A second-long burst of cough kills ~5% of hashes — rest still match.

Why pairs and not single peaks

Single-peak hashes collide too much — many songs share a frequency peak at the same time. Pairs are far more discriminating: roughly 10^6 distinct pairs in the index vs 10^3 single peaks per band.

8Deep Dive 2: The Hash Database

180B entries × 16 bytes = ~3 TB. To answer ~200 hash lookups per query in < 100 ms, the index must be RAM-resident (or RAM-cached on heavy SSDs).

Sharding

Shard by hash_key % N across 50 nodes, each ~60 GB RAM hot index + posting lists on local SSD as overflow. Each shard handles ~2k QPS comfortably. With 50 shards × 2k QPS each, we can support 100k queries/s — overkill for our 1k QPS, but the layout is the right shape for scale-out.

Storage layout per shard

Each shard maintains a hashmap from hash_key → posting list (offset into a per-shard packed array). Posting lists are sorted by song_id and delta-encoded.

9Deep Dive 3: Time-Offset Voting

A query produces ~200 hashes. Each hash returns ~100 candidate (song, anchor_offset) pairs from the index. That's ~20,000 raw candidates. Most are random collisions across different songs — only the true match should produce consistent time offsets.

The voting trick

For each hash in the query, recorded at time t_q, and each candidate (song, t_a) in its posting list:

  • Compute delta = t_a − t_q.
  • For the true match, delta is the same across all ~200 hashes (it's "the offset of this clip into the song").
  • For false matches, delta is essentially random.

So bucket all candidates by (song_id, delta). The bucket with the most votes wins. A true match typically has ~150 of the 200 hashes voting for the same delta; runner-up false matches have ~5–10 random hits.

Confidence score

confidence = winning_bucket_size / total_hashes_in_query = e.g. 152 / 200 = 0.76 If confidence > 0.4 → declare match. If < 0.2 → no match. Between → tentative; rely on alternatives.

10Deep Dive 4: Noise Tolerance and False Positives

What noise does to fingerprints

  • White noise: raises the baseline; many peaks survive because they're relative maxima.
  • Conversation in background: similar — voice peaks rarely overlap musical peaks.
  • Other music in background: this is the killer — bleeds into the same frequency-time grid; voting can shift to the wrong song.
  • Bandwidth-limited audio (phone speaker → microphone): cuts off >8 kHz peaks. Index design uses peaks across full spectrum but more weight on robust mid frequencies.

False positive rate analysis

With ~10^9 possible hashes and ~10^11 stored, false collisions are common per hash. The voting step is what discriminates: random collisions don't produce a consistent delta, so they spread across buckets. The probability of 50 false hashes all producing the same delta by chance is astronomically low.

11Deep Dive 5: Ingesting Music — Building the Index

Ingest pipeline

  1. Record label drops new track in S3 (with metadata).
  2. Ingest service detects new file, runs fingerprint extraction (~10 s of compute per song).
  3. Extracted fingerprints written to a Kafka topic fingerprints.new.
  4. Index update service consumes, computes shard for each hash, writes to that shard's append-only log.
  5. Shards periodically compact their logs into the main index (background, no read impact).
  6. Metadata written to Postgres.

End-to-end: a new song is matchable within ~5 minutes of upload.

Index updates without downtime

Append-only segments. Reads consult both the main compacted index and recent segments. Compaction merges segments in the background, atomic switch when ready. Same pattern as Cassandra and Elasticsearch.

12Failure Modes & Recovery

FailureMitigation
Index shard downReplicas (2× each shard). Match service falls over to replica with negligible latency cost.
Slow shard slows queryHedge requests: after 50 ms with no reply, send to another replica; first response wins.
Ingest backlogAsync pipeline; new songs delayed by minutes during burst. Surface freshness lag in ops dashboard.
Fingerprint extractor bugCanary: compare output of new extractor vs old on a known corpus before deploy.
False match storm (degraded accuracy)Confidence thresholds tuned per recall/precision targets; ops alerts on a sudden rise in low-confidence matches.

13Scaling Path

StageArchitecture
1k songsSingle in-memory hashmap. Fingerprinting in app process.
1M songsOne dedicated fingerprint server; ~60 GB RAM. Postgres for metadata.
50M songsThis article's design: 50 shards × 60 GB RAM each. Match service scatter-gather.
Hum-based / voice searchDifferent fingerprint algorithm (pitch contour matching); parallel pipeline.

14Cross-Questions and Pushbacks

"Why not just store waveforms and use cross-correlation?"
Answer: Cross-correlation requires comparing the query against every song — O(N × len) computation. For 50M songs that's prohibitive. More fundamentally, cross-correlation breaks under noise and time stretching. Fingerprints discretise the audio into hashes that survive noise (only peak locations, not amplitudes) and allow inverted-index O(1) lookup. The combination of robustness + indexable representation is the whole reason fingerprinting works.
"3 TB index in RAM — that's expensive. Can we use SSD?"
Answer: The cost is real but manageable: 50 nodes × ~80 GB RAM ≈ $50/mo each = ~$2,500/mo for the index fleet. That's tiny next to a music-streaming infrastructure. SSDs could work but 200 random disk reads per query × 100 μs = 20 ms — bursts into our 3 s budget noticeably. Modern NVMe makes SSD viable; if we're cost-sensitive, hybrid (top postings in RAM, long tail on SSD) is a fine evolution. Shazam-the-product runs heavily RAM-biased.
How do you handle when a clip is recorded over the song's own background music in a video?
The voting mechanism handles it surprisingly well: the foreground song produces a consistent delta vote across ~80% of its hashes; the background song produces a different delta with ~30% of hashes. The winner is the foreground. For cases where both songs are equally strong, we return the top-2 with confidence scores and let the user pick.
What about cover versions / live performances of the same song?
Covers won't match because the fingerprints depend on exact timing, key, and instrumentation. This is by design — Shazam returns the recording you heard, not "any version of this song." For cross-version matching, a separate ML pipeline (mel-spectrogram → CNN embedding → ANN search) handles "hum-to-search" and cover detection. It's a totally different pipeline that lives alongside.
How would you support live broadcasts (e.g. radio identification)?
Reverse the model: streams the radio station, continuously fingerprints, matches against the index in real-time. Maintain a rolling buffer of the last 30 s. Every second, identify the song playing. Useful for royalty enforcement (proving a station played a track) and "what's playing now" services.
"How do you keep the index updated when labels release thousands of new tracks daily?"
Answer: 1000 tracks/day × 3,600 hashes each = 3.6M new entries/day = ~40 entries/s sustained — trivial for an append-only log per shard. Real-time inserts on the append side; periodic compaction (every ~6 h or by segment-size threshold) merges into the main compacted index. Reads see both: query the main index + the recent segments. The label-to-matchable delay is dominated by extraction CPU (~10 s/song), not write throughput.

Twitter's photo cousin — same fanout problem, but with media-heavy storage, ephemeral Stories, ranked Reels, and an Explore feed that's a separate recommendation system.
