1Context and Why This Problem Matters

Instagram looks like Twitter-plus-photos at first glance. In practice it has four largely independent product surfaces (Feed, Stories, Reels, Explore), each with different data-flow characteristics. A good design recognises that one architecture does not fit all four and articulates the differences.

2Requirements Gathering

Functional

  • Post photos and videos with captions, tags, location.
  • Home feed: latest posts from accounts you follow, ranked.
  • Stories: 24-h ephemeral posts arranged at top of feed.
  • Reels: short-form video, infinite recommended scroll.
  • Explore: discovery grid based on interests, no follow graph required.
  • Likes, comments, DMs (out of scope here — DMs use the chat system from P3).
  • Search by user, hashtag, location.

Non-functional

  • 2 B total users, 500 M DAU.
  • Feed read P99 < 200 ms.
  • Media upload time < 5 s for a typical photo.
  • Video playback starts < 1 s on 4G.
  • Availability 99.95%; durability of user content 11 9's.

3Capacity Estimation

MetricNumber
DAU500 M
Posts/user/day (avg)~0.2
Posts created/day~100 M
Feed reads/user/day (avg)~30
Feed reads/day~15 B
Feed reads/sec (avg)~175 k/s
Feed reads/sec (peak)~500 k/s
Stories posted/day~500 M
Reels watched/day~30 B
Media size avg (photo)~2 MB
Media size avg (video, 30s)~15 MB
Daily upload volume~1 PB
Storage at 5 yr × 3 replicas~5 EB
🔑 From Numbers to Architecture
  • ~500 k peak feed reads/sec → pre-computed per-user feed in Redis (fanout-on-write); read = ZRANGE in < 1 ms.
  • Pure fanout-on-write breaks on celebrities (one post → millions of writes) → hybrid push-pull: push for normal users (< 1 M followers), pull-on-read for celebrities; merged at feed-fetch time.
  • ~1 PB/day uploads × 5 yr × 3 replicas = ~5 EB → S3 with intelligent tiering; never proxy through app servers (presigned multipart).
  • Photos & videos → CDN (CloudFront) absorbs > 95% of media reads; transcoding pipeline produces multiple variants (resolutions, formats).
  • ~30 B reels watches/day → vertical scrolling feed = autoplay; client prefetches next 3 reels; per-user reel ranking ML model.
  • Stories TTL 24 h → metadata in Cassandra with TTL; S3 lifecycle deletes media after 25 h; stories are write-mostly, low read after first day.

4API Design

Post creation

POST /v1/uploads // multipart, resumable → { upload_id, ... } POST /v1/posts { "upload_ids": ["..."], "caption": "Sunset 🌅", "tags": ["#sunset"], "location": { "lat":..., "lng":... } } → { post_id, state: "PROCESSING" }

Feed

GET /v1/feed?cursor=eyJ0aW1lIjoxNjI...&limit=20 → { items: [ {post, author, engagement}, ... ], next_cursor: "..." }

Stories

GET /v1/stories // list of authors with active stories GET /v1/stories/{author_id} // their current story reel POST /v1/stories { upload_id } // adds a story, ttl 24 h

Reels

GET /v1/reels // personalised infinite feed POST /v1/reels/{id}/like

5Data Model

posts (Postgres, sharded by post_id)

CREATE TABLE posts ( post_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, author_id UUID NOT NULL, caption TEXT, media JSONB, -- [{type, url, dims, duration}, ...] location_id UUID, tags TEXT[], state VARCHAR(20), -- PROCESSING | READY | DELETED visibility VARCHAR(20), -- PUBLIC | FOLLOWERS | PRIVATE created_at TIMESTAMPTZ ); CREATE INDEX idx_author_time ON posts(author_id, created_at DESC);

follows (Postgres, sharded by follower_id)

CREATE TABLE follows ( follower_id UUID, followee_id UUID, created_at TIMESTAMPTZ, PRIMARY KEY (follower_id, followee_id) ); CREATE INDEX idx_followee ON follows(followee_id); -- for reverse queries

user_feed (Redis Sorted Set, one per user)

// ZSET feed:{user_id} // score = post timestamp (epoch ms), member = post_id ZADD feed:{u} 1747396523000 p_abc ZADD feed:{u} 1747396789000 p_xyz ZREVRANGEBYSCORE feed:{u} +inf -inf LIMIT 0 20 // TTL: 7 days; rebuild on miss

stories (Cassandra with TTL)

CREATE TABLE stories ( author_id UUID, story_id TIMEUUID, media BLOB_URL, view_count COUNTER, ttl_seconds 86400, PRIMARY KEY ((author_id), story_id) ) WITH default_time_to_live = 86400;

6High-Level Architecture

Client (mobile-dominant) │ ▼ API Gateway (auth, rate-limit, request routing) │ ┌───┴────┬─────────┬─────────┬────────┐ ▼ ▼ ▼ ▼ ▼ Post Feed Stories Reels Explore Svc Svc Svc Svc Svc │ │ │ │ │ │ Redis user_feed + Postgres posts │ ▼ Media pipeline: Upload → S3 → Transcoding workers → CDN (CloudFront) Async pipelines: • post.created → Fanout workers → write to user_feed:{follower} • like / comment → Engagement counters in Redis + Postgres • Reels watches → ML training pipeline • Stories view → counter

7Deep Dive 1: Media Upload & CDN Delivery

Upload flow

  1. Client requests presigned URL → server returns S3 multipart-upload URL.
  2. Client uploads directly to S3 (bypasses our servers; saves egress).
  3. Upload-complete webhook fires → kicks off processing pipeline.

Processing

  • Photos: re-encode to consistent JPEG quality; generate multiple sizes (thumbnail 150×, feed 1080×, hi-res 2160×).
  • Videos: transcode to HLS with 3 quality tiers (480p, 720p, 1080p). Generate cover thumbnail.
  • Content moderation: ML classifier flags NSFW/violent content; quarantine if flagged.

CDN strategy

All ready media is served via CDN with long TTL (1 year). The content URL contains a content hash so updates produce a different URL — no invalidation needed. Edge POPs world-wide; videos use range requests for ABR.

8Deep Dive 2: Home Feed — Hybrid Fanout

Same problem as Twitter (P2). Two strategies and a hybrid:

Push fanout (default for most users)

When user X posts, find all of X's followers; for each, ZADD into feed:{follower}. Cost: O(follower_count) per post; cheap for accounts with < 1M followers.

Pull fanout (for "celebrities" with > 1M followers)

Don't fan out. On feed read, for each followee, pull their last N posts and merge. This avoids the "Justin Bieber problem" — fanning to 100M followers per post.

The hybrid

Each user's home feed = (push-pre-computed entries) + (live-pulled entries from celebrities they follow). Merged at read time. This is exactly the Twitter pattern from P2.

Ranking

The merged set isn't chronological. ML scores each post by (predicted engagement × recency × relationship strength). Top-N returned. Models trained offline on user-post interaction logs.

9Deep Dive 3: Stories — Ephemeral 24-Hour Posts

Why a separate system

Stories have very different characteristics:

  • High write rate (~500 M/day, 5× posts).
  • Short lifetime (24 h auto-expire).
  • Sequential consumption (you watch a friend's whole reel).
  • Per-viewer state (who has watched what).

Storage

Cassandra with TTL=24 h. Partition key is author_id, sort by story_id (time-based). Rows auto-expire — no cleanup job needed.

View state

Per (viewer, story) view records. Redis Sorted Set per viewer: viewed:{user_id} with story_ids and timestamps; TTL 24 h. On retrieval of an author's stories, intersect with viewed set to know which are unseen.

Active-stories list

For the top-of-feed list of friends with active stories: maintain per-user "friends with active stories" set in Redis. Updated on every story post (add author to all followers' sets) and on story expiry (remove). Read at feed time is O(1).

10Deep Dive 4: Reels — The Recommendation Engine

Reels are NOT chronological. They're personalised, infinite, recommendation-driven. Closer to TikTok than to a feed.

Two-stage recommendation

  1. Candidate generation: from billions of Reels, narrow to ~hundreds per user. Done by:
    • Two-tower neural network producing user embedding and reel embedding; ANN search (FAISS) finds nearest.
    • Trending boost (recently popular Reels).
    • Editorial / safety filters.
  2. Ranking: a heavier model (XGBoost / DNN) scores each candidate by predicted P(complete | watch), P(like), P(share). Top-N returned per page.

Online signals

As the user scrolls, every dwell-time and skip event streams to Kafka, updates per-user features in real-time. Subsequent batches reflect very recent behaviour ("you skipped 3 cooking videos in a row — show less of those").

11Deep Dive 5: Explore — Discovery Without Follows

Explore shows content from accounts you don't follow. Used to discover. Different from Reels: grid layout, mix of photos and short videos.

Cohort-based recommendation

Cluster users into ~10k cohorts by behavioural similarity. For each cohort, periodic top-K content (most-liked by cohort members in the last 24 h). User sees their cohort's top-K with deduplication against what they've already seen.

Hashtag and location

Searching "#sunset" returns posts tagged sunset, ranked by recency × popularity. Stored as a separate inverted index in Elasticsearch with a CDC mirror from posts.

12Failure Modes & Recovery

FailureMitigation
S3 region outageMulti-region replication; CDN continues serving from replicas. Posts in flight may pause.
Feed Redis downFall back to Postgres-pulled chronological feed; degraded UX but works.
Fanout backlogAuto-scale workers. Worst case: new posts take minutes to appear in followers' feeds.
Stories TTL missCassandra handles TTL natively; rare. Background sweeper catches stragglers daily.
Recommendation model badA/B canary catches relevance regressions; auto-rollback.

13Scaling Path

StageArchitecture
1k usersMonolith. Photos in S3. Simple chronological feed.
1M usersSplit services. Push fanout. Redis feed cache.
100M usersHybrid fanout. Cassandra stories. Reels candidate generator.
2B usersMulti-region. ML ranking tier. Edge ML for personalisation.

14Cross-Questions and Pushbacks

"Why use 4 different architectures for 4 surfaces — isn't that over-engineering?"
Answer: They have orthogonal characteristics that one architecture serves poorly. Feed is chronological-with-rank, Stories is ephemeral-with-view-state, Reels is recommendation-heavy, Explore is cohort-driven. Trying to force one design (e.g. unified feed) creates pathologies: stories' high write rate would overwhelm the feed pipeline; reels' ML scoring would dominate per-request cost; explore's broad-discovery doesn't fit a follow-graph feed. Engineering teams are usually organised by surface for the same reason.
How does Instagram handle the "celebrity post" problem differently from Twitter?
Same hybrid principle, but Instagram's celebrities have much larger follower counts (BTS at 70M, Cristiano Ronaldo at 600M). The pull path becomes the primary mechanism for these accounts. We don't fan out their posts; on each follower's feed read, we pull their last K posts on-demand and merge. The push path serves 99% of accounts (those with < 1M followers); pull serves the 1% with huge audiences.
How do you keep the Reels recommendation fresh as new videos go viral?
Real-time signals via Kafka. As likes/shares accumulate on a new video, its score in the candidate pool rises. Within minutes, it begins surfacing to relevant cohorts. A bursty engagement signal (50× normal in a 5-minute window) triggers "potentially viral" flagging; ML model boosts that video's exposure for the next hour. This is how content goes from 1k views to 1M views in a day.
"Stories at 5 B writes/day to Cassandra — won't that be expensive?"
Answer: Cassandra's write cost is ~$0.001/k operations on managed services; 5B writes = $5,000/day, ~$150k/month — small for a $30B revenue product. But more importantly, Cassandra's TTL + append-only structure is the only thing that scales at this rate cheaply. Postgres would need explicit deletion jobs and indexes that fight the write rate. Cassandra's columnar layout with TTL is purpose-built for this exact workload.
How do you measure feed quality and roll out ranking changes?
Holdout A/B tests: random 1% of users see the new ranker, rest see control. Metrics watched: engagement rate, dwell time, return rate, complaint rate. New ranker promoted only if it lifts at least one core metric without regressing others by > statistical-significance threshold. Some metrics are negative-signal (bounce rate, "I don't want to see this" clicks).
How do you handle bulk operations like "delete all posts of a banned user"?
Async pipeline. Banning the user emits an event; consumer iterates over the user's post IDs (paginated query against posts table) and marks state=DELETED with a tombstone marker. CDN URLs become 410 Gone. Feed entries with deleted post IDs are filtered out at read time (cheaper than rewriting all followers' feed lists). Backfill cleanup runs nightly to purge tombstoned entries from feed Redis after 7 days.

Hard Money / Billing Cron Scheduler Dunning Proration Tax

Problem 14: Designing a Subscription Management System

Netflix, Spotify, AWS — billing cycles, plan changes, retries on failed charges, taxes per jurisdiction, and a dunning workflow that recovers ~30% of declined cards if you do it right.

1Context and Why This Problem Matters

Subscriptions look simple until you ship them. Three flavours of complexity bite:

  • Money math — proration, refunds, tax, multi-currency, idempotency. Mistakes cost real money and reputation.
  • Time — billing on the 31st in a 30-day month, leap years, DST, time-zone-aware quiet hours, retries spread over days.
  • Dunning — a failed card isn't a lost customer. ~30% recoverable with the right retry strategy.

2Requirements Gathering

Functional

  • Sign up for a plan with a billing cycle (monthly, annual).
  • Auto-renew on cycle end; charge payment method on file.
  • Trial periods (free for N days, then auto-charge).
  • Plan changes (upgrade, downgrade) with proration.
  • Cancel — at cycle end, or immediate with refund.
  • Failed payments → dunning workflow → eventual involuntary churn.
  • Tax computation per recipient jurisdiction.
  • Email receipts; invoice PDFs.

Non-functional

  • 100 M active subscribers, ~10 M billings/day at peak (1st of month).
  • Billing P99 latency < 30 s (acceptable for an offline scheduler).
  • No double-charges. Ever.
  • Auditability for tax/regulatory.
  • Availability 99.99% for self-service (changes, cancellations).

3Capacity Estimation

MetricNumber
Active subscribers100 M
Avg billing cycles per year~13 (mostly monthly)
Billing events/year~1.3 B
Billing events/day (avg)~3.5 M
Billing events/day (peak, 1st of month)~10 M
Billing peak/sec~115/s if uniform; up to 1000/s if synchronised
Failed-charge rate~5–10% (industry typical)
Daily failed charges~350 k
Average dunning retries~4 over 14 days
Tax jurisdictions~200 countries + 50 US states + …
🔑 From Numbers to Architecture
  • ~10 M billing events/day peak on the 1st (~1000/s synchronised) → easily handled by Postgres; but spread the load via "billing anniversary" (each customer's renewal date is their signup date) — eliminates the 1st-of-month spike.
  • ~5–10 % failed charges/day (~350 k) → dunning state machine with timed retries (1, 3, 7, 14 days) via job scheduler; not a tight loop.
  • Money-critical → idempotency keys on every charge call; outbox pattern → CDC ensures every state change emits exactly one event.
  • 200+ tax jurisdictions → tax computation is a separate microservice (Stripe Tax / TaxJar / Avalara); never compute tax in code.
  • Subscription state machine (trialing → active → past_due → canceled) → modelled explicitly; saga handles rollback if any step fails.
  • Webhooks from payment processor are the source of truth for "did the charge succeed?" → idempotent webhook handler; signature-verified.

4API Design

POST /v1/subscriptions { "user_id": "u_abc", "plan_id": "plan_premium_monthly", "payment_method_id": "pm_123", "trial_days": 14, "promo_code": "WELCOME10" } → { subscription_id, state: "TRIALING", next_billing_at: "..." } GET /v1/subscriptions/{id} PATCH /v1/subscriptions/{id}/plan { new_plan_id: "plan_premium_annual" } // upgrade POST /v1/subscriptions/{id}/cancel { at_period_end: true } // or immediate

5Data Model

subscriptions (PostgreSQL)

CREATE TABLE subscriptions ( subscription_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, user_id UUID NOT NULL, plan_id VARCHAR(64) NOT NULL, state VARCHAR(20), -- TRIALING, ACTIVE, PAST_DUE, CANCELLED, CHURNED current_period_start TIMESTAMPTZ, current_period_end TIMESTAMPTZ, next_billing_at TIMESTAMPTZ, billing_anchor_day INT, -- e.g. "15" for "15th of every month" timezone VARCHAR(50), payment_method_id UUID, cancel_at_period_end BOOLEAN, trial_end TIMESTAMPTZ, created_at TIMESTAMPTZ, updated_at TIMESTAMPTZ ); CREATE INDEX idx_next_billing ON subscriptions(next_billing_at) WHERE state IN ('ACTIVE','PAST_DUE');

invoices (PostgreSQL)

CREATE TABLE invoices ( invoice_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, subscription_id UUID, amount_cents BIGINT, tax_cents BIGINT, currency CHAR(3), state VARCHAR(20), -- DRAFT, OPEN, PAID, FAILED, VOID billing_period_start TIMESTAMPTZ, billing_period_end TIMESTAMPTZ, due_at TIMESTAMPTZ, paid_at TIMESTAMPTZ, pdf_url TEXT, idempotency_key VARCHAR(255) UNIQUE );

payment_attempts (PostgreSQL)

CREATE TABLE payment_attempts ( attempt_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, invoice_id UUID, attempt_number INT, result VARCHAR(20), -- SUCCEEDED, DECLINED, ERROR error_code VARCHAR(50), -- 'insufficient_funds', 'card_expired', ... attempted_at TIMESTAMPTZ, next_retry_at TIMESTAMPTZ );

6High-Level Architecture

Customer / Admin UI │ ▼ Subscription Service (HTTP) │ ▼ Postgres subscriptions, invoices, payment_attempts Async pipelines: • Billing Scheduler — every minute polls subscriptions where next_billing_at <= NOW() AND state IN (ACTIVE, PAST_DUE) → emit billing.due • Invoice Generator — consumes billing.due → creates invoice → emit invoice.created • Charger — consumes invoice.created → calls Payment Service → records attempt • Dunning Worker — consumes payment.failed → schedules next_retry_at → emits notification • Notification Service (P8) — sends receipt, dunning email, cancel email • Payment Service (P21) — token vault, smart routing

7Deep Dive 1: Billing Cycle Calculation

"Charge them on the 15th of every month" — surprisingly subtle.

Anchor day pinning

Store billing_anchor_day = 15 at signup. On each cycle end, next_billing_at = (this period + 1 month, day=15). If the month has no day 15 (never happens for 15, but does for 31), clamp to the last day of the month. February 29 → March 28 (the same "month-of-day" arithmetic).

Time zones

Store timezone per subscription. "Charge at start of day in their local time" means converting next_billing_at to UTC at signup using that tz. DST changes are handled by the cron library (croniter / Joda) — never compute by hand.

Drift avoidance

Recompute from the original anchor, not from the most recent attempt. A subscription billed on 2025-01-15, then again on 2025-02-15, should still be 2025-03-15 — even if the Feb attempt fired at 02:00 instead of 00:00 due to delay. Always: next = anchor + N × interval, not next = last_attempt + interval.

Trials

Trial period: state=TRIALING, no charge yet. trial_end → first billing. On trial_end, immediately try to charge; if successful, transition to ACTIVE; if not, transition to PAST_DUE and enter dunning.

8Deep Dive 2: Dunning — Recovering Failed Payments

A card declines. Don't immediately churn — many declines are transient (insufficient funds today, paid tomorrow; card expired but auto-updater rolls in).

Smart retry schedule

Decline → retry at +1d, +3d, +5d, +7d. Total 4 attempts over 7 days. After all retries: state=CHURNED. Subscription cancelled. Final email sent.

Per-error customisation

  • insufficient_funds: retry as above; statistically high recovery.
  • card_expired: solicit new payment method via email/in-app; pause retries until user updates.
  • fraudulent: do not retry; require user-initiated re-auth.
  • do_not_honor (issuer's vague decline): retry with smart routing (different processor).

Card Updater services

Visa Account Updater / Mastercard ABU automatically refresh card details when a card is replaced. Saves ~30% of expired-card churn. Run a daily job to refresh tokens.

Communication during dunning

  • 1st decline: low-touch email "we tried to charge your card."
  • 2nd: more direct "please update payment method."
  • 3rd: in-app banner + push notification.
  • Final: "subscription expiring" with one-click resubscribe offer.
🔑 The Quiet Hours Rule for Dunning

Never send dunning emails between 10 pm and 9 am user time. Negative-sentiment messages during off-hours are statistically worse at recovery. Worth ~5% recovery delta.

9Deep Dive 3: Plan Changes and Proration

The formula

User upgrades from $10/month to $30/month mid-cycle, 10 days into a 30-day cycle. They've already paid $10. Cost recovery:

unused_credit = $10 × (20/30) = $6.67 upgrade_cost = $30 × (20/30) = $20.00 charge_now = $20.00 − $6.67 = $13.33 new_period_end = unchanged (keeps same anchor)

Implementation

  1. Compute prorated credit from old plan.
  2. Compute prorated charge for new plan.
  3. Issue a one-off invoice for the delta.
  4. Update plan_id; keep cycle anchor unchanged.

Downgrades

Usually deferred — switch takes effect at end of current period (no proration credit). Avoids "switch to cheap, get refund, switch back" gaming.

10Deep Dive 4: Tax Compliance

Subscription tax is determined by:

  • Recipient's address (country + state/region).
  • Product type (subscription, digital, physical).
  • Customer type (B2C, B2B with valid VAT ID).

Tax services

Outsource the rate lookup to a specialist (Avalara, TaxJar, Stripe Tax). Pass them the invoice line items and address; they return the tax breakdown. Cache rates per country×state for 24 h; invalidate on official updates.

VAT IDs

EU B2B sales: collect customer's VAT ID, validate against VIES API, reverse-charge mechanism (no VAT collected, customer self-assesses). Audit logged.

Tax invoicing

Generated PDF invoices must include: seller's tax ID, buyer's name and address, tax breakdown, jurisdiction-specific fields. Stored long-term (7 years typical) for audits.

11Deep Dive 5: Churn Prediction

Predict which subscribers are likely to cancel; target them with retention offers before they ask.

Features

  • Engagement: logins, usage minutes, content consumption.
  • Billing: failed payment recently, tenure, plan changes.
  • Support: number of contact instances, sentiment.

Model and action

Gradient-boosted model trained on historical cancellations. Daily batch scores all active subscribers. Top X% by predicted churn risk get a targeted offer (discount, plan downgrade option, content recommendation). Retention rate uplift measured via control group.

12Failure Modes & Recovery

FailureMitigation
Billing scheduler down for hoursIdempotent charges with idempotency_key = subscription_id:period_id. On recovery, scheduler picks up where it left off; no double charges.
Payment processor outageSmart routing to secondary processor. Pause charges if both down; resume when up; users not impacted unless outage > 24 h.
Tax service downUse cached rates for 24 h; mark invoices as "tax estimate" needing reconciliation if outage persists.
Bug causes wrong charge amountAll charges go through a dual-entry ledger; daily reconciliation catches discrepancies. Refund process automated for confirmed errors.
User claims they were charged after cancellationAudit log of state transitions resolves it. Issue refund if confirmed; tighten cancel→charge race window.

13Scaling Path

StageArchitecture
1k subscribersStripe handles everything. Webhook into your app.
100k subscribersOwn subscriptions table; Stripe just for payment processing. Custom dunning.
10M subscribersInternal billing scheduler. Dunning ML. Multi-processor smart routing. Local tax engine.
100M subscribersMulti-region. Currency-aware ledger. Per-jurisdiction tax compliance. Churn prediction integrated.

14Cross-Questions and Pushbacks

"Just use Stripe Billing — why build any of this?"
Answer: Below ~$5M ARR, Stripe Billing is the right answer; the cost of building > cost of Stripe fees. As you scale, three reasons to build: (1) fees — at $1B ARR, even 0.5% saves $5M/year. (2) flexibility — bespoke plan structures, custom dunning rules, regional pricing. (3) data ownership — own the customer relationship, support has full visibility, churn analysis can use raw data. Most companies migrate gradually: keep Stripe for processing, own the subscription layer.
"What if your billing scheduler double-charges a subscription?"
Answer: Idempotency at multiple layers. (1) Invoice creation uses idempotency_key = subscription_id:period_id with a unique constraint — concurrent attempts result in one invoice. (2) Payment attempts pass that idempotency key to the payment processor; even if our charger fires twice, the processor recognises the dupe. (3) Daily reconciliation: sum of invoices = sum of charges, mismatches alerted. The chance of a "real" double charge slipping through is negligible; defensive design assumes it will happen and detects.
How do you handle currency for a multi-region product?
Each plan has prices in multiple currencies (USD, EUR, INR, etc.). Customer picks the currency at signup, locked for the subscription's lifetime. Invoices issued in that currency. Exchange-rate fluctuation doesn't change the billed amount — only the merchant's converted revenue. Tax computed in customer's local currency. Payment processor receives the local currency and settles to the merchant in their preferred currency at the daily rate.
How does a refund work end-to-end?
Admin triggers refund via API → invoice flagged for refund with amount and reason → call to payment processor's refund API → on success, ledger entry created (debit revenue, credit refund), state=REFUNDED → email customer. Partial refunds supported (refund $5 of a $20 charge). Refunds cannot be reversed once processed — guarded by an admin double-confirmation.
How do you prevent users from gaming free trials with multiple emails?
Trial eligibility tied to multiple signals: card fingerprint (same card = same person, regardless of email), device fingerprint, address-of-record. Combination of these flags repeat trial-creation. Hard block after detection; user must convert to a paying account to continue. Edge cases (family sharing same card) require human review — small enough fraction to handle manually.
"On the 1st of the month, 10M subscriptions all fire — that's a thundering herd. How do you handle it?"
Answer: Jitter the schedule. Each subscription's next_billing_at is anchored to its signup day, not literally the 1st. So users who signed up on the 15th are charged on the 15th. Naturally spreads load over 30 days. If a particular day still has a spike (last day of month + monthly anchor), we add deterministic intra-day jitter (hash(subscription_id) % 14400 seconds = within the first 4 h of the day). Result: peak billings/sec is ~600, easily handled. Also: billing is non-time-critical (it can take 30 min) so the scheduler doesn't need wall-clock precision.

Problem 15: Designing a Generic Tagging Service

Tag any entity (post, photo, ticket, user) with arbitrary strings; query both directions efficiently; handle aliases, casing, multi-tenancy, and the inevitable "show me everything tagged #foo" performance trap.

1Context and Why This Problem Matters

Tagging is the "polymorphic association" of modern systems: one mechanism applies to many entity types. It looks trivial — a many-to-many relation — but the production version has to handle hashtag-style explosions (one tag attached to billions of posts), Unicode/emoji edge cases, user-generated aliases, multi-tenant SaaS isolation, and bidirectional queries with very different cardinalities.

2Requirements Gathering

Functional

  • Attach one or more tags to any entity (entity is opaque: just type + id).
  • List all tags on an entity.
  • List all entities tagged with a given tag (paginated).
  • Tag search / autocomplete by prefix.
  • Bulk tag operations (apply N tags to M entities atomically).
  • Aliases: "JavaScript" = "JS" = "javascript" — queries unify them.
  • Per-tenant isolation: Tenant A's tags don't bleed into Tenant B's autocomplete.

Non-functional

  • 1 B tagged entities, ~100 M distinct tags.
  • Read latency P99 < 50 ms.
  • Write latency P99 < 200 ms.
  • Throughput: ~50 k read QPS, ~5 k write QPS.
  • Eventual consistency between the two indexes is acceptable.

3Capacity Estimation

MetricDerivationNumber
Total tag-entity edges1B entities × avg 5 tags~5 B
Edge row size (entity_id, tag_id, timestamps)~50 B—
Storage for edges (one direction)5B × 50 B~250 GB
Storage for both directions × 3 replicas2 × 250 × 3~1.5 TB
Unique tags—~100 M
Hottest tag size (#love on Instagram)—~2 B entities
Read QPS peak—~50 k/s
Write QPS peak—~5 k/s
🔑 From Numbers to Architecture
  • ~50 k read QPS / 5 k write QPS → Cassandra for both directions; partition key chosen per access pattern (dual table pattern).
  • "Tags on this entity" returns ~5 → partition by entity_id; tiny read.
  • "Entities for this tag" can return billions for hot tags (#love) → partition by tag_id, bucket within tag ((tag_id, time_bucket)) to avoid single huge partitions.
  • Hot tag fanout → top-K most-popular entities per tag pre-computed and cached in Redis; cold tags fall through to Cassandra.
  • Free-form tag search (autocomplete on tag names) → Elasticsearch index of tags (~100 M); decoupled from the entity-tag mapping store.
  • Spam / abuse tags → moderation queue + per-user rate limit on tagging operations.

4API Design

// Tag an entity (idempotent) POST /v1/tags { "tenant_id": "t_acme", "entity": { "type": "POST", "id": "p_123" }, "tags": ["javascript", "tutorial", "beginner"] } → 200 { "tagged_count": 3, "deduplicated": 0 } // Remove a tag from an entity DELETE /v1/tags { "entity": {...}, "tags": ["beginner"] } // List tags on an entity (small result) GET /v1/entities/{type}/{id}/tags → { "tags": ["javascript", "tutorial"] } // List entities for a tag (paginated, big result) GET /v1/tags/javascript/entities?type=POST&cursor=...&limit=20 → { "entities": [{type, id, tagged_at}, ...], "next_cursor": "..." } // Autocomplete tag names GET /v1/tags/suggest?q=jav&tenant_id=t_acme → { "suggestions": ["javascript", "java", "javase"] } // Alias management POST /v1/tags/aliases { "canonical": "javascript", "alias": "js" }

5Data Model

tags (the canonical tag registry)

CREATE TABLE tags ( tag_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, tenant_id UUID NOT NULL, canonical_form VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL, -- lowercase, normalised display_form VARCHAR(100), -- preserve original casing for UI usage_count BIGINT DEFAULT 0, -- denormalised popularity counter created_at TIMESTAMPTZ, UNIQUE (tenant_id, canonical_form) ); CREATE INDEX idx_tag_search ON tags(tenant_id, canonical_form text_pattern_ops);

tag_aliases

CREATE TABLE tag_aliases ( alias_form VARCHAR(100), tenant_id UUID, canonical_tag_id UUID REFERENCES tags(tag_id), PRIMARY KEY (tenant_id, alias_form) );

tags_by_entity (forward index — "tags on entity X")

CREATE TABLE tags_by_entity ( tenant_id UUID, entity_type VARCHAR(50), entity_id UUID, tag_id UUID, tagged_at TIMESTAMPTZ, PRIMARY KEY (tenant_id, entity_type, entity_id, tag_id) ); -- Sharded by (tenant_id, entity_id)

entities_by_tag (reverse index — "entities tagged X")

CREATE TABLE entities_by_tag ( tenant_id UUID, tag_id UUID, entity_type VARCHAR(50), entity_id UUID, tagged_at TIMESTAMPTZ, PRIMARY KEY ((tenant_id, tag_id), tagged_at, entity_id) ) -- In Cassandra: partition by (tenant_id, tag_id), cluster by tagged_at DESC -- In Postgres: shard by tag_id; secondary index on (tenant_id, tag_id, tagged_at DESC)

6High-Level Architecture

Client │ POST /tags / GET /entities/{id}/tags ▼ ┌─────────────────────────────┐ │ Tag Service (HTTP) │ │ - canonicalise input │ │ - resolve alias → canonical │ │ - dual-table write │ └────────┬────────────────────-┘ │ ┌───────┴───────────┐ ▼ ▼ tags_by_entity entities_by_tag (forward) (reverse) Postgres/Cassandra Cassandra (hot tags) Emits Kafka events: • tag.added — for analytics, search index, audit log • tag.removed Search: Tag registry (Postgres) → CDC → Elasticsearch tag autocomplete index

7Deep Dive 1: The Dual-Table Pattern

The fundamental insight: (entity → tags) and (tag → entities) are different query patterns with different cardinality and access shapes. Storing them as two independent tables lets each be optimised for its own read.

Why not one table with two indexes

You can — and at small scale (a few million edges) it's fine. At billions of edges, the secondary index becomes huge and write-amplifying. In Postgres, every insert updates the primary B-tree + the secondary B-tree. In Cassandra, secondary indexes are local-per-partition and don't satisfy a "all entities for this tag" query without scatter-gather. The dual-table pattern shows up exactly when scale forces this fork.

Write path

Adding tag T to entity E writes both rows in a transaction (Postgres) or in a write-batch (Cassandra: LWT or just relying on per-row atomicity if eventual consistency is acceptable). If one side succeeds and the other fails, a background reconciliation job sweeps mismatches every hour.

Read paths

  • "Tags on entity E" → one PK lookup in tags_by_entity → ~5 rows. Sub-millisecond.
  • "Entities tagged T" → range scan on entities_by_tag partition for tag T → paginate by tagged_at. Each page sub-millisecond; entire result set may be billions of rows.

8Deep Dive 2: Canonicalisation and Aliases

Canonicalisation pipeline

Every input tag passes through:

  1. Trim whitespace.
  2. Unicode NFKC normalisation (compose accented chars, half-width to full-width, etc.).
  3. Lowercase (using Unicode-aware ICU rules, so İ → i correctly).
  4. Strip leading "#" if present.
  5. Validate against allowed-character regex (Unicode letters + digits + a few connectors).
  6. Apply alias substitution: if the input matches an alias, route to the canonical tag.

Why display vs canonical

Canonical "javascript" is used for storage and joins. Display "JavaScript" is shown to users (preserving the first-seen casing). Aliases ("js", "javascripty") share the same canonical tag but display their preferred form when set.

Alias creation

Admin-initiated: a moderator or auto-classifier proposes "ny" → "newyork". Past taggings on the alias remain attached to the alias' tag_id, but queries against either form return unified results because the resolver maps both to the canonical tag_id at query time.

⚠ The Merge Trap

Don't physically merge alias rows into canonical rows. The migration is too expensive and risky for billion-row tables. Instead, keep both tag_ids and add a query-time fan-out: SELECT … WHERE tag_id IN (canonical, alias_1, alias_2). Cheap at read time, zero migration risk.

9Deep Dive 3: Multi-Tenant Isolation

This is a SaaS-style service: tenant A and tenant B should never see each other's tags.

Tenant in every key

Every table starts with tenant_id. Indexes start with tenant_id. Partition keys start with tenant_id. Tags are isolated by physical separation in the storage layout.

Authorisation

JWT contains tenant_id. Service rejects any request where the URL/body tenant_id doesn't match the JWT's. Tenants can't impersonate via API.

Sharding by tenant

Large tenants (millions of entities) sit on dedicated shards. Small tenants share shards. Per-tenant rate limits prevent a single noisy customer from impacting others.

10Deep Dive 4: Tag Search and Autocomplete

"Show me tag names starting with 'java'": this is the autocomplete problem (P11), scoped to the tenant.

Implementation

The tag registry (Postgres) is mirrored to Elasticsearch via CDC. Per-tenant index (or per-tenant alias on a shared index). Tags ranked by usage_count. Query is a prefix search filtered by tenant_id, returning top-10. Latency < 30 ms.

Why not query Postgres directly

With 100 M tags and 50 k QPS suggest calls, Postgres B-tree on tag name handles it but with worse latency curves. Elasticsearch gives sub-30 ms P99 and better ranking flexibility (fuzzy match, typo correction). Adds operational cost; worth it past a threshold.

11Deep Dive 5: The "Popular Tag" Hot-Key Problem

Some tags accumulate billions of entries: #love, #fashion, #food. Querying "all entities tagged #love" is impossible to satisfy in any reasonable latency. Two defences:

Paginated reads with cursor

Never return more than a page (e.g. 100). The cursor encodes (tag_id, last_tagged_at). Range scan on the next page is bounded by LIMIT, returning in ~5 ms regardless of total partition size.

Hot-tag partition splitting

When a single partition exceeds ~10 GB (Cassandra recommendation), split it:

  • Original: partition key = (tenant_id, tag_id)
  • Split: partition key = (tenant_id, tag_id, bucket) where bucket = hash(entity_id) % 16

Reads must now query all 16 buckets in parallel and merge by tagged_at. More expensive per read but bounded; without the split, partition operations would degrade catastrophically.

12Failure Modes & Recovery

FailureMitigation
Dual-write partial failureReconciliation job (hourly) compares forward and reverse indexes; repairs mismatches. Mismatches expected but bounded.
Hot tag overwhelms one nodeBucketed partition split; cache the top-K popular tag reads in Redis.
Alias misconfigured (loop a → b → a)Validate at alias creation: walk alias chain; reject if cycle or depth > 1.
Cassandra TTL miss for old archived tagsTags don't expire by default. Optional archive-old job moves entries > 5 yrs to cold storage.
Search index lagAutocomplete may not show very-newly-created tags for 30 s. Acceptable.

13Scaling Path

StageArchitecture
1k entitiesPostgres single table with many-to-many. No service.
10M entitiesDedicated tag service. Dual table both in Postgres. Indexes in Postgres.
1B entitiesThis article's design: Cassandra for reverse index, Postgres for registry. Elasticsearch for autocomplete.
10B+ entitiesPer-tenant dedicated shards. Hot-tag bucket splitting. Edge-cached popular tag pages.

14Cross-Questions and Pushbacks

"Why not store tags as a JSONB array on the entity itself?"
Answer: For "tags on entity" reads, JSONB is fine — one row fetch, parse array. But for "entities tagged X", you'd need to scan every entity row checking the JSONB array. A GIN index on the array makes it queryable but at scale (1B entities) the index is huge and updates are write-amplifying. The dual-table pattern is the established answer for billion-edge graphs; storing as array works up to ~10M entities.
"Cassandra for reverse index — why not Elasticsearch for everything?"
Answer: Elasticsearch is great for text search, less great for billion-entry inverted lookups by exact key. ES with 100M tag-shards and a billion entries would be expensive operationally (cluster size, memory, GC pressure). Cassandra's partitioning model maps perfectly onto "entries per tag partition" — append-only writes, time-ordered scans, native pagination. We do use ES, just for autocomplete on tag names, where its strengths (text matching, ranking) shine.
How do you handle bulk tagging (tag 1M entities with one tag in a campaign)?
Async job. Producer service POSTs a bulk-tag request → service returns a job_id and creates work units (e.g. 10k entities per batch). Workers consume from Kafka, write in batched transactions, emit per-entity events for downstream listeners. Progress is queryable via job_id. Idempotency key per batch prevents double-tagging on retries.
How do you support tag-renaming (e.g. typo "fasion" → "fashion")?
Two strategies. (1) Soft rename via alias: create an alias "fasion" → "fashion". Reads naturally unify; writes prefer the canonical form. No data migration. (2) Hard rename: schedule a migration job that updates all entries in entities_by_tag from tag_id_A to tag_id_B; takes hours; risk of write conflicts during. Soft rename is almost always preferred; hard rename only if you must clean up the registry.
How do you handle tag deletion?
"Delete tag T everywhere it appears" is expensive — must touch the tag's partition in entities_by_tag (could be billions of rows) and update every affected entity's row in tags_by_entity. We mark tag_id as DELETED in the registry; reads filter it out. Async cleanup job sweeps over time. For privacy-required deletes (GDPR), expedite the cleanup with priority workers.
"Eventual consistency between forward/reverse indexes is dangerous — what if a user removes a tag but it still shows on the tag's page?"
Answer: Reads from entities_by_tag include a per-row "active" check against tags_by_entity (or use a small Redis "recently deleted" filter for hot tags). The discrepancy window is ~seconds, not hours. For absolute correctness on a high-stakes tag (compliance-flagged content), use transactions on both tables — adds latency, applied only where needed. For typical UGC tagging, the window is acceptable.

Problem 16: Designing a Distributed Job Scheduler

"Run this task at 2 am IST every weekday, retry on failure, resume from step 3 if step 4 fails, never lose a job, never run it twice." Sounds like Airflow — and you should be able to defend it against Cassandra at the table.

  2. Requirements Gathering
  3. Capacity Estimation
  4. API Design
  5. Data Model
  6. High-Level Architecture
  7. Deep Dive 1: Why PostgreSQL Over Redis or Cassandra
  8. Deep Dive 2: Partial Index + SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
  9. Deep Dive 3: Multi-Step Jobs and Resume-From-Failure
  10. Deep Dive 4: Cron Expressions and next_run_at
  11. Failure Modes & Recovery

1Context and Why This Problem Matters

Every backend has scheduled work: billing runs, retries, email digests, ML batches. Building a fault-tolerant scheduler exposes a lot of distributed-systems thinking: exactly-once semantics, leader election, retry storms, the cron correctness problem, and the under-appreciated power of SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED. Real systems with this shape: Airflow, Temporal, Sidekiq, GoodJob, Oban.

2Requirements Gathering

Functional

  • Submit a job to run once at time T, or recurring per cron.
  • Multi-step jobs: chain of N steps; on step failure, retry just that step.
  • Failure retries with exponential back-off.
  • Cancel and pause/resume.
  • Tenant isolation, priority queues.
  • At-least-once guarantee (idempotent steps required); exactly-once not promised.

Non-functional

  • 10M scheduled jobs, ~1M cron jobs.
  • Peak: 10k jobs/sec firing on the hour boundary.
  • Scheduling latency: jobs fire within 5 s of their scheduled time at P99.
  • Availability 99.95%.

3Capacity Estimation

MetricNumber
Total jobs in flight~10 M
Jobs created/day~10 M
Avg job firings/sec~116
Peak firings/sec (top of hour)~10 k
Steps per job (avg)~3
State writes per job~6 (start, per-step transitions, complete)
State writes/sec (avg)~700
State writes/sec (peak)~60k
Hot jobs partial-index size~3500 rows × 30 s window
🔑 From Numbers to Architecture
  • ~3 500 jobs in the 30-s lookahead window → partial index on (status='PENDING' AND run_at < now+30s) is tiny; fits in RAM; scheduler query is O(log n) regardless of 100 M total jobs.
  • ~60 k peak state writes/sec → easily within Postgres write budget; group_commit + batched UPDATEs keep latency low.
  • Many concurrent workers competing for the same job → SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED lets each worker claim disjoint job rows atomically; no Redis lock needed.
  • Worker crash mid-job → lease/heartbeat watchdog re-queues jobs whose lease expired; idempotent job execution is the contract.
  • Cron schedules → next-fire-time computed at insert/update and stored as run_at; no live cron evaluation; same partial-index path handles cron + one-off.
  • Audit / retry history → append-only job_runs table partitioned by date; queryable for ops; cold-tier to S3 after 90 days.

4API Design

POST /v1/jobs { "name": "send_digest", "schedule_type":"CRON", // ONE_TIME | CRON "cron_expr": "0 9 * * MON-FRI", "timezone": "Asia/Kolkata", "steps": [ { "type": "HTTP", "url": "https://...", "method": "POST", "body": {...}, "max_retries": 3 }, { "type": "LAMBDA", "function_arn": "...", "max_retries": 2 } ], "priority": "HIGH", "payload": { ... }, // shared context for all steps "tenant_id": "t_abc" } → { job_id, state: "PENDING", next_run_at: "..." } POST /v1/jobs/{id}/pause POST /v1/jobs/{id}/resume POST /v1/jobs/{id}/cancel GET /v1/jobs/{id} // current state + per-step progress GET /v1/jobs?state=FAILED&cursor=...

5Data Model

jobs (PostgreSQL, sharded by tenant_id)

CREATE TABLE jobs ( job_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, tenant_id UUID NOT NULL, name VARCHAR(255), schedule_type VARCHAR(10), -- ONE_TIME | CRON cron_expr VARCHAR(100), timezone VARCHAR(50), state VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL, -- PENDING|RUNNING|COMPLETED|FAILED|PAUSED|CANCELLED priority SMALLINT DEFAULT 5, next_run_at TIMESTAMPTZ, -- UTC; the partial index column current_step INT DEFAULT 0, total_steps INT NOT NULL, retry_count INT DEFAULT 0, max_retries INT DEFAULT 3, payload JSONB, last_error TEXT, worker_id UUID, heartbeat_at TIMESTAMPTZ, created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW(), updated_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW() ); -- THE critical index: partial on PENDING only CREATE INDEX idx_pending_jobs ON jobs (next_run_at ASC) WHERE state = 'PENDING';

job_steps

CREATE TABLE job_steps ( step_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, job_id UUID REFERENCES jobs, step_index INT NOT NULL, step_type VARCHAR(50), step_config JSONB, state VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL, input JSONB, output JSONB, error_msg TEXT, retry_count INT DEFAULT 0, max_retries INT DEFAULT 3, started_at TIMESTAMPTZ, completed_at TIMESTAMPTZ, UNIQUE (job_id, step_index) ); CREATE INDEX idx_job_steps_resume ON job_steps(job_id, step_index) WHERE state != 'COMPLETED';

6High-Level Architecture

Producer services │ POST /jobs ▼ ┌────────────────────────┐ │ Submission API │ │ - validate cron │ │ - compute next_run_at │ │ - INSERT into jobs │ └────────────────────────┘ ┌─────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────────────┐ │ Watchdog │ │ Scheduler (3 nodes, │ ◀── leader elect ──▶ │ - finds stuck │ │ leader-elected) │ │ RUNNING jobs │ │ every 5s: │ │ - resets to PEN│ │ SELECT FOR UPDATE │ └─────────────────┘ │ SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 500 │ │ WHERE next_run_at <= │ │ NOW() + 30s │ │ → push to Kafka │ └────────┬────────────────┘ │ ▼ ┌─────────────────────────┐ │ Kafka: jobs.due │ — partitioned by job_id └────────┬────────────────┘ │ ▼ ┌─────────────────────────┐ │ Workers (auto-scaled) │ │ - claim by UPDATE state │ │ - execute each step │ │ - on each step done: │ │ UPDATE job_steps │ │ UPDATE jobs progress │ │ - on cron complete: │ │ recompute next_run_at│ │ state ← PENDING │ └────────────────────────-┘ Postgres = source of truth. Kafka = transport between scheduler and workers.

7Deep Dive 1: Why PostgreSQL Over Redis or Cassandra

This is the most common pushback in the interview. The defence has four parts:

1. We need ACID across (job + step) updates

On cron recurrence: "mark last step COMPLETED, set job.state=PENDING, set new next_run_at, reset all steps" must be one transaction. If it's three writes that can be partially applied, you get duplicate fires, missed fires, or zombie jobs. Cassandra can't do multi-table transactions natively; Redis Multi-EXEC is fragile and lacks the schema.

2. We need SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED

The lynchpin of multi-worker claiming. 50 schedulers run the same query simultaneously; each gets a disjoint set without an external lock manager. Redis doesn't have row-level locks; you'd need a separate distributed lock service per claim.

3. Quantify the writes — Postgres handles them easily

Peak ~60k writes/s. Postgres handles 10k/s on a single node, 50k+ with batching. Sharded across 4 instances by tenant_id, each does 15k/s — within bounds. The interviewer's "Postgres can't scale" is wrong with numbers.

4. Cassandra's "denormalise into the job row" loses correctness

To use Cassandra, you'd put steps as a list inside the job row. Updating one step = read full list, modify, write back. Not atomic; race conditions under concurrent worker updates. The relational shape isn't a stylistic choice — it's required for correctness here.

8Deep Dive 2: Partial Index + SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED

The query

BEGIN; SELECT job_id FROM jobs WHERE state = 'PENDING' AND next_run_at <= NOW() + INTERVAL '30 seconds' ORDER BY next_run_at ASC LIMIT 500 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED; UPDATE jobs SET state='RUNNING', worker_id=$1, heartbeat_at=NOW() WHERE job_id IN (...); -- emit to Kafka in the same transaction (Outbox pattern) COMMIT;

Why partial index makes it cheap

The partial index WHERE state='PENDING' contains only ~3,500 rows (the next 30 s of due jobs). The B-tree fits in L1 cache. Query scans ~12 entries (log2 3,500) — sub-millisecond regardless of total table size.

Why SKIP LOCKED gives lock-free concurrency

Worker 1 selects rows, locks them. Worker 2 simultaneously selects, sees those rows locked, skips them, returns the next batch. No retry loop, no Redis lock, no idle workers. Postgres feature; battle-tested in Sidekiq Pro, Oban, GoodJob.

9Deep Dive 3: Multi-Step Jobs and Resume-From-Failure

The execution loop

function executeJob(job_id): loop: step = SELECT * FROM job_steps WHERE job_id = ? AND state != 'COMPLETED' ORDER BY step_index ASC LIMIT 1 if no step → mark job COMPLETED, RETURN UPDATE job_steps SET state='RUNNING' WHERE step_id = ? result = execute(step.step_type, step.step_config, input=step.input) if success: UPDATE job_steps SET state='COMPLETED', output=result.out UPDATE next step.input = result.out continue loop if failure: step.retry_count++ if step.retry_count <= max_retries: sleep(exponential_backoff) continue loop else: UPDATE job_steps SET state='FAILED' UPDATE jobs SET state='FAILED' RETURN

The resume-from-failure flow

When a 5-step job fails at step 3, steps 0–1 stay COMPLETED forever. Step 2 was the one that failed → reset to PENDING + reset retry_count. User triggers retry → job picked back up → query returns step 2 → resume from exactly that step. Steps 0 and 1 never re-run. This is why "send welcome email" doesn't fire twice when step 4 had a connection error.

Watchdog for worker crashes

If a worker crashes mid-step, the job sits in RUNNING with no heartbeat. Watchdog service every 30 s: WHERE state='RUNNING' AND heartbeat_at < NOW() − 5 min; reset to PENDING; another worker picks it up. Steps must be idempotent.

10Deep Dive 4: Cron Expressions and next_run_at

The executor never parses cron at run time. Cron → UTC next_run_at at three moments:

  1. At job creation: next_run_at = cron_parser.next(expr, from=NOW(), tz=user_tz). Stored UTC.
  2. After each successful run: next_run_at = cron_parser.next(expr, from=last_run_at, tz=user_tz). Crucial: from=last_run_at, not NOW(), to prevent drift.
  3. On user edit: recompute immediately.

Why from=last_run_at

If a 9 am job runs 2 min late at 9:02, computing from NOW() schedules the next at 9:02 + 24 h = 9:02 tomorrow. Drift accumulates. Computing from last_run_at (the intended anchor 9:00) schedules tomorrow's run at 9:00 sharp. No drift over months.

Cron library does the edge cases

DST transitions, month-end (Feb has no 31), leap years (Feb 29 only in leap years) — all handled by croniter / cron-parser / Quartz. Never reimplement.

11Failure Modes & Recovery

FailureMitigation
Worker crash mid-stepWatchdog detects stale RUNNING (heartbeat > 5 min); resets to PENDING. Steps must be idempotent.
Scheduler crashThree scheduler nodes with leader election (Raft via etcd). Followers take over within seconds.
Postgres failoverStandby promoted in ~30 s. Jobs paused; SCHEDULER waits; resumes cleanly.
Kafka backlogAuto-scale workers. Scheduling SLA may briefly slip; alerting fires.
Bad job (poison message)After max_retries, move to FAILED with error_msg; dead-letter queue for ops review.
Clock skewNTP everywhere. Postgres clock is the source of truth for next_run_at comparisons.

12Scaling Path

StageArchitecture
1k jobsIn-process scheduler in monolith. setInterval / Sidekiq.
100k jobsStandalone scheduler service. Postgres with this article's design. Single scheduler instance.
10M jobsMulti-scheduler with leader election. Partition Postgres by tenant. Watchdog separate.
100M jobsPostgres sharded by job_id hash across 8 instances. Per-tenant Kafka topics for priority.

13Cross-Questions and Pushbacks

"Writing next_run_at to Postgres after every run — too many writes, no?"
Answer: Quantify. ~116 jobs/s × 6 row writes per completion = ~700 writes/s. Postgres handles 5–10k writes/s. We're at 7% utilisation. With batching closer to 20k/s capacity. If we hit 10k jobs/s some day, PgBouncer + batched UPDATEs + write-behind for non-critical fields keep it comfortable. "Postgres can't" without numbers is the red flag.
"OK use Cassandra then" → "But what about the relations?"
Answer: Walking that back. Cassandra would force denormalisation (steps as a list inside the job row). Updating one step = read full list → modify → write back. Not atomic, race conditions under concurrent worker updates. Even worse: no multi-table ACID — cannot atomically reset job to PENDING + reset job_steps. The reset transaction would partial-apply on crash and produce duplicate fires. The relational shape isn't a stylistic choice; it's a correctness requirement.
Does the scheduler scan all 100M jobs every 5 seconds?
No. The partial index on state='PENDING' contains only ~3,500 rows (next 30 s of due jobs). Index is ~70 KB, lives in cache. Query is a B-tree scan of 3,500 entries with range filter — sub-millisecond regardless of total table size. The 100M rows do not affect this query.
How do you prevent two workers from running the same job?
SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED inside a transaction. Worker 1's SELECT acquires row locks; the UPDATE marks state=RUNNING atomically. Worker 2's simultaneous SELECT skips those locked rows, gets a disjoint set. Native Postgres feature; no Redis or external lock needed.
What happens when the worker crashes after completing all steps but before updating next_run_at?
Job sits in RUNNING with no heartbeat. Watchdog detects after 5 min and resets to PENDING with the same next_run_at. The job will re-fire all steps once. Steps must be idempotent. The right fix: update next_run_at inside the same transaction that marks the final step COMPLETED — atomic commit; on crash before commit, all rolled back; on commit, nothing to re-do.
"For crons that run every 5 minutes — won't writes overwhelm Postgres?"
Answer: Compute: 100k cron jobs × every-5-min = 333 fires/s × 6 writes each = 2k writes/s. Postgres handles 10k/s. We're 20% utilised. Real concern at this rate is not throughput but index bloat from next_run_at updates: mitigate with fillfactor=70 and aggressive autovacuum. Real concern at top-of-hour synchronised fires: mitigate with deterministic jitter (hash(job_id) % 60 seconds) so the spike spreads.

Groww / Zerodha-style: receive orders, route to exchanges, match where you can, compute risk, settle, all under sub-100 ms — without ever placing an order the user didn't authorise or letting them buy more than they can pay for.

1Context and Why This Problem Matters

A retail broker (Robinhood, Zerodha, Groww) is not the exchange itself — it's a customer-facing intermediary that routes orders to exchanges (NSE, BSE, NASDAQ). But the broker has its own hard problems: pre-trade risk checks, position tracking, real-time portfolio updates to millions of users, FIX/binary protocol integration, T+1 settlement, and the regulatory burden of being a money-handling system.

2Requirements Gathering

Functional

  • Place buy/sell orders: market, limit, stop-loss, stop-loss-market, GTT (good-till-trigger).
  • Modify or cancel pending orders.
  • Real-time market data feed to user apps (LTP, bid/ask, depth).
  • Portfolio view: holdings, P&L, margin available.
  • Funds management: deposit, withdraw, ledger.
  • Risk checks: margin sufficient? Position limit OK? Settlement OK?
  • Daily reports: trade book, contract notes, P&L statement.

Non-functional

  • 10 M users, 1 M concurrent during market hours.
  • Peak order rate: ~10 k orders/s (around open/close).
  • Order placement P99 < 100 ms (broker side; total round-trip includes exchange).
  • Market data fan-out: 100 k+ ticks/s to ~1 M WS connections.
  • Zero data loss; full audit trail (regulatory).
  • 9–3:30 market hours availability 100%; off-hours can have planned maintenance.

3Capacity Estimation

MetricNumber
Users10 M
DAU during market hours~1 M
Orders/day~50 M
Orders/sec (avg)~2.3 k/s
Orders/sec (peak open)~10 k/s
Ticks from exchange/sec~100 k/s
WS connections (market hours)~1 M concurrent
Symbols (NSE+BSE)~5,000
Daily storage~500 GB (ticks + orders + audit)
🔑 From Numbers to Architecture
  • ~10 k peak orders/sec → modest QPS; the real challenge is correctness + audit, not throughput.
  • ~100 k ticks/sec from exchange → market-data fanout via a separate path: Kafka → tick processor → per-symbol topic → WebSocket fan-out to ~1 M clients.
  • Strict ordering per symbol → matching engine partitioned by symbol; single-threaded per partition (lock-free in-memory order book); avoids cross-symbol contention.
  • SEBI / regulatory audit → every order + tick written to an append-only Kafka log + cold-tier to S3 for ≥ 7 years; queryable from BigQuery / Athena.
  • FIX gateway translates exchange protocol ↔ internal events; isolated from business logic; can be replaced without touching matching.
  • End-of-day settlement is a batch job, not on the hot path → reads the day's order log; produces statements + tax filings.

4API Design

Order placement

POST /v1/orders Idempotency-Key: ord_uuid { "symbol": "TCS", "exchange": "NSE", "side": "BUY", "qty": 10, "order_type": "LIMIT", // MARKET, LIMIT, SL, SL-M, GTT "limit_price": 3520.50, "product": "CNC", // CNC, MIS (intraday), NRML "validity": "DAY" } Response 201: { "order_id": "o_uuid", "broker_order_id": "bo_xxx", "status": "PLACED", // PLACED | REJECTED | PARTIAL | FILLED | CANCELLED "exchange_order_id": "..." // populated after exchange ack }

Modify and cancel

PATCH /v1/orders/{id} { qty?, limit_price? } DELETE /v1/orders/{id}

Portfolio and funds

GET /v1/portfolio/holdings // CNC holdings (T+1 settled) GET /v1/portfolio/positions // open intraday + delivered GET /v1/funds // available margin, used margin, ledger

Market data (WebSocket)

WSS /v1/market → Subscribe: { "action": "subscribe", "symbols": ["TCS","INFY","..."] } ← Tick: { "symbol":"TCS","ltp":3521.10,"bid":3521.0,"ask":3521.2,"vol":12343,"ts":... } ← Depth: { "symbol":"TCS","bids":[[p,q,n],...],"asks":[[p,q,n],...] }

5Data Model

orders (PostgreSQL, partitioned by date)

CREATE TABLE orders ( order_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, user_id UUID NOT NULL, symbol VARCHAR(20), exchange VARCHAR(10), side CHAR(4), -- BUY / SELL qty INT, filled_qty INT DEFAULT 0, order_type VARCHAR(10), limit_price NUMERIC(12,4), trigger_price NUMERIC(12,4), status VARCHAR(20), -- NEW, PLACED, PARTIAL, FILLED, CANCELLED, REJECTED product VARCHAR(10), validity VARCHAR(10), idempotency_key VARCHAR(64) UNIQUE, placed_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW(), updated_at TIMESTAMPTZ ); CREATE INDEX idx_user_placed ON orders(user_id, placed_at DESC); CREATE INDEX idx_open ON orders(symbol, status) WHERE status IN ('PLACED','PARTIAL');

positions and holdings

CREATE TABLE positions ( user_id UUID, symbol VARCHAR(20), exchange VARCHAR(10), product VARCHAR(10), net_qty INT, avg_price NUMERIC(12,4), PRIMARY KEY (user_id, symbol, exchange, product) ); CREATE TABLE holdings ( user_id UUID, symbol VARCHAR(20), qty INT, -- T+1 settled qty avg_price NUMERIC(12,4), PRIMARY KEY (user_id, symbol) );

funds_ledger (PostgreSQL, immutable append-only)

CREATE TABLE funds_ledger ( ledger_id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY, user_id UUID, type VARCHAR(30), -- DEPOSIT, WITHDRAW, BUY_BLOCK, BUY_DEBIT, SELL_CREDIT, FEE amount NUMERIC(15,4), balance_after NUMERIC(15,4), ref_id UUID, ts TIMESTAMPTZ );

6High-Level Architecture

User mobile/web app │ HTTPS / WSS ▼ ┌────────────────────────┐ │ Edge / API GW │ — JWT, rate-limit └─┬──────┬──────────┬────┘ │ │ │ ▼ ▼ ▼ Order Market Portfolio Svc Data WS Svc │ │ │ ▼ │ │ Risk Engine (synchronous pre-trade) │ │ ▼ │ FIX Adapter → Exchange (NSE / BSE) │ ▲ │ │ exchange ack / fills ▼ │ orders DB (Postgres) ▲ │ on fill events │ ┌───────────┴──────────┐ │ Fills Consumer │ │ - update positions │ │ - update funds_ledger │ │ - emit kafka event │ └──────────────────────┘ Market data path: Exchange feed → Tick ingester → Kafka (ticks.{symbol}) → WS fanout (1M conns) → Snapshot store (Redis: latest tick per symbol)

7Deep Dive 1: The Order Book

The broker itself doesn't have an internal matching engine in the retail-broker case — the exchange does. But the broker maintains a local view of open orders for risk and display.

Open-orders representation

Each user's open orders are in Postgres (state=PLACED or PARTIAL). For display: in Redis Sorted Set per user: open_orders:{user_id} ordered by placed_at; updates on every state change.

Per-symbol view

For "how many of this symbol can I sell?" we maintain per-user-per-symbol position in Redis: position:{user}:{symbol}. Updated synchronously on fill events. Used by risk engine.

When broker DOES match (internalisation)

Large brokers can internalise: match a buyer and seller on their own books before going to the exchange. Saves exchange fees, captures spread. Requires a real matching engine (price-time priority, two heaps) similar to an exchange's. In an interview, mention this for advanced credit; not always built.

8Deep Dive 2: The Pre-Trade Risk Engine

Every order passes through the risk engine before being sent to the exchange. Checks (all in < 10 ms):

  1. Margin check: available_margin >= order_value × margin_pct(symbol, product).
  2. Position limits: per-symbol position size cap (compliance).
  3. Per-user trade-count limit: anti-pattern-trading.
  4. Symbol availability: is this symbol banned today (circuit, T2T)?
  5. Price band: is the limit price within the daily circuit (±20%)?
  6. Order rate limit: max orders/sec per user (5–20).
  7. Self-trade prevention: same user can't buy and sell same symbol at same price simultaneously.

State for risk: all in Redis

The risk engine cannot afford Postgres round-trips. Available_margin, current positions, rate counters all live in Redis with synchronous updates on every fill. Postgres is the durable mirror.

Concurrent orders for the same user

Two orders arriving within 1 ms from the same user must not both pass margin check based on stale state. Use Lua-atomic decrement of available_margin: order is approved only if Redis DECRBY succeeds without going negative. If it does, rollback (INCRBY back) and reject.

9Deep Dive 3: Real-Time Market Data Feed

The exchange sends 100k+ ticks/s. We fan these out to ~1M user WS connections, each subscribed to a different subset of symbols.

Tick ingest

FIX or binary protocol from exchange. Tick ingester parses, normalises, writes to Kafka topic ticks partitioned by symbol. Latest LTP per symbol cached in Redis.

WS fan-out

WS terminator nodes (~20) hold 50k conns each. Each terminator subscribes to a subset of Kafka ticks partitions (every terminator gets every symbol; but a user only listens to symbols they subscribed to). For each tick: filter by user subscription set; push.

Bandwidth

1M users × 10 symbols subscribed × ~50 B per tick × 5 ticks/sec/symbol = ~2.5 GB/s aggregate. Compression (binary protocol, delta encoding) and rate-limited UI updates (max 5 updates/s/symbol shown to user) keep this manageable.

10Deep Dive 4: Settlement and Reconciliation

Indian equities settle T+1: a trade on Monday is settled on Tuesday. The broker handles the cash leg between the user and the clearing corporation.

Daily reconciliation

After market close, broker reconciles:

  1. Compare internal fills (from order events) with exchange's contract notes.
  2. Compute net obligation per user per symbol.
  3. Block / debit user funds for buys; credit funds for sells.
  4. Update holdings table at T+1 EOD.
  5. Generate contract notes (PDF + email).

Brokerage and taxes

Compute brokerage (flat or % per trade), STT, GST, stamp duty, exchange charges. Debited from user funds same day. The contract note shows all charges. Discrepancies in reconciliation are exchange-controlled; broker accepts the exchange's view and resolves with the user.

11Failure Modes & Recovery

FailureMitigation
Exchange feed lagReconnect; consume backlog; mark UI "delayed" until caught up.
Broker matching/sending engine downReject new orders with clear error. Existing orders still tracked at exchange (we don't lose them).
Risk engine slow → orders pile upReject excess via API rate-limit; faster fail-loud than slow-cause-corruption.
WS fanout backpressureDrop oldest unsent ticks per connection; we send latest LTP, missing intermediate ticks. Acceptable for retail UI.
Exchange order accepted but our internal write failedThis is the classic. We must reconcile: at end of day, exchange's contract note is the source of truth. Our system updates state to match. Brief inconsistency tolerated; auditable.
Mass corporate action (split, dividend)EOD batch adjusts holdings table; daily reconciliation catches.

12Scaling Path

StageArchitecture
10k usersMonolith. Single Postgres. Polling for portfolio updates.
1M usersService split. WebSocket for ticks. Redis for risk state.
10M usersThis article's design. Sharded Postgres by user_id. WS fleet.
100M usersMulti-region with sticky-by-country routing; co-located exchange adapters; sub-ms internal RTT.

13Cross-Questions and Pushbacks

"How do you ensure no double-buy when the user double-taps the button?"
Answer: Idempotency-Key on the POST /orders. Client generates a UUID per order intent; second tap sends the same key. Postgres unique constraint on idempotency_key — second insert no-op; returns the same order_id. Critically, the risk-margin block also uses the idempotency key — second pass doesn't double-debit margin. End result: one order regardless of taps.
"FIX is old. Why not REST?"
Answer: Exchanges run on FIX (or proprietary binary protocols). We don't get a choice. Internally we can use anything (gRPC, JSON); only the FIX adapter touches FIX. The adapter is a translation layer; the rest of our stack is normal microservices. FIX persists because exchanges value its standardisation, deterministic message ordering, and ~30 years of stability — not because it's pleasant.
How do you handle a sudden 10× spike in orders at market open?
Three layers: (1) Pre-warm connection pools and Redis state at 9:00 (1 min before open). (2) Auto-scale risk engine and order service ahead of opening based on historical patterns. (3) Backpressure via order rate-limit per user (5–20 orders/s) so a single algo client can't monopolise capacity. The exchange itself becomes the bottleneck eventually; we surface its 503s as "exchange busy, try again."
How do you handle GTT (good-till-trigger) orders that may sit unfilled for months?
GTT orders are not sent to the exchange until the trigger condition is met. Stored in a separate GTT table. A monitoring service subscribes to ticks for all symbols with active GTTs (Redis Set: gtts_active:{symbol}). On each tick crossing a trigger price, publish to gtt.triggered Kafka topic. The GTT executor reads, validates (margin still available, account still active), places the order via the same order API. Multiple GTTs at the same price queued by user_id.
What's "auto square-off" and how is it implemented?
Intraday (MIS) positions must close before market end (3:30 pm). At 3:15 pm, a scheduled job scans open MIS positions, places offsetting market orders. SELL MARKET for long; BUY MARKET for short. Market orders ensure execution before close. Bypasses the user's rate limit but still goes through risk engine. If user already squared off manually, the job detects (net_qty=0) and skips. Notifications sent at 3:00 pm warning.
"Postgres for orders at 10k/s peak — is it enough?"
Answer: Single-node Postgres handles ~10k writes/s tuned. We shard by user_id hash across 4 instances, ~2.5k/s each — comfortable. Reads (status polling, history) go to replicas. The risk path is in Redis (microsecond response). Postgres is in the durability path, not the latency path. We accept the ~5 ms commit latency on the write because the order isn't "live" with the user until we return success — and Postgres makes us correct.

Problem 18: Designing Pastebin

URL shortener's heavier cousin — same key-generation problem, but the payload is up to 10 MB of text. Storage choices, expiry, dedup, and syntax highlighting separate a 1-hour build from a real product.

1Context and Why This Problem Matters

Pastebin is a deceptively simple system that teaches the right answer to a recurring question: "where does my content live?" The naive answer (Postgres TEXT column) works at first and fails badly at scale. Choosing blob storage with metadata-in-DB is the canonical pattern that recurs across image hosting, document storage, log archives, and even videos.

2Requirements Gathering

Functional

  • Create a paste from a text body (up to 10 MB).
  • Get a short URL — both anonymous and authenticated users.
  • View paste; optionally raw view (plain text, no UI chrome).
  • Expiry: never, 10 min, 1 hr, 1 day, 1 week, custom.
  • Syntax highlighting per language (auto-detect or user-chosen).
  • Visibility: public, unlisted, private (auth-only).
  • Edit and delete by owner.

Non-functional

  • Read-heavy: ~100× more reads than writes.
  • P99 read latency < 100 ms.
  • Throughput: 1k writes/s, 100k reads/s peak.
  • Cheap storage — durability over latency on writes.

3Capacity Estimation

MetricNumber
Pastes/day~10 M
Write QPS (avg)~115/s
Write QPS (peak)~1 k/s
Avg paste size~10 KB
Read/write ratio~100:1
Read QPS (peak)~100 k/s
Storage/day~100 GB
Storage/year~36 TB
Storage 5 yr × 3 replication~540 TB
🔑 From Numbers to Architecture
  • ~100 k peak read QPS / 1 k peak write QPS → ~100:1 read:write ratio → aggressive caching wins; Redis caches the paste body (~10 KB) and absorbs 95%+ of reads.
  • ~540 TB cumulative storage → never store paste bodies in Postgres; metadata in Postgres, body in S3 (cheap, durable, infinitely scalable).
  • Short slug generation → Base62 from a 6-char counter (~56 B combinations); collision check via Postgres unique constraint; or pre-generate slugs in a Redis pool.
  • Optional features (syntax highlighting, expiry, password) → metadata flags on the row; body remains unchanged in S3.
  • Public discovery / trending → small Postgres view; OK to be slightly stale.
  • Abuse / takedown → soft-delete sets a flag; S3 lifecycle removes body lazily; metadata kept for audit.

4API Design

POST /v1/pastes { "content": "...up to 10MB...", "language": "python", // optional "expires_in": 86400, // seconds; 0 = never "visibility": "PUBLIC", "title": "Quick notes" } → 201 { "paste_id": "abc123", "url": "https://p.example/abc123", "expires_at": "..." } GET /v1/pastes/{id} // metadata + content GET /v1/raw/{id} // plain text, content-type text/plain PATCH /v1/pastes/{id} // owner only DELETE /v1/pastes/{id}

5Data Model

pastes (PostgreSQL — metadata)

CREATE TABLE pastes ( paste_id VARCHAR(12) PRIMARY KEY, -- short key user_id UUID, -- nullable for anonymous title VARCHAR(200), language VARCHAR(20), content_hash CHAR(64), -- sha256 for dedup content_url TEXT, -- S3 URL size_bytes INT, visibility VARCHAR(20), -- PUBLIC | UNLISTED | PRIVATE expires_at TIMESTAMPTZ, created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW(), view_count INT DEFAULT 0 ); CREATE INDEX idx_expires ON pastes(expires_at) WHERE expires_at IS NOT NULL; CREATE INDEX idx_user ON pastes(user_id, created_at DESC); CREATE INDEX idx_content_hash ON pastes(content_hash);

Content storage

Content body in S3 (or any blob store) at s3://pastes/{shard}/{paste_id}.txt.gz with gzip compression. Metadata only in Postgres.

6High-Level Architecture

Client │ POST /pastes / GET /pastes/{id} ▼ ┌─────────────────────────────┐ │ API Gateway │ └────────┬────────────────────-┘ │ ▼ ┌─────────────────────────────┐ │ Paste Service │ │ - generate short key │ │ - compute content hash │ │ - dedup check │ │ - upload to S3 │ │ - insert metadata in PG │ └─────┬──────────────────┬─────┘ │ │ ▼ ▼ Postgres S3 + CDN (metadata) (content blobs) │ ▼ CDN cache 60s Background: • Expiry sweeper — daily job deletes pastes WHERE expires_at <= NOW() • View counter aggregator — Redis HINCRBY → flush to PG hourly

7Deep Dive 1: Storage — DB vs Blob

Why not Postgres TEXT

At 10 KB avg × 10M pastes = 100 GB/day of text. Postgres can store it, but:

  • Postgres backups multiply by the size — backups are slow and expensive.
  • VACUUM and reindex operations slow as the TOAST'd text accumulates.
  • CDN-cached delivery from a database is not natural; from S3 it is.
  • S3 storage is ~$23/TB-month; EBS is ~$80/TB-month.

The split

Metadata (~200 B per row) → Postgres. Content (~10 KB avg) → S3 with the content_hash + paste_id as the key. CDN sits in front of S3 for read-heavy hot content. Postgres is small, fast, indexed; S3 is huge, cheap, durable.

Compression

Gzip the content at the service layer before S3 upload. Text compresses ~5×, so 10 KB → 2 KB stored. Decompress at retrieval (or set Content-Encoding: gzip and let the browser handle).

8Deep Dive 2: Key Generation

Same problem as URL shortener (P1). Three approaches:

  1. Hash the content: base62(sha256(content)[:8]) = ~12-char URL. Pure: same content → same URL (automatic dedup). Cons: cannot pre-mint keys; collision check needed.
  2. Counter-based: base62(monotonic_counter). Distributed counter via Snowflake or KGS (Key Generation Service). Predictable, but URLs are guessable.
  3. Random + collision retry: 8-char random base62 (≈ 218 trillion space). Check uniqueness in DB; retry on the rare collision.

Most production pastebins use approach 3 with a KGS pre-minting pool to avoid in-line collision checks.

9Deep Dive 3: Deduplication

Two users paste identical content (think: error messages from popular libraries). Storing the body twice in S3 wastes space.

Content-hash indirection

On paste creation:

  1. Compute sha256(content).
  2. Lookup in pastes by content_hash; if a recent one exists with matching content, reuse its S3 URL.
  3. Each new paste gets its own paste_id (so URLs differ) but its content_url may point to a shared S3 object.
  4. Reference-counting: a separate blob_refs table tracks count of pastes pointing to each blob. Decrement on paste expiry; delete blob when count hits 0.

When to skip dedup

If content is < 1 KB, just store inline in the DB (avoid blob round-trip). Dedup overhead exceeds storage savings for tiny payloads.

10Deep Dive 4: Expiry and Cleanup

Soft expiry on read

On every read of a paste, check expires_at <= NOW(). If expired, return 410 Gone (don't serve content). Users see "this paste has expired."

Background cleanup

Daily job sweeps the expires_at index for the past 24 h: paginate, delete paste row, decrement blob_ref. When blob_ref hits 0, delete the S3 object. Run during off-hours; rate-limited to avoid DB pressure.

S3 lifecycle as a backstop

Set an S3 lifecycle policy: "delete objects older than max_paste_age (e.g. 2 years) regardless of metadata." Catches anything the cleanup job missed. Defensive double-delete.

11Deep Dive 5: Syntax Highlighting Strategy

Highlighted view is the second-most-requested feature after raw view. Two implementation paths:

Server-side pre-rendering

At paste creation: run Pygments / Highlight.js → produce HTML → store alongside raw. Read serves the HTML. Pros: fast read, consistent rendering. Cons: 5× storage (HTML is verbose), can't update highlighter without re-rendering all pastes.

Client-side rendering

Server returns raw text + detected language. Browser-side library renders. Pros: storage is just raw text, highlighter updates apply immediately. Cons: blocks page render briefly; mobile clients pay CPU cost.

Hybrid: server returns raw + a renderer-version hash. CDN caches the rendered HTML page (with hash as part of cache key). Updates to the highlighter invalidate cache; storage stays small.

12Failure Modes & Recovery

FailureMitigation
S3 region outageCross-region replication; CDN serves stale; reads fail over after 30 s.
DB primary downStandby promotion. Brief pause in writes; reads continue from replicas.
Hot paste (viral) overwhelms CDN miss pathCDN with long TTL absorbs; backend rate-limited; per-paste-id caching.
Cleanup job lagsExpired-but-undeleted pastes return 410 anyway; storage cost incurred until cleanup runs.
Malicious content / illegal materialML moderation queue, takedown API, S3 deletion + DB tombstone.

13Scaling Path

StageArchitecture
1k pastesSingle Postgres with TEXT column. Done.
1M pastesMove content to S3; CDN.
100M pastesDedup via content_hash. Postgres sharded by paste_id.
1B pastesMulti-region S3 buckets; geo-routed CDN; analytics in ClickHouse.

14Cross-Questions and Pushbacks

"Just use Postgres for everything — why complicate with S3?"
Answer: At < 100 GB total content, Postgres TEXT is fine. Above that, three things bite: (1) backups grow with content size, multiplying RTO/RPO. (2) Read-from-DB doesn't benefit from CDN; every read is a DB round trip. (3) Storage cost: EBS is $80/TB-mo, S3 is $23/TB-mo; at 100 TB that's $5,700/mo difference. The split is the right pattern; doing it from day one isn't wrong either.
How do you prevent malicious actors from using Pastebin to host illegal content?
Multi-layer. (1) ML classifier on submission checks for known categories (CSAM hashes via PhotoDNA, malware patterns). (2) Rate-limit anonymous pastes by IP. (3) Crawl-based abuse reports route to a human review queue with takedown SLA. (4) For pastes flagged as high-risk, the URL contains a redirect-through page with a "this content may be malicious" warning. Compliance with takedown requests (DMCA, EU laws) within SLA.
How do you handle very large pastes (10 MB) without timing out?
Resumable / chunked upload using S3 multipart. Client requests presigned multipart URL; uploads chunks of 5 MB; on completion, S3 stitches; metadata row inserted at the end. Same pattern as YouTube upload (P4). Backend never sees the bytes — saves egress costs and timeouts.
"Content-hash dedup leaks information — I can guess if someone else posted the same content."
Answer: Correct concern. Two defences. (1) Each paste still has its own paste_id and URL; an attacker can't enumerate. (2) The hash table is internal — never exposed via API. (3) For privacy-sensitive use cases (private pastes), disable dedup: store a fresh copy, accept the storage cost. The dedup is opt-out at the paste creation level.
How do you support paste editing without breaking existing URLs?
The URL maps to the paste_id, which persists. On edit, a new content_hash is computed; a new S3 object is uploaded; metadata's content_url is updated. Old blob's ref-count decremented; deleted when zero. Edit history can be retained via a paste_versions table linking version_id → content_hash. Roll-back to a previous version updates the metadata back. URL semantics: same URL always returns latest version.

End of Problem 18. Next: Google Docs (P19) — real-time collaborative editing.

Hard Real-Time Collab OT CRDT WebSocket Versioning

Problem 19: Designing Google Docs (Real-Time Collaboration)

Two people typing in the same paragraph at the same instant, with 100 ms of network latency between them, must converge to the same document. Operational Transformation and CRDTs are the only known answers — and choosing between them is the interview.
