1Context and Why This Problem Matters

Real-time collaborative editing is one of the hardest distributed-systems problems shipped to consumers. Two users 100 ms apart, both editing the same word, must always end up with the same document. The algorithm has been studied for 40 years and the two practical solutions (Operational Transformation, CRDTs) have very different shapes. An interview that asks "design Google Docs" is testing whether you can articulate the correctness invariant (convergence + intention preservation) before you draw a single box.

2Requirements Gathering

Functional

  • Multiple users edit the same document concurrently; see each other's changes in < 1 s.
  • See other users' cursors and selection ranges.
  • Version history; revert to a previous state.
  • Comments, suggestions ("track changes" mode).
  • Offline editing with later sync.
  • Permission model: owner, editor, commenter, viewer.

Non-functional

  • 100 M users, ~5 M concurrent active sessions.
  • Edit latency end-to-end < 200 ms.
  • Document size: typical 50 KB, can grow to ~10 MB.
  • Convergence guaranteed: all users see same final state.
  • Durability: no data loss; full edit history.

3Capacity Estimation

MetricNumber
Users100 M
Active concurrent sessions~5 M
Edits/user/min during active editing~30 keystrokes
Edits/sec (peak across all users)~2.5 M ops/s
Documents~10 B
Avg document size~50 KB
Total storage~500 TB
WebSocket connections5 M concurrent
🔑 From Numbers to Architecture
  • ~2.5 M edit ops/sec peak → ops are tiny (5–50 B) and per-document; sharded by doc_id → no single bottleneck.
  • ~5 M concurrent WebSocket connections → dedicated WS gateway fleet (~50 nodes), each holding ~100 k conns; sharded by doc_id so all collaborators on one doc hit one server (simplifies OT/CRDT).
  • OT (Operational Transformation) or CRDT for concurrent edits → server stores op log + periodic snapshots; clients apply ops in order; conflicts merged automatically.
  • ~10 B docs × ~50 KB avg = ~500 TB → docs in Postgres / Cassandra (snapshot + tail op log); cold docs evicted to S3.
  • Presence (cursor / selection of other users) → ephemeral; broadcast via WebSocket, not persisted.
  • Snapshots + op-log → recover any historical state; "version history" feature falls out naturally.

4API Design

WebSocket protocol per document

WSS /v1/docs/{doc_id} → Server sends initial state: { "type":"INIT", "doc_id":"...", "revision":42, "content":"...", "collaborators":[...] } → Client sends an operation: { "type":"OP", "client_id":"...", "base_rev":42, "ops":[ {"retain":10}, {"insert":"Hello"}, {"retain":5} ] } ← Server acks + broadcasts transformed op to all other clients: { "type":"OP", "rev":43, "ops": [...] } { "type":"ACK", "client_op_id":"..." } ← Server pushes presence: { "type":"PRESENCE", "user_id":"u_xyz", "cursor": 14, "selection": [10,18] }

REST endpoints

POST /v1/docs // create GET /v1/docs/{id} // snapshot + metadata GET /v1/docs/{id}/history?from=...&to=... // version history POST /v1/docs/{id}/restore?revision=... // revert POST /v1/docs/{id}/permissions { user, role } // sharing

5Data Model

documents (PostgreSQL — metadata only)

CREATE TABLE documents ( doc_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, title VARCHAR(255), owner_id UUID, created_at TIMESTAMPTZ, current_revision BIGINT, snapshot_url TEXT -- S3 url of latest snapshot ); CREATE TABLE doc_permissions ( doc_id UUID, user_id UUID, role VARCHAR(20), PRIMARY KEY(doc_id, user_id) );

operations log (Cassandra — append-only)

CREATE TABLE doc_ops ( doc_id UUID, revision BIGINT, client_id UUID, ops_json TEXT, applied_at TIMESTAMP, PRIMARY KEY ((doc_id), revision) ) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (revision ASC);

Snapshots (S3, every 100 ops)

// s3://docs/{doc_id}/snapshot_{revision}.json // Contains full document at that revision // Allows fast initial load (last snapshot + ops since then)

6High-Level Architecture

Browser │ WSS — long-lived ▼ ┌─────────────────────────────┐ │ WS Terminator │ ← 100s of nodes, ~50k conns each │ (sticky by doc_id) │ └────────┬─────────────────────┘ │ ▼ ┌─────────────────────────────┐ │ Doc Server (per doc) │ ← one logical "owner" per active doc │ - holds in-memory state │ │ - transforms incoming ops │ │ - broadcasts to all clients │ │ - persists to log + snapshot│ └────┬───────────┬─────────────┘ │ │ ▼ ▼ Cassandra ops log S3 snapshots │ ▼ Postgres metadata

The "doc server" concept

Each active document has a designated server holding its authoritative state in RAM. All ops for that doc are routed there. Routing by consistent hash of doc_id. The doc server is responsible for the single global order of operations and serves as the OT central server. When all collaborators leave, the in-memory state is flushed to a snapshot and the server is freed.

7Deep Dive 1: Operational Transformation

OT solves the convergence problem by transforming incoming ops to account for ops applied earlier. Best understood with a tiny example:

Initial document: "ABC" User A inserts "X" at position 0 User B inserts "Y" at position 3 A's op: { insert "X" at 0 } B's op: { insert "Y" at 3 } Both arrive at server simultaneously. Server applies A first → "XABC" Server transforms B's op against A's: B was at position 3 in original; now A inserted 1 char before, so B → position 4 Server applies transformed B → "XABCY" When A's client receives B's op (transformed): also "insert Y at 4" → "XABCY" When B's client receives A's op: "insert X at 0" → "XABCY" Both converge to "XABCY". ✓

Transform functions

For each pair of operation types (insert vs insert, insert vs delete, delete vs delete), define a transform(op_a, op_b) function that produces a new op_b' that, when applied after op_a, has the same intent. Mathematically, these must satisfy "transformation property 1" (TP1): applying op_a then transform(op_b, op_a) = applying op_b then transform(op_a, op_b).

Server-centric OT (Google Docs approach)

Single server defines the canonical order. Clients send ops with base_revision; server transforms against any ops since that revision; assigns the next revision number; broadcasts. Simpler than peer-to-peer OT (which needs TP2 — much harder).

⚠ Why OT is hard to "just implement"

OT for plain text inserts is undergrad-level. OT for rich text with formatting, lists, tables is much harder — getting it right for every operation pair took Google's team years and many bug reports. The Apache Etherpad project has open-source OT code; the Google internal code is famously thousands of lines of edge cases.

8Deep Dive 2: CRDTs (Alternative Approach)

Conflict-free Replicated Data Types eliminate the need for a central transform server. Each character in the document is given a globally unique ID (e.g. site_id + counter + position). Concurrent insertions are resolved by the IDs themselves — no transformation needed.

RGA (Replicated Growable Array) sketch

Each insertion stores: (id, value, predecessor_id). To insert "X" after "A", the op references A's id. When merging concurrent inserts after the same predecessor, ties are broken by site_id. Result: all replicas see the same sequence.

Trade-offs vs OT

  • CRDT pro: peer-to-peer friendly; no central server required for correctness.
  • CRDT pro: simpler reasoning per op type; no quadratic transform-function explosion.
  • CRDT con: per-char overhead (every character carries a UUID-sized ID). 50 KB document → potentially 500 KB CRDT state.
  • CRDT con: less mature for rich text; complexity moves into the merge algorithm.

Modern verdict

Google Docs uses OT. Figma uses CRDTs. Both at scale. The choice depends on whether a central server is acceptable: docs has one, peer-to-peer apps don't. In the interview, either answer is defensible; the discriminator is whether you can articulate the trade-off.

9Deep Dive 3: Persistence — Log + Snapshots

Every applied operation is logged in Cassandra. The log lets us reconstruct any past state by replaying from the beginning. But for a doc with 1M edits, replay is slow.

Periodic snapshots

Every 100 revisions: take the current state and write to S3 as snapshot_{revision}.json. Update the doc's metadata to point at the latest snapshot. To open the doc later: load snapshot + replay ops from snapshot.revision to current. ~100 ops to replay = milliseconds.

Version history UI

"Show me yesterday's version": find the closest snapshot, replay forward to a specific revision. Each named version (revision number, optional label) is exposed in the UI.

Cleanup

Old ops can be discarded after a snapshot covers them. We keep ~30 days of granular ops for "see who typed what" + named snapshots forever for restore.

10Deep Dive 4: Presence, Cursors, Selections

Per-doc presence channel

The same WebSocket carries presence messages. Each client sends its cursor position every 100 ms when active. Server broadcasts to other clients. No persistence — presence is ephemeral.

Cursor transformation

A cursor at position 14 is invalidated when an op modifies text around it. The server transforms cursor positions through the operation stream the same way it transforms ops. After typing happens "before" my cursor, my cursor moves; if my cursor was at the typing point, it shifts to the right.

Color and label assignment

Each user is assigned a stable color and shown by name. Client-side rendering; backend doesn't care.

11Deep Dive 5: Offline Edits and Reconciliation

Users edit on a plane, then reconnect. Their local edits must merge with the central document.

Local buffer

While offline, edits are applied to a local copy and appended to an outbound op queue with the local base_revision. The UI shows changes immediately for the user.

Reconnect flow

  1. Client reconnects with its base_revision = R.
  2. Server returns all ops since R.
  3. Client transforms its pending local ops against the server ops (OT works both ways).
  4. Client sends the transformed local ops to the server.
  5. Server applies and broadcasts to other clients.

For long offline periods (days), divergence might be large enough that the user is shown a "merge conflicts" UI before sending — letting them review.

12Failure Modes & Recovery

FailureMitigation
Doc server crashPersisted state in Cassandra + last snapshot in S3; new doc server elected via consistent-hash failover; replays from snapshot to recover; clients reconnect and resync.
Client disconnect mid-typingBuffered ops with base_revision; on reconnect, sync as in offline flow.
Network blip causes duplicate opEach op has a client_op_id; server dedups.
Two doc servers think they own the same docLeader election via etcd / Raft; the one without lease must yield. Brief split possible but resolved within seconds.
Lost message → missed revisionEach op message has the new revision number; client detects gaps and requests resync.

13Scaling Path

StageArchitecture
10 users / docSingle backend instance owns all docs. Postgres for log.
10k concurrent docsMultiple doc-server instances; consistent-hash routing by doc_id.
1M concurrent docsCassandra for op log. S3 snapshots. WS terminator fleet.
5M+ concurrent sessionsMulti-region with home-region pinning per doc; cross-region read replicas for view-only access.

14Cross-Questions and Pushbacks

"Why OT instead of CRDTs?"
Answer: We have a central authoritative server in the architecture anyway (for permissions, version history, snapshots). OT exploits that: simpler per-op state (no UUIDs per character), smaller wire format, more mature rich-text support. CRDTs win when there's no central server (P2P collaboration tools, local-first apps). For Google Docs as a hosted product, OT is the better fit. Figma chose CRDTs because their layered design tree benefits from CRDT's automatic merging properties — context-dependent.
How do you handle a doc with 200 concurrent editors?
Single doc server in memory; ops are tiny (~50 B avg), so even 200 users × 10 ops/s = 2k ops/s = handleable. Broadcast cost: 200 ops × 200 recipients = 40k messages/s = ~1 MB/s — comfortable. The doc server's CPU isn't the bottleneck until ~thousands of editors. Beyond that, partition the doc (e.g. per-section ownership) — but that's not a Google Docs use case.
"How is OT correct when ops can arrive out of order?"
Answer: The server enforces total order. Every op gets a monotonically increasing revision number. Clients receive ops in revision order; if they see a gap (rev 45 but they're at 43), they request the missing ops. Ops are never applied out of order. The transformation happens at the server, not the client. Client-side is "apply this transformed op against your current state" — straightforward.
How do you handle rich text (bold, lists, tables, images)?
The op model extends to include "attribute" ops: retain 10 with {bold: true}. Inserts can include attributes. Transformation rules for attribute ops are mostly straightforward (the position arithmetic is the same; attributes attach to positions). Tables are harder — they're nested structures that need per-cell op handling. Google's internal model is a tree of nodes; ops operate at that tree level, not flat text. Years of edge-case work.
How do you scale presence at 5M concurrent users?
Presence is ephemeral and high-frequency. WS terminator nodes hold presence in memory locally; when a presence change happens, broadcast only to other clients on the same doc-server's roster. Cross-shard presence not needed — only people in the same doc see each other. Worst case: 200 collaborators on one doc × 10 presence msg/s = 2k presence msg/s on that doc-server — trivial.

End of Problem 19. Next: Ticket Booking (P20) — seat holds and flash sales.

Hard Transactional / Hot Inventory Seat Hold Redis Lua Virtual Queue

Problem 20: Designing a Ticket Booking System

BookMyShow / Ticketmaster — 100k people clicking the same Coldplay concert seats at 9 am sharp, with the user holding a seat in their cart for 7 minutes before paying. Get it slightly wrong and you double-sell a seat.

  2. Requirements Gathering
  3. Capacity Estimation
  4. API Design
  5. Data Model
  6. High-Level Architecture
  7. Deep Dive 1: Seat Hold with Redis Lua
  8. Deep Dive 2: Virtual Queue for Flash Sales
  9. Deep Dive 3: Payment Integration & Idempotency
  10. Deep Dive 4: Seat Layout and Availability Map
  11. Deep Dive 5: Reconciliation & Anti-Oversell

1Context and Why This Problem Matters

Seat-based ticketing is the most concentrated form of the inventory problem from P10 (E-Commerce). Unlike generic SKUs, every seat is uniquely identified, two-person hold-time is mandatory, and the system has to gracefully handle "1M users clicking seat A12 at the same instant." It also combines almost every distributed-systems trick: virtual queues, atomic decrement, optimistic locking, idempotent payments, and reservation TTLs.

2Requirements Gathering

Functional

  • Browse events / movies / shows by city, date.
  • See seat-by-seat availability for a show.
  • Reserve specific seats; hold for ~7 min while user pays.
  • Atomic checkout: payment success → booking confirmed; failure → seats released.
  • Cancellation, refund, transfer (per-event policy).
  • Flash sales: handle 100k+ users at sale open.

Non-functional

  • 1 M registered users; 100 M+ shows tracked across the platform.
  • Peak: 100 k concurrent users on a single hot show.
  • Zero double-bookings.
  • Seat-hold race resolution < 100 ms.
  • Availability 99.95% during sales.

3Capacity Estimation

MetricNumber
Users100 M
Shows tracked~10 M
Bookings/day (avg)~1 M
Bookings/sec (avg)~12/s
Bookings/sec (peak flash)~5 k/s for short windows
Browse QPS (peak)~50 k/s
Seats per show (avg)~200
Big-venue shows~50 k seats
Hold TTL7 minutes
🔑 From Numbers to Architecture
  • ~5 k peak bookings/sec but with intense contention on a few hot shows (Taylor Swift, IPL final) → Redis-backed seat-hold with TTL 7 min for the inventory reservation hot path.
  • ~50 k peak browse QPS → cached show / venue / seat map in Redis + CDN; origin Postgres serves only the long-tail.
  • Big venues with ~50 k seats → seat map stored as a compact structure (bitmap or per-section list); rendering on client.
  • Booking = hold → payment → confirm → multi-step process with strict consistency; saga pattern handles partial failures (release hold on payment failure).
  • Audit trail for every state change → outbox + Kafka → analytics warehouse; financial reconciliation against payment processor.
  • Fraud / bot defence → rate-limit per user/IP; CAPTCHA for repeated rapid hold-then-release patterns.

4API Design

// Browse GET /v1/events?city=Mumbai&date=2026-06-15 GET /v1/shows/{show_id} // details + section pricing GET /v1/shows/{show_id}/seats // availability map // Hold (one or more seats) POST /v1/holds Idempotency-Key: h_uuid { "show_id": "s_abc", "seat_ids": ["A12","A13"] } → 200 { "hold_id": "h_xyz", "expires_at": "2026-06-15T19:07:00Z", "total_cents": 24000 } or 409 { "error": "SEAT_UNAVAILABLE", "unavailable_seats": ["A12"] } // Checkout (uses hold) POST /v1/bookings { "hold_id": "h_xyz", "payment_method_id": "pm_..." } → 201 { "booking_id": "b_abc", "state":"CONFIRMED", "tickets":[...] } // Cancel hold (release seats early) DELETE /v1/holds/{hold_id} // Cancel booking (if policy allows) POST /v1/bookings/{id}/cancel

5Data Model

shows (PostgreSQL)

CREATE TABLE shows ( show_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, event_id UUID, venue_id UUID, starts_at TIMESTAMPTZ, state VARCHAR(20), -- DRAFT | ON_SALE | SOLD_OUT | COMPLETED total_seats INT, available_seats INT -- denormalised counter for browse list );

seats (PostgreSQL — one row per seat per show)

CREATE TABLE seats ( show_id UUID, seat_id VARCHAR(20), -- "A12" section VARCHAR(20), -- "Orchestra" price_cents BIGINT, state VARCHAR(20), -- AVAILABLE | HELD | BOOKED | BLOCKED hold_id UUID, -- non-null when state=HELD booking_id UUID, -- non-null when state=BOOKED version BIGINT, -- optimistic-lock token PRIMARY KEY (show_id, seat_id) ); CREATE INDEX idx_show_state ON seats(show_id, state);

Per-show seat availability (Redis, the hot path)

// Hash per show: seat_id → "AVAILABLE" | "HELD:user_id:exp" | "BOOKED" HSET seats:{show_id} A12 "AVAILABLE" A13 "AVAILABLE" ... // Holds with TTL SET hold:{hold_id} "{show_id, seats[], user_id}" EX 420 // 7 min

bookings (PostgreSQL)

CREATE TABLE bookings ( booking_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, show_id UUID, user_id UUID, seat_ids VARCHAR[] NOT NULL, state VARCHAR(20), -- PAYMENT_PENDING | CONFIRMED | CANCELLED | REFUNDED total_cents BIGINT, hold_id UUID, payment_id UUID, idempotency_key VARCHAR(64) UNIQUE, created_at TIMESTAMPTZ );

6High-Level Architecture

Client (mobile/web) │ ▼ ┌─────────────────────────────┐ │ Edge / CDN │ ← caches show pages, seat-map JS └────────┬────────────────────-┘ │ ▼ ┌─────────────────────────────┐ │ Booking API Gateway │ ← auth, rate-limit, virtual queue gate └─┬──────┬───────┬─────────────┘ │ │ │ ▼ ▼ ▼ Browse Hold Booking Svc Svc Svc │ │ │ ▼ ▼ ▼ Postgres Redis hot inventory Postgres bookings (catalog) (per-show hash + holds) Payment Svc (P21) ↔ Booking Svc Background: • Hold-expiry sweeper — Redis TTL handles 99%; reconciler cleans missed • Daily reconciliation — Postgres seats vs Redis vs bookings

7Deep Dive 1: Seat Hold with Redis Lua

The core operation: atomically check + mark seats as HELD, fail if any seat is unavailable.

-- KEYS[1]: seats:{show_id} (Redis hash) -- KEYS[2]: hold:{hold_id} (Redis string) -- ARGV: seat_ids comma-separated, user_id, expires_at_unix, hold_metadata local seat_ids = split(ARGV[1], ",") -- check all seats are AVAILABLE for i, sid in ipairs(seat_ids) do local cur = redis.call('HGET', KEYS[1], sid) if cur ~= 'AVAILABLE' then return { err = "UNAVAILABLE", seat = sid } end end -- all good, mark each for i, sid in ipairs(seat_ids) do redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], sid, "HELD:" .. ARGV[2] .. ":" .. ARGV[3]) end redis.call('SET', KEYS[2], ARGV[4], 'EX', 420) -- 7 min return { ok = true }

This Lua script runs atomically — no other Redis command interleaves. Two concurrent requests for the same seat: one wins, the other gets UNAVAILABLE. Sub-millisecond.

Hold release

Two paths:

  • Explicit: user cancels hold or completes booking → another Lua script atomically clears HELD entries and the hold key.
  • TTL expiry: after 7 min, Redis automatically deletes the hold key. A background sweeper subscribes to __keyevent@*__:expired notifications, finds the seat_ids that the hold referenced, and resets them from HELD to AVAILABLE.

8Deep Dive 2: Virtual Queue for Flash Sales

Coldplay tickets go on sale at 12:00:00 IST. 500k users hammer F5. Direct access to the booking API would saturate everything. Solution: virtual queue.

The flow

  1. At 11:55, users land on a waiting page. JS asks for a queue ticket: POST /v1/queue/{show_id}/join.
  2. Server replies with a position number (via Redis INCR queue:{show_id}) and a signed JWT containing position.
  3. Page polls every 5 s for status; backend admits N positions per second into the booking flow.
  4. When the JWT's position is within the "admitted window", client gets the green light and proceeds to seat selection.
  5. Admission rate is tuned to what the booking pipeline can handle (e.g. 200 admits/s).

Why this works

The booking inventory pipeline only sees admitted traffic — never the raw 500k spike. Backend load is bounded. Users see "you're in line, ~5 min wait" instead of a 500 error.

Anti-bot

Captcha before queue entry; per-user/IP rate limits on admission; behavioural signals to demote bots. Bots that get tickets are reversed after the fact via fraud rules.

9Deep Dive 3: Payment Integration & Idempotency

The 3-state booking flow

  1. User has a HELD seat → POSTs /bookings with hold_id + payment method.
  2. Server creates booking row in PAYMENT_PENDING, with idempotency_key = hold_id.
  3. Server calls payment service (P21) with idempotency_key + amount + payment_method.
  4. Payment success → state=CONFIRMED, seats moved from HELD to BOOKED (atomic Lua), tickets emailed.
  5. Payment failure → state=CANCELLED, seats released (HELD → AVAILABLE), user shown the error.

Race conditions to handle

  • User retries: idempotency_key prevents duplicate bookings.
  • Hold expires while payment in flight: tight timing window. The payment service must succeed within the hold TTL; if not, payment is reversed and booking rejected. We mitigate by reserving for 7 min and capping payment timeout at 5 min.
  • Server crash mid-flow: PAYMENT_PENDING bookings are reconciled — call payment provider to query status; finalise state accordingly.

10Deep Dive 4: Seat Layout and Availability Map

Static layout

Each venue has a static seat map (sections, rows, seat numbers, x/y coordinates, accessibility flags). Stored in a JSON document per venue, served via CDN.

Dynamic availability

On show page load, client fetches GET /shows/{id}/seats → returns the current state of every seat. For 50k-seat venues, this is ~2 MB JSON; gzip ~200 KB. CDN-cached for ~5 s with frequent updates as users hold.

Real-time updates

WebSocket per-show channel; when a seat changes state, broadcast a delta to subscribers. Other users browsing the same show see seats "grey out" as others hold them. Improves UX (less "this seat was just taken" disappointment).

11Deep Dive 5: Reconciliation & Anti-Oversell

Redis is the hot path; Postgres is the source of truth. They can diverge under failure. We reconcile every hour:

  1. For each show that had bookings in the last hour, compare Redis hash with Postgres seats table.
  2. Each booking_id in Postgres → seats should be BOOKED in Redis. If not, sync.
  3. Active holds in Redis without backing rows in Postgres (a corrupted state) → release.
  4. If overselling is detected (e.g. two bookings reference the same seat), trigger an incident: refund one customer (the later booking by timestamp), apology, possibly a free upgrade.

Detection is critical; recovery is graceful (refunds, apologies). The system minimises oversell to near-zero via Lua atomicity, but humans handle the residual cases.

12Failure Modes & Recovery

FailureMitigation
Redis crash mid-flash-saleAOF every-second + Postgres as backup. Recover Redis from snapshot; replay Kafka booking events. Surface "demand spike, retry" rather than 500.
Postgres failoverStandby promoted; writes pause briefly; Redis continues serving holds; reconcile after recovery.
Payment provider timeoutHold TTL is 7 min; payment timeout is 5 min. Expired hold? Payment is reversed.
User pays but booking marked CANCELLEDReconcile by calling payment service; if charge succeeded, restore booking; if hold long expired, refund user + offer alternative.
Hot show overloads one Redis shardShard by show_id; one show fits one shard easily. For mega-events (Wimbledon), pre-warm a dedicated shard.

13Scaling Path

StageArchitecture
10 showsSingle Postgres with row-level locking on seats.
10k showsAdd Redis for hot show inventory. Lua atomic holds.
1M showsRedis sharded by show_id. Virtual queue for flash sales. WS for real-time seat-map updates.
10M shows + globalMulti-region with venue-pinning (a venue's shows stay in one region). Cross-region read replicas for browse.

14Cross-Questions and Pushbacks

"Two users click seat A12 within milliseconds — who wins?"
Answer: The Lua hold script. It runs atomically inside Redis; only one of the two HSET commands successfully changes the seat from AVAILABLE to HELD. The other returns UNAVAILABLE. Both requests took the same path; Redis serialised them on the single-threaded execution. No lock, no race. The "loser" sees an error within ~10 ms and is shown alternative nearby seats.
"What if the user pays but Redis lost the hold?"
Answer: Postgres is the source of truth. We mark the booking PAYMENT_PENDING with seat_ids before calling the payment provider. Payment success means: (1) attempt Lua to confirm booking by moving seats HELD→BOOKED; (2) if seats are not in HELD state (lost hold), reconcile: are they AVAILABLE? Try to claim them. Are they BOOKED by another user? Refund and offer alternatives. Are they HELD by someone else? Same. The Postgres record proves the user paid; we trade seat assignment for refund-and-apology — never lose their money.
How long should the hold TTL be?
7 minutes is industry-standard. Long enough for slow typists / international users on bad connections to enter card details + 3DS auth. Short enough that bots can't squat on all seats by holding indefinitely. Per-user concurrent-hold limit (e.g. 3 holds at once) prevents seat-blocking attacks. For pre-sale events with manual queue management, holds can extend to 15 min.
How would you support group bookings (e.g. 10 friends, adjacent seats)?
Same hold mechanism — single hold with multiple seat_ids. UI shows recommended "10 adjacent" sets (computed from seat coordinates in the layout). The hold is atomic: all 10 succeed or all fail. If a partial subset becomes unavailable mid-hold, the request returns 409 with which seats are unavailable; client retries with alternatives. For very large groups (50+ seats), an admin path is offered — pre-block the section.
"Virtual queue is great until users get bored and refresh — does the queue position reset?"
Answer: The signed JWT stores the position; refresh re-sends it. Position is preserved. We also store position-by-user in Redis as a backup. Users keep their place. The polling page shows estimated wait time to keep them engaged. If they close the tab and come back hours later, their slot is gone (queue expires after a window), but at that point the tickets are sold out anyway.

Problem 21: Designing a Payment Gateway (Stripe / Razorpay)

Sit between merchants and card networks, tokenise PANs you'll never see in plaintext, route each charge to the processor most likely to approve it, handle 3DS authentication, and never lose money or auth.

1Context and Why This Problem Matters

A payment gateway is the lubricant of e-commerce: merchant calls "charge $50 to this card"; gateway handles tokenisation, fraud screening, authentication, routing to a processor (or directly to a card network), capturing the auth, returning success/failure — and later settling money into the merchant's bank account. The interview tests:

  • Compliance literacy (PCI scope, tokenisation, why you never store PANs).
  • Reliability engineering (smart routing, retries, idempotency for money).
  • Multi-party flows (issuer, acquirer, network, gateway).
  • Reconciliation and settlement — the unsung part.

2Requirements Gathering

Functional

  • Merchant uses our SDK / hosted checkout to tokenise a card.
  • Merchant calls Charges API with token + amount; receives auth/decline.
  • Capture (one-step or two-step: auth-then-capture).
  • Refunds (full or partial).
  • 3D Secure flow for regulated regions (EU SCA, India RBI).
  • Webhooks: charge.succeeded, charge.failed, refund.processed.
  • Settlement: daily aggregate transfer to merchant's bank account.

Non-functional

  • PCI DSS Level 1 compliance.
  • P99 charge latency < 1 s (external processor dominates).
  • 10k TPS peak (Black Friday).
  • 99.99% availability for the charge API.
  • Zero financial discrepancies; full audit trail.

3Capacity Estimation

MetricNumber
Charges/day~50 M
Charge QPS (avg)~580/s
Charge QPS (peak)~10 k/s
Average ticket size~$50
Daily volume~$2.5 B
Charge record (~2 KB)—
Storage/day~100 GB
Tokens in vault~500 M
External processor latency (avg)~300 ms
🔑 From Numbers to Architecture
  • ~10 k peak charges/sec → easy DB QPS; the real complexity is correctness, idempotency, and external processor latency, not throughput.
  • ~300 ms external processor latency → never block the user thread; charge call is itself an async state machine (initiate → processor → webhook → finalise).
  • Money movement is sacred → idempotency_key on every POST + dedup table; same key returns the same response forever.
  • 500 M card tokens → PCI-scoped vault (separate service, separate network, separate audit boundary); app servers handle only opaque tokens.
  • Multiple processors (Stripe / Razorpay / Adyen) → processor-router abstraction; fallback chain; per-processor circuit breaker.
  • Double-entry ledger underneath every charge → guarantees auditability; reconciled daily against processor settlement reports.
  • 3DS / SCA hops → asynchronous redirect flow; pending → confirmed transition driven by webhook; idempotent.

4API Design

Tokenise a card (PCI-scoped frontend SDK direct to vault)

POST https://vault.example.com/v1/tokens { "card_number": "4242...", "cvc": "...", "exp_month": 12, "exp_year": 2028 } → { "token": "tok_abc...", "last4": "4242", "brand": "Visa", "exp_month": 12, "exp_year": 2028 } // Card data never touches merchant's servers.

Create a charge (merchant backend)

POST /v1/charges Authorization: Bearer {merchant_api_key} Idempotency-Key: ch_uuid { "amount_cents": 5000, "currency": "USD", "source": "tok_abc", // tokenised card "customer_id": "cus_xyz", "description": "Order #1234", "capture": true, // immediate capture vs auth-only "metadata": {"order_id":"1234"} } → 200 { "charge_id": "ch_...", "state": "SUCCEEDED", "amount_cents":5000, "fee_cents": 145, "net_cents": 4855, "processor_response": {...} }

Refunds and other

POST /v1/refunds { "charge_id":"ch_...", "amount_cents": 5000 } GET /v1/charges/{id} POST /v1/webhooks/configure { "url":"https://merchant.com/wh", "events":[...] }

5Data Model

charges (PostgreSQL, partitioned monthly)

CREATE TABLE charges ( charge_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, merchant_id UUID, amount_cents BIGINT, currency CHAR(3), state VARCHAR(20), -- PENDING | AUTHORIZED | SUCCEEDED | FAILED | REFUNDED source_token_id UUID, -- link to vault token processor VARCHAR(50), processor_charge_id VARCHAR(100), auth_code VARCHAR(20), decline_reason VARCHAR(50), idempotency_key VARCHAR(64) UNIQUE, fee_cents BIGINT, net_cents BIGINT, three_ds_status VARCHAR(20), created_at TIMESTAMPTZ, captured_at TIMESTAMPTZ ); CREATE INDEX idx_merchant_created ON charges(merchant_id, created_at DESC);

tokens (PCI-scoped vault, separate DB / cluster)

// Lives in PCI-scope environment ONLY CREATE TABLE tokens ( token_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, encrypted_pan BYTEA, -- KMS-encrypted, never queryable pan_hash CHAR(64), -- HMAC-SHA256 for dedup last4 CHAR(4), brand VARCHAR(20), exp_month INT, exp_year INT, created_at TIMESTAMPTZ ); CREATE INDEX idx_pan_hash ON tokens(pan_hash); -- for "same card already tokenised?"

refunds, webhook_deliveries, settlement_batches — separate tables

6High-Level Architecture

Merchant browser │ tokenise card direct ▼ ┌────────────────────────┐ │ PCI Vault │ ← isolated VPC, audited, KMS encryption │ - tokenise / detokenise │ └────────────────────────┘ ▲ │ │ │ │ token only │ │ ▼ Merchant backend │ POST /charges ▼ ┌────────────────────────┐ │ Gateway API │ │ - idempotency check │ │ - fraud screen │ │ - INSERT charges row │ └────────┬───────────────-┘ │ ▼ ┌────────────────────────┐ │ Smart Router │ │ - pick processor │ │ - retry strategy │ └────────┬───────────────-┘ │ ┌───────┴───────┐ ▼ ▼ Adyen Stripe ← processor adapters (FIX-like) Worldpay Razorpay │ ▼ Card network (Visa / Mastercard) │ ▼ Issuer bank │ ▼ auth response (response propagates back up) Async pipelines: • Webhooks fan-out to merchants (durable retry queue) • Settlement batch (EOD): roll up to merchant payouts • Reconciliation: gateway records vs processor reports

7Deep Dive 1: PCI Tokenisation Vault

PCI DSS scope is the set of systems that touch card data. Reducing scope is the single most expensive/important compliance lever.

What the vault does

  1. Browser submits card via our hosted iframe (Stripe Elements, Razorpay Checkout). Card data goes directly from browser to vault.example.com — never via merchant's server.
  2. Vault encrypts PAN with envelope encryption: data_key = KMS.generate(); encrypted_pan = AES-GCM(pan, data_key); store (encrypted_data_key, encrypted_pan).
  3. Issue an opaque token_id (UUID, no structure). Return to browser.
  4. Merchant uses token_id for all subsequent calls. Token alone cannot be used outside this gateway.

Detokenisation

When the gateway needs to send the actual PAN to a processor, it asks the vault to detokenise. Audit logged. Only the processor-call code path can detokenise; merchants never can.

Scope reduction

Merchants integrate via tokens; their servers are out of PCI scope. Our vault is in scope, and we contain it to a small isolated VPC with separate audit. The rest of our gateway (smart router, charges DB) handles tokens — also out of scope.

8Deep Dive 2: Smart Routing

We integrate with multiple processors (Adyen, Stripe, local acquirers). Each has different success rates, fees, and supported networks. Smart routing picks the right one per charge.

Inputs

  • BIN of the card (first 6 digits) → issuer, country, type (debit/credit).
  • Merchant's allowed processors (some have direct relationships).
  • Real-time processor health (last 5 min approval rate, latency).
  • Historical success rate for (BIN, processor) combination.
  • Per-processor fee.

Decision

For each charge: score each viable processor by (approval_probability − fee_ratio). Pick the highest. If declined by processor A, retry on processor B (controlled — not all declines are retryable; a 51-insufficient-funds shouldn't be retried, but a 91-issuer-unavailable should).

Result

+5–10% approval rate vs single-processor routing. Worth real money at scale ($billions of incremental revenue across the gateway industry).

9Deep Dive 3: 3D Secure (SCA)

EU PSD2 and Indian RBI rules require customer authentication for online card payments above thresholds. 3DS adds a step (OTP, biometric) between authorisation and capture.

Flow

  1. Gateway receives charge request → determines 3DS is required (regulation + amount + frictionless-flow eligibility).
  2. Gateway calls processor with 3DS init → processor responds with a challenge URL.
  3. Gateway returns to merchant with state=REQUIRES_ACTION + redirect URL.
  4. User redirected to issuer's bank page; enters OTP.
  5. Issuer redirects back to gateway with auth result.
  6. Gateway calls processor with the 3DS auth result → final approve/decline.
  7. Gateway updates charge state, returns to merchant.

Frictionless 3DS

For low-risk transactions (returning customer, low amount, trusted device), the issuer can approve without challenge. Gateway sends device fingerprint, IP, browser data; issuer's risk engine decides. Frictionless is the goal — challenge converts ~70%, frictionless converts ~95%.

10Deep Dive 4: Idempotency End-to-End

The merchant-to-gateway hop

Merchant supplies Idempotency-Key. Gateway INSERTs charges with unique constraint on idempotency_key + merchant_id. Duplicate request returns the same charge_id with current state.

The gateway-to-processor hop

Gateway passes its own idempotency token to the processor. If our service crashes after the processor charged but before we recorded success, on retry the processor recognises the idempotency token and returns the existing result. No double-charge.

The reconciliation backstop

Daily reconciliation compares our charges table with the processor's settlement report. Any charge they have that we don't (or vice versa) is investigated; manual or automated repair.

11Deep Dive 5: Reconciliation & Settlement

Daily processor reports

Each processor delivers a daily file (or API) of all charges, refunds, and chargebacks. Our reconciliation job loads these, joins with our charges table by processor_charge_id, validates totals match. Discrepancies create incident tickets.

Settlement to merchants

Per merchant, daily aggregate: sum of net_cents (charges − refunds − fees). Initiate ACH/bank transfer for the rolled-up amount. Settlement timing depends on merchant's plan: standard (T+2), instant (T+0 for a higher fee).

Chargebacks

Customer disputes a charge with their bank; bank issues a chargeback. Gateway receives notification (via processor webhook). State transitions to DISPUTED; we hold the disputed amount + chargeback fee. Merchant has a window to contest; depending on outcome, money flows.

12Failure Modes & Recovery

FailureMitigation
Processor timeoutSmart router retries with secondary processor. The first one's outcome (charged or not) must be reconciled later; if a duplicate charge occurred, refund automatically.
Vault failureVault is multi-AZ; KMS keys replicated. If vault is unreachable, new charges fail loudly; old tokens still work because card data is encrypted at rest with key references.
Charge succeeds, our DB write failsThe processor charged the user. Reconciliation catches in EOD report. Auto-create the charges row backfill; webhook merchant of the late-arrived success.
Merchant webhook endpoint downDurable retry queue: 1 min → 5 min → 30 min → 1 hr → 6 hr → 1 day. After max retries, escalate to merchant alerting.
Catastrophic processor outageRouting automatically prefers other processors; merchant approval rate dips slightly but charges still go through.

13Scaling Path

StageArchitecture
10 TPSSingle Postgres. One processor. No routing.
1k TPSThis article's design. Smart router. Multi-processor. Vault separate.
10k TPSPostgres sharded by merchant_id. Webhook fleet auto-scaled.
Multi-regionPer-region gateways with local processors; cross-region recon at EOD.

14Cross-Questions and Pushbacks

"How do you handle a charge that succeeded at the processor but our system crashed before recording it?"
Answer: Three layers. (1) Idempotency token passed to processor — retrying the request returns the existing result, no double-charge. (2) Pre-flight INSERT: we write charges row with state=PENDING before calling the processor. On crash, the row is in PENDING; a reconciliation worker checks status via processor API and finalises the state. (3) EOD reconciliation against processor's settlement file catches anything else. The user is never double-charged; the merchant gets a delayed webhook in the worst case.
How do you handle PCI scope when storing token vault separately?
Vault is a separate VPC with strict access controls: only specific service roles can detokenise; all access audited. The vault's database is encrypted at rest with KMS keys; key rotation enforced annually. Merchants never touch the vault directly. Internal services that detokenise (the processor-adapter only) are themselves PCI-scoped but minimal. Annual external audit (QSA) reviews scope. The rest of the gateway — charges DB, smart router, webhooks — handles tokens, not PANs, and is out of scope.
"Smart routing with retries — won't that approve some charges twice (e.g. issuer responds slowly so you retry to a second processor)?"
Answer: Retries are not automatic on all decline codes. Specifically: timeouts (issuer didn't respond) are not retried to a second processor — we wait and use the original. Hard declines (insufficient funds, fraud) are not retried at all. Soft declines (issuer unavailable, do_not_honor) trigger one retry to a different processor. Even with retries, processor-level idempotency tokens + EOD reconciliation catches accidental dupes; auto-refund. The retry policy is tuned per decline code with empirical data.
How do you handle currency conversion?
Two modes. (1) Single-currency: merchant prices in USD, charges in USD; we settle USD to merchant's USD account. No FX. (2) Local-currency: merchant prices in INR; we use a local Indian processor, charge in INR, settle INR. (3) Multi-currency settlement: merchant prices in EUR for a USD customer; we charge USD, convert at our published rate (with FX margin), settle to merchant's EUR account. FX margin is a revenue line. Rates updated every hour.
How does the merchant know when a charge succeeded?
Two paths. (1) Synchronous: their POST /charges returns 200 with state=SUCCEEDED. Most common. (2) Asynchronous: 3DS requires user action; merchant gets state=REQUIRES_ACTION and must poll or wait for webhook. Webhooks are durable with retries; we sign webhooks (HMAC) so merchant can verify authenticity. Merchant must implement webhook idempotency on their side. Best practice: rely on webhooks as source of truth for state, treat synchronous response as best-effort indication.

Problem 22: Designing a Change Data Capture Pipeline

Stream every insert/update/delete from your OLTP database to downstream consumers (search, cache, warehouse, microservices) with low latency, exactly-once semantics, and graceful schema evolution.

Article Contents
  1. Context and Why This Problem Matters
  2. Requirements Gathering
  3. Capacity Estimation
  4. API / Configuration
  5. Data Model — Events & Schema Registry
  6. High-Level Architecture
  7. Deep Dive 1: Reading the WAL / Binlog
  8. Deep Dive 2: Schema Evolution
  9. Deep Dive 3: Exactly-Once Delivery
  10. Deep Dive 4: Initial Snapshot + Ongoing CDC
  11. Deep Dive 5: Consumer Patterns
  12. Failure Modes & Recovery
  13. Scaling Path
  14. Cross-Questions and Pushbacks

1Context and Why This Problem Matters

CDC is the spine of any modern data platform. Whenever you've said "write to the DB and publish to Kafka" you've created a dual-write problem — the two can diverge on failure. CDC solves it by reading the DB's own write-ahead log (Postgres WAL, MySQL binlog, MongoDB oplog) and turning every row change into a stream event. Search indexes update, caches invalidate, downstream microservices react — all from a single authoritative source.

2Requirements Gathering

Functional

  • Capture every insert/update/delete from configured tables.
  • Emit ordered events per row (insert → update → update → delete).
  • Schema metadata included in or referenced by each event.
  • Initial snapshot of existing data (when a connector is first turned on).
  • Multiple downstream consumers, each at its own pace.
  • Replay from any point in history (within retention).

Non-functional

  • End-to-end latency P99 < 5 s (DB commit → consumer receives).
  • Throughput: 100k events/sec sustained, 500k peak.
  • Exactly-once semantics per consumer (with proper consumer logic).
  • Zero data loss on connector restart.
  • Schema changes (add column, drop column) handled without downtime.

3Capacity Estimation

MetricNumber
Source DB write rate (peak)~50 k writes/s
CDC event rate (peak)~100 k events/s (one row update = 1 event)
Avg event size (key + value + metadata)~2 KB
Bandwidth (peak)~200 MB/s
Kafka topics~1 per source table
Partitions per topic12–32 (sized for parallel consumers)
Kafka retention7 days (or compacted forever for snapshot tables)
🔑 From Numbers to Architecture
  • ~100 k events/sec peak → Kafka can take 1 M+ per broker; the constraint is per-topic partition count (sized for consumer parallelism).
  • Source DB has WAL / binlog → Debezium reads it directly, never queries the DB (no extra load on the source).
  • Exactly-once delivery to downstream → Kafka transactions + idempotent consumers; same row update produces the same Kafka message even on connector restart.
  • Ordering matters per-key → events for one row land on one Kafka partition; consumers process in order per partition.
  • Schema evolution (column added) → Schema Registry (Confluent / Karapace); consumers use Avro/Protobuf; backward-compatible by default.
  • Snapshot tables (need "current state per key") → log-compacted Kafka topic; eventually only the latest value per key is retained.

4API / Configuration

Most CDC infrastructure is configured, not API-driven. A typical Debezium connector config:

{ "name": "orders-connector", "config": { "connector.class": "io.debezium.connector.postgresql.PostgresConnector", "database.hostname": "prod-orders.rds.aws", "database.dbname": "orders", "database.user": "cdc_user", "plugin.name": "pgoutput", "publication.name": "dbz_publication", "slot.name": "orders_slot", "table.include.list": "public.orders,public.line_items", "topic.prefix": "orders.v1", "snapshot.mode": "initial", "schema.history.internal.kafka.bootstrap.servers": "kafka:9092", "schema.history.internal.kafka.topic": "schema.history.orders" } }

Health API

GET /connectors // list GET /connectors/{name}/status // running, paused, FAILED POST /connectors/{name}/pause POST /connectors/{name}/resume POST /connectors/{name}/restart

5Data Model — Events & Schema Registry

Event envelope (Debezium-style)

{ "op": "u", // c=create, u=update, d=delete, r=read (snapshot) "ts_ms": 1747396523123, "source": { "version": "2.5", "connector": "postgres", "name": "orders.v1", "snapshot": false, "lsn": 7654321, "txId": 89, "schema": "public", "table": "orders" }, "before": { // null on insert "id": "o_abc", "amount": 5000, "state": "PENDING", "version": 1 }, "after": { // null on delete "id": "o_abc", "amount": 5000, "state": "CONFIRMED", "version": 2 }, "transaction": null, // present for transaction-aware mode "schema_id": 12345 // reference to Schema Registry }

Schema Registry

Holds versioned Avro/Protobuf/JSON-Schema definitions of each topic's keys and values. Producers serialise with a schema ID; consumers deserialise using the registered schema. Compatibility checks (backward / forward) enforced on registration.

6High-Level Architecture

Source DB (Postgres / MySQL / MongoDB) │ │ WAL / binlog / oplog ▼ ┌─────────────────────────────┐ │ Debezium Connector │ ← runs on Kafka Connect / standalone │ - reads WAL │ │ - decodes change events │ │ - resolves schema │ └────────┬─────────────────────┘ │ ▼ ┌─────────────────────────────┐ │ Kafka topics │ ← one per table, partitioned by PK │ orders.v1.public.orders │ │ orders.v1.public.line_items │ └────────┬─────────────────────┘ │ ┌───────┴────────────────┐ │ │ ▼ ▼ Search consumer Cache invalidator → Elasticsearch → Redis HDEL keys │ ▼ Warehouse loader → Snowflake / BigQuery Schema Registry: separate service (Confluent / Apicurio)

7Deep Dive 1: Reading the WAL / Binlog

The trick to CDC: don't poll the DB; read its own change log.

Postgres logical replication

  • Create a replication slot: CREATE_REPLICATION_SLOT slot_name LOGICAL pgoutput.
  • Connector subscribes; receives a stream of BEGIN / COMMIT / INSERT / UPDATE / DELETE events with LSN (Log Sequence Number).
  • Each event has the row data; connector publishes to Kafka.
  • Postgres holds WAL until the slot's LSN is acked → important to keep consumers running, else WAL grows unbounded.

MySQL binlog

Similar concept: GTID or file+position. Server must be configured with binlog_format=ROW and binlog_row_image=FULL.

MongoDB oplog

Tailable cursor on local.oplog.rs. Each entry is an op (insert/update/delete) with the resulting document. Watch for collection-level change streams in modern MongoDB.

8Deep Dive 2: Schema Evolution

Tables change. Add a column → CDC must keep working without dropping events.

Compatibility levels

  • Backward compatible: new schema can read old data. Default; safest. Add a column with a default value: ok.
  • Forward compatible: old schema can read new data. Useful when consumers can't upgrade in lock-step.
  • Full compatible: both. Strictest.

Schema Registry rejects incompatible changes at registration time. Producer cannot publish events that violate the topic's compatibility setting.

Breaking changes (rare)

Renaming a column, changing type, dropping a non-nullable column: requires a new topic version (orders.v2). Producers dual-write to v1 and v2 during migration; consumers migrate one-by-one. After all consumers move, v1 is retired.

9Deep Dive 3: Exactly-Once Delivery

Kafka itself is at-least-once by default. Exactly-once requires producer + consumer cooperation.

Producer side (CDC connector)

Kafka transactional producers + idempotent send: each batch of events gets a producer epoch + sequence number; Kafka brokers reject duplicates. The connector commits its source-LSN offset and the Kafka transaction in lock-step. No event written twice; no event lost on restart.

Consumer side

Two options:

  • Transactional consumer: read events, write to a transactional sink, commit Kafka offset and sink transaction together. True exactly-once. Hard to implement against non-transactional sinks.
  • Idempotent consumer: use the event's primary key + LSN as idempotency key. Sink stores last-seen LSN per row; ignores events with LSN ≤ stored. Effectively exactly-once even with at-least-once delivery.

10Deep Dive 4: Initial Snapshot + Ongoing CDC

When you turn on CDC against a table with 1B existing rows, you need to backfill before the WAL stream becomes useful.

Snapshot phase

  1. Connector takes a read lock briefly (or uses MVCC snapshot — no lock with Postgres).
  2. Captures the current WAL position as the cutover point.
  3. Reads the table in chunks, emits op=r (read/snapshot) events.
  4. When done, switches to streaming WAL from the captured position.

Consumer view

Consumer sees a stream of r events (the historical state) then c/u/d events (ongoing changes). Most consumers treat r like c. After snapshot, throughput drops to the steady rate.

Incremental snapshot (Debezium 1.6+)

For very large tables, traditional snapshots block. Incremental snapshot interleaves chunks of the historical read with streaming CDC, so the WAL never falls too far behind.

11Deep Dive 5: Consumer Patterns

Search index sync

Consumer reads CDC topic; applies inserts/updates/deletes to Elasticsearch. Ordering preserved per-row via Kafka partition key = primary key. ~seconds of lag.

Cache invalidation

On update events for table X, DEL the cache keys derived from the row. Useful for cache-aside patterns where the writer might not know to invalidate — CDC handles it as a side-channel.

Warehouse / analytics ingestion

Hourly: batch up the last hour of events, write to S3, COPY into Snowflake / BigQuery. Stream-style: tools like Fivetran / Snowpipe consume continuously.

Microservice integration

Service B reacts to changes in service A's DB by subscribing to A's CDC topic — without A needing to publish events explicitly. Couples on schema but decouples on code.

12Failure Modes & Recovery

FailureMitigation
Connector down for hoursPostgres retains WAL because slot's LSN is unacked. On restart, connector resumes from last LSN; no events lost. Risk: WAL disk filling up; alert before that happens.
Schema registry downProducer caches recent schemas; can continue for a brief window. Consumers similarly cache. Extended outage halts new schema registrations.
Kafka cluster downConnector stops producing; replication slot accumulates WAL. Source DB still operational. Recover Kafka → connector drains backlog.
Replication slot abandonedWAL accumulates → disk fills → DB writes fail. Monitor slot lag as a top-priority alert. If a connector is decommissioned, drop the slot.
Schema change breaks consumerSchema registry's compatibility check prevents incompatible registration. If a real break happens, consumer skips bad events (DLQ) and alerts.

13Scaling Path

StageArchitecture
One table, low trafficSingle Debezium connector + single Kafka topic + one consumer.
Dozens of tablesOne connector per source DB; topics per table; consumer groups for fanout.
100s of tables, multiple DBsKafka Connect cluster; per-connector partitioning. Schema Registry mature.
Multi-regionPer-region CDC; MirrorMaker 2 for cross-region replication of selected topics.

14Cross-Questions and Pushbacks

"Why not just dual-write to DB and Kafka in the application?"
Answer: The dual-write problem. If you write to DB and Kafka, the two can diverge: DB write succeeds, Kafka write fails — now downstream is stale; or vice versa. Worse, retries cause duplicates. CDC reads the DB's authoritative log, so there's a single source of truth. Anything committed to the DB is in the WAL; events emit deterministically. The "Outbox pattern" is a variant: app writes to DB + an outbox table in the same transaction; CDC reads the outbox. Either way, you're using CDC to avoid dual-writes.
"Exactly-once is a myth — Kafka can't guarantee it across heterogeneous sinks."
Answer: Correct — exactly-once is end-to-end, and only achievable when both producer and consumer cooperate. Within Kafka itself, transactional producers + read_committed consumers give exactly-once. With external sinks, you fall back to effectively exactly-once via idempotent consumers (PK + version stored alongside the sink record, dedup on consume). For non-idempotent sinks (e.g. sending an email), at-least-once is the best we can do; the sink itself must handle dedup. We don't pretend; we tell consumers exactly what guarantees they have.
How does ordering work across partitions?
Kafka guarantees order within a partition, not across. We partition by primary key, so all events for a given row land on the same partition in order: insert → update → delete. Cross-row ordering is not preserved across partitions, which is usually fine because consumers process rows independently. If you need transaction-level ordering across rows, use Debezium's "transaction-aware" mode (emits BEGIN/COMMIT events) and have consumers group by transaction.
How do you handle a table with 1B rows for the initial snapshot?
Incremental snapshot mode. Connector reads the table in PK-ordered chunks (e.g. 1000 rows at a time) and interleaves with WAL streaming. While snapshot is running, current changes also flow as c/u/d events. Consumer sees a mix; idempotency by PK ensures the final state is correct. For very large tables, snapshot takes hours but the database is never blocked, and the WAL doesn't grow unbounded.
"What happens when someone drops a critical column from the source table?"
Answer: Schema registry rejects backward-incompatible changes by default; if registry compatibility is set to BACKWARD, the connector cannot publish events with the new schema. The DBA's ALTER TABLE DROP COLUMN succeeds at the DB level, but the CDC pipeline halts with a clear error. Recovery: either restore the column, or explicitly rotate to a new topic version (orders.v2) after coordinating with consumers. Workflow: schema changes go through a CI check that simulates the registry's compatibility rules before deploy.

Problem 23: Designing UPI (Unified Payments Interface)

India's account-to-account real-time payments rail. 10 B transactions/month, P99 under 5 s, mediated by NPCI's central switch, across 300+ banks — and "successful" means money actually moved at both banks.

1Context and Why This Problem Matters

UPI is the rare system-design problem where the architecture isn't a tech company's choice — it's a national rail. The interview question "design UPI" is really "explain a multi-party real-time payments network with strong correctness." It exercises four-corner flows (payer bank, payee bank, NPCI, PSP apps), idempotency across organisations, deemed-approval semantics, and the genuinely interesting netting / settlement story.

2Requirements Gathering

Functional

  • Users have a VPA (virtual payment address, e.g. name@bank) linked to a bank account.
  • P2P send: pay another VPA an amount.
  • P2M: pay a merchant via VPA or QR.
  • Collect request: payee initiates, payer approves.
  • Mandate / auto-debit: recurring or one-tap pull (e.g. SIPs, subscriptions).
  • Refunds and reversals.

Non-functional

  • ~10 B transactions/month, 4k–8k TPS peak.
  • P99 end-to-end < 5 s.
  • Available 24×7 (no batch windows like legacy ACH).
  • Strong correctness — money never moves at only one bank.
  • Regulatory: audit trail, AML, OFAC checks, RBI reporting.

3Capacity Estimation

MetricNumber
Total UPI users~400 M
Transactions / month~10 B
Transactions / sec (avg)~3,800/s
Transactions / sec (peak, festival)~10 k/s
Avg ticket size₹500 (~$6)
Connected banks~300
Connected PSPs (apps like GPay, PhonePe)~40
End-to-end SLAP99 < 5 s
🔑 From Numbers to Architecture
  • ~10 k TPS peak across ~300 banks → NPCI as the central switch (a managed message bus, like Kafka + routing); PSPs and banks connect as participants.
  • P99 < 5 s end-to-end → no synchronous chain of 4 hops > 1 s each; banks respond from in-memory account cache + async settlement.
  • VPA → bank mapping (~400 M users) → distributed lookup at NPCI; cached at each PSP for the user's own VPA.
  • Settlement: real-time intra-bank (direct ledger), deferred-net for inter-bank (NPCI nets transactions every few hours).
  • Idempotency on every leg → unique transaction reference (UTR); retries safe; reconciliation possible 24 h later.
  • Disputes / refunds → separate flow over the same rails; each transaction has a 24-hour SLA for chargebacks.

4API Design

From PSP app to PSP backend

POST /v1/pay Authorization: device PIN re-confirmed { "from_vpa": "ramesh@hdfcbank", "to_vpa": "merchant@icicibank", "amount_inr": 1499.00, "note": "Coffee", "txn_ref_id": "TXN_uuid" // client-generated idempotency token } → 202 { "txn_id": "...", "state": "INITIATED" } // success when settled final state pushed via webhook / poll: { "txn_id":"...", "state":"SUCCESS"|"FAILED"|"DEEMED_SUCCESS" }

NPCI-facing API (between PSP / bank and NPCI)

Defined by NPCI specs: ISO-20022-like XML messages over HTTPS with mutual TLS. Each PSP and bank implements an "UPI Switch" microservice that speaks these protocols.

5Data Model

VPAs (Bank's mapping service)

CREATE TABLE vpas ( vpa VARCHAR(255) PRIMARY KEY, -- 'ramesh@hdfcbank' account_no VARCHAR(20), ifsc VARCHAR(11), customer_id UUID, active BOOLEAN, created_at TIMESTAMPTZ ); CREATE INDEX idx_vpa_active ON vpas(vpa) WHERE active;

Transactions (immutable, per-side)

CREATE TABLE transactions ( txn_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, npci_txn_id VARCHAR(35) UNIQUE, -- the canonical NPCI reference from_vpa VARCHAR(255), to_vpa VARCHAR(255), amount_paisa BIGINT, state VARCHAR(20), -- INITIATED, AUTHENTICATED, DEBITED, COMPLETED, FAILED, REVERSED, DEEMED_SUCCESS initiated_at TIMESTAMPTZ, debit_at TIMESTAMPTZ, credit_at TIMESTAMPTZ, reversed_at TIMESTAMPTZ, idempotency_key VARCHAR(64) UNIQUE );

6High-Level Architecture

User (PSP app: GPay/PhonePe/Paytm) │ HTTPS POST /pay (with UPI PIN) ▼ ┌────────────────────────┐ │ PSP App Backend │ │ - device + PIN check │ │ - constructs request │ └────────┬───────────────-┘ │ ▼ ┌────────────────────────┐ │ PSP's UPI Switch │ ← speaks NPCI protocol └────────┬───────────────-┘ │ mutual TLS, ISO-style XML ▼ ┌────────────────────────┐ │ NPCI Switch │ ← the central hub │ - validates VPAs │ │ - routes to banks │ │ - tracks transaction │ └─┬────────────────────┬─┘ │ │ ▼ ▼ Payer Bank Payee Bank UPI Switch UPI Switch │ │ ▼ ▼ Core Banking Core Banking (DEBIT account) (CREDIT account) │ │ └────── ack ───────┘ │ ▼ NPCI marks SUCCESS │ ▼ PSPs notified → user notified Side pipes: • Settlement (NPCI clearing house) — multilateral netting • Audit feeds to RBI, fraud monitoring

7Deep Dive 1: The NPCI Switch

NPCI is the central orchestrator. Every UPI transaction passes through it. It serves three functions:

  1. VPA resolution: given a VPA, look up the customer's bank + account.
  2. Transaction routing: forward the debit instruction to the payer bank; forward the credit to the payee bank.
  3. Settlement bookkeeping: track every transaction for end-of-day net settlement.

The two-phase flow

  1. PSP submits payment request to NPCI with payer + payee VPAs.
  2. NPCI resolves payee VPA → confirms payee exists.
  3. NPCI sends debit instruction to payer bank.
  4. Payer bank validates PIN (UPI PIN is bank-validated, not PSP-validated), checks balance, debits account, returns "Debit Success."
  5. NPCI sends credit instruction to payee bank.
  6. Payee bank credits account, returns "Credit Success."
  7. NPCI marks transaction SUCCESS, notifies both PSPs.

If any step fails

If credit fails after debit succeeded, NPCI initiates a reversal: instructs the payer bank to credit back. Within minutes. Reversals are a normal part of the flow, not an edge case.

8Deep Dive 2: VPA Resolution

The address book

Each bank manages VPAs for its customers. The VPA ramesh@hdfcbank tells everyone: "go ask HDFC's UPI switch to resolve this."

Resolution flow

  1. NPCI parses the VPA → identifies the handle (hdfcbank) → maps to HDFC's PSP code.
  2. NPCI sends a "validate VPA" request to HDFC's UPI switch.
  3. HDFC returns the customer's name, account exists confirmation.
  4. NPCI returns customer name to the payer (so the payer sees "Sending to RAMESH KUMAR" and can confirm).

Why not store all VPAs centrally at NPCI

Privacy + autonomy + scale. Each bank owns its customer data. NPCI is a router, not a name registry. Banks can change account mappings without coordinating with NPCI.

9Deep Dive 3: Multilateral Netting & Settlement

For every UPI transaction, the payer bank owes the payee bank the amount. With 10 B transactions/month across 300 banks, settling each individually would be impractical.

Multilateral netting

Throughout the day, NPCI tracks every txn: bank A → bank B by ₹X. At the settlement window (multiple times per day, modern UPI), NPCI computes the net position per bank pair, then per bank against all others. Each bank either owes (or is owed) a single net amount.

Settlement

Banks transfer the net amounts via the RTGS (Real Time Gross Settlement) system run by RBI. Instead of 10M individual transfers, NPCI does ~300 net transfers per cycle.

Why this matters for design

The customer-visible UPI flow is real-time (5 s). The bank-to-bank money movement is netted and settled in batches. This separation is essential — without netting, the underlying rail couldn't carry the volume. Customers and banks see different timelines.

10Deep Dive 4: End-to-End Idempotency

A UPI transaction crosses 5 systems (App, PSP, NPCI, payer bank, payee bank). Each can timeout / retry independently. Idempotency is non-negotiable.

The npci_txn_id is the global identifier

NPCI assigns a unique 35-character txn_id at the start of every transaction. Every system stores it; every retry uses it. If the payer bank receives the same debit instruction twice (a retry from NPCI), it recognises the npci_txn_id and returns the previous result, not a second debit.

Per-hop idempotency

Each hop (App↔PSP, PSP↔NPCI, NPCI↔Bank) has its own retry / timeout. Each side stores the npci_txn_id with its local state and dedups on receipt. Network blips don't double-debit; client retries don't double-debit; bank-side queue replays don't double-debit.

11Deep Dive 5: Deemed-Approved & Reversal

Sometimes a bank's response is delayed beyond SLA. UPI defines "deemed-approved" / "deemed-failed" semantics to handle this.

Deemed success

If the payer bank debited the account but the credit confirmation didn't arrive at NPCI within the SLA window, NPCI marks the transaction as "DEEMED_SUCCESS" and notifies the user that it's processed. The actual credit happens on the next scheduled settlement.

Deemed failure

If neither bank confirmed, NPCI marks DEEMED_FAILED. If any bank later replies "actually I did debit," NPCI triggers a reversal back to the payer.

Why this matters

Users can't be left in limbo for hours. The system says "ok, treat this as decided" after a timeout, and uses delayed reconciliation to make money flows match. The customer experience is decisive; the bookkeeping catches up.

12Failure Modes & Recovery

FailureMitigation
Payer bank slowNPCI times out; transaction returned as PENDING. App polls; bank may reply later; reconcile.
Debit OK, credit failedNPCI triggers reversal: instructs payer bank to credit back. Reversal flows guaranteed by NPCI rules.
Both banks debited (impossible in normal flow but seen with double-submission)npci_txn_id dedup; the second submission is rejected at the bank with "duplicate transaction."
NPCI switch outageUPI stops nationally — extremely rare and historically resolved within minutes. PSPs queue transactions; replay when up.
VPA misresolution (payer typed wrong handle)Customer name confirmation before final submit catches most. Wrong account = customer's mistake; refund requires the payee's cooperation.
Mass fraud detectionBank/NPCI can pause specific VPAs or block specific handles in real time.

13Scaling Path

UPI is the canonical "designed for scale from day one" system — capacity growth is regulatory, not architectural. NPCI has expanded the switch capacity over time (currently around 4k–8k TPS sustained, with headroom). Banks scale their UPI switches independently. PSPs scale their app backends.

StageArchitecture
Bootstrap (2016)NPCI built single switch. PSPs (banks themselves) connected.
Mass adoption (2019+)3rd-party PSPs (GPay, PhonePe, Paytm). Switch capacity quadrupled.
TodayMulti-DC switch, real-time fraud detection, mandate framework, international integrations (UPI in UAE, Singapore).

14Cross-Questions and Pushbacks

"Why does NPCI sit in the middle — couldn't banks just talk to each other directly?"
Answer: Bilateral connectivity would require 300 banks × 299 = ~90,000 connections. Operationally infeasible. NPCI is the hub-and-spoke model that makes a network with hundreds of participants tractable. Each bank maintains one connection to NPCI; NPCI routes between them. Settlement also benefits: netting requires a central party to compute positions. The U.S. equivalent (FedNow) and EU's TIPS use the same hub design.
How is the UPI PIN secured?
PIN is encrypted at the device with a public key from the user's bank (not the PSP, not NPCI). Encrypted PIN travels through PSP and NPCI as opaque bytes; only the payer bank can decrypt. PSP never sees the PIN. NPCI never sees the PIN. This is the cornerstone of UPI's trust model — even a malicious PSP cannot harvest PINs.
"5 second SLA across 5 hops is tight. Where does the latency budget go?"
Answer: Budget breakdown: device-to-PSP ~500 ms (mobile network), PSP-to-NPCI ~100 ms (same-region datacenter), NPCI-to-bank ~200 ms × 2 (debit + credit), bank core processing ~500 ms × 2. Total ~2 s typical. The 5 s P99 accounts for retries on slow banks. Bank core systems are the slowest hop — they're typically Java monoliths on mainframes; modernising them is a multi-year initiative. NPCI publishes per-bank latency metrics to incentivise improvement.
How do recurring mandates (SIP / subscription) work?
User signs a mandate once (via UPI PIN). The mandate is registered at NPCI + payer bank with parameters: max amount, frequency, payee VPA, expiry. On each scheduled charge, the merchant initiates via PSP → NPCI → payer bank: "execute mandate M, charge ₹X." Bank checks mandate validity, debits without re-PIN, settles. User can revoke any time at the bank or app level.
How is multi-currency / cross-border supported?
UPI is INR-only domestically. Cross-border extensions (UPI in Singapore via PayNow integration, in UAE, etc.) involve bilateral agreements between NPCI and the partner national rail. Currency conversion happens at one of the participating banks; the user sees the converted amount before approving. End-to-end protocol details extend NPCI's existing message set with currency fields. Slower scaling because each country needs a separate bilateral negotiation.

Problem 24: Designing a Payment System with Double-Entry Ledger

The internal money-of-record system: wallets, transfers, holds, refunds — all backed by an immutable double-entry ledger that the CFO can audit and that survives any single-component failure without losing a cent.
