1Context and Why This Problem Matters

If P21 (Payment Gateway) is the external interface to money networks, P24 is the internal source of truth for "who has how much." It's the system a fintech keeps the books on. Get the data model right and reconciliation is easy; get it wrong and you discover years later that your platform is short by millions. The two ideas that matter: double-entry bookkeeping (centuries old, still right) and immutable append-only ledger (modern engineering for what accountants have done since 1494).

2Requirements Gathering

Functional

  • Maintain a wallet/balance per user (or merchant, or any account).
  • Transfer money between accounts (P2P, P2M, refunds, fees, payouts).
  • Place holds (auth-then-capture pattern) and release.
  • Reverse / refund transactions.
  • Query: balance, transaction history, statement, audit log.
  • Multi-currency, with FX conversion lines.
  • Daily / monthly statements; CSV export for accounting.

Non-functional

  • Throughput: ~5k transfers/sec sustained, ~50k peak.
  • P99 transfer latency < 100 ms (it's an internal hop, must be fast).
  • Strict consistency: sum of all balances = sum of all funded amounts, always.
  • Audit-grade durability: every transaction is immutable, signed, retained 7+ years.
  • Reconcilable with external sources (bank statements, payment gateway).

3Capacity Estimation

1 day = 100k sec; that's the only math we need.

MetricNumber
Accounts~100 M
Transfers/day~500 M
Transfers/sec (avg)500M / 100k = 5 k/s
Transfers/sec (peak)~50 k/s (festival/payroll)
Ledger lines per transfer (double-entry)2 (one debit, one credit) minimum
Ledger writes/sec (peak)~100 k/s
Avg ledger row size~300 B
Storage/day~150 GB
7-year storage × 3 replicas~1.1 PB
🔑 From Numbers to Architecture
  • ~100 k ledger writes/sec peak → sharded Postgres (or NewSQL) by account_id; double-entry guarantees every transfer is exactly 2 rows.
  • Append-only journal → no UPDATE / DELETE on ledger rows; corrections happen via reversing entries; preserves audit forever.
  • Ledger lines must balance to zero → enforced by a transactional INSERT of both legs in one DB transaction.
  • Account balance = sum of ledger lines → too slow to compute on every read; maintain a denormalised "balance snapshot" column updated atomically via SERIALIZABLE transaction.
  • 7-year regulatory retention × 3 replicas = ~1.1 PB → hot in Postgres for 1 year, then archive to S3 + columnar warehouse for queries.
  • Daily reconciliation against external statements → batch job compares ledger totals to processor / bank statements; alerts on any mismatch.

4API Design

// Money movement POST /v1/transfers Idempotency-Key: tx_uuid { "from_account": "acc_alice", "to_account": "acc_bob", "amount": { "value": "100.00", "currency": "USD" }, "memo": "Splitting dinner", "metadata": { "external_ref": "..." } } → 201 { "transfer_id": "tr_abc", "state": "POSTED", "posted_at": "..." } // Authorisation + capture pattern POST /v1/holds { from, amount, expires_in_min: 60 } POST /v1/holds/{id}/capture { amount? } // amount<=hold; release rest POST /v1/holds/{id}/release // explicit release before expiry // Reverse / refund POST /v1/transfers/{id}/reverse { reason } // Query GET /v1/accounts/{id}/balance → { available, pending, currency } GET /v1/accounts/{id}/statement?from=...&to=... GET /v1/transfers/{id}

5Data Model

accounts

CREATE TABLE accounts ( account_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, owner_id UUID, -- user / merchant / system account type VARCHAR(20), -- USER_WALLET | MERCHANT | FEE_REVENUE | SUSPENSE | BANK currency CHAR(3), status VARCHAR(20), -- ACTIVE | FROZEN | CLOSED created_at TIMESTAMPTZ );

ledger_entries (immutable, append-only, the source of truth)

CREATE TABLE ledger_entries ( entry_id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY, transfer_id UUID NOT NULL, -- groups all entries of one transfer account_id UUID NOT NULL, direction CHAR(1) NOT NULL, -- 'D' debit | 'C' credit amount_minor BIGINT NOT NULL, -- integer minor units (cents) currency CHAR(3) NOT NULL, balance_after BIGINT NOT NULL, -- running balance for fast queries posted_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(), CONSTRAINT amount_positive CHECK (amount_minor > 0) ); CREATE INDEX idx_acct_time ON ledger_entries(account_id, posted_at DESC); CREATE INDEX idx_transfer ON ledger_entries(transfer_id); -- IMPORTANT: no UPDATE, no DELETE. Append-only. -- Reversals are MORE entries, not changes to existing.

transfers (transfer-level metadata, atomic with the entries)

CREATE TABLE transfers ( transfer_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, type VARCHAR(30), -- TRANSFER | REFUND | FEE | PAYOUT | HOLD | CAPTURE state VARCHAR(20), -- POSTED | REVERSED | HELD | CAPTURED | RELEASED idempotency_key VARCHAR(64) UNIQUE, -- dedup initiator_id UUID, amount_minor BIGINT, currency CHAR(3), posted_at TIMESTAMPTZ, metadata JSONB );

account_balances (denormalised hot read; eventually consistent with ledger)

CREATE TABLE account_balances ( account_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, available_minor BIGINT NOT NULL, pending_minor BIGINT NOT NULL, version BIGINT NOT NULL, -- optimistic-lock token updated_at TIMESTAMPTZ ); -- Computed: available = sum(credits) − sum(debits) − sum(holds) -- Stored for O(1) reads; reconciled vs ledger nightly

6High-Level Architecture (with rationale)

Producer services (Payment Gateway, Refund, Payroll, etc.) │ POST /transfers (Idempotency-Key) ▼ ┌────────────────────────┐ │ Ledger API │ — stateless, horizontally scaled └────────┬───────────────-┘ │ ▼ ┌────────────────────────┐ │ Transfer Coordinator │ — enforces idempotency, runs the tx │ - BEGIN tx │ │ - INSERT 2+ ledger_entries (atomic) │ - UPDATE account_balances (optimistic lock) │ - emit ledger.posted event │ - COMMIT │ └────────┬─────────┬──────-┘ │ │ ▼ ▼ Postgres Kafka (Source of (ledger.posted → truth) downstream consumers: analytics, fraud, notif, reconciliation) Read paths: Balance → Redis hot cache (account_balances row) Statement → Postgres replica (read replica) History → ClickHouse mirror (analytics) Long archive → S3 (compressed Parquet, 90+ days)
🔑 Why Each Component (Memorise This for Interview)
  • Postgres as source of truth — money requires ACID. Multi-row transactions (debit + credit + balance update) must commit atomically. Postgres single-node handles ~10k writes/s; sharded by account_id_hash across 8 nodes gives ~80k/s — well above our 100k peak. We do not use Cassandra/Mongo here: no multi-row ACID, no SELECT FOR UPDATE, would force us to invent transactions in app code (the leading cause of money bugs).
  • Redis cache for balances — balance is read 100× per write (every page load shows it). Postgres can do 50k reads/s; Redis does 200k/s. We cache balances in Redis with cache-aside; invalidate on every write. Source of truth remains Postgres; Redis is the speed layer.
  • Kafka for downstream events — fraud monitoring, analytics, notifications all need to react to every transfer. Direct calls would couple the ledger to N consumers. Kafka decouples: ledger publishes once, N consumers eat at their own pace. Choose Kafka over SQS/RabbitMQ because throughput (100k events/s) exceeds RabbitMQ's comfort zone and we need replay for backfills.
  • ClickHouse for analytics — column-store DB optimised for aggregations ("revenue by merchant, by month"). Postgres can do these but slowly and at the cost of OLTP performance. We CDC-ship to ClickHouse (P22) so analysts query a copy, never the live OLTP DB.
  • S3 + Parquet for cold archive — old entries (>90 days) compressed and shipped to S3. Storage cost drops 30× ($23 → $1/TB-month for Glacier Instant). Queryable via Athena when an auditor needs 2020 data.
  • No CDN — this is internal API, B2B traffic, no edge caching needed. CDN would just add cost and a stale-cache risk on balance reads.
  • What scales easily: Postgres read replicas (add more for read QPS), Kafka partitions (add more for event throughput), Redis cluster (consistent-hash shard for cache QPS).
  • What breaks first: write throughput on Postgres. At ~10k writes/s on a single node, the only fix is sharding by hash(account_id). Each tenant/account always lands on the same shard, so within-shard transactions still ACID. Cross-shard transfers (which exist) require a 2-phase commit or a Saga — see Deep Dive 2.

7Deep Dive 1: Double-Entry Ledger

The rule, unchanged since 1494: every transaction debits at least one account and credits another by the same total amount. The ledger is in balance if and only if SUM(credits) − SUM(debits) = 0 across the entire system.

Example: Alice sends Bob $100

transfer_id = T-001 ledger_entries inserted (in one atomic tx): (T-001, acc_alice, D, 10000 USD) -- debit Alice $100 (T-001, acc_bob, C, 10000 USD) -- credit Bob $100 After: sum debits − sum credits = 0. Books balance.

Example with fees

Alice sends Bob $100; we charge a $1 fee. ledger_entries: (T-002, acc_alice, D, 10100) -- Alice paid 10100 total (T-002, acc_bob, C, 10000) -- Bob received 100 (T-002, acc_fee_revenue, C, 100) -- We earned 1 debits = 10100, credits = 10100. Balanced.

Why this is correct under all conditions

The double-entry invariant is enforced at the application level (the coordinator refuses to write entries that don't sum to zero) and validated nightly by a reconciliation job that scans the entire ledger and confirms SUM(D) = SUM(C). If they ever diverge, alerts fire — it means a bug in the coordinator and is a P0 incident.

Why immutability is non-negotiable

UPDATEs and DELETEs to ledger entries are forbidden. You don't fix a wrong transfer; you post a reversal: a new transfer with opposite directions. Original entry stays in history; new entries undo it. This preserves audit trail and prevents "the transaction that vanished" class of bugs.

8Deep Dive 2: Idempotency & Saga Patterns

Idempotency

Every POST /transfers carries an Idempotency-Key. Postgres unique constraint on idempotency_key rejects duplicate inserts. Retry returns the existing transfer's state — never creates two.

Cross-shard transfers — the Saga

If Alice's account is on shard A and Bob's on shard B, a single transaction can't span them. Saga pattern:

  1. Debit Alice on shard A (locally atomic). State: PENDING.
  2. Credit Bob on shard B (locally atomic).
  3. If credit succeeds → mark transfer POSTED.
  4. If credit fails → compensating action: credit Alice back on shard A. State: REVERSED.

The window between debit and credit/reversal is brief but exists. During this window, Alice's available balance reflects the debit (money is "in flight"). Funds never disappear — at every moment, they're either with Alice, in the suspense account, or with Bob. The reconciliation job tracks suspense balances and aging.

9Deep Dive 3: Holds, Authorisations, and Pending Balances

"Hold $100 on Alice's card until restaurant captures actual amount" — a standard pattern.

Hold as a ledger operation

POST /holds { from: acc_alice, amount: 10000 } → creates a hold_id, plus ledger entries: (H-001, acc_alice, D, 10000) -- debit Alice (H-001, acc_alice_hold, C, 10000) -- credit a per-user "hold" sub-account Alice's available balance drops by $100 immediately. Her total balance (available + hold) is unchanged — money is still hers, just earmarked.

Capture (partial or full)

POST /holds/H-001/capture { amount: 7500 } → ledger entries: (CAP-001, acc_alice_hold, D, 10000) -- debit hold (full release) (CAP-001, acc_alice, C, 2500) -- credit back the un-captured part (CAP-001, acc_merchant, C, 7500) -- credit merchant the captured part

Hold expiry

Holds carry expiry (e.g. 7 days). A scheduled job (see P16) releases unused holds:

(EXP-001, acc_alice_hold, D, 10000) (EXP-001, acc_alice, C, 10000) -- Hold returns to available; net zero impact.

10Deep Dive 4: Reconciliation & Suspense Accounts

External money rails (bank, payment gateway) maintain their own books. Our ledger must match theirs.

Suspense accounts

When money "should be in transit" — debited from our books, not yet confirmed on the bank's books — we credit a suspense account. The bank later confirms via webhook / settlement file; we move from suspense to the target account.

The aging of suspense balances is a top reconciliation metric: every entry in suspense should clear within hours (or days, for bank rails). Aged entries are alerts: something didn't settle.

Daily reconciliation job

  1. For each external rail (bank, gateway, processor), load their settlement file or query their API.
  2. Group by transaction reference.
  3. Compare amounts: ours vs theirs.
  4. Match: clear suspense entries.
  5. Mismatch: flag for human investigation.
  6. Total credit-debit invariant verified across all accounts at end.

11Deep Dive 5: Money Representation & Currency

Never use floats

Floats lose precision. $0.10 might be stored as 0.0999999... and 100 transfers add up to $9.99 instead of $10.00. Two safe representations:

  • Integer minor units: store cents (or paisa for INR, satoshi for BTC). $100 → 10000. Math is exact integer arithmetic. The choice for almost all payment systems.
  • Arbitrary precision decimal: NUMERIC(15,4) in Postgres, BigDecimal in Java. Slower but no precision loss; useful for FX rates with sub-cent precision.

Multi-currency

Every account has a currency. Transfers between same-currency accounts are direct. Cross-currency transfers go through an FX leg:

Alice (USD) → Bob (INR), 100 USD at rate 83.4 INR/USD = 8340 INR (acc_alice, D, 10000 USD) (acc_fx_pool_USD, C, 10000 USD) (acc_fx_pool_INR, D, 834000 INR) -- 8340.00 INR in paisa (acc_bob, C, 834000 INR) -- USD side balances; INR side balances; FX margin retained by acc_fx_revenue (small fraction)

Each currency's ledger must balance independently. You never sum across currencies — apples and oranges. The FX revenue account captures spread; reconciled against the FX desk's hedging positions.

12Failure Modes & Recovery

FailureMitigation
Coordinator crashes mid-transfer (debit done, credit not done)The transfer state is PENDING in DB. A reconciliation worker every 30 s scans PENDING transfers; commits or rolls back based on whether the credit side's row exists. Suspense entries make this deterministic.
Cross-shard credit fails permanentlyCompensating debit reversal on the source shard. Audit log records both the failed credit and the reversal. Net change: zero.
Redis balance cache staleStale read possible for ~ms after a write. Solution: write-through invalidation (delete cache key on write); next read re-fetches from Postgres. For strict reads (just-charged users checking balance), read directly from Postgres replica.
Postgres primary failureFailover to standby in ~30 s. In-flight transactions either commit (already on standby's WAL) or roll back (lost between primary and standby). Clients retry — idempotency makes retries safe.
Bug introduces non-balancing transferNightly invariant check fires. Block further writes from the affected coordinator version. Issue investigation + correcting reversal entries.
External bank says "you sent us $X" but our ledger says $YSuspense entries pinpoint the discrepancy. Manual investigation; corrective ledger entry to align with bank's reality (we believe the bank for legal disputes).

13Scaling Path

StageArchitecture
10 transfers/sSingle Postgres. App + DB on the same box. Synchronous everything.
1 k/sAdd Redis balance cache. Async event publishing via outbox table.
10 k/sShard Postgres by account_id hash; ~8 shards. Cross-shard via Saga + suspense.
100 k/sMulti-region with same-region transfers majority. Cross-region transfers explicit, batched.

14Cross-Questions and Pushbacks

"Why double-entry? Just track balances in one column."
Answer: Single-balance designs have failed every fintech that tried them. The problems: (1) no audit trail — when balance is wrong, you don't know what made it wrong. (2) no reconciliation invariant — without "sum of all entries = 0," you have no way to detect drift. (3) partial-failure ambiguity — if A → B fails mid-flight, did A's balance decrease? Did B's increase? Double-entry makes it explicit: each side is its own row. Centuries of accounting practice converged on this for a reason. Modern systems (Stripe Ledger, Square Cash, every bank) use double-entry.
"Postgres at 100k writes/s — won't it die?"
Answer: Sharded by hash(account_id) across 8 nodes, each handles ~12.5k writes/s — within Postgres's ~10–20k/node ceiling. Within-shard transfers (~95% of traffic) are local ACID. Cross-shard transfers use Saga + suspense. We do not switch to a NoSQL DB because we'd lose multi-row ACID — and that's what makes the double-entry invariant enforceable in the first place.
How do you compute balance — sum all entries every time?
No. We maintain a denormalised account_balances row updated in the same transaction as new ledger entries. Hot reads hit Redis cache of this row → ~1 ms. The full sum-of-entries query is only run during the nightly invariant check. We also store balance_after per entry as a denormalised "running balance" for statement rendering — avoids re-aggregating to generate a statement.
How do you handle accounting changes — say a fee model update applies retroactively?
You don't change history. You post correcting entries: ledger entries with reason="FEE_CORRECTION" that reverse the old fee and apply the new one. Audit trail shows the original transaction, the correction, and a link to the policy change. Books always balance at every moment. Customer sees the net effect in their statement.
What's a "suspense account" and why does it matter?
A suspense account holds money "in transit" — debited from the source, not yet credited to the destination. Used heavily for external bank rails (we debited our customer to send to their bank, but the bank hasn't confirmed receipt yet). The credit-debit invariant still holds: money is in our books, just in suspense. When the bank confirms, we move from suspense to the customer's bank-side account. Aged suspense entries (>48h) are alerts: something didn't settle and needs investigation.
"At 100k writes/s, won't the WAL be huge and replication lag?"
Answer: At 300 B/row × 100k/s = 30 MB/s WAL. NVMe SSDs handle 500+ MB/s; replicas catch up in real time. We provision replicas in the same AZ for <1 ms lag. The bottleneck would be cross-AZ replicas (~50 ms lag at peak) — that's why writes go to primary only; reads use sync replicas. Async cross-region replicas exist for DR but aren't on the read path.

Problem 25: Designing a Malicious URL Detection Service

Google Safe Browsing-style: every browser checks every URL before navigating; you must serve 100k+ QPS with ~1 ms latency, near-zero false positives, and updates as fast as new phishing pages appear.

1Context and Why This Problem Matters

Every Chrome / Firefox / Safari user is silently protected by a URL safety check every time they navigate. Google's Safe Browsing service handles ~10 B URL checks/day across ~3 B users. The interview question is famous because it has a textbook-perfect answer for the hot path (Bloom filters) and an opportunity to discuss ML, privacy, and operational scale.

2Requirements Gathering

Functional

  • Given a URL, return safety verdict: SAFE | MALWARE | PHISHING | UNWANTED_SOFTWARE.
  • Add new malicious URLs (from crawler, user reports, partner feeds).
  • Remove cleared URLs (false positives, remediated sites).
  • Fast updates: a phishing page reported now should be blocked everywhere within minutes.
  • Privacy: don't expose individual user browsing to the central service (k-anonymity).

Non-functional

  • ~10 B URL checks/day → 10B/100k = 100k QPS average; ~500k peak.
  • P99 latency: < 5 ms (client-side cache hits are sub-ms).
  • ~10M malicious URLs in the index, growing.
  • False positive rate < 0.0001% (one in a million).
  • Update propagation: minutes globally.

3Capacity Estimation

MetricNumber
URLs checked/day~10 B
Checks/sec (avg, ÷100k)100 k/s
Checks/sec (peak, 5×)~500 k/s
Malicious URLs in index~10 M
Per-URL hash (SHA-256 prefix)8 B
Full hash database~80 MB
Bloom filter for 10M entries at 0.01% FPR~30 MB
Client-side cache TTL30 min
🔑 From Numbers to Architecture
  • 99.99% of URLs are safe → optimise for the no-op case; tiny client-side Bloom filter (~30 MB for 10 M URLs at 0.01% FPR) avoids any network call for safe URLs.
  • Bloom false positives → secondary lookup to central service; only on positive hits (rare); central service sized for ~0.01% of traffic, not all traffic.
  • ~10 M malicious URLs × 8 B hash → 80 MB database; full hash list cheaply distributed; clients pull deltas every ~30 min.
  • Threat-intel pipeline (offline): web crawler + ML classifier + analyst review → produces additions / removals → packaged into delta files → CDN.
  • Privacy → client never sends full URL to central service; only the 32-bit hash prefix; server returns all matches sharing that prefix; client checks locally.
  • Bloom filter updates → versioned; clients refresh on schedule; bit-set difference applied incrementally to minimise bandwidth.

4API Design

Browser → safety service (the hot path)

// k-anonymous lookup: client sends only a HASH PREFIX of the URL POST /v1/lookup { "hash_prefixes": ["a3f7b2", "9c14e0", ...] // 32-bit prefixes of SHA-256(url) } → 200 { "matches": [ { "prefix":"a3f7b2", "full_hashes":[ { "hash":"a3f7b2...e1", "threat":"MALWARE" }, { "hash":"a3f7b2...f2", "threat":"PHISHING" } ]} ] } // Client side then checks if its actual full hash matches any returned full hash. // Privacy: the service sees only prefixes, never the full URL or hash.

Bulk threat-list updates (client pulls)

GET /v1/update?lists=malware,phishing&state={last_seen_state} → { "lists": { "malware": { "state":"...", "adds":[...], "removes":[...] }, "phishing": { ... } } } // Client downloads diffs; updates local Bloom filter and hash prefix index.

Internal admin / submission

POST /v1/admin/urls { "url":"...", "threat":"PHISHING", "evidence":"..." } DELETE /v1/admin/urls/{id} GET /v1/admin/stats

5Data Model

malicious_urls (PostgreSQL — source of truth for admin / appeals)

CREATE TABLE malicious_urls ( url_hash BYTEA PRIMARY KEY, -- SHA-256(url) full url_canonical TEXT, -- original URL after normalisation threat_type VARCHAR(20), -- MALWARE | PHISHING | UNWANTED_SOFTWARE source VARCHAR(50), -- crawler | user_report | partner_feed | ml_classifier confidence SMALLINT, -- 0..100 added_at TIMESTAMPTZ, expires_at TIMESTAMPTZ, -- some URLs auto-expire if site is cleaned state VARCHAR(20), -- ACTIVE | REMOVED | DISPUTED evidence_ref TEXT -- link to crawl artifact or report ); CREATE INDEX idx_state_added ON malicious_urls(state, added_at DESC);

Bloom filter (in-process, on every client)

Not a "table" — a precomputed binary blob distributed to clients. Constructed from all ACTIVE malicious URLs. Size: ~30 MB at 0.01% FPR for 10M entries. Embedded in browser binaries; updated by diff.

Hash prefix index (server-side hot path)

// Redis sorted set per threat type, sharded by prefix // Key: prefixes:malware:{shard}, member: 8-byte prefix, score: insertion timestamp // On lookup: GET full hashes for all matching prefixes

6High-Level Architecture (with rationale)

Browser (every user, ~3B clients) │ │ 1. Local Bloom filter check ~99.99% return SAFE here, no network call │ │ 2. If Bloom says "maybe match" → hash prefix lookup to server ▼ ┌────────────────────────┐ │ Lookup API │ — stateless, sized for 500k QPS peak └────────┬───────────────-┘ │ ▼ ┌────────────────────────┐ │ Prefix Index (Redis) │ — ~80 MB, fits in RAM, 1 ms lookups └────────────────────────┘ Async pipelines: ┌────────────────────────┐ • Crawler → Classifier → Postgres │ Postgres source-of-truth│ ◀───── • Partner feeds → ingest job │ (admin, audit, appeals) │ • User reports → manual review queue └────────────────────────┘ • Postgres → CDC → Bloom filter rebuild (hourly) → S3 → clients pull Client-update path: Postgres delta → diff generator → S3 (versioned blobs) → CDN → Browser pulls every 30 min
🔑 Why Each Component (Memorise This for Interview)
  • Bloom filter on the client — at 100k QPS per user × 3B users globally, calling our service for every URL is 300 trillion checks/day. Impossible. Bloom filter pushes 99.99% of the load to client-side memory: a 30 MB embedded data structure absorbs the no-op case for free. False positives (saying "maybe malicious" when not) trigger one server call to confirm. False negatives are impossible by Bloom's definition — we never miss a real threat.
  • Hash prefix lookup, not full URL — preserves user privacy (k-anonymity). The server sees the prefix and can't reconstruct what URL the user visited. ~256 URLs share each 32-bit prefix on average, so the service knows the user visited one of 256 URLs — not enough to identify a specific page. This is exactly Google Safe Browsing's design.
  • Redis for prefix → full-hash lookup — server-side, 1 ms lookup latency at 500k QPS. 80 MB index fits in RAM; sharded by prefix range across a small Redis cluster. Postgres-backed lookups would add ~5 ms per call; Redis is 5× faster, which matters at hot-path scale. Source-of-truth still in Postgres.
  • Postgres as source of truth (NOT hot path) — admin operations (add/remove URL, dispute resolution, audit) need ACID. The DB is ~10M rows, well within single-node capacity. Throughput is low (hundreds of admin writes/day vs 500k client QPS), so Postgres is the obvious fit.
  • S3 + CDN for client updates — every browser pulls the Bloom filter every 30 min. 3B clients × 30 MB = 90 PB of egress if we served direct. CDN absorbs 99% of these; origin sees only cold-cache misses. Cheapest possible distribution path.
  • No Kafka in the hot path — the read path is synchronous and read-only. Kafka shows up only in the ingest path (crawler events, partner feeds → classifier) where decoupling helps. The lookup API doesn't need it.
  • What scales easily: Lookup API (stateless, horizontal scale); Redis prefix index (shard by prefix); CDN egress (CloudFront capacity is effectively unlimited).
  • What breaks first: client-side Bloom filter size. As the malicious URL list grows from 10M to 100M, Bloom filter grows from 30 MB to 300 MB. Mitigate by splitting per threat type (one filter per list) so users only download active threats; old expired URLs are removed from filters.

7Deep Dive 1: The Layered Check Pipeline

Defense in depth: each layer filters most traffic so the next layer sees less. From cheapest to most expensive:

  1. Local Bloom filter (client memory): O(1) lookup, ~1 μs. 99.99% of URLs return "definitely safe."
  2. Local hash prefix list (client memory, larger): for the 0.01% Bloom-positive URLs, check if our actual 32-bit hash prefix is in the downloaded list. If not, false positive — return safe.
  3. Server hash prefix lookup (network call): for prefix matches, ask server for all full hashes sharing this prefix. Client checks against own full hash. Latency ~5 ms.
  4. ML classifier (server, async or on submission): when a new URL is submitted, ML scores it; high confidence → auto-add; low confidence → human review queue.

The funnel: 100% → 0.01% → 0.001% → matches. Most layers are local and free.

8Deep Dive 2: Bloom Filter — Why It's the Hot-Path Star

How a Bloom filter works

An m-bit array, initially all zeros. To insert element x: hash x with k different hash functions; set those k bits to 1. To check element y: hash with the same k functions; if any of those bits is 0, y is definitely not in the set; if all are 1, y is probably in the set (small false-positive rate).

Sizing for our use case

For n=10M elements at 0.01% false-positive rate: m ≈ 1.44 × n × log2(1/p) ≈ 192M bits ≈ 24 MB. We use 30 MB for headroom. k = 10 hash functions.

Why no false negatives matter

Bloom filters can have false positives ("might be in set") but never false negatives ("not in set" is always correct). For URL safety, this is perfect: a true threat is never missed; some safe URLs trigger a confirming server call, which is cheap.

Updates to Bloom filter

Bloom filters don't support deletion (a deleted entry might share bits with kept entries). Solution: rebuild from scratch hourly when the threat list changes. 10M URLs hashed × 10 hash functions = ~100M operations, runs in seconds on a single CPU. Diff against last version → small delta blob → distributed via CDN.

9Deep Dive 3: URL Ingestion & Classification

Sources

  • Crawler: visits URLs, detects malware, exploit kits, phishing patterns.
  • User reports: "Report site" button in browsers.
  • Partner feeds: PhishTank, OpenPhish, AV vendors.
  • ML classifier on incoming URLs: heuristic patterns (suspicious TLD, lookalike domain, IP-based URL, unusual punycode).

Submission pipeline

Each submission goes through: dedup → URL canonicalisation (lowercase host, strip tracking params, follow redirects to final destination) → classifier → if high confidence, insert; if medium, queue for human review; if low, drop.

Removals

Sites get cleaned. We periodically re-crawl previously-flagged URLs; if they're now clean for X days, expire from the list. Disputed entries (operator appeals) get manual review.

10Deep Dive 4: Fast Updates to Billions of Clients

A new phishing campaign starts at noon. We want every browser to block it by 12:15. Three pillars:

Quick-add to server prefix index

Admin/automated submission writes to Postgres → CDC stream → Redis prefix index updated within seconds. Clients that hit a server lookup for the same prefix will catch the new threat immediately (no Bloom filter update needed yet).

Bloom filter delta distribution

Every 15 min, regenerate Bloom filter; compute diff from prior version; sign with our key; upload to S3; invalidate the latest-pointer at CDN. Clients pull on their next 30-min poll; diff is <100 KB.

Emergency push channel

For catastrophic threats (large active phishing campaign), browser has an emergency channel that triggers immediate filter refresh on a server-pushed signal (silent push notification to active browser sessions). Used sparingly.

11Deep Dive 5: ML Classifier for Real-Time Decisions

Most URLs we see have never been seen before. Heuristic + ML scoring decides whether to admit them.

Features

  • Lexical: URL length, number of dots, suspicious keywords, look-alike substrings ("paypa1.com"), IP literal as host, very-recent registration of domain.
  • Network: hosting provider reputation, AS number history, DNS resolution to known-bad IPs.
  • Content (if we crawled): forms requesting credentials, mismatched branding, JS obfuscation patterns.
  • Behavioural: did this URL just receive a sudden surge of click-throughs from random Discord servers?

Models

Gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost / LightGBM) are the workhorse. For features that need sequence understanding, character-level CNNs on URLs. Models retrained nightly on the past month's data, with active learning prioritising uncertain cases for human review.

12Failure Modes & Recovery

FailureMitigation
Lookup API outageBrowser falls back to local Bloom filter and prefix list — slightly stale but functional. Known-safe URLs unaffected.
Bloom filter corruption / bugVersioned filters; signed blobs; client verifies signature before using; on failure, retain prior version.
False positive blocks a legitimate siteAppeal API; manual review; if confirmed false, remove from list — propagates within 15 min via the same update pipeline.
New phishing campaign exceeds throughputIngest pipeline auto-scales; manual prioritisation flag for known-bad operators.
Privacy leak via prefix collisionk-anonymity: each prefix maps to ~256 URLs on average. Server sees the prefix; can't single out the specific URL the user visited.

13Scaling Path

StageArchitecture
1 M users, 10k URLsServer-only lookups; no Bloom filter; Postgres handles it.
100 M users, 1M URLsAdd Bloom filter on the client. Redis prefix index server-side.
1 B users, 10M URLsThis article's design. Per-threat-type filters. CDN distribution of updates.
3 B users globallyMulti-region CDNs. Regional ingest pipelines. Edge-side lookups for the prefix step.

14Cross-Questions and Pushbacks

"Bloom filter false positives mean some safe URLs incur a network call — wasteful?"
Answer: At 0.01% FPR, 1 in 10,000 safe URLs incurs the call. Even if a user visits 100 URLs/day, that's a 1% chance per day of one network call — < 1 call/user/week. Aggregate: 3 B users × 1 call/week ÷ 700k sec/week ≈ 4k calls/sec. Trivial. The Bloom filter saves the other 99.99% — billions of calls/sec we'd otherwise be forced to handle. The trade is wildly favorable.
"How do you guarantee zero false negatives — what if Bloom filter says 'safe' when site is actually malicious?"
Answer: Bloom filters mathematically can't produce false negatives. If a URL was inserted, all k of its bits are 1. A lookup checking those same k bits will always find them set. The only error mode is false positives (claim "present" when absent), which we handle with a server confirmation. The actual real risk: a new threat URL that hasn't been added to the filter yet — purely a race against the update cycle (15 min). For high-urgency threats, the emergency-push channel cuts that to seconds.
How does the privacy/k-anonymity scheme actually preserve privacy?
Client sends a 32-bit hash prefix instead of the full URL or full hash. With 4 billion possible prefixes and ~10M malicious URLs in the index, ~256 URLs share each prefix on average. The server sees the prefix and returns all matching full hashes; the client locally checks if its actual full hash is among them. The server knows "this user visited one of 256 URLs" but not which one. Crucially: legitimate URLs the user visits also resolve to prefixes that happen to share with malicious entries — the server can't even tell whether the user visited a malicious URL or a coincidentally-prefix-colliding safe one.
What about HTTPS or signed-binary updates — what stops a man-in-the-middle from injecting a malicious "safe list"?
All update blobs are signed with the service's private key; clients embed the public key. A modified blob fails signature verification and is rejected. The update server is reached via HTTPS with cert pinning. Even if a state-level adversary intercepts the network, they can't forge a signed update. Compromised signing key would be catastrophic — keys are HSM-backed with two-person physical access controls.
"30 MB Bloom filter × 3B users = 90 PB of distribution. Can the CDN even handle that?"
Answer: Not all 3B users update simultaneously, and we ship diffs, not full filters. A typical diff is <100 KB. 3B users × 100 KB / 30 min = ~1.5 GB/s sustained CDN egress — well within CloudFront's per-region capacity. The full 30 MB filter is downloaded only on first install (or after a long offline period) — heavily cached at CDN edge POPs; origin sees almost zero traffic. Cost: ~$30k/month in CDN egress at this scale, against billions in user trust value.
How would you handle Punycode / IDN homograph attacks (apple.com vs аpple.com using Cyrillic 'а')?
URL canonicalisation step before insertion + lookup. Detect mixed-script domains (Latin + Cyrillic letters); flag for review. Also maintain a "known-good brand → variants" mapping; any new domain that's edit-distance-1 from a brand is suspicious. The ML classifier features include character-set mixing and lookalike detection. Browsers themselves now warn on suspicious Punycode, but the safety service backs that with reputation data.

1Context — How OTT Differs from YouTube

Both stream video, but the underlying design pressures are very different. Understanding the differences shapes every decision below.

ConcernYouTube (UGC)Netflix / Prime (OTT)
Content sourceUsers upload millions of videos/dayStudios deliver ~10–50 titles/week (curated)
Catalogue sizeBillions of videos~15k titles (movies + episodes)
Per-title sizeFew MB to GB3–10 GB (1080p), 30–60 GB (4K HDR)
Avg watch session~5–15 min~60–90 min (entire movie or 2-3 episodes)
DiscoverySearch + browse drivenRecommendation-driven (80%+ of plays)
DRMOptional (most videos open)Mandatory — every stream
Cross-deviceNice-to-haveCritical — start on TV, resume on phone
Geographic restrictionsPer-video age/country gatingPer-title licensing varies sharply by country
Offline viewingYouTube Premium featureCore mobile feature; DRM-protected expiry
Concurrent peaksSpread across millions of videosConcentrated on a few hot titles (finale, premiere)

The big takeaways:

  • OTT has a much smaller catalogue but much larger per-title files → totally different storage/CDN economics.
  • OTT's concentrated viewing means CDN caching is wildly effective (a single title can serve 50M+ viewers).
  • OTT's DRM and licensing requirements are load-bearing design constraints, not afterthoughts.
  • OTT's recommendation engine is the product's primary surface; not an add-on.

2Requirements Gathering

Functional

  • Browse the catalogue (rows of cards, categories, genres) with infinite-scroll personalisation.
  • Search by title, actor, genre.
  • Stream video on phone, tablet, TV, web — with adaptive bitrate based on network.
  • Multi-profile per account (parent + kids); per-profile watch history and recommendations.
  • Resume watching across devices ("Continue Watching" row reflects last position).
  • Subscription tiers: SD / HD / 4K, with-ads / ad-free, 1 / 2 / 4 simultaneous streams.
  • Parental controls, content rating filters.
  • Offline downloads on mobile (DRM-protected, time-limited).
  • Personalised home screen and "Because you watched X" rows.

Non-Functional

  • Subscribers: 250M globally; DAU: ~100M; avg 2 h watch/day per active user.
  • Peak concurrent viewers: ~50M (major release / live sport finale).
  • Playback start latency: P99 < 2 s from tap-to-first-frame.
  • Seek latency: P99 < 1 s.
  • Availability: 99.99% — every minute down is a measurable cancellation event.
  • Geographic: global; per-region licensing must be enforced server-side.
  • DRM: every premium stream must be license-protected end-to-end.
  • Cost: CDN egress is the dominant infra cost; must be aggressively optimised.

Out of Scope (this design)

  • Content production / studio workflows.
  • Live sports / live linear TV (mention briefly in scaling path — different ingest pipeline).
  • Ad insertion mechanics (touched as a hook into the manifest pipeline).

Clarifying Questions to Ask the Interviewer

  • "How big is the catalogue? 1k, 10k, or 100k titles?" — drives ingest pipeline scale.
  • "Are we doing live or only on-demand?" — live needs separate ingest + low-latency packaging.
  • "What's the device mix? Mostly mobile, mostly TV?" — drives DRM choice (Widevine/FairPlay/PlayReady).
  • "Single region or global?" — single-region halves the CDN complexity.
  • "Subscription model or one-time-rental?" — billing complexity, license duration semantics.

1 day = 100,000 sec (the rule).

🔧 From Numbers to Architecture — what these estimates force

Every tech choice in the HLD below traces back to a number we just computed. Read these bullets as "number → constraint → tech choice".

  • 100 Tbps peak streaming bandwidth → utterly impossible from any origin. CDN absorbs ~99% of egress. Multi-CDN (CloudFront + Akamai + Fastly, or proprietary Open Connect appliances) required for resilience.
  • ~50M concurrent on a single hot title → without edge caching, even a "small" 100 Mbps origin gets melted instantly. Pre-warm popular titles to every POP before release; cache popularity-decays over weeks.
  • 180 PB/day delivered, $50–85/TB egress cost → CDN bills can hit $10M+/day. Drives every decision: bitrate ladders tuned to network, codec choice (AV1 is 30–50% smaller than H.264), per-region edge contracts.
  • 15 k titles, 1.5 PB packaged → fits comfortably in S3 as origin; not a storage problem. The hard problem is distributing this to 200 POPs efficiently.
  • 1.7 M heartbeats/sec peak (and they must persist for "Continue Watching") → far beyond Postgres. Cassandra (partition by user_id, cluster by ts) for heartbeats; Redis cache for "latest position per (user, title)".
  • P99 playback start < 2 s → cannot fetch master + transcode on demand. Pre-packaged variants, edge-cached manifests, DRM license server geo-distributed.
  • Every stream needs a DRM license → 50M concurrent license requests at peak. DRM License Server fleet with regional replicas; license cached per device for the session.
  • Recommendations drive 80% of plays → cannot compute personalised rows on-request. Precomputed nightly via Spark/Flink on watch logs; served from Cassandra/S3 + Redis hot cache.
  • ~25 k watch heartbeats/sec avg → 2 B events/day → great training data for recommendations + analytics. Kafka → Spark batch nightly + Flink streaming for "trending now" rows.
  • Per-region licensing → cannot serve a title to the wrong country. Catalogue filtered server-side per IP geo; manifest URLs signed with region tokens; CDN refuses to serve out-of-region.
  • Subscription billing for 250M users → relational ACID needed. Postgres for subscription state; separate Subscription Service (use the P14 design).
  • Offline downloads on mobile → DRM license with offline mode, time-limited (e.g. 30-day rental window, 48-hour active-play window after first play). Standard Widevine "persistent license" pattern.

4API Design

Catalogue and Browse

GET /v1/catalog/home?profile_id={pid} Response 200: { "rows": [ { "title": "Continue Watching", "items": [{title_id, name, poster, watched_position_sec, ...}] }, { "title": "Trending Now", "items": [...] }, { "title": "Because you watched Breaking Bad", "items": [...] }, ... ] } GET /v1/titles/{title_id} GET /v1/search?q=...&profile_id=...

Playback

POST /v1/play/session { "title_id":"t_abc", "profile_id":"p_xyz", "device_id":"dev_uuid" } Response 201: { "session_id": "sess_uuid", "manifest_url": "https://cdn.example/m/sess_uuid/manifest.m3u8?token=...", "license_url": "https://drm.example/license?session=sess_uuid", "start_position_sec": 0 // or resume from continue-watching } POST /v1/play/heartbeat { "session_id":"...", "position_sec":420, "buffer_health":"OK", "bitrate_kbps":3500 } Response 204 POST /v1/play/stop { "session_id":"...", "position_sec":3420 }

DRM License

POST /drm/license Body: device challenge blob (Widevine / FairPlay / PlayReady format) Authorization: Bearer {session_token} Response: signed license blob (binary)

Watch State

GET /v1/profiles/{pid}/continue-watching GET /v1/profiles/{pid}/history?from=...&to=... POST /v1/profiles/{pid}/dismiss-from-row { title_id, row_id }

Offline Downloads

POST /v1/downloads/start { "title_id":"...", "quality":"720p", "device_id":"..." } Response 201: { manifest_url, license_url (persistent), expires_at }

5Data Model

titles (PostgreSQL — small catalogue, indexed for search)

CREATE TABLE titles ( title_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, type VARCHAR(10), -- 'MOVIE' | 'SERIES' | 'EPISODE' name VARCHAR(255), description TEXT, release_year INT, duration_sec INT, rating VARCHAR(10), -- 'PG-13', 'R', etc. genres TEXT[], cast_ids UUID[], poster_url TEXT, trailer_url TEXT, master_url TEXT, -- S3 path to master file ingestion_state VARCHAR(20), -- 'INGESTING' | 'READY' | 'BLOCKED' created_at TIMESTAMPTZ ); -- Mirrored to Elasticsearch for search; updated via CDC.

title_variants (PostgreSQL — per-title packaged outputs)

CREATE TABLE title_variants ( title_id UUID, quality VARCHAR(10), -- '240p', '720p', '1080p', '4K' codec VARCHAR(10), -- 'h264', 'h265', 'av1' bitrate INT, -- in kbps manifest_url TEXT, -- HLS .m3u8 or DASH .mpd drm_id VARCHAR(50), -- license server reference PRIMARY KEY (title_id, quality, codec) );

licensing (PostgreSQL — geographic availability)

CREATE TABLE title_licensing ( title_id UUID, country CHAR(2), -- ISO 3166 country code available_from TIMESTAMPTZ, available_until TIMESTAMPTZ, PRIMARY KEY (title_id, country) ); CREATE INDEX idx_country ON title_licensing(country, available_until);

watch_events (Cassandra — high-write event log)

CREATE TABLE watch_events ( user_id UUID, ts TIMEUUID, title_id UUID, profile_id UUID, device_id UUID, event_type TEXT, -- 'START', 'HEARTBEAT', 'STOP', 'SEEK', 'BUFFER' position_sec INT, bitrate_kbps INT, buffer_health TEXT, PRIMARY KEY ((user_id), ts) ) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (ts DESC); -- 30-day TTL on the table; older data moves to S3 archive.

continue_watching (Cassandra + Redis hot copy)

CREATE TABLE continue_watching ( profile_id UUID, title_id UUID, position_sec INT, updated_at TIMESTAMPTZ, device_id UUID, PRIMARY KEY ((profile_id), title_id) ); -- Redis: HSET cw:{profile_id} {title_id} "{position_sec, updated_at}" -- TTL on Redis side: 7 days (refresh on every play).

recommendations (precomputed in Cassandra, Redis cache for hot users)

CREATE TABLE recommendations ( profile_id UUID, row_id VARCHAR(50), -- 'home_top_picks', 'trending_now', 'because_x' rank INT, title_id UUID, PRIMARY KEY ((profile_id), row_id, rank) ); -- Refreshed nightly by Spark batch job + Flink streaming for 'trending'.

subscriptions (PostgreSQL — see P14 for full design)

CREATE TABLE subscriptions ( user_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, plan_tier VARCHAR(20), -- 'BASIC_SD', 'STANDARD_HD', 'PREMIUM_4K' ads_enabled BOOLEAN, max_concurrent_streams INT, state VARCHAR(20), -- 'ACTIVE', 'PAST_DUE', 'CANCELLED' current_period_end TIMESTAMPTZ, ... );

6High-Level Architecture

Devices: phone, tablet, TV, web │ │ catalogue + manifest + license + heartbeats ▼ ┌──────────────────────────────┐ │ Edge: API Gateway + CDN │ │ (region-aware routing) │ └──┬───┬───┬───┬───┬───┬────────┘ │ │ │ │ │ │ ┌────────┘ │ │ │ │ └─────────────┐ ▼ │ │ │ ▼ ▼ Catalog Svc │ │ │ DRM License Svc CDN edge POPs │ │ │ │ │ (HLS/DASH segments ▼ │ │ │ ▼ served from edge) Postgres │ │ │ Widevine / ▲ (titles + │ │ │ FairPlay / │ licensing) ──CDC─┼───┘ │ PlayReady │ │ │ │ keys & policies │ ▼ │ │ ▲ │ Elasticsearch │ │ │ │ (search) ▼ │ │ │ Playback Svc │ Content Mgmt Svc │ - session │ - ingest pipeline │ - manifest │ - DRM packaging ─────────┘ signing │ - distribute to CDN - regional │ │ eligibility│ ▼ │ │ S3 Origin ▼ │ (packaged variants Watch State Svc│ + master files) - heartbeats │ - position │ │ │ ▼ │ ┌──────────────┴──────┐ │ Kafka │ — watch.events │ (heartbeats, plays)│ └─┬──────────┬────────┘ │ │ ▼ ▼ Cassandra Flink + Spark (watch_events, (recommendations continue_ training) watching) │ │ ▼ │ Recommendations │ (Cassandra + │ Redis cache) │ ▲ └──────────────────┘ Subscription Svc ──► Postgres (billing state)

7Deep Dive 1: CDN & Edge Caching at Planetary Scale

The CDN is the platform. 99%+ of bytes delivered come from edge POPs. Three real-world models:

Model A: Multi-CDN aggregation (Prime Video pattern)

Buy edge capacity from multiple commercial CDNs (CloudFront, Akamai, Fastly). At play start, a CDN selector picks the best one for that user's region, ISP, and current health. Failover is automatic.

  • Pros: no infrastructure to operate at the edge; resilience via diversification.
  • Cons: expensive ($50–85 / TB egress); margins thin on heavy traffic; you compete with everyone for capacity during big events.

Model B: Own appliances at ISPs (Netflix Open Connect)

Netflix ships custom storage appliances ("Open Connect Appliances") to ISPs worldwide. ISPs host them inside their network for free (saves them transit bandwidth). Netflix pushes new content nightly via S3 sync. Users stream from the ISP-local appliance.

  • Pros: cost ~$5–10/TB (just hardware amortisation); zero CDN bills; near-zero last-mile latency.
  • Cons: massive operational investment; ISP relationships needed; not feasible until you're huge.

Model C: Hybrid (most common today)

Use commercial CDN for the long tail and edge appliances for hot content. Live sports → commercial CDN with low-latency mode; on-demand → Open-Connect-style appliances.

Cache warming and the "Stranger Things problem"

When a major season drops at 00:00, traffic to that title can hit 30–50% of all platform traffic. If even one POP cache-misses on that title, the origin is instantly overwhelmed. Solution: pre-warm every POP with the new title before release. Push happens during off-peak hours over the days leading up to launch.

Manifest signing for region enforcement

The manifest URL handed to the client is signed with a short-lived JWT containing user/region/time fields. The CDN edge validates the signature before serving segments. Out-of-region or expired tokens get 403. Prevents URL sharing and enforces geo-licensing at the CDN edge, not the origin.

8Deep Dive 2: DRM — Widevine / FairPlay / PlayReady

Every premium stream must be protected by a DRM license. Three industry-standard systems cover all major devices:

DRMOwnerDevices
WidevineGoogleAndroid, Chrome, Chromecast, most smart TVs
FairPlayAppleiOS, iPadOS, Safari, Apple TV
PlayReadyMicrosoftWindows, Xbox, some smart TVs (Samsung, LG)

How a DRM-protected play works

  1. Client requests a play session → server returns manifest URL + license URL.
  2. Client begins fetching encrypted segments from CDN.
  3. Client generates a challenge (device-specific, keyed to its hardware-backed trust chain).
  4. Client POSTs the challenge to the license server.
  5. License server validates: (a) is the user's subscription active? (b) is the title licensed in their region? (c) is the device under the simultaneous-stream limit?
  6. License server returns a signed license blob containing the decryption key + a policy (max output resolution, HDCP requirements, validity duration).
  7. Client passes license to the device's secure media path; player decrypts segments in trusted hardware.

Why three DRMs?

Apple won't allow Widevine on iOS. Microsoft built PlayReady before Widevine. The licensing requirements from studios mandate that "premium" content (Hollywood movies, 4K, HDR) be served only via hardware-backed DRM — which means using the platform's native DRM.

CMAF + Common Encryption (CENC)

To avoid storing three copies of every segment (one per DRM), the industry standardised on CMAF (Common Media Application Format) with CENC (Common Encryption). The video bytes are encrypted once with AES-128-CTR; each DRM provides its own license format wrapping the same underlying key. One set of segment files; three license-server flavours.

9Deep Dive 3: Adaptive Bitrate Streaming (HLS / DASH)

Standard pattern, same as P4 YouTube, with OTT-specific tweaks:

  • Bitrate ladder: 5 levels (240p / 480p / 720p / 1080p / 4K-HDR), each as ~6-second segments.
  • Manifest: HLS (.m3u8) for Apple devices, DASH (.mpd) for everyone else. Both reference the same underlying CMAF segments.
  • Adaptive logic: client measures network throughput, buffer health, and screen size. Upshifts when bandwidth is good; downshifts on stalls.
  • Trick play: low-resolution thumbnails ("storyboard") delivered as a single sprite-sheet image for fast scrubbing preview.
  • Per-title encoding: Netflix found that animated content compresses very differently from live action. Each title gets a custom bitrate ladder, optimised offline. Saves ~20% bandwidth vs. fixed ladders.
📐 The "first 2 seconds" trick

To hit P99 < 2s startup, clients start with the lowest bitrate (240p), then upshift after the first second of playback. Looks ugly for half a second, but the viewer is already watching — vastly better than a 4-second buffering spinner.

10Deep Dive 4: Content Ingestion Pipeline

When a studio delivers a master file, the pipeline transforms it into the cached, DRM-protected segments served at the edge. Heavy compute, batched, runs days before release.

Studio uploads master (4K HDR ProRes, 100–500 GB per title) │ ▼ S3 Origin (master) │ ▼ Kafka content.uploaded │ ┌────────┴─────────────┐ ▼ ▼ Encoding Workers QC/Metadata Workers - 15 outputs: - extract: duration, (5 quality × chapters, subtitles 3 codec) per title - run automated QC - parallel per shot - generate thumbnails - GPU-accelerated - storyboard sprite │ ▼ DRM Packaging - encrypt with CENC AES-128 - generate per-DRM key wrappers - sign manifests │ ▼ S3 Origin (packaged variants) │ ▼ CDN Distribution - push to ALL POPs for top-tier titles - push to "tier-1 regions" only for niche titles - completes 24–72 h before release

Why batch, not on-demand

Transcoding a 4K 90-min movie takes hours of compute. Doing it on the first viewer's play request would mean catastrophic startup latency. By pre-encoding everything, the first viewer's experience is identical to the millionth viewer's.

11Deep Dive 5: Recommendation Engine

The home screen is ~20 rows of personalised content; ~80% of plays start from a recommendation row. Three recommendation flavours combine:

  1. Collaborative filtering: users who watched X also liked Y. Matrix factorisation over user × title matrix; periodically retrained on watch logs.
  2. Content-based: title metadata (genre, cast, director, tags) → embedding. Recommend nearest neighbours.
  3. Contextual / sequence: "you just watched episode 3, here's episode 4" + "you've finished Breaking Bad, try Better Call Saul".

Serving architecture

Nightly Spark/Flink job consumes watch logs (Kafka → Cassandra → batch). Per-profile recommendations computed for ~20 rows × top 50 titles each. Written to recommendations table in Cassandra, keyed by profile_id. Home screen fetches in one query (~1 KB response per row); Redis caches the hot 1% of profiles for sub-ms reads.

Streaming "Trending Now"

Real-time top-K via Flink: 5-minute sliding window of play-start events, group by title, keep top-50 globally. Refreshed every minute. Same Count-Min-Sketch + Heavy-Hitters pattern as Twitter's trending topics (P2).

Cold-start problem

New subscriber → no watch history → can't run collaborative filtering. Solutions:

  • Onboarding questionnaire: "pick 3 titles you like" → seed embeddings.
  • Show universally-popular rows for the first session.
  • After 5–10 plays, switch to personalised.

12Deep Dive 6: Watch State Sync Across Devices

"Pause on TV, resume on phone" is core OTT UX. The plumbing:

Heartbeat protocol

Every 30 seconds during playback, client POSTs a heartbeat with current position. Watch State Service writes to Kafka watch.events and updates Redis cw:{profile_id}. Cassandra ingests Kafka events for durability.

Resume position

When the user opens any device and asks for "Continue Watching", the Watch State Service reads from Redis (sub-ms). If the cache misses (Redis evicted), it falls back to Cassandra. The displayed position is the latest seen, regardless of which device produced the heartbeat.

Multi-device race

User pauses TV at minute 12; opens phone 30 seconds later. Phone gets position=12:00 from Watch State. Phone starts playing from 12:00. But TV is still showing the paused frame at 12:00 — when they later wake the TV, it will use the heartbeat's position. Last-writer-wins on Redis.

End-of-title detection

When position ≥ 90% of duration, the row is removed from "Continue Watching" and the title moves to "Watched". The 90% threshold accounts for credits the user may have skipped.

13Deep Dive 7: Offline Downloads

Mobile users download titles to watch on planes / commutes without burning data. DRM still applies.

Persistent license model

The client requests a persistent license from the DRM server — same protocol as streaming, but the license carries a longer expiry (e.g. 30 days) and an "offline playback" flag. The license is stored on the device alongside the encrypted segments.

Two-clock policy (industry standard)

  • Rental clock: 30 days from download. After 30 days, the license expires; the file is unplayable.
  • Active-play clock: 48 hours from first play. After first play, the user has 48 hours to finish.

Device limits

Most plans allow downloads on N devices simultaneously (e.g. 2 devices for Basic, 4 for Premium). Tracked server-side via the DRM license server's session table: a request beyond the limit is rejected.

14Failure Modes & Recovery

FailureBlast radiusMitigation
CDN POP outageUsers in that POP's region see slow/failed playbackMulti-CDN failover; client retries to alternate CDN within ~3 s.
DRM license server overloadNew plays cannot startRegional license-server fleet; licenses cached per-device for the session; client retries with backoff.
Origin S3 region outageEdge cache misses fail; new content cannot ingestCross-region S3 replication; popular content is at the edge already.
Recommendation pipeline lag (Spark job fails)Home screen shows yesterday's recsFall back to "Trending Now" + universal-popular rows; alert ops; rerun pipeline.
Mass concurrent stress (finale release)License + manifest signing services see 50× normal QPSPre-scale at known events; pre-warm caches; circuit-break new plays if licenses queue.
Cassandra (watch_events) under-provisionedHeartbeats accumulate in Kafka backlogKafka durability buffers; auto-scale Cassandra; backlog drains within minutes.
Subscription downgrade not honoredUser watches 4K despite SD planLicense server checks subscription state at every license issuance; downgrades take effect on next license request.

15Scaling Path

StageArchitecture
10k users, 100 titlesSingle S3 bucket + CloudFront. No DRM (or basic AES). Synchronous transcoding.
1M usersAdd Widevine DRM. Async transcoding via SQS. Recommendations via simple "most popular".
10M usersMulti-CDN. Three-DRM coverage. Real recommendations via Spark batch. Cassandra for watch events.
100M usersThis article's design. Per-region edge appliances or hybrid CDN. Real-time trending via Flink. Multiple subscription tiers.
Live streaming addedSeparate live-ingest pipeline (low-latency CMAF, ~5–10 s glass-to-glass); manifests refreshed every few seconds.

16Cross-Questions and Pushbacks

"Why not just use AWS MediaConvert + CloudFront end-to-end? Why design anything?"
Answer: For a startup with < 1M users, that's the right answer — managed services beat building. The custom design matters at scale because: (1) CDN egress costs at 100 Tbps are crushing — Netflix saves billions by running Open Connect. (2) Per-title encoding and DRM-packaging pipelines are deeply customised for optimal bitrate ladders. (3) Recommendation engine is the product's primary surface; can't outsource. (4) Watch state sync requires custom protocol design. Managed services scale to ~10M MAU comfortably; past that, custom infra pays off.
"Cassandra for watch_events at 1.7 M peak writes/s — won't that need a huge cluster?"
Answer: Quantify: 1.7M writes/s ÷ 100k writes/s per Cassandra node = ~17 nodes minimum, with replication factor 3 we need ~50 nodes. With per-region sharding (peak in NA region is ~700k writes/s, EMEA peaks separately) we run regional clusters of ~25–30 nodes each. That's a noticeable cluster but not insane. The alternative — keeping heartbeats in Postgres — would melt the DB instantly. LSM-tree append is exactly what this workload needs.
How does the manifest URL prevent URL sharing?
The manifest URL contains a signed JWT with claims: user_id, session_id, region, expires_at (e.g. 8 hours from issuance), device_id. CDN edge validates the signature on every segment request. A shared URL: (a) expires within hours; (b) only works in the original region; (c) the actual segments are still DRM-encrypted, so even a valid manifest URL without the license is useless. Layered defence.
How would you add live sports streaming to this?
Live needs a totally different ingest path: source signal → encoder → packager → live origin → CDN, all with end-to-end latency < 10 s (or < 3 s for low-latency CMAF / LL-HLS). Players use live manifests that get refreshed every 2-6 s with new segment URLs. DRM and CDN reuse the on-demand stack. Recommendation engine doesn't apply to a single live event. Scaling: live events have catastrophic concentration — 50M concurrent on one match — so pre-warm CDN and have a "broadcast mode" where new client connects pull from edge cache instantly.
"Why CDN-first instead of letting requests hit the origin?"
Answer: At 100 Tbps peak streaming bandwidth, even a tiny percentage hitting origin is catastrophic. 1% miss rate = 1 Tbps to origin = ~125 GB/s = $30k+/hour just in egress, plus the origin servers themselves can't handle that bandwidth. With 99%+ cache hit at edge, origin sees ~1 Gbps — handled by a modest server fleet. The economics demand CDN-first; nothing else fits.
How do recommendations handle the cold-start of a new title?
A brand-new title has no watch data → collaborative filtering gives it zero score. Three workarounds: (1) Content-based ranking: cast/genre/director embeddings place the title near similar known titles; gets shown to fans of those. (2) Editorial boost: marketing team manually promotes the title to home-page rows for the first 2 weeks. (3) Cohort sampling: random ~5% of users see the title in a "New This Week" row; their engagement seeds the CF model. By week 2, recommendations stabilise.
What's the typical bitrate ladder?
Industry standard ladder (Netflix-derived, in kbps): 235 (240p) · 375 (240p) · 560 (360p) · 750 (480p) · 1050 (480p) · 1750 (720p) · 2350 (720p) · 3000 (1080p) · 4300 (1080p) · 5800 (1080p) · 8000 (1080p HDR) · 12000 (4K) · 16000 (4K HDR). Each level is encoded with both H.264 (universal) and H.265 (50% smaller). AV1 adopted for top-tier titles (saves another ~30%). Per-title encoding tweaks the exact bitrates per content (animation needs less, action needs more).

End of Problem 26.

In a Hurry: Introduction

A week to your interview? Start here. This page tells you exactly what the interview is, what's being graded, and the minimum content from this guide to skim.

1What a System-Design Interview Actually Tests

It is not a coding interview, a trivia quiz, or a Wikipedia recall. The interviewer is grading you on four things:

  1. Requirement gathering: do you ask the right clarifying questions before designing?
  2. Trade-off reasoning: when you pick X over Y, can you defend it with numbers?
  3. Component intuition: do you know which tool solves which sub-problem (Kafka vs SQS, Cassandra vs DynamoDB, etc.)?
  4. Communication under pressure: can you hold a structured conversation while drawing on a whiteboard?

2How to Spend 45–60 Minutes

TimePhaseWhat you do
0–5 minRequirementsFunctional + non-functional; ask clarifying Qs. Negotiate scope.
5–10 minCapacity estimationDAU → QPS → storage. Drives your architecture choices.
10–15 minAPI + Data model3–5 key endpoints; entity relationships.
15–30 minHigh-level designBoxes + arrows. Defend each box with the numbers.
30–50 minDeep divesPick 2–3 hardest sub-problems. Drive them; don't wait to be prompted.
50–60 minFailure modes + scale"What if X dies?" "How would this look at 10×?"

The Interview Framework page elaborates each phase.

3Level Expectations (rough industry signal)

LevelWhat's expected
L3 / SDE-1Component knowledge; the interviewer drives.
L4 / SDE-2You drive the design; defend each choice with numbers.
L5 / SeniorYou also surface trade-offs proactively (consistency vs availability, push vs pull). Multiple deep-dives.
L6 / StaffYou discuss operational concerns (deployments, oncall, blast radius), cost, evolution over 3 years.

4The Minimum Viable Reading List (1-week plan)

  • Cheatsheet — the back-of-napkin numbers you'll need every interview.
  • Interview Framework — the 6-phase structure above, with example phrasing.
  • Core Concepts: Caching, Sharding, CAP, Numbers, Indexing. ~30 min each.
  • Key Technologies: Redis, Cassandra, Kafka, Postgres. ~20 min each. The other five only if you have time.
  • Patterns: Real-time, Contention, Scaling Reads, Scaling Writes. The four most-asked.
  • Problems: do P1 (URL Shortener), P2 (Twitter), P3 (WhatsApp), P4 (YouTube) end-to-end. Skim the rest by skimming each problem's HLD diagram + cross-questions section.

5The Mindset

  • Show your work. "I'm choosing Cassandra because we have 500k writes/sec and the access pattern is partition-keyed by user_id" beats "Cassandra."
  • Numbers first. Never propose an architecture without doing the QPS / storage math first — your architecture follows from those numbers.
  • Don't bluff. If you don't know a technology, say "I'd reach for X because it solves Y, but I haven't operated it." Interviewers respect honesty.
  • Be the driver. Silence is bad. Narrate as you draw.
🔑 If You Remember Only Two Things

(1) Capacity estimation comes before architecture, never after. (2) Every architectural choice must be justified by a number you wrote down in the estimation step.

How to Prepare

Three concrete study plans depending on how much runway you have. Each plan tells you exactly what to read each day.

DayReadDrill

2One-Month Plan (Recommended)

  • Week 1 — Foundations: all Core Concepts + Cheatsheet + Interview Framework. Drill numbers daily.
  • Week 2 — Toolbox: all Key Technologies + all Patterns. Read with a "when would I pick this?" lens.
  • Week 3 — Problems batch 1: P1–P15. One per day. After reading, close the page and whiteboard from memory in < 45 min.
  • Week 4 — Problems batch 2: P16–P31. Same routine. Mock interviews on weekends.

3Three-Month Plan (Comfortable)

  • Month 1 — Reading: every page of the guide, taking notes. No deadline pressure.
  • Month 2 — Active Recall: re-whiteboard each problem cold. For weak spots, build a small Anki deck (latency numbers, "when to use X" one-liners).
  • Month 3 — Mocks & Variations: do 8–10 mock interviews, mixing problem types. For each, time yourself; reflect on what slowed you down and revisit those pages.

4Mock-Interview Drills

  • Random-pick drill: roll a die, pick a problem you haven't done in 2 weeks, whiteboard cold in 45 min.
  • Cross-question drill: after whiteboarding, read the Cross-Questions section and try to answer each one in 30 s.
  • Number drill: open the Cheatsheet, cover the right column, recite the latency / QPS / size numbers from memory.
  • Component drill: open Key Technologies, randomly pick two (e.g. Cassandra vs DynamoDB) and articulate "when would I pick each" in 60 s.

5Using the Quick Reference During the Actual Interview

If your interview is open-book, the Quick Reference (separate file in this project) is your single-page-per-problem cheat sheet. Don't read it during the interview — glance at the HLD diagram and the "Why These Choices" section if you stall. The rest of the time, your eyes should be on the whiteboard or the interviewer.

6What to Do the Day Before

  • Re-read the Cheatsheet (10 min).
  • Re-read the Interview Framework (10 min).
  • Whiteboard one familiar problem cold (45 min).
  • Sleep 8 hours. Don't cram new material.

Core Concepts — Quick Intro

One-paragraph summaries of every Core Concept. Read this 30 minutes before the interview to refresh.

1Numbers Every Engineer Should Know

L1 ~1 ns, RAM ~100 ns, SSD ~150 µs, intra-DC RTT ~0.5 ms, cross-region RTT ~80–180 ms. 1 day ≈ 100 k seconds → 1 M events/day ≈ 10 QPS. A single Postgres handles ~10 k writes/s; Redis ~100 k+ ops/s; Kafka ~1 M+ msgs/s/broker.

2Networking

Round-trip cost is set by speed of light through fibre — you can't beat it, only avoid it. Cold HTTPS connection costs ~3–4 RTTs (TCP + TLS); HTTP/2 keep-alive amortises this. CDNs win by serving from a POP 5 ms away instead of 180 ms away — a 30× latency win for static assets.

3API Design

REST for public + mobile, gRPC for internal microservices, WebSocket for bidirectional realtime, SSE for one-way push. Idempotency keys on POSTs that move money / send messages. Cursor pagination, not offset. Right status codes (201 / 202 / 204 / 409 / 410 / 422 / 429 / 503) signal intent precisely.

4Data Modeling — Picking the Database

Default: Postgres until proven otherwise. Switch to MongoDB for flexible / JSON-shaped data where you'd embed instead of join, Cassandra / DynamoDB for write-heavy partition-keyed workloads, Elasticsearch for full-text + faceted search, Redis for caching / leaderboards / locks, Redis Streams for a durable task queue without Kafka, Kafka for high-volume event streaming, S3 for blobs, ClickHouse for analytics, TSDB for metrics, Vector DB for embeddings, Graph DB only when the workload is genuinely graph-shaped (multi-hop traversal).

5Caching

Three strategies: cache-aside (most common), read-through (cache fetches on miss), write-through/write-back. Eviction: LRU (general-purpose), LFU (long-tail traffic), FIFO (write-heavy). Watch for stampedes (request coalescing + jittered TTL) and hot keys (consistent hashing + per-key replication).

6Partitioning & Sharding

Partitioning splits one table into pieces on the same machine (faster scans, smaller indexes, cheap mass deletes). Sharding splits across different machines (to scale beyond one box). Strategies: range / hash / consistent-hashing / geo. The shard key dictates which queries are fast forever — pick it for your dominant access pattern. Pre-shard generously (64 logical shards) so you can move shards between machines without re-mapping. Hot keys mitigated by salting, dedicated shards, or sharded counters.

7Consistent Hashing

Place nodes and keys on a hash ring; each key goes to the next clockwise node. Adding/removing a node only remaps ~1/N keys (vs nearly all keys with naive hash % N). Use virtual nodes (~150 per real node) to even out distribution. Foundational for Cassandra, DynamoDB, Memcached/Redis clusters, CDN routing.

8CAP Theorem

Under partition, you must choose Consistency or Availability — not both. CP systems (Postgres failover, ZooKeeper, etcd, HBase) refuse writes when split. AP systems (Cassandra, DynamoDB default, Dynamo-style stores) accept writes everywhere and reconcile later. Most real systems are PACELC: even without a partition, you trade latency for consistency.

9Database Indexing

B-tree for range + equality (Postgres / MySQL default). Hash for equality. GIN/Inverted for JSONB and full-text. BRIN for huge ordered tables. Partial for sparse predicates ("WHERE status = 'pending'"). Covering / INCLUDE for index-only scans. Every index slows writes and costs storage — index your hot read paths only.

Key Technologies — Quick Intro

When-to-pick one-liners for the 9 technologies that appear in nearly every system-design problem.

The Ladder of Picks

TechReach for it when…Avoid when…
PostgreSQL (SQL)You need ACID, joins, ad-hoc queries; data fits ~10 TB. The default for 80% of problems.You need > 10 k writes/s sustained on one key partition, or multi-region writable.
MongoDBFlexible / evolving schema, hierarchical or JSON-shaped data; you'd rather embed than join.Heavy joins / strict referential integrity / financial transactions — Postgres is stronger.
CassandraYou have a partition-keyed write-heavy workload (> 100 k writes/s) and can tolerate eventual consistency.You need joins, transactions, ad-hoc queries.
DynamoDBYou're on AWS and want managed Cassandra-like store with auto-scale and zero ops.Costs at very high scale (Cassandra on EC2 is cheaper).
RedisYou need < 1 ms reads, distributed locks, leaderboards, rate-limit counters, ephemeral state.You need durability + ACID. (Redis is best as a cache or fast scratchpad.)
Redis StreamsDurable task queue / event log with consumer groups + replay — without standing up Kafka.Throughput > ~100 k msgs/s sustained, or you need multi-day retention on disk.
ElasticsearchFull-text search, autocomplete, faceted filters, log analytics.Source-of-truth for money / canonical state.
KafkaDurable event streams, replayable feeds, decoupling producers from consumers, CDC, > 100 k events/s.Simple task queues with low volume (use SQS / Redis Streams).
Apache FlinkReal-time stream aggregations with exactly-once semantics, watermarks, windowing.Stateless transforms (Kafka Streams is lighter); batch reports (Spark).
API GatewaySingle edge entry point for auth, rate limit, routing, TLS termination across many services.You only have one service — gateway adds latency for no win.
ZooKeeper / etcdCoordination — leader election, distributed locks, config, service discovery.As a general DB. As a metadata store for < 5 nodes (overkill).

Common Combinations You'll See

  • Web app default: Postgres + Redis + CDN.
  • Chat / feed: Cassandra + Kafka + Redis + WebSockets.
  • Search-heavy: Postgres source + CDC → Elasticsearch.
  • Analytics: Kafka → Flink/Spark → ClickHouse / Snowflake.
  • Distributed coordination: ZooKeeper / etcd alongside the DB layer.

Common Patterns — Quick Intro

One-paragraph summaries of every Pattern. Each pattern recurs across 5–10 problems in this guide.

1Real-time Updates

Two distinct sub-problems: pushing data to clients as it happens (WebSockets for bidirectional, SSE for one-way, long-polling as fallback) and keeping internal services in sync as DB state changes (CDC + Kafka). Used in chat, live dashboards, collaborative editing, stock tickers.

2Dealing with Contention

Multiple workers fight over the same resource. Toolbox in order of cost: optimistic CAS (compare-and-set, no lock), advisory locks (Postgres), distributed locks (Redlock / ZooKeeper), pessimistic SELECT FOR UPDATE, queue-based serialisation (route all writes for one key to one worker). Used in ticket booking, payment ledgers, inventory.

3Multi-step Processes

One user action spans many services. Saga pattern (each step has a compensating undo); outbox pattern (atomic DB-write + event emit); durable execution engines (Temporal, Step Functions) for long-lived workflows. Used in payments, order fulfilment, account creation.

4Scaling Reads

Escalation order: in-process cache → Redis cache → read replicas → CDN for static assets → pre-computed materialised views → denormalisation. Last resort: shift to eventual consistency and serve stale reads from edge. Used everywhere — almost every problem.

5Scaling Writes

Escalation order: tune the box → batch writes → shard the relational DB → switch to LSM-tree store (Cassandra / DynamoDB) → put Kafka as a buffer in front of the DB → write-back caches → denormalise to remove writes entirely. Hot keys mitigated by salting / sharded counters. Used in chat, social feeds, click events.

6Handling Large Blobs

Three rules: never proxy blobs through your app server (use S3 presigned URLs), split metadata in DB from blob in object store, deliver via CDN. TUS / S3 multipart for resumable upload; HTTP range requests for chunked download; S3 lifecycle tiering for cost. Used in YouTube, Instagram, Dropbox.

7Managing Long-Running Tasks

Standard pattern: return 202 Accepted + job_id; client polls a status endpoint or registers a webhook. Job queue choices: Kafka / SQS / Redis Streams / Postgres SKIP LOCKED / Sidekiq-style. Always idempotent + exponential-backoff retry + dead-letter queue. Lease/heartbeat watchdog re-queues jobs from dead workers. Used in video transcoding, batch reports, ML inference.

Networking Essentials

The minimum networking knowledge you need to defend latency claims in a system-design interview. Numbers and round-trips you should have at the tip of your tongue.

1Round-Trip Time (RTT) — The Number That Drives Everything

PathTypical RTT
Within the same data centre / AZ0.5–1 ms
Cross-AZ (same region)1–2 ms
Cross-region within continent (us-east ↔ us-west)60–80 ms
Cross-continent (us ↔ eu)80–110 ms
Trans-Pacific (us ↔ ap)130–180 ms
Mobile last-mile (4G)30–80 ms
Mobile last-mile (5G)10–30 ms

This is set by the speed of light through fibre — you cannot beat it. The whole reason CDNs exist is to shorten the geographic distance the request must traverse.

2TCP Handshake (3-Way) and TLS Handshake

  • TCP open: SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK = 1 RTT before any data flows.
  • TLS 1.2: 2 RTTs after TCP open before encrypted data flows.
  • TLS 1.3: 1 RTT after TCP open. With 0-RTT resumption (session tickets), 0 extra RTTs on reconnect.
  • QUIC / HTTP/3: TCP and TLS combined; new connections in 1 RTT, resumed in 0 RTT.

So a "fresh" HTTPS request from India to a us-east origin pays: TCP (180 ms) + TLS 1.3 (180 ms) + actual request/response (180 ms) ≈ 540 ms before the user sees anything. That's why you serve the SSL handshake from a CDN edge POP 5 ms away from the user.

3HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3

HTTP/1.1HTTP/2HTTP/3 (QUIC)
ConnectionTCP, one streamTCP, multiplexedUDP, multiplexed
Head-of-line blockingYes (per connection)Yes (TCP-level)No
Header compressionNoneHPACKQPACK
Server pushNoYes (mostly deprecated)Yes
Resilience to packet lossBadBad (TCP)Good (per-stream)

Modern browsers default to HTTP/2 for HTTPS, HTTP/3 if available. Always run keep-alive: 1 RTT setup amortised across many requests is the difference between a fast and slow page.

4DNS Resolution Flow

client → recursive resolver (ISP / 1.1.1.1 / 8.8.8.8) ↓ (cache miss) root NS → TLD NS (.com) → authoritative NS for example.com ↓ returns A record (IP) — TTL applied client cached for < TTL seconds

Every public DNS lookup is 20–80 ms cold; cached lookups are local and free. Use short TTL (60s) when you need fast failover; long TTL (1 day) when you don't.

5Anycast — How CDNs Route You to the Nearest Edge

Many CDN POPs advertise the same IP via BGP. Routers naturally route the user to the topologically closest POP. So a single IP serves Tokyo from Tokyo and London from London. CloudFront, Cloudflare, Google all use anycast for their edge IPs.

6The Latency Budget — How to Defend "We Need a CDN"

A user in Mumbai requests a static asset from a us-east-1 origin:

  • TCP + TLS 1.3 cold: 4 × 180 ms = 720 ms
  • TLS resumed: 1 × 180 ms = 180 ms
  • Same asset via Mumbai CDN edge (5 ms away): cold 4 × 5 ms = 20 ms; resumed 5 ms

30–100× improvement for static assets. That's the math you give when an interviewer asks "do you really need a CDN?"

7Bandwidth vs Latency

Bandwidth (bytes/sec) and latency (sec/RTT) are independent. A 10 Gbps link from US to AP still has 180 ms RTT. Throwing more bandwidth at a chatty (many-RTT) protocol does not help — you reduce latency only by reducing distance or round-trips.

8Connection Pooling and Keep-Alive

Service-to-service calls inside your DC: always keep-alive, always pool. A typical service should hold 8–32 long-lived connections to each downstream peer; closing+reopening per request adds 1+ ms × your QPS in pure waste.

9Things to Remember in Interviews

  • Speed of light = ~5 µs/km in fibre. Mumbai ↔ NYC ≈ 12,500 km × 5 µs ≈ 62 ms one-way ≈ 125 ms RTT minimum.
  • Every cross-region call costs 80–180 ms. Design to avoid them on the request path.
  • CDN edge for static + TLS termination + DDoS scrubbing = the standard front door.
  • Mobile is the lossiest network; HTTP/3 / QUIC matters most there.

API Design

Every system-design interview includes "show me the API." A few principles let you knock out a clean, defensible spec in two minutes flat.

1Choose the Right Style

StyleBest forAvoid when
REST / JSON over HTTPPublic APIs, web/mobile clients, broad ecosystemVery high QPS internal service-to-service
gRPC (protobuf over HTTP/2)Internal microservices, strong typing, ~5× faster than JSON, built-in streamingBrowser clients (no native support)
GraphQLMobile clients fetching deeply-nested data; over-fetch problemPublic unauth APIs (query complexity attacks); simple CRUD
WebSocketBidirectional realtime (chat, collab, trading)One-way server→client only (use SSE)
Server-Sent Events (SSE)Server→client push (live feeds, AI streaming)Bidirectional needs

Default for an interview answer: REST for public endpoints, gRPC for internal service-to-service.

2REST Resource Design

  • Resources are nouns, not verbs: POST /messages not POST /sendMessage.
  • Use plural for collections: /users/42 not /user/42.
  • Nest only one level: /users/42/messages. Deeper nesting → use query params.
  • Filtering / sorting / paging via query: ?cursor=abc&limit=20&sort=-createdAt.

3HTTP Verbs and Idempotency

VerbActionIdempotent?Safe (no side effects)?
GETReadYesYes
