POSTCreate / generic actionNo (use idempotency key)No
PUTReplace whole resourceYesNo
PATCHPartial updateUsually yesNo
DELETERemoveYesNo

Network retries are inevitable. Make POSTs idempotent via an Idempotency-Key header (Stripe, GitHub, every modern API). Server stores the key + response; duplicate request → return cached response.

4The Status Codes You Actually Need

CodeMeaningUse for
200OKSuccessful read / update with body
201CreatedPOST that created a resource (return Location header)
202AcceptedAsync work queued; client polls for result
204No ContentSuccessful action, no body to return
400Bad RequestMalformed JSON / missing field
401UnauthorizedNo / invalid auth
403ForbiddenAuthenticated, but not allowed
404Not FoundResource doesn't exist
409ConflictVersion mismatch, concurrent edit
410GoneUsed to exist; permanently removed
422Unprocessable EntityValid syntax but semantically invalid
429Too Many RequestsRate limited (return Retry-After)
500Internal Server ErrorUnexpected server crash
503Service UnavailableOverloaded / circuit open (transient)

5Pagination — Offset vs Cursor

  • Offset: ?page=5&limit=20. Easy. Breaks if rows are inserted between pages. OFFSET 100000 is slow on large tables.
  • Cursor: ?cursor=eyJ0aW1lIjoxMjM0fQ&limit=20. Server returns next-cursor in response. Stable under inserts. Always-O(log n) seek.

Use cursor for everything customer-facing. Offset is fine for admin tools.

6Versioning

  • URI versioning: /v1/users, /v2/users. Most common; trivially debuggable.
  • Header versioning: Accept: application/vnd.api+json;version=2. Cleaner URIs; less obvious in logs.
  • Date versioning (Stripe): Stripe-Version: 2024-04-10. Most flexible; lets each customer upgrade independently.

7The Standard Headers

  • Authorization: Bearer <token> — auth.
  • Idempotency-Key: <uuid> — POST de-dup.
  • X-Request-Id: <uuid> — distributed tracing.
  • Retry-After: 30 — when returning 429 / 503.
  • X-RateLimit-Limit / -Remaining / -Reset — clients can self-throttle.
  • ETag + If-None-Match — conditional GETs (304 Not Modified saves bandwidth).
  • If-Match — optimistic concurrency control on PUT/PATCH.

8Error Response Shape (consistent across the API)

{ "error": { "code": "INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS", "message": "Account balance $5 less than transfer amount.", "request_id": "req_abc123", "details": { "balance_cents": 1495, "transfer_cents": 2000 } } }

9What Interviewers Look For

  • Resource-based REST naming.
  • Right verb + right status code.
  • Idempotency keys on POSTs that move money / send messages.
  • Cursor pagination for list endpoints.
  • Auth header (mention JWT or API key).
  • One example error response shape.

Data Modeling — Picking the Right Store

The most common interview pushback: "why did you pick this database?" Memorise the table below so you can answer with one sentence per option.

1The Shortlist

DatabaseTypePick whenSingle-node ceiling
PostgreSQL / MySQLRelational, ACIDDefault OLTP. Joins, transactions, strong consistency. Up to ~10 TB on one node.~10 k writes/s, 50 k reads/s
Cassandra / ScyllaDBWide-column, LSM-treeWrite-heavy (100 k+/s/node), time-series, event logs. Partition key designed around query.~100 k+ writes/s/node
DynamoDBManaged key-valueKey-value at scale, predictable per-partition QPS, want to skip ops.1 k writes/s, 3 k reads/s per partition
MongoDBDocument storeSchemaless / nested documents (e.g. CMS, user profiles with varied fields).~10–20 k writes/s
RedisIn-memory KVCache, rate limits, sessions, leaderboards, pub/sub. Sub-ms latency.~100 k–1 M ops/s/node
Elasticsearch / OpenSearchSearch engineFull-text search, log analytics, faceting, geo queries. Never primary.~10 k indexing/s, 10 k+ search/s
S3 / object storageBlob storageFiles, images, videos, backups, data lake. Cheap; 11 9's durability.Unlimited; pay per GB-month
ClickHouse / BigQuery / SnowflakeColumnar OLAPAnalytical queries over billions of rows (aggregations, time-bucketing).Trillions of rows scanned in seconds
InfluxDB / TimescaleDBTime-seriesMetrics, IoT sensor data, monitoring. Built-in down-sampling and retention.~1 M points/s
Neo4j / NeptuneGraphMulti-hop traversals (friends-of-friends, recommendation graphs, fraud rings).~100 M nodes
HBase / BigtableWide-column, CPMassive datasets with strong row-level consistency (Google's choice for indexes).PB-scale; linear with regions
Spanner / CockroachDB / TiDBNewSQL (distributed ACID)Need both ACID transactions AND horizontal scale across regions.Scales horizontally

2Decision Tree

Q: Do you need ACID transactions across multiple rows / tables? ├── Yes → relational (Postgres / MySQL). │ ├── Need to scale beyond ~10 TB? → shard MySQL OR use NewSQL (Spanner / CockroachDB). │ └── Otherwise → single Postgres + read replicas. Move on. │ └── No, eventual consistency is fine. Then ask: │ ├── Is it search / faceting / full-text? → Elasticsearch (mirror from primary). │ ├── Is it analytics / aggregations? → ClickHouse / BigQuery (mirror via CDC). │ ├── Is it cache / session / rate-limit? → Redis. │ ├── Is it blobs / files / videos? → S3. │ ├── Is it time-series metrics? → InfluxDB / TimescaleDB. │ ├── Is it heavy graph traversal? → Neo4j. │ ├── Are you write-heavy with simple per-row access? → Cassandra. │ └── Need managed key-value with auto-scale? → DynamoDB.

3Trade-off Matrix (the famous 4 dimensions)

DatabaseConsistencyScale shapeQuery flexibilityOperational cost
Postgres / MySQLStrong (single-leader)Vertical (then sharded)Very high — full SQL, joinsLow — mature ops
CassandraTunable (eventual default)Linear horizontalLow — must design tables per queryHigh — repair, compaction
MongoDBTunableShardedMedium — flexible docs, limited joinsMedium
DynamoDBTunableAuto-scaled by AWSLow — PK + GSI onlyMinimal (managed)
RedisNone (cache); CRDTs availableCluster shardedKey-based + rich data typesLow
ElasticsearchEventual (~1 s refresh)Sharded + replicatedVery high for text / aggregationsHigh — JVM tuning, mapping conflicts
ClickHouseEventualShardedOLAP-style SQL; great aggregationsMedium
Spanner / CockroachDBStrong (global)Linear horizontalFull SQLMedium-high

4Modelling for Each Store

  • Postgres / MySQL: 3NF normalised by default; denormalise selectively for read perf. Use JSONB / JSON for genuinely flexible-shape data.
  • Cassandra: design tables around your queries. The same data may be denormalised into 3 tables, one per access pattern.
  • DynamoDB: single-table-design philosophy. Hash + sort key, GSIs for alternate access paths. The whole schema fits in one table with composite keys.
  • MongoDB: embed nested data when read together; reference when accessed independently.
  • Elasticsearch: never your primary. Mirror from Postgres / Mongo via CDC.
🔑 The Universal Pattern: One Source of Truth + Many Specialised Views

Almost every real system has:

  • One OLTP DB (Postgres / MySQL / Cassandra) as the source of truth.
  • Multiple specialised views kept in sync via CDC: Elasticsearch for search, ClickHouse for analytics, Redis for cache, S3 for archive.

Don't try to make one DB do everything — that's the route to a stack you can't operate. Specialise per workload; sync via CDC.

Caching — Strategies and Eviction

Picking the right read/write pattern (4 main + 2 bonus) and the right eviction policy is what separates "fast" from "broken under load."

1Cache Strategies — The Four Read/Write Patterns

Pick the right pattern based on (a) is the workload read-heavy or write-heavy, (b) how stale can the cache be, and (c) what happens if the cache or DB fails mid-write.

1. Cache-Aside (Lazy Loading) — the default

READ: app → cache? ┌── hit → return value └── miss → DB → write into cache → return value WRITE: app → DB app → cache.DEL(key) // invalidate; next read re-populates
  • Pros: simple; cache only holds what's actually read; cache failure doesn't break writes.
  • Cons: cache miss = slow (one DB round-trip + one cache write); stale data possible if writer forgets to invalidate; stampede risk on hot-key expiry.
  • Use when: read-heavy workload, can tolerate brief staleness (URL shortener, product catalog, user profiles).

2. Read-Through — cache fronts the DB transparently

READ: app → cache ┌── hit → return └── miss → cache loads from DB → returns to app WRITE: app → cache → cache writes to DB // combined with write-through usually
  • Pros: app code is simpler — no DB code on the miss path; cache and DB are coupled by configuration, not code.
  • Cons: requires a cache layer or library that "knows" the DB schema; harder to override per-query.
  • Use when: managed caches that proxy a DB (DAX for DynamoDB, Hibernate L2 cache, NGINX caching proxy).

3. Write-Through — cache and DB updated together, synchronously

WRITE: app → cache.SET(key, val) cache → DB.write(key, val) // synchronous; both must succeed return success to app READ: app → cache → hit (always; even fresh writes are cached)
  • Pros: cache and DB always consistent; readers never see stale data; read-after-write is guaranteed.
  • Cons: write latency = max(cache, DB); pollutes the cache with data that may never be read; cache failure can block writes.
  • Use when: read-after-write consistency is critical and write rate is moderate (e.g., user profile updates that the user immediately re-reads on next page).

4. Write-Back (Write-Behind) — cache absorbs writes, flushes to DB async

WRITE: app → cache.SET(key, val) // returns immediately cache → buffers writes cache → DB.batchWrite(...) // asynchronously, e.g. every 100 ms or 1000 entries READ: app → cache → hit (cache is source of truth between flushes)
  • Pros: extremely high write throughput; absorbs spikes; batched DB writes are 10–100× more efficient.
  • Cons: data loss if cache crashes before flush; cache becomes temporary source of truth; complicated recovery semantics.
  • Use when: write-heavy, tolerable durability loss — view counters, click events, leaderboard scores, like counts. Never for money or auth data.

Bonus pattern: Write-Around

Writes go directly to the DB, bypassing the cache. Reads use cache-aside. Useful for write-once-read-rarely data so the cache isn't polluted by writes that won't be read soon (e.g., audit logs, archival writes).

Bonus pattern: Refresh-Ahead

Cache proactively refreshes hot keys before their TTL expires. Eliminates cold-miss latency cliffs on popular keys. Trade-off: wasted refreshes for keys that aren't actually re-accessed. Use when you have a predictable hot-key access pattern.

Decision matrix

WorkloadStrategyExample
Read-heavy, stale OKCache-AsideURL shortener, product catalog
Read-after-write must be freshWrite-ThroughUser profile, cart contents
Write-heavy, durability tolerantWrite-BackView counts, like counts, analytics
Managed cache fronting DBRead-ThroughDAX, ORM L2 cache, CDN
Write-once, read-rarelyWrite-AroundAudit logs, cold archives
Predictable hot keysRefresh-AheadTop-N lists, leaderboards

2Eviction Policies — Choosing What to Throw Out

When the cache hits its memory limit, something must go. The policy decides which key. Get this wrong and your hit rate tanks.

PolicyRuleStrengthsWeaknesses
LRU (Least Recently Used)Evict the key not accessed for the longest timeO(1) with doubly-linked list + hash map; matches typical temporal-locality workloadsScan pollution: a full-table scan evicts every hot key in one shot
LFU (Least Frequently Used)Evict the key with the lowest hit-countResists scan pollution; stable popular keys stay hotOld hot keys that stop being accessed linger forever (mitigated by aging variants)
FIFOEvict the oldest-inserted, regardless of accessSimplest; cheap O(1)Ignores actual access patterns; usually worst hit rate
RandomEvict a random keyTrivially simple; surprisingly OK; no metadata to trackCan evict the hottest key by bad luck
TTL-basedEach key auto-expires after a set timePredictable memory pressure; great for time-bounded data (sessions, rate-limit windows)Not a true eviction; need a fallback if you fill up before TTLs hit
ARC (Adaptive Replacement)Two lists (recency + frequency); balance shifts based on workloadBetter hit rate than LRU on mixed workloadsMore complex; was IBM-patented (now expired)
W-TinyLFUWindow-LRU front + Count-Min Sketch frequency estimator; admit new key only if estimated freq > victim'sBest hit rate in published benchmarksMore complex; small CMS memory overhead

Picking a policy (quick guide)

  • LRU — safe default for typical app workloads with temporal locality.
  • LFU — when you have analytical scans that mustn't pollute the working set.
  • TTL-based — when data is naturally time-bound (sessions, OTPs, rate-limit windows). Combine with another policy as fallback.
  • W-TinyLFU — when you need the best possible hit rate and can afford the complexity (Caffeine library is the reference).
  • Random — when you genuinely don't care or you're aiming for minimum metadata overhead.

Redis eviction policies

Redis's maxmemory-policy setting controls behaviour when maxmemory is reached:

PolicyWhat it does
noeviction (default)Reject new writes with an error. Reads keep working.
allkeys-lruLRU across all keys, whether they have a TTL or not. Most common for a pure cache.
allkeys-lfuLFU across all keys (added in Redis 4.0; uses a probabilistic counter).
volatile-lruLRU but only on keys that have a TTL set. Keys without TTL are protected.
volatile-lfuLFU but only on keys with TTL.
volatile-ttlEvict keys closest to expiry first. Useful when TTLs encode "freshness need."
allkeys-random / volatile-randomRandom eviction.
🔑 Two practical Redis defaults

If Redis is a pure cache: use allkeys-lru and don't bother setting TTLs unless you want them for staleness reasons.

If Redis holds some "must keep" state mixed with cache (e.g., sessions you can't lose alongside cached data you can): use volatile-lru and set TTLs only on the cache keys; the session keys without TTL are safe from eviction.

3Stampede Prevention

A hot key expires at T=0. Between T=0 and T=ε, a thousand concurrent requests all see MISS and all hit the DB. The DB melts. Three defences:

  • Request coalescing (singleflight): in each app server, when a MISS triggers a DB read, mark the key as "in flight"; subsequent concurrent MISSes for the same key wait on the in-flight promise.
  • Probabilistic early refresh (XFetch): as TTL nears expiry, each requester probabilistically refreshes the cache asynchronously even while the cached value is still valid. Eliminates synchronised expiry storms.
  • TTL jitter: set TTL to base + random(±10%) so synchronised sets don't expire synchronously.

Partitioning & Sharding

Splitting one logical dataset into pieces. Same idea at the algorithmic level — different things at the operational level. People (and interviewers) frequently confuse the two; getting the distinction crisp is a fast credibility win.

1Partitioning vs Sharding — The Distinction

Both split a logical table into smaller pieces by some key. The difference is where the pieces live:

PartitioningSharding
Where pieces liveAll on the same machine, inside one DB instanceAcross different machines / DB instances
GoalFaster queries, smaller indexes, easier maintenanceScale storage / throughput beyond one machine
RoutingThe DB does it transparently — same SQL worksApplication or middleware (Vitess, Citus) routes to the right shard
TransactionsCross-partition ACID is free (same DB)Cross-shard transactions are hard (2PC / saga)
Failure blast radiusOne disk / one node dies = whole table downOne shard down = only that shard's data unavailable
Operational complexityLow — built into Postgres / MySQL nativelyHigh — connection routing, resharding, cross-shard queries
ExamplesPostgres PARTITION BY RANGE/LIST/HASH; MySQL partitionsVitess, Citus, manual app-level sharding, DynamoDB partitions across nodes

One-line mental model: "Partitioning = one table split into pieces on one machine. Sharding = one table split into pieces on many machines."

Why partition (even if you don't shard)?

  • Faster scans — query planner reads only relevant partitions (partition pruning). A WHERE ts > yesterday on a daily-partitioned table touches one partition, not the whole 100 TB table.
  • Smaller indexes per partition — index lookups are O(log per-partition), not O(log total). Big wins on very large tables.
  • Cheap mass deletes — DROP PARTITION events_2023_01 is instant; DELETE WHERE ts < ... on 100M rows takes hours and bloats indexes.
  • Storage tiering — old partitions on slow / cold storage, hot partitions on SSD.
  • Per-tenant isolation — if you partition by tenant_id, queries are tenant-scoped and noisy neighbours can't scan a full table.

Partitioning strategies (Postgres / MySQL syntax)

-- RANGE: each partition owns a contiguous range
CREATE TABLE events (id BIGINT, ts TIMESTAMPTZ, ...)
  PARTITION BY RANGE (ts);
CREATE TABLE events_2026_05 PARTITION OF events
  FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-05-01') TO ('2026-06-01');

-- LIST: explicit value list per partition
CREATE TABLE users PARTITION BY LIST (region);
CREATE TABLE users_us PARTITION OF users FOR VALUES IN ('us-east','us-west');
CREATE TABLE users_eu PARTITION OF users FOR VALUES IN ('eu-west','eu-north');

-- HASH: even distribution by hash(key) % N
CREATE TABLE messages PARTITION BY HASH (user_id);
CREATE TABLE messages_p0 PARTITION OF messages FOR VALUES WITH (MODULUS 8, REMAINDER 0);
-- ... messages_p1 ... messages_p7

The full picture: vertical vs horizontal, partitioning vs sharding

TermWhat it splitsDirection
Vertical partitioningColumns — split a wide table into users_core + users_profileSplits the schema
Horizontal partitioningRows — split by a key on the same machineSplits the data, same machine
ShardingRows — split by a key across different machinesSplits the data, many machines
FederationTables — different services own different tables (microservices DB-per-service)Splits ownership

In day-to-day usage, "partitioning" almost always means horizontal partitioning on one machine, and "sharding" almost always means horizontal sharding across many machines.

The natural progression

1.  Single Postgres
       (works fine up to ~1 TB / 10k writes/sec)
            ↓
2.  + Read replicas       ← scale reads
            ↓
3.  + Partitioning        ← scale single-table size; faster maintenance
       (still one machine — just cleaner internals)
            ↓
4.  + Sharding            ← scale beyond one machine
       (Vitess / Citus / app-level shards)

Don't skip step 3. A partitioned single Postgres handles workloads that people often unnecessarily shard for.

2Why Shard at All?

You shard when a single node can't keep up — even after partitioning, replicas, and vertical scale. Symptoms:

  • Storage: dataset > ~10 TB on one box.
  • Write throughput: > ~10 k writes/sec on Postgres / MySQL.
  • Read throughput: > ~50 k reads/sec even after read replicas.
  • Per-tenant isolation: noisy neighbour drowning others.

Until then, vertical scale + read replicas + partitioning are cheaper and simpler. Shard last, not first.

3The Three Strategies

StrategyHowWinsLoses
RangeEach shard owns a key range (user_id 0–1M, 1M–2M...)Range queries are single-shard; intuitive splitsHot ranges if traffic is non-uniform; manual splits
Hashshard = hash(key) % NEven distribution by constructionRange queries scatter to all shards; resharding remaps everything
Consistent hashingHash to a ring; key goes to next clockwise nodeAdding/removing nodes only remaps 1/N of keysSlightly more code; uneven without virtual nodes
Geo / lookupShard by region or by an explicit lookup tableData residency; per-tenant isolationLookup table becomes a hot spot if not cached

4Choosing the Shard Key — the Permanent Decision

The shard key dictates which queries are fast forever:

  • Single-shard queries (those filtering by the shard key) are O(1) shards.
  • Cross-shard queries are O(N) shards — scatter-gather; latency = slowest shard; unbearable at 100+ shards.

Pick a key that:

  1. Has high cardinality (millions of distinct values).
  2. Distributes traffic uniformly (no celebrity that takes 10× normal load).
  3. Appears in the WHERE clause of your most common queries.

Bad shard keys: country (only ~200 values; some 50× larger than others), gender, status. Good shard keys: user_id, tenant_id, order_id.

5Hot Keys / Hot Shards

One key = celebrity user, one tenant = enterprise giant. Even with a perfect shard key, traffic is rarely uniform. Mitigations:

  • Salting: append a random suffix celeb#42#0...celeb#42#9. Distribute writes across 10 keys; reads must aggregate.
  • Dedicated shard for the heavy tenant.
  • Sharded counter instead of one row.
  • Cache the hot read paths in Redis.

See the Scaling Writes Patterns page §8 for the full toolbox.

6Resharding — the Pain You Want to Avoid

Doubling shard count when N is fixed (hash % N) remaps almost every key. Strategies to make it less painful:

  • Pre-shard generously (start with 64 logical shards even if you have 4 physical nodes — move logical shards between nodes later).
  • Consistent hashing — only 1/N keys move per added node.
  • Vitess / Citus / Spanner-style splits — automated background range splits with zero downtime.
  • Dual-write window — for hash-sharded systems, dual-write to old + new shards, backfill in background, switch reads, drop old.

7Cross-Shard Operations

OperationApproach
Cross-shard JOINAvoid. Denormalise. Or do it in the app via two queries.
Cross-shard transactionSaga pattern with compensating actions, or 2PC (slow).
Cross-shard countFan out, sum locally on each shard, aggregate.
Cross-shard paginationPull top-K from each shard, merge in app. Pricey.
Reporting / OLAPCDC stream all shards into a separate columnar warehouse (ClickHouse / Snowflake).

8The Standard Milestones

WorkloadSharding
0–10k QPS, < 1 TBSingle Postgres + replica
10k–50k QPS, 1–10 TB4 shards (room to grow to 16)
50k–500k QPS, 10–100 TB16–64 shards, or move to Cassandra/DynamoDB
500k+ QPS, 100 TB+Hundreds of shards, regionally partitioned
🔑 The One Rule

The shard key you choose at minute one determines what's fast for the lifetime of the system. Pick it for your dominant query pattern, not for what feels natural.

Consistent Hashing

The technique that lets you add and remove nodes from a sharded cluster while remapping only ~1/N keys instead of all of them. Used by Cassandra, DynamoDB, Akamai CDN, Riak, and every Memcached/Redis client.

1The Problem: Naïve Sharding Is Catastrophic

The obvious sharding is node = hash(key) mod N. Add one node → almost every key remaps to a different node:

N=10: hash("user_42") mod 10 = 2 → node #2 N=11: hash("user_42") mod 11 = 5 → node #5 N=12: hash("user_42") mod 12 = 6 → node #6 When you scale up, you basically invalidate the entire cache. For a stateful sharded DB, this is even worse — you'd have to move ~all the data to new nodes during a single deploy.

2The Idea: A Hash Ring

Imagine a circle with positions 0 to 2³². Each server gets one (or more) positions on the ring. Each key is hashed to a position. The key is "owned" by the next server clockwise.

0 │ ┌─────────┼─────────┐ N3 N1 │ │ │ key_X │ │ (lands here)│ ├──── owned by N1 ─┤ │ │ N4 N2 │ │ └─────────┼─────────┘ 2^32 / 2

Adding a node: drop it onto the ring at some position. It takes over the keys between its position and the previous server's position. Only those keys move; everything else is untouched. About 1/N of all keys remap.

Removing a node: its keys go to the next clockwise neighbour. Same minimal-remap property.

3Virtual Nodes (the production essential)

With one position per server, key distribution is uneven (some servers hold 5%, some 0.5%). Solution: each physical server owns 100–200 virtual positions on the ring (random hashes of node_id|0, node_id|1, …).

Benefits:

  • Smooths out load distribution.
  • When a node dies, its keys redistribute across many neighbours instead of dumping all on one — no thundering herd.
  • Lets you give bigger machines more vnodes proportional to their capacity.

4Replication Via the Ring

To replicate, copy each key to the next K-1 distinct physical nodes clockwise. Replication factor 3 = primary + 2 replicas. The ring topology naturally gives you replication geography for free; Cassandra and DynamoDB both work this way.

5Where It's Used

  • Cassandra — every cluster is a consistent-hash ring with vnodes (default 256).
  • DynamoDB — partition assignment uses the same idea.
  • Akamai CDN — content distributed across edge nodes via consistent hashing.
  • Memcached client libraries (libketama, mc-router) — clients hash keys to servers, no central coordinator.
  • Redis Cluster — uses 16,384 hash slots assigned to nodes; not exactly consistent hashing but the same minimal-remap principle.

6Trade-offs

  • Pros: minimal remap on add/remove; auto-rebalance friendly; no central coordinator needed.
  • Cons: harder to do range queries (data isn't sorted); requires gossip-based membership protocol.

CAP Theorem

In a distributed system you can have at most 2 of: Consistency, Availability, Partition tolerance. Since network partitions do happen, the real choice is CP vs AP.

1The Formal Statement (and the Real-World One)

Formal: a distributed system cannot simultaneously provide all three of:

  • Consistency — every read sees the most recent write.
  • Availability — every request gets a (non-error) response.
  • Partition tolerance — the system keeps working despite the network dropping messages between nodes.

Real-world: network partitions happen — power outage, switch failure, intercontinental cable cut, NAT timeout. So P is non-negotiable. The actual choice you're making is: when (not if) a partition happens, do I sacrifice C or A?

2CP vs AP — Real Systems

SystemCAP ChoiceWhy
PostgreSQL primary-replicaCPIf primary partitioned from replicas, primary refuses writes until quorum
CassandraAP (tunable)Available during partitions; you choose consistency level per operation
DynamoDBAPAlways available; eventual consistency default; optional strong consistency
HBase / BigtableCPIf region server fails, region unavailable until reassigned
etcd / ZooKeeperCPQuorum required for any write — coordination service must be consistent
Spanner / CockroachDBCPStrong global consistency; latency cost of cross-region quorum on writes
S3APAlways available globally; eventually consistent for cross-region reads
DNSAPAlways answers; might serve a stale record during propagation

3How to Pick

WorkloadPick
Financial transactions, inventory, ledgerCP — better to be unavailable than wrong
Social feeds, DNS, CDNAP — stale post is fine; downtime is not
User profile / session storeAP usually — eventual is fine
Coordination (leader election, locks)CP — split-brain is catastrophic
Analytics / event logAP — losing a few events is OK; downtime kills training
Authentication tokensAP with short TTL — old tokens still verify

4Tunable Consistency (the modern view)

Modern AP systems (Cassandra, DynamoDB, MongoDB) let you tune per-operation: a read from a single replica is fast and possibly stale; a quorum read sees recent writes. The famous formula: if W + R > N (writes confirmed by W replicas, reads from R replicas, total N), you get strong read-after-write consistency without giving up the AP benefits.

5PACELC — the extension you should know

CAP only describes behaviour during a partition. PACELC adds: else (when there's no partition), you still trade Latency vs Consistency. Most "AP" systems are actually "PA/EL" — they sacrifice consistency even when there's no partition, to keep latency low. Spanner is "PC/EC" — strict consistency at the cost of cross-region write latency.

6How to Defend Your Choice in Interviews

🔑 The Stock Answers

"Why AP for our social feed?" "Users tolerate a slightly stale feed (eventual consistency over a few seconds is invisible). They don't tolerate the app being down. So we accept eventual consistency to keep availability."

"Why CP for inventory?" "Overselling a single unit is a refund + apology. Overselling 10,000 is the news. We'd rather refuse the order than risk inconsistency, so we pick CP — which means a partitioned region cannot accept new orders."

Database Indexing

An index is a separate data structure that lets you find rows by a column without scanning the table. Picking the right index type for the right access pattern is what makes a query 1000× faster.

1Index Types — When to Use Each

IndexBest forUsed by
B-TreeEquality + range queries on a sorted column. The default in nearly every relational DB.Postgres, MySQL InnoDB, SQLite, Oracle
LSM-TreeHeavy write workload; reads are slower (must check multiple SSTables, helped by Bloom filters).Cassandra, RocksDB, LevelDB, HBase
HashPure equality lookups; no range queries. Constant-time lookup.Postgres (HASH index), DynamoDB, Redis (internally)
InvertedFull-text search: term → list of documents.Elasticsearch / Lucene, Solr
GIN (Generalized Inverted)JSONB containment queries, array containment, full-text in Postgres.Postgres
GiST / SP-GiSTGeo-spatial, range types, custom data types.Postgres + PostGIS
BRIN (Block Range)Huge tables where data is naturally ordered (time-series). Tiny index size.Postgres for time-series
PartialIndexes only the rows matching a WHERE clause. Tiny index for sparse data.Postgres, SQL Server
Covering / IncludedIndex includes extra columns so the query doesn't need a heap fetch. Index-only scans.Postgres, SQL Server, MySQL 8

2B-Tree Mechanics (the most common index)

A B-tree is a balanced tree where each node holds many keys (matched to a disk page). Lookup is O(log N), and because each node holds many keys, the tree is shallow — typically 3–5 levels for a billion-row table, so 3–5 disk reads worst case.

  • Index lookup: walk from root to leaf comparing keys; the leaf points to the row's heap location.
  • Range scan: walk to the start of the range, then traverse leaves linearly (leaves are linked).
  • Insert: find the leaf, insert the key. If the leaf is full, split (and propagate up).
  • Update: usually a delete + insert in the index, even if the row's heap location stays the same.

3The Power of Partial Indexes (PostgreSQL)

From the Job Scheduler problem: a partial index dramatically reduces index size.

CREATE INDEX idx_pending ON jobs(next_run_at) WHERE status = 'PENDING';

Without WHERE: index has 100M rows. With WHERE: index has only ~3,500 rows (the PENDING ones). Index fits in CPU cache. Queries that match the WHERE clause use this tiny index. Queries that don't match it use a different index (or full scan).

Use whenever you have a small subset of rows that's queried far more often than the rest.

4Composite Indexes & Column Order

A composite index (a, b, c) can be used for queries that filter on:

  • a alone
  • a + b
  • a + b + c

It cannot be used for queries on b alone or c alone. Lead with the column you filter on most often; equality before range.

5When Indexes Hurt

  • Write amplification: every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE updates every index on the table. 10 indexes = 10× write cost.
  • Storage: each index is a copy of the indexed columns + pointers. A heavily-indexed table can be 2–3× the size of the data alone.
  • Plan complexity: too many indexes confuses the query planner; sometimes adding an index makes a query slower.

Rule of thumb: index every query you run regularly; remove indexes that aren't used (Postgres has pg_stat_user_indexes for this).

6Index-Only Scans (the fastest read)

If all the columns you SELECT are in the index (covering index), the database never reads the heap — it returns directly from the index. 5–10× faster on cold caches.

-- Original: must do heap fetch for `name` SELECT name FROM users WHERE email = ?; CREATE INDEX idx_email ON users(email); -- Covering: returns name directly from index (Postgres / MySQL 8+) CREATE INDEX idx_email_name ON users(email) INCLUDE (name); -- or in MySQL: CREATE INDEX idx_email_name ON users(email, name);

7JSONB Indexing (Postgres)

You can index JSONB fields with GIN for general containment, or with B-tree on a specific extracted path. JSONB B-tree indexes give SQL-like behaviour for specific keys; GIN is for "find documents where any path matches".

-- B-tree on a specific path CREATE INDEX idx_status ON events ((data ->> 'status')); -- GIN for general containment CREATE INDEX idx_data_gin ON events USING GIN (data jsonb_path_ops);

CDN — Content Delivery Networks

A globally distributed cache that sits between users and your origin. The single biggest latency win available for any read-heavy workload. Used by ~99% of large-scale web/mobile/streaming systems.

1What a CDN Actually Is

A CDN is a fleet of edge POPs (Points of Presence) — datacentres scattered across cities worldwide (Cloudflare ~300, CloudFront ~450, Akamai ~4 000+). Each POP holds a local cache. Users get routed to the topologically nearest POP via anycast BGP; the POP serves cached responses from local SSD/RAM; only cache misses hit your origin.

  • Latency: cuts request RTT from "user to your origin" down to "user to nearest POP" — typically ~5–20 ms vs 80–180 ms.
  • Bandwidth offload: 90–99 % of requests served from POP; origin sees only the long tail.
  • DDoS shield: CDN absorbs volumetric attacks at the edge.
  • TLS termination: heavy crypto work happens at the edge, close to the user.
  • Edge compute: modern CDNs (Cloudflare Workers, Lambda@Edge, Fastly Compute) run code at the POP for personalisation, A/B tests, auth.

2The Number That Sells the CDN

User in Mumbai, origin in us-east-1:

  • Without CDN: TCP + TLS 1.3 cold open = 4 × 180 ms ≈ 720 ms before first byte.
  • With CDN edge in Mumbai (~5 ms away): 4 × 5 ms ≈ 20 ms.
  • 30–100× latency reduction for static assets and cached API responses.

This is the math you cite when an interviewer asks "do you really need a CDN?"

3Anycast — How the User Gets to the Nearest POP

Many POPs advertise the same IP via BGP. Internet routers naturally route the user to the topologically closest one. So 1.1.1.1 reaches Cloudflare's London POP from a UK user and Cloudflare's Tokyo POP from a Japan user — same IP, different physical machine.

4Push vs Pull Origin Models

Pull (lazy)Push (proactive)
HowPOP fetches from origin on first miss; caches locallyYou explicitly upload content to the CDN
First requestCold — origin hit + cache fillAlways cached — zero cold misses
Best forLong-tail assets, web pages, API responsesVideo premieres, software releases, major launches
EffortNone (set Cache-Control and forget)Manual or pipeline-driven uploads

~99% of CDN usage is pull-based. Push is for pre-warming high-stakes drops (Netflix pre-warms new-release titles to every Open Connect box hours before launch).

5Cache Hit/Miss Flow

Client GET /image.png ▼ POP receives request │ ├── HIT (object in POP cache, not expired) │ → serve from local SSD/RAM (~5 ms) │ └── MISS (cold POP / expired / new asset) ▼ origin shield POP (regional aggregation layer) │ ├── HIT → serve, populate edge POP │ └── MISS → origin server → serve, populate shield + edge → next request to that region = HIT

Origin shield: an intermediate caching layer between edges and origin. Concentrates misses from many edges into one fetch from origin. Critical when you have hundreds of POPs — without shield, a viral asset causes a "thundering herd" of misses against origin.

6Headers That Control CDN Behaviour

  • Cache-Control: public, max-age=86400 — cache for 24h at edge.
  • Cache-Control: private — only browser cache, never CDN. Use for user-specific responses.
  • Cache-Control: s-maxage=3600 — separate edge TTL distinct from browser TTL.
  • Cache-Control: no-cache — must revalidate with origin (ETag); cheaper than no-store.
  • Cache-Control: no-store — never cache (auth tokens, secrets).
  • Cache-Control: stale-while-revalidate=60 — serve stale while fetching fresh in background. Hides origin latency from users.
  • ETag: "abc123" + client's If-None-Match: "abc123" → CDN returns 304 Not Modified (no body) when unchanged.
  • Vary: Accept-Encoding — store separate cache entries per encoding (gzip vs br).

7Cache Invalidation — the Hard Part

  • TTL expiry — easiest; let it expire naturally. Cheap, but means brief staleness.
  • Versioned URLs — /static/v123/main.css; never invalidate, just deploy a new URL. The standard for static assets.
  • Explicit purge — CDN API call to evict a path globally. Slow (seconds to propagate); use sparingly.
  • Soft purge — mark as stale but serve while revalidating; users never see a miss.
  • Cache tagging (Fastly's surrogate keys) — tag objects with logical labels ("user:42"); purge by tag → multi-asset invalidation.

8What to Cache vs Not

Cacheable at CDNNot cacheable
Static assets (CSS, JS, images, videos)Per-user dashboards / authenticated pages
Public API responses (catalogue, product, search)POST / PUT / DELETE requests
HTML pages for logged-out usersAuth tokens, secrets, payment data
API responses with short TTL (newsfeed, hot products)Real-time data with strong freshness
Anything with same response for many usersAnything with Set-Cookie typically

9Multi-CDN Strategy

At very high scale, no single CDN can serve everything. Real systems use multiple CDNs simultaneously:

  • DNS-based routing: NS record returns different CDN IPs per region (or based on RUM latency data).
  • RUM (Real-User Measurement): clients report perceived latency back; routing engine picks the best CDN per region in real time.
  • Vendor isolation: one CDN outage doesn't take you down.
  • Cost arbitrage: route traffic to the CDN with the best per-GB cost in each region.
  • ISP-embedded CDN (Netflix Open Connect, YouTube Google Global Cache): hardware boxes placed inside ISPs; effectively LAN-speed delivery.

10When NOT to Use a CDN

  • Single-region B2B tool where users are all in one office → CDN is wasted complexity.
  • Truly real-time data (sub-second freshness) where CDN TTL would lie → put it at the API layer instead.
  • End-to-end encrypted content where the CDN can't see / serve bytes meaningfully.
  • Tiny startup with one Postgres + one app server — until you have measurable origin load, CDN is premature.
🔑 The Mental Model

A CDN is a tiered cache: browser cache → edge POP → regional shield → origin. Each tier absorbs the next tier's load. Design your URLs and headers so each level caches what it should, and your origin serves only the long tail of genuinely uncached requests.

CDC — Change Data Capture

Streaming every row-level change in a source database to downstream systems in near-real-time. The standard glue for syncing your OLTP DB to search indexes, caches, warehouses, microservices, and analytics pipelines.

1The Problem CDC Solves

You write to Postgres. You also want that change reflected in Elasticsearch (for search), Redis (for cache), ClickHouse (for analytics), Service B (downstream), and S3 (audit). Two naïve approaches:

  • Dual writes — app writes to Postgres and to each downstream in the same code path. Broken: if Postgres succeeds but Elasticsearch is down, you have permanent drift. Distributed transactions across heterogeneous systems are infeasible.
  • Polling — downstreams periodically SELECT * WHERE updated_at > last. Wastes DB load, misses hard-deletes, scales poorly past a few thousand rows/sec.

CDC is the right answer. The source DB itself becomes the single source of truth; every change emits an event; downstreams subscribe.

2Two Flavours: Polling-based vs Log-based

Polling-based (timestamp / trigger)Log-based (WAL / binlog / oplog)
MechanismPeriodic SELECT, or DB triggers writing to a changes tableTail the DB's replication log directly
DB loadAdds queries / triggers; affects production~Zero impact (just reads the WAL the DB already writes)
Delete captureHard — row is gone before the next pollNative — DELETE events are in the log
LatencySeconds to minutesSub-second
Order preservationApproximate (by updated_at)Exact (log order)
Setup complexityTrivialHigher (Debezium, replication slots, etc.)

Modern systems default to log-based CDC; polling exists only as a fallback for legacy DBs without accessible replication logs.

3Log-Based CDC — How It Works

Every relational DB writes a replication log for its own crash recovery and replicas — Postgres' WAL, MySQL's binlog, MongoDB's oplog, SQL Server's transaction log. CDC tools tail this log:

App writes ──► Postgres ──► WAL (durable, sequential) │ ▼ Debezium reads as replication client │ ▼ (one event per row-level change) Kafka topic per source table │ ┌───────────────────┼────────────────────┬──────────────┐ ▼ ▼ ▼ ▼ Elasticsearch Redis cache ClickHouse Service B

Each event contains: table name, primary key, before-image, after-image, operation (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE), commit timestamp, LSN/position. Consumers process events in order.

4The Standard Stack: Debezium + Kafka

  • Debezium — open-source CDC connector, runs as Kafka Connect source. Supports Postgres, MySQL, MongoDB, SQL Server, Oracle, Cassandra.
  • Kafka Connect — the platform that hosts Debezium; provides offset management, restart-recovery, scaling.
  • Kafka topics — one topic per source table; partitioned by primary-key hash for ordering within a key.
  • Schema Registry — Avro / Protobuf schemas with backward-compatible evolution.
  • Consumers — your code or Kafka Connect sinks (Elasticsearch sink, JDBC sink, S3 sink).

5The Outbox Pattern — CDC's Sibling

Sometimes you want to emit a business event ("OrderPlaced") atomically with a DB write — not just the row diff. The outbox pattern:

BEGIN; INSERT INTO orders (...) VALUES (...); INSERT INTO outbox (event_type, payload) VALUES ('OrderPlaced', '{...}'); COMMIT;

CDC then tails the outbox table and emits to Kafka. The DB transaction ensures the business write and the outbox row commit together (or both roll back). No dual-write inconsistency possible.

  • You control the event schema (decoupled from DB row shape).
  • One transaction-level guarantee for business + event.
  • Periodic cleanup job deletes already-emitted outbox rows.

6Delivery Semantics

  • At-least-once (default) — Kafka transactions + idempotent consumers ensure no events lost; consumer must handle duplicates via primary-key upsert or idempotency key.
  • Exactly-once — Kafka transactional producer + transactional consumer (or sink that upserts by PK). Achievable inside the Kafka ecosystem.
  • Ordering — events for the same key arrive in commit order (Kafka partition + PK-based hashing).
  • Snapshot then stream — Debezium's initial snapshot copies the existing table, then transitions to log-tailing. Critical for bootstrapping a new consumer.

7Where CDC Shines (canonical use cases)

  • Search index sync — Postgres → Debezium → Kafka → Elasticsearch (always-fresh search).
  • Cache invalidation — Postgres row update → CDC → Redis DEL key (eliminates stale-cache bugs).
  • OLTP → OLAP — Postgres → Snowflake / BigQuery / ClickHouse for analytics.
  • Microservices decoupling — service A owns its DB; service B reads via CDC; no shared schema.
  • Audit trails — every change written to S3 as parquet; queryable forever.
  • Zero-downtime migrations — old + new DBs both running; CDC syncs old → new; cut over once caught up.

8Failure Modes & Gotchas

  • Replication slot bloat (Postgres) — if Debezium falls behind, WAL accumulates on disk; can fill the volume and crash the DB. Monitor slot lag religiously.
  • Schema changes — ALTER TABLE can break consumers if not handled. Use Schema Registry + only backward-compatible changes (add column nullable; never drop/rename in place).
  • Initial snapshot duration — large tables take hours to snapshot; plan window for migrations.
  • DELETEs in compacted topics — represented as a "tombstone" (null value); consumers must handle.
  • Transaction boundaries — events from one DB transaction appear individually; consumers can't see "all events in this txn" without correlating commit IDs.

9When NOT to Use CDC

  • You have one DB and one app — no downstream needs the data.
  • Source isn't a relational/operational DB with a tail-able log (e.g. third-party SaaS — use webhooks instead).
  • You need business events, not row diffs — use the outbox pattern within CDC.
  • Your team has no operational capacity for Kafka + Debezium — start with synchronous webhooks or simple polling.
🔑 The One-Line Pitch

"Every row change in Postgres becomes a Kafka event in < 1 second, with no impact on the DB and no dual-write inconsistency. Everything downstream (search, cache, analytics, microservices) consumes from there."

Proximity Search & Geo Indexing

"Find everything within 2 km of me." A 2-D problem that B-trees can't answer efficiently. The trick is mapping 2-D space to a 1-D key that preserves locality — Geohash, Quadtree, H3, S2 — or using a purpose-built geo extension (PostGIS, Elasticsearch geo_point, Redis GEO).

1Why You Can't Just Use a B-Tree

A B-tree is 1-D — it can sort by one axis (lat or lng), not both. A query "WHERE lat BETWEEN ... AND lng BETWEEN ..." filters by one axis via the index, then full-scans the rest. At millions of rows, the latency is unbearable.

The fix: convert (lat, lng) into a 1-D key where nearby points get nearby keys. Now a range scan on the 1-D key returns nearby points. All proximity-search techniques are variants of this idea.

2Geohash — Z-Order Curve

Recursively divide the world into rectangles, encoding the path as base-32 characters. Each character adds 5 bits of precision (alternating lng/lat halvings).

LengthCell sizeUse
4~20 km × 20 kmCity-scale
6~600 m × 600 mNeighbourhood
8~20 m × 20 mBuilding precision
12~3 cm × 3 cmCentimetre precision
  • Prefix property: 9q8yyk is inside 9q8yy is inside 9q8y. Range queries become prefix scans on a B-tree.
  • Query: compute geohash of query point at desired precision, scan that geohash + 8 neighbours.
  • Weakness: rectangles distort near the poles; edge cells differ wildly in area; the Z-order curve has jumps at boundaries (the antimeridian is a discontinuity).
  • Best for: simple proximity in any DB that can do prefix index lookups; small to medium scale; equator-ish workloads.

3Quadtree — Recursive 2-D Partitioning

Start with the world as one square. Recursively split each square into 4 children when it contains more than K points. Pure trees naturally adapt to data density (cities = deep subdivisions, oceans = shallow).

  • Insert: descend to the leaf; if it overflows, split.
  • Range query: recursively descend into all nodes overlapping the query rectangle.
  • Best for: in-memory geo indexes with sparse / clustered point distributions (game maps, simulations).
  • Weakness: harder to shard across machines; tree imbalance for naïvely-built trees.

4H3 (Uber) — Hexagonal Hierarchical Grid

Uber's open-source library. Tiles the sphere with hexagons at multiple resolutions (0 through 15). Each cell has a 64-bit integer ID.

  • Hexagons have uniform neighbour relationships — every cell has exactly 6 neighbours at equal distance. Squares have 4 cardinal + 4 diagonal neighbours at different distances → uneven.
  • Resolution 9 is ~150 m hex side — the sweet spot for ride-sharing dispatch.
  • Built-in operations: ring (k-step neighbours), polyfill (cells covering a polygon), compactness (merge into parent cells).
  • Best for: ride-sharing dispatch (Uber, Lyft), delivery, density-based clustering of geo events.
  • Weakness: cells aren't a perfect hexagonal lattice on a sphere (12 pentagons exist near poles) — usually irrelevant unless you operate near the poles.

5S2 (Google) — Hilbert Curve on a Sphere

Google's library. Projects the sphere onto a cube, subdivides each face hierarchically (level 0 to 30), serialises via a Hilbert curve into a 64-bit integer.

  • Hilbert curve locality — adjacent integers correspond to adjacent regions almost always (no antimeridian jump).
  • Cell coverings — any region (radius circle, polygon) decomposes into a small set of S2 cells at mixed resolutions.
  • Used by: Google Maps, MongoDB geo, Foursquare, Pokémon Go.
  • Best for: large-area planet-scale operations; high precision; SQL-friendly 64-bit integer keys.
  • Weakness: less intuitive than H3 / Geohash; library footprint heavier.

6Side-by-Side Comparison

GeohashQuadtreeH3S2
Cell shapeRectangleSquare (recursive)HexagonSquare (on sphere)
Key formBase32 stringTree path64-bit int64-bit int
Levels1–12Arbitrary0–150–30
Neighbour uniformityOK (4 + 4 diag)OK (4 + 4 diag)Excellent (6 equal)Good
Locality at boundariesWeak (antimeridian)OKGoodExcellent
Sharding-friendlyYes (prefix)HardYes (cell ID range)Yes (cell ID range)
Built by / forPublic domainGeneralUber dispatchGoogle Maps

7Use the Index a Database Already Has

Most production systems don't roll their own geo index — they use what their data store provides.

PostgreSQL + PostGIS

  • Extension that adds geography and geometry types, plus GiST spatial indexes.
  • SQL queries like ST_DWithin(loc, ST_MakePoint(?, ?)::geography, 2000) use a 2-D index efficiently.
  • Best for: small-medium scale, you already have Postgres, you want the geo data with the rest of your relational data.
  • Scale ceiling: tens of millions of points before sharding becomes necessary.
CREATE EXTENSION postgis;
ALTER TABLE places ADD COLUMN loc geography(POINT);
CREATE INDEX idx_loc ON places USING GIST (loc);
SELECT * FROM places
 WHERE ST_DWithin(loc, ST_MakePoint(:lng, :lat)::geography, 2000);

Elasticsearch geo_point

  • Built-in geo_point and geo_shape types; uses BKD (Block KD-tree) indexes under the hood.
  • Combine geo filters with full-text + structured filters in a single query — the killer feature.
  • Best for: search-shaped problems where geo is one of many filters (Yelp, Airbnb-style discovery).
{
  "query": {
    "bool": {
      "must":   [{ "match": { "name": "ramen" } }],
      "filter": [
        { "geo_distance": { "distance": "2km",
                            "location": { "lat": ?, "lon": ? } } },
        { "term": { "is_open_now": true } }
      ]
    }
  },
  "sort": [ { "_geo_distance": { "location": ..., "order": "asc" } } ]
}

Redis GEO

  • Implemented on top of Sorted Sets; the score is a Geohash-encoded integer.
  • GEOADD, GEOSEARCH (radius / box), GEODIST, GEORADIUSBYMEMBER.
  • Best for: low-cardinality, in-memory, "nearest driver to rider" style queries (Uber's hot dispatch path).
  • Scale ceiling: a single key tops out around ~100k entries; shard across multiple keys (e.g. one per H3 cell) for more.
GEOADD drivers -122.4 37.77 driver:42
GEOSEARCH drivers FROMLONLAT -122.4 37.77 BYRADIUS 2 km ASC COUNT 10

MongoDB 2dsphere

MongoDB's 2dsphere index uses S2 internally; supports $geoWithin, $near, polygon queries. Good if you're already on Mongo.

8How to Pick (Decision Tree)

  • Already on Postgres + medium scale → PostGIS. Done.
  • Search with geo as one of many filters → Elasticsearch geo_point.
  • "Find nearest X" in tight latency budget, in-memory → Redis GEO (sharded if needed).
  • Ride-sharing / delivery dispatch at scale → H3 cells as a partition key into Redis or Cassandra.
  • Planet-scale, large-area queries, polygon coverings → S2 (Google Maps territory).
  • Game / simulation with sparse-then-dense clusters → in-memory quadtree.

9The Standard Query Pattern

Whatever the underlying tech, the query flow looks the same:

  1. Determine the query's bounding region (radius circle, polygon, viewport).
  2. Convert to a small set of cells (geohash prefix, H3 cells, S2 covering) — the candidate set.
  3. Fetch all points in those cells (cheap, indexed).
  4. Apply exact-distance filter on the candidates (cheap; small N).
  5. Sort by distance and return top-K.

Step 2 is the trick — cells are coarse-grained so you over-fetch slightly, but step 4 cleans up. Bigger cells = more over-fetch but fewer cells to query.

🔑 The Universal Insight

"All geo indexes are 1-D mappings of 2-D space with locality preservation, so range-scan-friendly. Pick the encoding that matches your access pattern: prefix-friendly (Geohash), uniform neighbours (H3), planet-scale polygons (S2), or just let PostGIS / Elasticsearch do it for you."

Redis

In-memory data structure server. The swiss-army knife of system design — cache, rate limiter, session store, leaderboard, message queue, geo-index, all in one.

1How Redis Achieves Sub-Millisecond Latency

Redis serves 100K-1M ops/sec from a single node with sub-millisecond latency. The mechanisms:

  • Everything in RAM: data lives in memory, never disk. RAM access is ~100ns; SSD is ~100μs (1000× slower). No I/O wait.
  • Single-threaded event loop: one thread handles all commands using epoll (Linux) or kqueue (BSD). No context switches, no mutex locks. Each command runs to completion before the next starts → atomic by default, no race conditions.
  • Optimised data structures: hash tables for O(1) GET/SET, skip lists for sorted sets (O(log N)), Simple Dynamic Strings (SDS) for O(1) length queries on binary data.
  • Non-blocking I/O: thousands of client connections multiplexed by a single thread using epoll. No thread-per-connection overhead.
  • Pipelining: clients can send multiple commands without waiting for replies, then read all replies — amortises network round-trips.

Trade-off: single-threaded means a slow command (e.g., KEYS on a large DB) blocks everyone. Use SCAN, never KEYS. Use BLOCKING commands cautiously.

2Redis Data Types and Their Use Cases

TypeCommandsUse For
String / CounterSET / GET / INCR / DECR / EXPIRECaching, counters, simple flags, rate-limit tokens
HashHSET / HGET / HINCRBY / HMGETPer-user state (cart, preferences, session); avoids many small keys
ListLPUSH / RPOP / BLPOP / LRANGESimple FIFO queue, recent-N items, undo stack
SetSADD / SREM / SISMEMBER / SUNIONMembership tests, tags-per-entity, available pool (e.g. drivers in cell)
Sorted Set (ZSET)ZADD / ZREVRANGE / ZRANGEBYSCORELeaderboards, top-K, time-windowed event log, priority queue, sliding-window rate limit, user feeds
StreamXADD / XREAD / XGROUPLightweight Kafka-style log with consumer groups; good when Kafka is overkill
HyperLogLogPFADD / PFCOUNT / PFMERGEUnique-count estimation (DAU, unique IPs) at ~1.5 KB per counter
GeoGEOADD / GEOSEARCH / GEODISTNearest-K, radius search; fine up to ~100k entries per key
BitmapSETBIT / GETBIT / BITCOUNTUser-id boolean flags ("did user X do action Y today"); 12.5 MB for 100M users
Pub/SubSUBSCRIBE / PUBLISHFan-out notifications, real-time UI updates; non-persistent

3The ZSET (Sorted Set) — Deep Dive

If you remember one thing about Redis, make it ZSET. It is the single most useful data structure in system design interviews — half of the "non-cache" Redis problems boil down to "use a sorted set."

How it works internally

A ZSET stores (member, score) pairs. It's implemented as two structures kept in sync:

  • A hash map from member → score (O(1) score lookup).
  • A skip list indexed by score (O(log N) insert and range query).

All operations are O(log N); range queries return in O(log N + K) where K is the result size. Memory: ~80 bytes per entry overhead.

The seven canonical use cases

PatternScoreKey commands
Leaderboardplayer's pointsZADD lb 1500 alice
ZREVRANGE lb 0 9 WITHSCORES → top-10
Top-K trendingview / click count (INCR via ZINCRBY)ZINCRBY trending 1 video:42
ZREVRANGE trending 0 99
News feed / timelineunix timestamp of postZADD feed:u42 1715000000 post_abc
ZREVRANGE feed:u42 0 19 → latest 20
Priority queuepriority (lower = sooner)ZADD jobs 100 job_abc
ZPOPMIN jobs → next job
Sliding-window rate limittimestamp of each requestZADD rl:user:42 <now_ms> <uuid>
ZREMRANGEBYSCORE rl:user:42 0 <now-window>
ZCARD rl:user:42 → current count
Delayed job schedulerunix timestamp of "run at"ZADD jobs <run_at_ms> job_abc
ZRANGEBYSCORE jobs 0 <now> LIMIT 0 100 → ready jobs
Recent-N with deduptimestampZADD recent_searches:u42 <ts> "ramen"
ZREMRANGEBYRANK recent_searches:u42 0 -101 (keep last 100)

Two concrete deep-dive examples

(1) Sliding-window rate limiter (P6 building block) — limit 100 req / 60 s per user:

-- Lua script (atomic)
local key = KEYS[1]
local now = tonumber(ARGV[1])
local window = tonumber(ARGV[2])  -- 60000 ms
local limit = tonumber(ARGV[3])   -- 100

redis.call('ZREMRANGEBYSCORE', key, 0, now - window)  -- evict old
local count = redis.call('ZCARD', key)
if count < limit then
  redis.call('ZADD', key, now, now .. ':' .. ARGV[4])  -- now+uuid
  redis.call('EXPIRE', key, math.ceil(window / 1000))
  return 1   -- allowed
else
  return 0   -- 429
end

(2) Twitter-style timeline fanout (P2 / P13):

-- On post:
PUBLISH new_post user:42 post:xyz
-- For each follower f of user 42:
ZADD feed:f <timestamp_ms> post:xyz
ZREMRANGEBYRANK feed:f 0 -1001   -- keep latest 1000

-- On feed read:
ZREVRANGE feed:u42 0 19    -- top 20 most recent → O(log N + 20)

ZSET vs alternatives

  • ZSET vs List: List is O(N) to access by index in the middle; ZSET is O(log N). Use List for pure FIFO queues; ZSET when you need ordering by a score that changes.
  • ZSET vs Hash: Hash for unordered key→value; ZSET when you also need range scans by score.
  • ZSET vs Stream: Stream for append-only event logs with consumer groups; ZSET when you need arbitrary scoring and range queries.
  • ZSET vs Postgres: Postgres + ORDER BY + LIMIT works but at ~10 ms; ZSET does it in ~0.1 ms. Use ZSET for the hot path, Postgres as source of truth.

4Three More Patterns That Win Interviews

🔑 Lua scripts for atomicity

Redis is single-threaded, and Lua scripts run atomically — no other command interleaves. Anywhere you'd need "check-then-set" (rate limiter token decrement, seat hold, inventory decrement), wrap the read + check + write in a Lua script. One round trip, zero races, no distributed lock needed.

🔑 Pipelining vs MULTI/EXEC

Pipelining: send N commands without waiting for each reply; reduces round trips. Not atomic. MULTI/EXEC: queue N commands and execute atomically (no interleaving) but no conditional logic. Lua: atomic + can include conditionals + can read intermediate values. Pick by latency need (pipeline), strict atomicity (MULTI), or conditional logic (Lua).

🔑 Hash tags for multi-key operations on Cluster

In Redis Cluster, related data must hash to the same slot to allow multi-key ops (MULTI/EXEC, ZUNIONSTORE, Lua scripts touching multiple keys). Use hash tags: put a tag in curly braces, only that part is hashed. feed:{u42}:posts and feed:{u42}:scores both land on the same shard.

5Persistence (RDB + AOF)

Redis offers two persistence modes; usually you enable both:

  • RDB (snapshots): periodic full snapshot of the dataset to disk. Fast restart, low overhead, but a crash loses everything since the last snapshot (typically 5–15 min).
  • AOF (append-only file): every write command appended to disk. Configurable fsync: always (durability, slower), everysec (default, ~1s data loss on crash), no (OS-flushed). Combined with RDB gives best of both.

6Cluster Mode & Replication

For HA and scale: Redis Cluster shards the keyspace across N primary nodes (16,384 hash slots), each backed by 1+ replicas. Replication is async by default. Failover is handled by Sentinel (sentinel-mode) or by the cluster itself. Caveat: Redis Cluster doesn't support multi-key transactions across slots; design keys with hash tags ({user_id}) so related data lands on the same shard.

7When to Use Redis (and When Not)

Use whenDon't use when
Cache layer (cache-aside pattern)You need durable source of truth (Redis can lose data)
Rate limiting (token bucket via Lua)Dataset much larger than RAM (cost prohibitive)
Sessions / auth tokensComplex queries / joins (Redis is key-value)
Leaderboards, top-K, trendingMulti-key transactions across nodes
Real-time presence / online usersRange queries beyond ZSET / Geo capabilities
Pub/Sub for notificationsLong-lived persistent message queues (use Kafka)
Geo-spatial nearest-K (small scale)Massive geo-indexes (use H3 + sharded Redis or PostGIS)

Elasticsearch

Distributed search and analytics engine built on Apache Lucene. Think of it as "Postgres for text and aggregations" — but never as a primary source of truth.

1How an Inverted Index Works (the heart of Elasticsearch)

Instead of storing rows and scanning them, the index stores a mapping from term → list of documents containing that term:

Documents: doc1 = "The quick brown fox" doc2 = "The lazy brown dog" doc3 = "A quick fox jumped" Inverted index (after tokenize + lowercase + stemming): "the" → [doc1, doc2] "quick" → [doc1, doc3] "brown" → [doc1, doc2] "fox" → [doc1, doc3] "lazy" → [doc2] "dog" → [doc2] "jump" → [doc3] "a" → [doc3] Query: "quick fox" → intersect postings: [doc1, doc3] ∩ [doc1, doc3] = [doc1, doc3] → score each with BM25 → return ranked

2Pipeline per Query (the path of a search request)

  1. Tokenize — split the query into terms ("quick fox" → ["quick", "fox"]).
  2. Analyze — lowercase, stem ("running" → "run"), remove stop-words ("the", "a"), apply synonyms.
  3. Lookup — for each term, fetch its posting list from the inverted index (sub-ms; lists are sorted and compressed).
  4. Intersect / union — AND query intersects lists; OR unions.
  5. Score — each matching doc gets a BM25 score (term-frequency × inverse-document-frequency, length-normalised).
  6. Sort and return top-K — usually top-10 with highlights.

3Distributed Architecture

  • Index = collection of documents (think: a logical "table").
  • Shard = a Lucene index file; each index is split into N shards distributed across nodes.
  • Replica = a copy of a shard on another node; provides failover and parallel read throughput.
  • Refresh interval = how often new documents become searchable. Default 1 s — this is what people mean by Elasticsearch being "near real-time."
  • Coordinator node = receives the query, fans it out to all shards, gathers responses, merges top-K, returns to client.

4Strengths

  • Full-text search with relevance scoring (BM25), out of the box.
  • Faceted search and aggregations — "how many products in this filter combination?" computed at index time.
  • Fuzzy matching, synonyms, autocomplete (edge n-grams), phonetic search.
  • Geo-spatial queries (bounding box, distance, polygons).
  • Log/metric analytics — the "E" in ELK stack; analysts run ad-hoc queries on billions of log lines in seconds.

5Aggregations — The Other Killer Feature

Aggregations are pre-computed bucketing/counting at query time, comparable to SQL GROUP BY but optimised for the inverted index. Run sub-second on billions of docs.

  • Bucket aggregations — group by a field (terms), by a date range (date_histogram), by a numeric range (histogram), by geo cell (geohash_grid).
  • Metric aggregations — sum / avg / min / max / stats / percentiles / cardinality (uniques via HLL).
  • Pipeline aggregations — operate on other aggregations' output (moving avg, cumulative sum, derivatives).
  • Nested aggregations — bucket inside bucket: "for each category, top-3 products by sales."

This is why Kibana dashboards are fast — every chart is one or two aggs.

POST /products/_search
{
  "size": 0,
  "aggs": {
    "by_brand": {
      "terms": { "field": "brand", "size": 10 },
      "aggs": {
        "avg_price": { "avg": { "field": "price" } },
        "in_stock":  { "filter": { "term": { "stock": true } } }
      }
    }
  }
}

6Geo Capabilities

  • geo_point field type — single lat/lng. Use geo_distance, geo_bounding_box, geo_polygon queries.
  • geo_shape field type — polygons, lines, multi-shapes for territory / route queries.
  • Backed by BKD (Block KD-tree) indexes — efficient 2-D range queries.
  • Sort by _geo_distance from a query point; sub-100 ms on 100 M docs.
  • Combine with text + filter in one query — the killer Yelp / Airbnb pattern. See the Proximity Search page for details.

7Autocomplete & Suggesters

  • Edge n-gram analyser — at index time, generate prefix tokens ("apple" → "a", "ap", "app", "appl", "apple"). Query matches by prefix in O(log N).
  • Completion suggester — purpose-built FST (Finite-State Transducer) index; sub-ms suggestions; supports fuzzy + weighted.
  • Search-as-you-type field type — automatically maintains prefix + n-gram subfields; the modern default.

8Weaknesses (the reasons you don't make it your primary DB)

  • Not a source of truth — refresh interval, eventual consistency, no real transactions. Always feed it from your real DB via CDC.
  • Memory-hungry — JVM-heavy; ~50% of RAM for heap, the rest for OS page cache. A 1 TB index needs ~250 GB+ RAM across the cluster.
  • Writes are amplified — every doc update is a delete+insert in Lucene segments; high write rate causes segment merging pressure.
  • Cluster ops are operationally heavy — yellow/red status, shard rebalancing, mapping conflicts. Most teams use managed offerings (Elastic Cloud, AWS OpenSearch).
  • Deep pagination is expensive — going to page 100 forces every shard to materialise top-1000; use search_after (cursor) instead of from.

9When to Use Elasticsearch

Use caseWhy Elasticsearch wins
Search box (product, document, articles)BM25, fuzzy match, synonyms, highlighting — built-in
Log analytics (ELK / EFK stack)Aggregations over billions of lines in seconds; Kibana dashboards
Faceted filters (e.g. e-commerce filters)Fast counts per facet via pre-computed bucket aggregations
AutocompleteEdge n-gram analyser; prefix search at the edge
Geo-spatial queriesR-tree indexes; "within 5 km of point" in milliseconds

10When NOT to Use Elasticsearch

  • Primary key-value lookups (use Redis / DynamoDB; far cheaper and faster).
  • Transactional updates (use Postgres / MySQL).
  • Source of truth for business data (use a real OLTP DB + CDC-mirror to ES).
  • Tiny datasets (Postgres full-text search is enough up to ~10M rows).
🔑 The Mental Model

"Elasticsearch is for when SQL WHERE isn't expressive enough — multi-field filters, full-text relevance, geo, faceted aggregations, all in one query at billion-doc scale. Pair it with Postgres-as-source-of-truth via CDC, and you have the best of both worlds."

Kafka

Distributed, durable, partitioned event log. Decouples producers from consumers; supports replay; 1M+ messages/sec per broker. The backbone of every modern data platform.

1How Kafka Handles 1M+ Messages/Sec

Kafka achieves throughput that traditional message brokers can't:

  • Append-only log: every message is appended to a partition log file. Sequential disk writes, no random I/O.
  • Zero-copy sendfile(): when a consumer reads, Kafka uses the Linux sendfile() syscall to send data directly from disk cache to the network socket, skipping user space. Saves 2 memory copies and 2 context switches per message batch.
  • OS page cache: Kafka deliberately doesn't maintain its own RAM cache — it relies on the OS page cache. Recent messages are served from RAM. Free RAM caching.
  • Batching: producers batch messages before sending. Consumers receive in batches. Amortises per-message overhead (network frames, syscalls).
  • Partition parallelism: a topic is split into N partitions, each on a different broker. Linear throughput scaling.

Trade-off: Kafka is optimised for high throughput sequential consumption. Random access (read message at offset X) is fast, but seeking by message content is not — that's what databases are for.

2Topics, Partitions, Consumer Groups

  • Topic = named stream of messages.
  • Partition = ordered subset of a topic; each partition lives on one broker (with replicas elsewhere). Per-partition message order is guaranteed; across partitions it isn't.
  • Consumer group = set of consumers that share work — Kafka assigns each partition to exactly one consumer in the group. Add consumers to scale up reads (capped at #partitions).
  • Producer partitioning = pick by key (same key → same partition → ordered) or round-robin.

3Delivery Semantics

ModeHowUse when
At-most-onceCommit offset before processingLogs/metrics where dropping is OK
At-least-once (default)Commit offset after processing; failures replayMost cases — make consumers idempotent
Exactly-onceIdempotent producer + transactional writes (atomic across partitions)Billing, ledgers — but read the docs carefully

4Retention & Replay

Kafka retains messages for a configurable time (default 7 days) or until size limit. Consumers commit their offset; you can rewind to replay any range. This is what makes Kafka different from a queue: messages don't disappear when consumed. Multiple independent consumer groups can read the same topic.

5Kafka vs Alternatives

SystemUse when
KafkaHigh-throughput streaming, replay needed, multiple consumers, durable log
RabbitMQLower throughput (~50k msg/s), rich routing (topics, fanout), traditional task queue
SQS / Cloud queuesYou want managed; throughput modest; no replay needed; per-message visibility timeout
Redis StreamsYou already run Redis; throughput < ~100k msg/s; simple consumer groups
PulsarMulti-tenant, geo-replication, separate compute/storage layers

6When to Use Kafka

  • Async fan-out (one producer → N independent consumers).
  • CDC pipelines (DB → Kafka → consumers).
  • Audit logs, event sourcing.
  • Decoupling microservices.
  • Buffering ahead of slower processors (smoothing spikes).
  • Real-time analytics ingest (→ Flink / Spark Streaming).

API Gateway

The single entry point that sits between clients and your microservices. It handles cross-cutting concerns (auth, rate limiting, routing, observability) so individual services don't each implement them.

1What an API Gateway Does (the Cross-Cutting Layer)

  • Authentication / Authorization: validate JWT or API keys; reject unauthenticated calls before they touch your services.
  • Rate limiting: per-user / per-IP / per-API-key token bucket. See P6 Rate Limiter.
  • Routing: path-based or header-based — /api/v1/users/* goes to user-service.
  • Request transformation: rewrite paths, inject headers, transform protocols (REST to gRPC).
  • Response aggregation: a single client request fans out to N internal services; gateway combines responses (the BFF pattern).
  • TLS termination: HTTPS at the gateway; internal traffic can be HTTP for performance.
  • Caching: cache response bodies for idempotent reads.
  • Observability: log every request, emit traces, expose metrics.
  • Circuit breaking: trip a circuit when a downstream service is failing; return a stale response or 503.

2Common Implementations

ChoiceTypeBest for
AWS API GatewayManaged (AWS)Pay-per-request; tight Lambda integration; minimal ops
Cloud-flare / Cloud Front + WorkersEdge gatewayEdge-side logic, DDoS, CDN colocated with auth
KongSelf-hosted (open-source + enterprise)On-prem, plugin-rich, popular in K8s
Envoy + IstioSelf-hosted (service-mesh)Microservices at scale; mTLS between services; advanced routing
NGINX / OpenRestySelf-hosted reverse proxyLightweight; battle-tested; Lua scripting for custom logic
ApigeeManaged (Google)Enterprise API mgmt with full lifecycle (publish, monetise)

3Edge Gateway vs Internal Gateway

Two distinct roles, sometimes the same product:

  • Edge gateway: faces the internet; handles auth, TLS, rate limit, DDoS. Cloudflare / CloudFront / AWS API Gateway typical here.
  • Internal gateway / service mesh: between microservices; handles mTLS, retries, circuit breaking, traffic shaping. Envoy / Istio / Linkerd here.

4The BFF Pattern (Backend For Frontend)

A specialised gateway that aggregates multiple service calls into one client-friendly response. Mobile gets a different gateway than web; each tunes its responses to its client's needs.

Mobile app → Mobile BFF → 5 microservice calls → 1 trimmed response Web app → Web BFF → 8 microservice calls → 1 verbose response Both BFFs talk to the same backend services.

5Pitfalls — When NOT to Put Logic at the Gateway

  • Business logic: don't write order-processing in gateway plugins. Gateways are infrastructure; business logic belongs in services.
  • Stateful operations: gateways should be stateless. State (rate-limit counters, sessions) lives in Redis, not the gateway.
  • Heavy compute: don't transcode video at the gateway. Push to dedicated workers.
  • Tight coupling: don't add a gateway plugin for every small need; that's how you build an unmaintainable monolith.

6Rate Limiting at the Gateway (Standard Pattern)

Client request hits gateway: 1. Extract identity (JWT user_id, API key, IP) 2. Lua script in Redis (atomic): - DECR token bucket for that identity - if >= 0 → forward request - if < 0 → return 429 Too Many Requests 3. Forward (or reject) within ~5 ms total

7Observability — What to Log at the Gateway

  • Request ID (propagate as X-Request-Id); used for distributed tracing.
  • User ID, API key prefix (never the full key).
  • Path, method, status code, latency.
  • Upstream service called, upstream latency.
  • Cache hit/miss for cached endpoints.
  • Rate-limit decisions (allowed / 429).

8When the Gateway Itself Becomes the Bottleneck

  • Horizontal scale: stateless gateway → run many instances behind LB.
  • Move TLS to the LB or CDN: TLS handshake is CPU-heavy.
  • Move auth to a sidecar: each service validates its own JWTs; gateway only checks signature, not claims.
  • Use anycast + many edge POPs: terabits-per-second capacity (Cloudflare scale).

Cassandra

Wide-column LSM-tree DB. Linear horizontal scaling, 100k+ writes/sec per node, tunable consistency. Built for write-heavy workloads where you can design tables around your access patterns.

1How Cassandra Achieves High Write Throughput

Cassandra writes 100K+ ops/sec per node. Why? LSM-Tree architecture.

  1. Step 1 — Commit Log: every write is first appended to the Commit Log on disk. Sequential disk writes are ~500 MB/s on modern SSDs — comparable to RAM throughput. No seeks.
  2. Step 2 — MemTable: the write is also placed in an in-memory sorted structure. Subsequent reads see the new write immediately from memory.
  3. Step 3 — SSTable flush: when the MemTable fills (~64 MB), it's flushed to disk as an immutable SSTable. Sequential write, very fast.
  4. Step 4 — Compaction: background process merges older SSTables, removing overwritten values. Pays the "cost" of LSM-Tree's write speed asynchronously.

Compare to MySQL B-Tree: writes find a leaf node (random I/O), may split nodes (more random I/O), update indexes (more random I/O). 10× slower for write-heavy workloads.

Trade-off: Cassandra reads can be slower (multiple SSTables to check; Bloom filters mitigate), and you must plan partition keys carefully because Cassandra doesn't support arbitrary queries.

2The Partition Key — The Most Important Choice You'll Make

⚠ Terminology heads-up

Cassandra's partition key is what most non-Cassandra people would call a shard key: it determines which node across the cluster owns a row. This is different from Postgres' native partitioning, which splits a table into pieces on the same machine. Both Cassandra and DynamoDB use the word "partition" for what is effectively the shard concept. See the Partitioning & Sharding Core Concepts page for the full disambiguation.

Cassandra distributes data by hashing the partition key; rows with the same partition key live on the same node and are sorted by the clustering key.

CREATE TABLE messages ( user_id UUID, -- partition key (which node) ts TIMEUUID, -- clustering key (sort order on that node) message TEXT, PRIMARY KEY ((user_id), ts) ) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (ts DESC);

Rules of thumb:

  • Each query you want to support needs its own table (denormalisation is normal).
  • Partition size must stay under ~100 MB; if a partition could grow unbounded, add a bucket: (user_id, year_month).
  • Hot partition = hot node. Avoid partition keys that concentrate traffic on one user/account/timestamp bucket.

3Tunable Consistency (the AP-with-knobs feature)

Each read and write specifies a consistency level. Common choices:

LevelWhat it meansUse for
ONEWait for 1 replicaLowest latency; can read stale data
QUORUMWait for majority of replicasBalanced — strong consistency if W+R>N
ALLWait for every replicaMaximum durability (rare; sacrifices availability)
LOCAL_QUORUMQuorum within local data centreMulti-DC default — avoids cross-DC latency

The classic recipe: W + R > N for read-after-write consistency. With RF=3: write at QUORUM (2), read at QUORUM (2), 2+2 > 3 ✓.

4vnodes & Cluster Topology

Each physical node owns ~256 virtual nodes (vnodes), each a small slice of the hash ring. This:

  • Distributes data evenly even with non-uniform node capacity.
  • Speeds up rebalancing when adding/removing a node (only 1/N of the data moves).
  • Is invisible to application code; you just specify partition + clustering keys.

5When to Use Cassandra

Use whenDon't use when
Write throughput > 10k/sec sustainedYou need joins or ad-hoc queries
Time-series / event logs / chat messagesMulti-row ACID transactions required
Linear scale-out across many nodes / DCsStrong consistency on every read
Tunable per-query consistency needsSmall dataset (Postgres + replicas is simpler)
You can design tables around the queriesSchema evolves frequently in unpredictable ways

DynamoDB

AWS's managed wide-column NoSQL. Predictable per-partition throughput, single-digit-ms latency, auto-scaling. Effectively "Cassandra without the operational pain — at AWS prices."

1Core Concept: Partition Key + Sort Key

Every DynamoDB table has:

  • Partition key (required): hashed to determine which physical partition holds the row.
  • Sort key (optional): orders rows within the same partition. Lets you do range queries: "all messages for user 42 from yesterday".

Together (partition + sort) form the primary key; must be unique.

2The Partition Limit (the most-asked interview gotcha)

⚠ The Hard Cap You Need to Know

Each partition in DynamoDB caps at ~1 k writes/sec and ~3 k reads/sec. Hit this and DynamoDB throttles you with ProvisionedThroughputExceededException.

To scale past these limits, your partition key cardinality must be high — i.e., load is distributed across many partition keys. A table that hammers a single partition key is broken at scale, no matter how many RCUs/WCUs you've provisioned.

3Hot Partition Problem

If 80% of your traffic hits one partition key (e.g., a single celebrity user), you're throttled at 1k/3k regardless of total table provisioning. Mitigations:

  • Add a random suffix: celebrity#42#shard0...celebrity#42#shard9. Distributes writes across 10 keys.
  • Cache hot keys in DAX: in-memory cache fronts DynamoDB; reads served at sub-ms.
  • Adaptive capacity (built-in since 2018): DynamoDB automatically gives more throughput to hot partitions.

4Indexes: GSI vs LSI

Index TypeWhat It IsConstraints
LSI (Local Secondary Index)Alternate sort key on the same partition keyMust be defined at table creation; max 5 per table
GSI (Global Secondary Index)Different partition key + sort key entirely. Like a separate table that auto-syncsEventually consistent; pay separate RCUs/WCUs; max 20 per table

Use GSI for "alternate access patterns": e.g., primary keyed by order_id, GSI keyed by user_id for "user's orders" queries.

5Single-Table Design (the DynamoDB philosophy)

Unlike relational DBs where you have many tables and JOINs, DynamoDB encourages stuffing all entity types into one table using composite keys:

PK SK Entity USER#42 METADATA {name: "Alice", email: ...} USER#42 ORDER#2026-05-18 {amount: 100, status: "PAID"} USER#42 ORDER#2026-05-19 {amount: 50, status: "PENDING"} USER#42 ADDR#home {street: ..., city: ...} ORDER#xyz METADATA {user: 42, total: 100, ...} ORDER#xyz ITEM#1 {sku: "abc", qty: 2}

One Query(PK="USER#42") returns the user + all orders + addresses in one round trip. Counter-intuitive coming from relational, but it's the DynamoDB optimum.

6Pricing Models

ModeUse when
