ProvisionedPredictable load. Pay for RCUs/WCUs reserved.
On-DemandSpiky / unknown load. Pay per request. ~6× more per-request than provisioned but no capacity planning.

Most teams start On-Demand to learn the workload, switch to Provisioned + Auto-Scaling once patterns stabilise.

7DAX (DynamoDB Accelerator)

A managed in-memory cache that fronts DynamoDB transparently. Reads cached locally — sub-ms latency vs ~5 ms to DynamoDB. Cache-aside semantics; writes go through to DynamoDB then update DAX.

Use when you have repeated reads of the same hot keys at very high QPS. Avoid when reads are random / non-cacheable.

8Global Tables (Multi-Region)

Replicates a DynamoDB table across multiple AWS regions, all writable. Last-writer-wins conflict resolution (uses item timestamp). Use for global apps where users want low latency from any region.

Caveat: write conflicts on the same key from two regions = silent data loss for the older write. Design partition keys to be region-pinned (e.g. include region in PK) to avoid this.

9When DynamoDB Beats Cassandra — and Loses

Pick DynamoDB whenPick Cassandra when
You're on AWS and don't want to run a clusterYou need the absolute lowest cost at very high scale
Auto-scaling matters more than per-request costYou need on-prem / multi-cloud
Workload fits the partition + sort key modelYou need fully tunable consistency per request
You can use DAX for hot readsYour team has Cassandra ops experience

10When NOT to Use DynamoDB

  • Multi-row ACID transactions (DynamoDB has TransactWriteItems but it's limited to 100 items, costs 2× normal writes).
  • Ad-hoc queries / analytics (DynamoDB has no full SQL; use Athena over a DynamoDB export instead).
  • Joins across tables.
  • Cost-sensitive workloads at very high scale (DynamoDB egress + storage adds up vs running Cassandra on EC2).

PostgreSQL

The default OLTP database. ACID, joins, indexes, JSONB, replication, partitioning — all in one. If you don't have a strong reason to pick something else, the answer is "Postgres." It scales much further than people expect.

1WAL + MVCC — How Postgres Survives Crashes and Concurrent Writes

Two foundational mechanisms:

  • Write-Ahead Log (WAL): every change is appended to the WAL before being applied to the data files. On crash, replay the WAL → data is consistent. Sequential disk writes; ~500 MB/s on modern SSDs.
  • MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control): every UPDATE creates a new row version; old versions stay until VACUUM cleans them. Readers see a consistent snapshot at the moment their transaction started; writers don't block readers, readers don't block writers.

The cost: dead row versions accumulate; autovacuum reclaims them in the background. A poorly-tuned autovacuum is the #1 cause of Postgres performance issues.

2Index Types (the rich toolbox)

  • B-tree (default) — equality + range queries.
  • Hash — equality only; rarely used.
  • GIN (Generalized Inverted) — JSONB containment, array containment, full-text search.
  • GiST / SP-GiST — geo-spatial (with PostGIS), range types.
  • BRIN (Block Range) — huge ordered tables (time-series); tiny index size.
  • Partial — index only the rows matching a WHERE clause; massively reduces index size for sparse data.
  • Covering / INCLUDE — index includes extra columns; index-only scans, no heap fetch.

See the Database Indexing Core Concepts page for full mechanics.

3JSONB — Flexible Schema in a Relational DB

JSONB stores binary JSON; supports indexed path queries:

CREATE TABLE events ( id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY, data JSONB NOT NULL ); CREATE INDEX idx_status ON events ((data ->> 'status')); -- B-tree on a path CREATE INDEX idx_data_gin ON events USING GIN (data jsonb_path_ops); -- GIN for general containment -- Query SELECT * FROM events WHERE data ->> 'status' = 'paid'; SELECT * FROM events WHERE data @> '{"user": {"country": "IN"}}';

Use JSONB when (a) the schema genuinely varies row-by-row (events, audit logs), (b) you want flexibility without giving up SQL. Don't JSONB-everything; columns are still cheaper to query.

4Table Partitioning (≠ Sharding)

⚠ Don't confuse these

Partitioning = one table split into pieces on the same machine, inside one Postgres instance. Sharding = one table split across multiple Postgres instances on different machines. Postgres has first-class native support for partitioning (this section). For sharding you reach for Citus, Vitess-style middleware, or app-level routing — see the Partitioning & Sharding Core Concepts page for the full distinction.

Native partitioning splits a logical table into multiple physical partitions on the same instance. Postgres routes inserts to the right partition; queries with the partition key filter scan only relevant partitions (partition pruning).

-- RANGE (most common for time-series) CREATE TABLE events (id BIGINT, ts TIMESTAMPTZ, ...) PARTITION BY RANGE (ts); CREATE TABLE events_2026_05 PARTITION OF events FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-05-01') TO ('2026-06-01'); CREATE TABLE events_2026_06 PARTITION OF events FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-06-01') TO ('2026-07-01'); -- LIST (categorical values) CREATE TABLE users PARTITION BY LIST (region); CREATE TABLE users_us PARTITION OF users FOR VALUES IN ('us-east','us-west'); -- HASH (even distribution by hash key) CREATE TABLE messages PARTITION BY HASH (user_id); CREATE TABLE messages_p0 PARTITION OF messages FOR VALUES WITH (MODULUS 8, REMAINDER 0);

Why partition (even if you don't shard):

  • Partition pruning — a WHERE ts > yesterday query touches one partition, not the whole 10 TB table.
  • Smaller indexes per partition → faster lookups; index fits in RAM where the whole one wouldn't.
  • Cheap mass deletes — DROP PARTITION events_2023_01 is instant; DELETE WHERE ts < ... on 100 M rows takes hours and bloats indexes.
  • Storage tiering — old partitions on cold/slow storage, hot partitions on SSD.
  • Per-tenant isolation — partition by tenant_id so noisy tenants can't scan a full table.

Rule of thumb: aim to keep individual partitions under ~100 GB for index efficiency.

5Replication

  • Streaming replication: primary streams WAL to replicas. Async by default; can be synchronous (slower writes, zero data loss).
  • Logical replication: subscribers receive logical change events (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on selected tables). Used for upgrades, partial replicas, and CDC pipelines.
  • Failover: not built-in. Use Patroni / Stolon / RDS / managed Postgres for automatic primary failover.

6SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED — The Distributed Job Pattern

Postgres has a unique-among-DBs feature: SKIP LOCKED lets multiple workers concurrently claim disjoint sets of rows from a "jobs" table without coordinating via Redis or ZooKeeper. See P16 Job Scheduler. Used in Sidekiq Pro, GoodJob, Que, Oban — battle-tested at scale.

7When to Shard, When to NewSQL

Single Postgres handles a surprising amount:

  • ~10 k writes/sec on a beefy box (m6i.4xlarge or similar).
  • ~50 k+ reads/sec with read replicas.
  • ~10 TB on a single SSD.

When you outgrow a single node:

  1. Read replicas first — gets you to 100k+ reads/sec.
  2. Vertical scale — bigger instance handles more writes than people expect.
  3. Application sharding — manually shard by hash(user_id) into N Postgres instances. Simple but loses cross-shard joins.
  4. Citus (Postgres extension) — distributed Postgres; same SQL, transparent sharding.
  5. NewSQL (CockroachDB, Spanner, TiDB) — when you genuinely need ACID across regions.

Most teams that "need to switch from Postgres" actually just need read replicas + caching.

8The Postgres Operational Tax (be honest about it)

  • Autovacuum tuning — default settings struggle on high-write tables.
  • Long-running queries — block VACUUM and accumulate dead rows; alert on them.
  • Connection limits — max ~200 connections per node. Use PgBouncer or RDS Proxy for connection pooling at scale.
  • Index bloat — REINDEX CONCURRENTLY periodically.
  • Failover — managed services (RDS, Aurora) handle this; self-hosted needs Patroni.

9When to Use Postgres (the strong defaults)

  • You need ACID transactions across multiple rows / tables.
  • You need joins.
  • You need ad-hoc queries / analytics.
  • Schema is mostly stable (with JSONB columns where flexibility helps).
  • Up to ~10 TB and ~10k writes/sec.
  • You want a battle-tested, well-documented DB with abundant ops knowledge.
🔑 The Universal Default

"Use Postgres until proven otherwise" is the right answer in 80% of system design problems. Specialise (Cassandra / Redis / DynamoDB / ES) only for clearly-justified workloads — and even then, keep Postgres as the source of truth.

MongoDB

Document-oriented NoSQL DB. Stores JSON-like documents (BSON) with flexible per-document schemas. Strong when your data is naturally hierarchical, schemas evolve fast, or you want one row to contain "the whole thing" without joins.

1What MongoDB Is — the Document Model

A document is roughly a JSON object — nested fields, arrays, sub-documents. A collection is a group of documents (loosely "a table"). Unlike a relational table, documents in one collection can have different shapes — fields added or omitted per row.

// One document in `users` collection
{
  "_id": ObjectId("..."),
  "email": "alice@example.com",
  "name": "Alice",
  "addresses": [
    { "label": "home", "street": "...", "city": "Mumbai" },
    { "label": "work", "street": "...", "city": "Pune" }
  ],
  "prefs": { "newsletter": true, "language": "en" },
  "tags": ["beta-user", "vip"]
}

// Another document in the same collection — different shape, that's fine
{
  "_id": ObjectId("..."),
  "email": "bob@example.com",
  "name": "Bob",
  "company_id": ObjectId("...")     // a field Alice doesn't have
}

2The Flexible Schema Win — and the Trap

The biggest sales pitch for MongoDB is schema flexibility: you can add fields without a migration, store optional sub-objects, model polymorphic entities without table-per-class gymnastics. Real wins:

  • Fast iteration — early-stage products where the schema isn't settled. Add fields freely; deal with the schema later.
  • Heterogeneous entities — products with wildly different attributes per category (a TV has resolution; a book has ISBN; a t-shirt has size).
  • Embedded relationships — store a user's addresses, a post's comments, an order's line items inside the parent document. One read fetches the whole thing.
  • Document-shaped APIs — your REST/GraphQL responses are already JSON; storing them as JSON eliminates an O/R mapping layer.

The trap: flexibility ≠ no schema. Without discipline, your collection becomes a graveyard of half-typed fields with three different spellings of "country." Real Mongo teams use schema validation ($jsonSchema) for important collections, treating schema as code.

3Querying — Find & Aggregation Pipeline

// Simple find
db.users.find({ "addresses.city": "Mumbai", "prefs.newsletter": true })

// Aggregation pipeline (SQL-like, but stage-based)
db.orders.aggregate([
  { $match:  { status: "PAID", created_at: { $gte: ISODate("2026-01-01") } } },
  { $group:  { _id: "$user_id", total: { $sum: "$amount_cents" } } },
  { $sort:   { total: -1 } },
  { $limit:  100 },
  { $lookup: { from: "users", localField: "_id", foreignField: "_id", as: "user" } }
])
  • find() — basic filter + projection; like SELECT … WHERE.
  • Aggregation pipeline — multi-stage pipeline ($match, $group, $sort, $lookup for joins, $unwind for arrays, $project to reshape). The serious query tool.
  • $lookup = join. Works but slow vs SQL JOINs; the Mongo idiom is to embed related data instead.

4Indexes

TypeUse
Single fieldThe default: db.users.createIndex({ email: 1 })
CompoundMultiple fields; same column-order rules as B-tree composite indexes
MultikeyIndex entries for every element of an array field — { tags: 1 } lets find({ tags: "vip" }) use the index
TextFull-text search on string fields (basic; for serious search reach for Elasticsearch)
2dsphereGeo queries — uses S2 internally; supports $near, $geoWithin, polygons
TTLAuto-expire docs after N seconds — sessions, OTPs, time-limited tokens
WildcardIndex "any field under this path" — useful for the truly schema-less corner of your data
HashedUsed as a shard key for even distribution

5Replication — Replica Sets

  • Replica set = 1 primary + N secondaries (typically 3 nodes). All writes go to primary; replicated to secondaries via the oplog.
  • Automatic failover — if primary dies, secondaries elect a new primary in seconds. Built-in.
  • Read preferences — primary (default, strongly consistent), secondary (stale but offloaded), nearest (latency-optimised).
  • Write concern — { w: 1 } = ack from primary only; { w: "majority" } = ack from majority before returning (safer; what you want for money).

6Sharding — Scaling Beyond One Replica Set

MongoDB's sharding is built-in (unlike Postgres). A sharded cluster has:

  • mongos — query routers (stateless); your app connects here.
  • Config servers — store the shard-map metadata.
  • Shards — each is its own replica set holding a range of the keyspace.
  • Balancer — background process that moves chunks between shards as data grows or skews.

Shard-key choice is the permanent decision (same as in Cassandra / DynamoDB). Hashed shard key for even distribution; ranged for locality. Note the terminology: MongoDB's "shard" is what most people call a shard. (Unlike Cassandra/DynamoDB which call it "partition" — see Partitioning & Sharding page.)

7Transactions — Multi-Document ACID (since 4.0)

For years MongoDB was famously single-document atomic only. Since 4.0 (2018) it supports multi-document transactions:

const session = client.startSession();
session.startTransaction();
try {
  await accounts.updateOne({ _id: a }, { $inc: { balance: -100 } }, { session });
  await accounts.updateOne({ _id: b }, { $inc: { balance:  100 } }, { session });
  await session.commitTransaction();
} catch (e) {
  await session.abortTransaction();
}

Caveats: transactions add latency and reduce throughput; use sparingly. The Mongo idiom is still to embed related data so one update touches one document.

8Atlas — the Managed Default

Most Mongo deployments now use MongoDB Atlas (the official managed cloud). Adds backups, monitoring, search (Lucene-backed), vector search, change streams, online schema management. Effectively the production target unless you have strict on-prem needs.

9When to Use MongoDB

Use whenWhy
Schema evolves rapidly (early-stage products, internal tools)Add fields without a migration
Data is naturally hierarchical (user with addresses, post with comments, order with line items)Embed it — one read fetches the whole tree
Polymorphic entities (different "kinds" sharing a collection)Flexible per-document shape; no table-per-class
Document-shaped APIs (REST / GraphQL returning JSON)Same shape end-to-end; no ORM mapping
Geospatial app2dsphere + S2 native; competitive with PostGIS
Content management, catalogues, IoT events, log-like dataDocument model fits naturally
Built-in sharding without extra middlewareCitus/Vitess equivalent comes in the box

10When NOT to Use MongoDB

  • Heavy joins across "tables" — relational DBs do this an order of magnitude better.
  • Financial / accounting with multi-row transactions — Postgres' ACID story is more mature; transactions in Mongo are possible but a code smell.
  • Analytics / OLAP — aggregation pipeline is decent but ClickHouse / Snowflake / BigQuery crush it on real analytics.
  • Strict schema enforcement is critical — Postgres' CHECK + NOT NULL + foreign-keys are stronger out of the box.
  • You'd rather have SQL — every analyst on Earth speaks SQL; Mongo's aggregation pipeline has a real learning curve.

11Common Pitfalls (the "we wished we'd known")

  • Unbounded array growth — embedding "all comments" in a post breaks when the post goes viral (16 MB document size limit; performance degrades long before that).
  • Schema drift — without validation, fields proliferate; old data gets stale shapes. Use $jsonSchema validation on important collections.
  • $lookup performance — works but doesn't replace SQL joins. Plan to embed instead.
  • Working-set in RAM assumption — Mongo expects your hot data to fit in RAM. When it doesn't, performance falls off a cliff.
  • Default write concern — older versions defaulted to w: 1 (single ack); production should use w: "majority" for durability.
🔑 The Mental Model

"MongoDB is excellent when your data is JSON-shaped and you embrace embedding over joining. It is mediocre when your data is relation-shaped and you keep reaching for $lookup. Choose by the natural shape of your data, not the brand of the database."

Redis Streams

A Kafka-style append-only log inside Redis. Adds durable, ordered, replayable events with consumer groups — without standing up a separate Kafka cluster. The pragmatic middle ground between Redis Lists/Pub/Sub and full Kafka.

1What Redis Streams Is

Introduced in Redis 5.0. A Stream is a per-key log: every XADD appends an entry with a server-assigned ID (timestamp-based, monotonically increasing). Consumers can read from any point in the log, replay, or coordinate via consumer groups.

// Producer — append events to a stream
XADD orders * order_id 42 amount 1500 status PAID
// Returns: "1715000000000-0"  (timestamp-seq)

// Simple consumer — read all entries
XREAD COUNT 100 STREAMS orders 0

// Block until new entries arrive
XREAD COUNT 100 BLOCK 5000 STREAMS orders $

2The Five Commands That Matter

CommandWhat it does
XADDAppend entry. Auto-IDs or explicit IDs. Optional MAXLEN to cap stream length.
XREADRead entries from one or more streams; blocking variant available.
XRANGE / XREVRANGERead a range by ID; like a SQL WHERE ts BETWEEN.
XGROUP CREATECreate a consumer group on a stream.
XREADGROUPRead entries as a named consumer in a group. Entry is "delivered" to that consumer.
XACKAcknowledge an entry as processed. Removes from the consumer's pending list.
XPENDINGList entries delivered but not yet acked. The retry / dead-letter path.
XCLAIMReassign a long-pending entry to a different consumer (recovering from a crashed worker).
XTRIMTrim the stream by length or by ID. Bounds memory growth.

3Consumer Groups — the Killer Feature

This is what separates Streams from Redis Lists / Pub/Sub. A consumer group lets N workers share processing of one stream, each worker getting different entries.

XADD orders ... ──► [ stream: orders ] │ ▼ ┌────────── consumer group: order-processors ────────┐ │ │ ▼ ▼ ▼ ▼ worker:1 worker:2 worker:3 worker:4 (gets entries 1,5,9) (gets 2,6,10) (gets 3,7,11) (gets 4,8,12) │ │ on success → XACK │ on crash → entry stays "pending"; XCLAIM by peer or watchdog
// Setup (once)
XGROUP CREATE orders order-processors $ MKSTREAM

// Worker loop
while (true) {
  const msgs = await redis.call(
    'XREADGROUP', 'GROUP', 'order-processors', 'worker:1',
    'COUNT', 10, 'BLOCK', 5000, 'STREAMS', 'orders', '>'
  );
  for (const [streamName, entries] of msgs) {
    for (const [id, fields] of entries) {
      try {
        await processOrder(fields);
        await redis.call('XACK', 'orders', 'order-processors', id);
      } catch (e) {
        // Don't XACK; entry stays pending; will be retried or claimed
      }
    }
  }
}

// Watchdog (periodic; recovers crashed workers' pending entries)
const pending = await redis.call(
  'XPENDING', 'orders', 'order-processors', 'IDLE', 60000, '-', '+', 100
);
for (const entry of pending) {
  await redis.call('XCLAIM', 'orders', 'order-processors', 'worker:1', 60000, entry.id);
}

4Typical Use Cases

Use caseWhy Streams fits
Task queue with retriesXREADGROUP delivers one entry per worker; XACK on success; XPENDING + XCLAIM is the retry/DLQ path
Lightweight event logMultiple consumer groups can independently read the same stream → fan-out without copying data
Audit trail / activity feedAppend-only, ordered, replayable; XRANGE for historical queries
Pub/Sub with replayPlain Redis Pub/Sub loses messages if consumer is offline; Streams preserves them
Outbox pattern (poor man's CDC)App writes to DB + appends to Stream in a Lua script; consumer drains Stream to Kafka / downstream
WebSocket fan-out coordinationOne worker XADDs notifications; each WS terminator XREADGROUPs and pushes to its connected clients

5Redis Streams vs Alternatives

Redis StreamsRedis Lists (LPUSH/RPOP)Redis Pub/SubKafka
PersistenceRDB + AOF (durable)RDB + AOFNone — lost if consumer offlineDisk; weeks of retention
Consumer groupsYesNo (one worker pops, gone)No (broadcast only)Yes (gold standard)
Replay / random readYes (XRANGE)No (LPOP is destructive)NoYes
Acks / pendingYes (XACK / XPENDING)NoNoYes (consumer offsets)
Throughput ceiling~50–100 k msgs/s/node~100 k+/nodeHighest (no persistence)Millions/s (distributed)
Operational costJust RedisJust RedisJust RedisWhole Kafka cluster + ZK/KRaft
Best forTask queues, durable fan-out at modest scaleSimple FIFO when one worker popsFire-and-forget real-time fan-outEvent streaming > 100 k/s, multi-day retention, exactly-once

6When to Use Redis Streams

  • You already have Redis and need a task queue with retries — don't spin up SQS / RabbitMQ / Kafka just for this.
  • You want replay / multiple consumer groups but throughput is under ~50 k msgs/s.
  • You need ordered delivery per-key (use the key as the stream name).
  • Latency matters more than retention — Streams adds ~1 ms vs Kafka's ~10 ms.
  • You want one log accessible from your app code without a separate operational surface area.

7When NOT to Use Redis Streams

  • Throughput > ~100 k msgs/s sustained — Kafka is purpose-built for this; Redis will run out of memory or single-thread CPU.
  • Long retention (days/weeks of history) — Streams lives in RAM; Kafka writes to disk much cheaper.
  • Exactly-once across heterogeneous sinks — Kafka transactions + Schema Registry are the standard; Streams doesn't compete.
  • Strict ordering across partitions — Kafka's per-partition ordering with N partitions is the model; Streams gives per-stream ordering, no built-in partitioning.
  • Cross-cluster mirroring / DR — Kafka MirrorMaker / Confluent Replicator are the standard; Streams replication is single-cluster.

8Capping Stream Growth

Streams grow forever if you let them. Bound them with:

  • XADD orders MAXLEN ~ 1000000 * ... — keeps roughly the last 1M entries; the ~ is approximate-but-fast.
  • XADD orders MINID ~ <timestamp_2_days_ago> * ... — keeps only entries newer than 2 days.
  • XTRIM orders MAXLEN ~ 1000000 — explicit trim from a separate maintenance task.
🔑 The Mental Model

"Redis Streams is the missing middle between Lists (no replay, no consumer groups) and Kafka (heavy operational surface). For task queues, fan-out, and audit logs at modest scale, it's the pragmatic choice — one fewer thing to operate."

Apache Flink

A true stream-first compute engine: low-latency, exactly-once aggregations on continuous event streams. The standard answer when an interviewer asks "how do you compute trending topics / real-time fraud / live aggregations?"

1What Flink Is (and Isn't)

  • Is: a distributed stream-processing engine. Reads from Kafka / Kinesis / Pulsar; emits to anywhere. Sub-second end-to-end latency.
  • Isn't: a database. State lives in RocksDB on each task manager, checkpointed to S3. You query it via the output sink, not directly.
  • Vs Spark Streaming: Spark is micro-batch (seconds of latency); Flink is true streaming (ms of latency).
  • Vs Kafka Streams: Kafka Streams is a library embedded in your app; Flink is a separate cluster you submit jobs to. Flink wins on heavy state and large jobs; Kafka Streams wins on simplicity.

2Event Time vs Processing Time (the most-tested concept)

  • Event time: the timestamp embedded in the event ("when it happened" in the real world).
  • Processing time: the timestamp when the engine processes the event ("now" in the cluster).

Real systems have late-arriving data: a phone offline for 2 hours emits its events when it reconnects. If you bucket by processing time, those events go into the wrong window. Flink's killer feature is handling event-time windowing correctly.

3Watermarks — Bounding Lateness

A watermark of T says "I think no more events with event-time < T will arrive." Flink uses watermarks to decide when to close a window. Lateness allowance is configurable (e.g. "wait 5 minutes after window end before finalising").

4Windowing

WindowDefinitionUse
TumblingFixed size, non-overlapping (every 1 min)"Clicks per minute"
SlidingFixed size, overlapping (5 min, slide every 1 min)Smoothed metrics; trailing 5-min averages
SessionCloses after gap of inactivityUser sessions, device sessions
Global + custom triggerSingle window, custom firing logicAnomaly detection, custom aggregations

5State and Checkpointing

Flink keeps per-key state (in RocksDB on each task manager). Periodically checkpoints all state to durable storage (S3 / HDFS). On failure, restores from the latest checkpoint. With Kafka source's offset committed in the same checkpoint, you get exactly-once end-to-end.

6Typical Use Cases

  • Real-time aggregations: clicks-per-ad-per-minute, trending hashtags, hot products.
  • Fraud / anomaly detection: pattern matching on user-behaviour streams (CEP — Complex Event Processing).
  • ETL / stream-to-warehouse: transform Kafka events and write to ClickHouse / Iceberg / Snowflake.
  • Joins between streams: enrich orders stream with customer profile stream.
  • Materialised views: compute and maintain pre-aggregated tables.

7When NOT to Reach for Flink

  • Simple "consume Kafka, write to DB" — use a plain consumer or Kafka Connect.
  • Stateless transformations — Kafka Streams is lighter.
  • Daily batch reports — Spark / Snowflake is cheaper.
  • Tiny throughput (< 100 events/s) — Flink's cluster overhead isn't worth it.

8The "Real-time Aggregator" Pattern (interview gold)

click events → Kafka → Flink job ├ keyBy(ad_id) ├ tumbling 1-min window ├ count + dedup via key state └ → sink to: • Redis (low-latency dashboard) • ClickHouse (long-term analytics)

This is the canonical answer for "Ad Click Aggregator," "Trending Topics," "Real-time Leaderboard."

Apache ZooKeeper

A small, strongly-consistent key-value store designed for distributed coordination — leader election, configuration, distributed locks, service discovery, membership. Modern systems often prefer etcd; the patterns are the same.

1What ZooKeeper Is (Mental Model)

Think "tiny hierarchical filesystem (like /services/orders/leader) replicated by Paxos-like consensus across 3 or 5 nodes." All writes are linearizable; reads are sequentially consistent.

  • Strong consistency over availability (CP system).
  • Cluster of odd size (3, 5, 7); tolerates ⌊N/2⌋ failures.
  • Designed for small, high-value metadata, not bulk storage.

2znodes — Persistent vs Ephemeral vs Sequential

TypeLifetimeUsed for
PersistentUntil explicit deleteConfiguration, partition assignments
EphemeralTied to client session; deleted when client disconnectsLiveness, presence, distributed locks
SequentialAuto-numbered (lock-0001, lock-0002...)Lock ordering, leader election

3Watches

Clients can register a one-shot watch on a znode. ZooKeeper notifies the client on the next change. The standard substrate for "tell me when something changes": leader change, config update, peer leaving.

4Leader Election Pattern

  1. Each candidate creates an ephemeral sequential znode under /election/.
  2. The candidate with the lowest sequence number is leader.
  3. Each non-leader puts a watch on the next-lower znode.
  4. If leader dies, its ephemeral znode disappears, the next candidate's watch fires, that candidate becomes the new leader.

Used by HBase, Solr, Kafka (legacy), countless internal systems.

5Distributed Lock Pattern

Same recipe as leader election: ephemeral sequential znode, lowest sequence holds the lock, others watch the next-lower. Lock is automatically released when the holder dies (its ephemeral znode disappears) — no leaked locks even on hard crash.

See the Distributed Locks page for the full Redlock vs ZooKeeper comparison.

6Service Discovery / Membership

Each service instance registers itself as an ephemeral znode under /services/<svc-name>/. Other services list children to discover live instances; watch the parent for changes. When an instance dies, its znode disappears automatically — no stale endpoints.

7Things ZooKeeper Is Famously Used For

  • Kafka (pre-KRaft): broker registration, controller election, partition assignment.
  • HBase: master election, region-server liveness.
  • Solr: cluster state, shard leader election.
  • Hadoop / YARN: HA master coordination.
  • Custom job schedulers: leader election for the scheduler.

8ZooKeeper vs etcd

ZooKeeperetcd
ConsensusZAB (Zookeeper Atomic Broadcast)Raft
APIznode tree, watchesflat key-value, watch ranges
Client librariesMature Java; others varyingModern gRPC, all languages strong
Run byJVMGo binary
Cloud-native?Predates KubernetesKubernetes' own backend

For new projects, default to etcd unless you're integrating with a system that requires ZooKeeper (Kafka in legacy mode, HBase, Solr).

9Operational Notes

  • Don't store anything > 1 MB per znode — degraded performance.
  • Don't use ZooKeeper as a general database; ~10 k writes/sec ceiling.
  • Always run odd cluster size; never 2 or 4 (split-brain risk).
  • Network partitions can stall the cluster; design clients to tolerate temporary unavailability.

Pattern: Real-time Updates

Two complementary problems: (1) pushing data to clients as it happens (WebSockets, SSE) and (2) keeping internal services in sync as DB state changes (CDC + Kafka). Both fall under "real-time updates."

1The Four Client-side Approaches

ApproachHow it worksDirectionBest for
Short pollingClient sends GET every N seconds; server immediately replies with current stateC ↔ S (request/response)Status checks, slow-changing data, batch job results
Long pollingClient sends GET; server holds the connection open until new data exists (or timeout); replies, client immediately reconnectsS → C effectivelyLegacy real-time fallback when WS / SSE blocked
Server-Sent Events (SSE)Single long-lived HTTP response that streams chunked events; auto-reconnect built into browsersS → C onlyLive feed, notifications, AI streaming responses, dashboards
WebSocketUpgrade HTTP → TCP-based bidirectional frame protocol; long-livedBi-directionalChat, collab editing, gaming, market data, anything truly bidirectional
Mobile Push (APNs / FCM)OS-managed channel; wakes the app even when killedServer → mobileNotifications when the app isn't running

2WebSocket vs Polling — When to Pick Which

The most-asked sub-question in real-time problems. Two perspectives matter: latency and cost.

Latency math

ApproachUpdate visible to client in…Server resources / client / minute
Polling every 60 s0–60 s (avg 30 s)1 request
Polling every 10 s0–10 s (avg 5 s)6 requests
Polling every 1 s0–1 s (avg 0.5 s)60 requests
Long polling (30 s timeout)~50 ms after event (one extra RTT)~2 requests (one per event or per timeout)
SSE / WebSocket~50 ms after event (one TCP push)0 requests (one persistent connection)

Cost math (1 M concurrent clients)

ApproachRequests/sec server-sideConnections held
Polling every 5 s1 M / 5 = 200 k req/sec~200 k transient (matches active req)
Polling every 30 s~33 k req/sec~33 k transient
SSE / WebSocket~0 (only event-driven)1 M persistent

Insight: polling trades CPU/bandwidth for connection slots; WebSocket/SSE trade connection slots for CPU/bandwidth. Above some break-even point, persistent connections are always cheaper.

The decision tree

  • Truly bidirectional, low-latency, high-frequency (chat, collab editing, gaming, trading) → WebSocket. No alternative.
  • Server-push only, browser-friendly (live feed, notifications, AI streaming, server logs view) → SSE. Simpler than WebSocket, runs over plain HTTP, native browser reconnect.
  • Updates < once per minute, latency tolerance is minutes (status pages, weather, batch job progress page) → Short polling. Stateless, trivially scalable, no connection-state ops.
  • Mobile app, user not on-screen → Push notification (APNs / FCM). The OS handles the channel; battery-friendly.
  • You wanted a WebSocket but it's blocked (corporate proxies, ancient browsers) → Long polling as a fallback. Most real WS libraries (Socket.IO, SignalR) downgrade automatically.

Polling isn't a hack — pick it when it's right

Engineers reach for WebSocket too quickly. Polling wins when:

  • Updates are infrequent and latency-tolerant (every few seconds is fine).
  • Statelessness matters — every request is independent, load balancer doesn't care which node serves it, no sticky sessions, no in-memory state to migrate.
  • Server is behind a CDN — polled endpoints can be CDN-cached with short TTL; WebSocket can't.
  • Auth model is HTTP-native — every request carries a normal Authorization header; no special auth-on-connect logic.
  • The client population is huge but per-client traffic is rare — holding 10 M idle WS connections is expensive; polling once a minute is cheaper.

Concrete picks across the guide

System / problemPickWhy
WhatsApp / chat (P3)WebSocketBidirectional, < 200 ms latency expected, billions of clients but with steady traffic
Stock broker price ticker (P17)WebSocket100 k ticks/sec fan-out; polling at this rate is infeasible
Google Docs (P19)WebSocketTruly bidirectional collaborative edits
Uber dispatch driver app (P5)WebSocketDrivers push GPS, server pushes ride offers — both directions
Live notification feedSSEServer → client only; HTTP-friendly; auto-reconnects
AI chat streaming responseSSESingle response progressively streamed; no client→server messages mid-stream
OTT "Continue Watching" sync (P26)Polling on app openOnce per app launch is enough; WebSocket is overkill
Job status endpoint (P16)Polling (or webhook)State changes seconds-to-minutes apart; no need for persistent connection
Payment processor callback (P21)Webhook (server → server push)Server-to-server; firewalled, retryable
"Has my crypto trade settled?"Long pollingSettles within ~seconds; user is actively waiting; cheaper than WebSocket for a one-shot wait

3Connection Management at Scale

  • ~50 k–100 k WebSockets per node typically (RAM-bound; ~5 KB per connection).
  • For 1 M concurrent users, plan ~10–20 WS terminator nodes behind a sticky LB.
  • Sticky session via JWT (not connection ID) so any node can take over after failover.
  • Heartbeat every 30 s; reconnect with exponential backoff on disconnect.

4Fan-out (Broadcast)

To push the same event to many connected clients (e.g. "Bieber tweeted"), use Redis Pub/Sub or Kafka topic per channel; each WS terminator subscribes and forwards to its connected clients filtered by interest.

5Internal Real-time: CDC Pipelines

Change Data Capture streams every insert / update / delete from a database into downstream consumers in near real time. Keeps your search index / cache / analytics warehouse in sync with the OLTP DB without the dual-write problem.

The dual-write problem (the reason CDC exists)

The naïve approach: when your app writes to the DB, it also publishes a message to Kafka.

app → DB.write() ✓ succeeded app → Kafka.publish() ✗ network error, retry? Result: DB has the new state, but downstream consumers never learn. Or worse — Kafka.publish() succeeds and DB.write() fails after.

Solutions: 2-phase commit (too slow), the Outbox pattern (write to DB + outbox table in one transaction; separate process publishes outbox), or — best — just read the DB's own log.

How CDC works

The DB already maintains a durable, ordered log of every change for its own crash recovery — the Postgres WAL, the MySQL binlog, the MongoDB oplog. CDC tools read that log and publish each event to Kafka.

Source DB (Postgres / MySQL / Mongo) │ │ WAL / binlog / oplog (append-only, ordered) ▼ CDC connector (Debezium / AWS DMS / Maxwell) │ - decodes binary log entries │ - resolves schema │ - emits one event per row change ▼ Kafka topic per table (e.g. `db.users`, `db.orders`) │ ┌──┴────────┬───────────────┬────────────────┐ ▼ ▼ ▼ ▼ Search Cache Data Warehouse Microservice index invalidator loader consumer (ES) (Redis) (Snowflake) (Service B reacts)

When to use CDC

Use caseWhy CDC
Search index syncPostgres → Elasticsearch via CDC. Whenever a row changes, ES is updated within seconds. No dual-write.
Cache invalidationPostgres → consumer → DEL on Redis. Frees the writer from remembering to invalidate.
Data warehouse / analyticsOLTP → Kafka → Snowflake / BigQuery / ClickHouse. Analysts query a near-live copy without touching production DB.
Microservices integrationService B reacts to Service A's data changes without coupling code.
Cross-region replicationStream changes from primary region to read replicas in other regions.
Audit logsEvery row change captured immutably to S3 / data lake.

When NOT to use CDC

  • You don't have access to the source DB's transaction log.
  • You need application-level events (e.g. "the user did a checkout") rather than row-level changes.
  • Latency requirements < 100 ms end-to-end — CDC adds 1–10 s of lag.
  • Your throughput is tiny (< 100 writes/s) — Outbox pattern + cron polling is simpler.
🔑 The Mental Model

Think of CDC as turning your database into an event stream. Every row change becomes a Kafka message; every downstream system subscribes. One source of truth, many consistent copies — without the dual-write bug.

Pattern: Dealing with Contention

Multiple writers want to update the same resource at the same time. Pick the right concurrency primitive and you avoid race conditions; pick wrong and you ship a corrupting bug.

1Pessimistic Locking (SELECT FOR UPDATE)

Acquire a row-level lock; everyone else blocks until you commit/rollback.

BEGIN; SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 42 FOR UPDATE; -- balance is now locked; other transactions wait UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 42; COMMIT;

Use when: contention is high and you want correctness over throughput. Avoid when: contention is rare; pessimistic locking serialises operations and creates deadlock risk.

2Optimistic Concurrency (Version Column)

Read the row + version; on update, require the version to match. Retry on conflict.

SELECT balance, version FROM accounts WHERE id = 42; -- compute new balance... UPDATE accounts SET balance = ?, version = version + 1 WHERE id = 42 AND version = ?; -- if 0 rows updated → someone else won; reread and retry

Use when: contention is rare; most updates succeed first try. Avoid when: contention is high (you'll spend more time retrying than working).

3SKIP LOCKED — The Multi-Worker Job Queue Pattern

The classic pattern for multi-worker job queues:

BEGIN; SELECT job_id FROM jobs WHERE status = 'PENDING' AND next_run_at <= NOW() ORDER BY next_run_at LIMIT 10 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED; UPDATE jobs SET status = 'RUNNING' WHERE job_id IN (...); COMMIT;

How it works:

  • FOR UPDATE: acquires a row lock on each returned row.
  • SKIP LOCKED: if another transaction holds the lock on a row, skip it (don't block). Return the next eligible row.
  • Result: 50 workers running the query concurrently each get a different set of 10 rows. No coordination needed. No external lock manager (Redis, Zookeeper) needed.

Used by: Sidekiq Pro, GoodJob, Que, Oban — battle-tested at scale.

4Atomic Operations (Redis Lua, atomic counters)

For counter-style contention (rate limit, inventory decrement, seat hold), the cleanest answer is to push the entire check-then-update into a single atomic operation. Redis Lua scripts are the standard:

-- Atomically: if balance >= cost, decrement and return new balance. local key = KEYS[1] local cost = tonumber(ARGV[1]) local cur = tonumber(redis.call('GET', key)) if cur < cost then return -1 end return redis.call('DECRBY', key, cost)

One round trip; no race; no lock. Used in P6 (rate limiter), P10 (e-commerce inventory), P20 (ticket booking seat hold).

5Compare-And-Swap (CAS)

Hardware-level atomic primitive: "set this value to X, but only if it's still Y." Available in atomic CPU instructions and at the database level (Cassandra LWT, DynamoDB conditional updates).

6Distributed Locks (Redlock and Its Caveats)

When you really need a lock spanning multiple processes/services, Redis-based Redlock is the most cited algorithm. However, Martin Kleppmann famously demonstrated that Redlock is unsafe under certain failure modes (clock skew, network delays). For correctness-critical use cases, prefer:

  • Postgres advisory locks (pg_advisory_lock) when your DB is the natural source of truth.
  • etcd / ZooKeeper for leader election or critical coordination — they use proper consensus (Raft / ZAB).
  • SKIP LOCKED for job queues — no distributed lock needed.

7Decision Guide

SituationPick
Counter-style decrement (inventory, rate limit)Redis Lua atomic
Multi-worker job claimSELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
Low-contention concurrent editsOptimistic version column
High-contention bank-style transfersSELECT FOR UPDATE
Leader election across servicesetcd / ZooKeeper lease
Hot-spot writes against a single rowSharded counter (N rows, aggregate on read)

Pattern: Multi-step Processes

A workflow that spans multiple services or DBs needs to handle partial failures. The toolbox: idempotency, outbox, sagas, durable execution.

1Idempotency — The Multi-Layer Defense

Network calls fail. Clients retry. Without idempotency, retries cause duplicates. Standard defense:

  1. Client-supplied idempotency key (UUID per request).
  2. Redis SETNX (atomic): if key exists → return cached result.
  3. DB UNIQUE constraint on idempotency_key: backup if Redis fails.
  4. Downstream gateway idempotency: pass the key to Stripe/Razorpay/etc. — they also dedupe.
  5. Reconciliation: nightly job compares records across systems to catch any missed.

4 layers seem like overkill until you've seen a single missed dedup cause a double-charge in production.

2The Outbox Pattern

You need to atomically (a) write to your DB AND (b) publish a message to Kafka. Doing both directly creates the dual-write problem (the network can fail between them).

Solution: in the same DB transaction that writes the business state, also INSERT a row into an outbox table. A separate process (or CDC connector) reads the outbox and publishes to Kafka, marking each row as published. If the publisher crashes, no problem — unpublished rows are still there to retry.

BEGIN; INSERT INTO orders (...) VALUES (...); INSERT INTO outbox (event_type, payload) VALUES ('order.created', '...'); COMMIT; -- separate worker reads outbox, publishes to Kafka, deletes/marks row

3The Saga Pattern

A long-running workflow that touches multiple services / DBs (book flight → book hotel → charge card). Cannot be a distributed transaction (too slow, requires 2PC). Saga = sequence of local transactions, each with a compensating action for rollback.

Choreography vs Orchestration

StyleHowTrade-offs
ChoreographyEach service emits events; other services react. No central coordinator.Loose coupling but harder to trace; emergent behaviour is hard to debug.
OrchestrationA central orchestrator calls each step in sequence and triggers compensations on failure.Easier to reason about; the orchestrator becomes a critical service.

Compensating transactions

For each forward action, you need a compensating "undo": cancel-flight, cancel-hotel, refund-charge. These must themselves be idempotent (the orchestrator may retry the compensation if it fails).

4Durable Execution (Temporal, Cadence, Step Functions)

For complex multi-step workflows, write the orchestration as plain code that runs on top of a durable execution engine. The engine persists every step's input/output to a DB, so if your worker crashes mid-workflow, it resumes from exactly where it left off.

  • Temporal / Cadence: code-as-workflow, popular in microservice stacks.
  • AWS Step Functions: state-machine-as-workflow, managed.
  • Airflow: DAG-as-workflow, batch-leaning, popular in data engineering.

5Retry & Backoff Strategy

  • Exponential backoff with jitter: backoff_ms = min(MAX, BASE × 2^attempt × (0.5 + random())). Prevents thundering herd.
  • Cap retries: after N attempts, send to dead-letter queue for human review.
  • Distinguish failure modes: permanent (don't retry — bad data, 4xx) vs transient (retry — 5xx, timeout, throttle).

6The Mental Model

🔑 The Three Defences

1. Idempotency keys protect against duplicate retries.

2. Outbox pattern protects against dual-write divergence.

3. Sagas / durable execution protect against partial-failure rollback gaps.

Use all three together for any business workflow that touches money or critical state.

Pattern: Scaling Reads

When read traffic outgrows your primary DB. The toolbox, in escalation order: read replicas → cache layer → CDN → pre-computed materialised views.

1The Escalation Ladder

Read QPSSolution
< 5 kSingle Postgres / MySQL primary, no help needed
5–50 kAdd read replicas (async)
50–500 kAdd Redis cache layer (cache-aside)
500 k+Add CDN at the edge for cacheable responses
1 M+Pre-compute materialised views (fanout-on-write timelines)

2Read Replicas

  • Sync replication: writes wait for replica ack. Strong consistency but write latency = max(primary, replica).
  • Async replication (default): writes commit at primary; replicas catch up asynchronously. Replica reads can be stale by ms to seconds (replication lag).
  • Routing: send writes + read-after-write queries to primary; everything else to a random replica.
  • Trap: replication lag during burst writes. App code that does UPDATE → SELECT may see stale data on a lagging replica. Use sticky reads ("read your writes" routing) to handle this.

3Cache Layer

Redis cache-aside is the default. Even at 95% hit rate, the cache absorbs 95% of read load — DB load drops 20×. See the Caching page for full strategy and eviction details.

4CDN — How It Reduces Latency (With Actual Numbers)

A Content Delivery Network is a globally distributed cache of HTTP responses. The user connects to the nearest CDN POP instead of your origin. This can speed up page loads 10× and cut your bandwidth bill by 90%.

The latency arithmetic

Real numbers for a typical "user in Mumbai, origin server in Virginia, USA":

StepWithout CDNWith CDN (cache hit)
TCP / TLS handshake3 round trips × ~200 ms = ~600 ms3 round trips × ~15 ms = ~45 ms
HTTP request → response (1 byte)1 round trip × 200 ms = 200 ms1 round trip × 15 ms = 15 ms
Download 200 KB asset~250 ms (long-distance throughput)~50 ms (POP throughput)
Total time-to-display~1,050 ms~110 ms

That's ~10× faster on first access. Compound across 50 page assets → 10 s → 0.75 s page load.

How CDN reduces latency, mechanically

  1. Anycast routing: same IP from every POP; BGP routes user to the nearest one.
  2. TCP / TLS termination at edge: handshakes happen between user and POP (low RTT) instead of user and origin (high RTT).
  3. Cache hit at edge: 90–99% of requests for popular static content served from POP RAM/SSD.
  4. HTTP/2 / HTTP/3 multiplexing: one connection, many concurrent streams.
  5. Connection pooling to origin: long-lived persistent connections; cache miss adds only 1 origin RTT.

What CDNs are great for

  • Static assets: images, CSS, JS bundles, fonts.
  • Video segments: HLS/DASH chunks with long TTL.
  • Frequently-read API responses: with proper Cache-Control headers.
  • HTTPS termination: TLS handshake at edge dramatically faster.
  • DDoS absorption: edge has terabits-per-second of capacity.

What CDNs are NOT great for

  • Personalised / per-user content — cache key per user → near-zero hit rate.
  • Strict consistency reads — CDN cache can be ~minutes stale.
  • POST/PUT writes — only saves the TLS-handshake latency.
  • One-off content — first request always misses.

Cost numbers

ItemOrder-of-magnitude
CDN egress (CloudFront, India zone)~$85 / TB
CDN egress (CloudFront, US/EU zones)~$50–60 / TB
Origin egress (EC2 to internet)~$90 / TB
Typical cache hit rate90–99% for static, 50–80% for dynamic
Net bandwidth savings~70–90% lower bill plus much faster page loads

5Pre-computed Views (Fanout-on-Write)

The ultimate "scale reads" trick: don't compute on read at all. Pre-compute the answer at write time and store it in the form the reader wants. Twitter / Instagram timelines: when a user posts, write the post into every follower's timeline cache. Read becomes O(1) ZRANGE.

Trade-off: write amplification scales with follower count. Use hybrid push/pull for celebrities (see P2 Twitter, P13 Instagram).

Pattern: Scaling Writes

A single Postgres / MySQL node tops out at ~10 k writes/sec. Past that, you reach for a small set of well-known techniques. Apply them in the order below — start simple, escalate only when the numbers say you must.

1The Escalation Ladder

Sustained writes/secSolution
< 5 kSingle Postgres / MySQL — no help needed
5–10 kTune the box: bigger SSDs, batch INSERTs, group commit
10–50 kShard the relational DB by hash(primary_key)
50–500 kSwitch to LSM-tree store (Cassandra / DynamoDB / ScyllaDB)
500 k+Add Kafka as a write buffer in front of the DB
1 M+Per-region sharding + write-back caches + eventual consistency

2Sharding Strategies

StrategyHowTrade-off
Hash shardingshard = hash(primary_key) % NEven distribution; no range queries; resharding is hard
Range shardingEach shard owns a range (e.g. user_id 0-1M, 1M-2M...)Range queries fast; risk of hot ranges; manual splits
Consistent hashingHash ring; key goes to next node clockwiseAdd/remove nodes minimally remaps; great for caches & Cassandra
Geo shardingShard key includes region (EU-user-42)Data residency / latency wins; cross-region queries expensive

Pick the shard key carefully — it determines forever which queries are fast (single-shard) and which are slow (cross-shard scatter-gather).

3LSM-Tree Stores (Cassandra, DynamoDB, ScyllaDB, RocksDB)

LSM-tree (Log-Structured Merge tree) trades read complexity for ridiculous write throughput. See the Cassandra page for full mechanics. Per-node ceiling: ~100 k+ writes/sec via sequential disk writes (commit log) → in-memory MemTable → SSTable flush → background compaction.

Use when:

  • Append-mostly workload (chat messages, event logs, time-series).
  • Partition key naturally exists in the query pattern.
  • You don't need joins / multi-row ACID.

4Batched Writes (Producer-side)

Most write paths can amortise per-message overhead by batching: 1 fsync per 1000 messages instead of per message. Order-of-magnitude wins.

  • Kafka producer: linger.ms=10 + batch.size=64KB turns 100 individual sends into 1 batched send.
  • Postgres batch insert: INSERT ... VALUES (...), (...), (...) 1000 rows in one round trip beats 1000 single inserts by 100×.
  • Cassandra logged batch: groups writes to the same partition for atomicity. Don't use cross-partition logged batches — anti-pattern.

5Async Pipelines (Kafka in Front of the DB)

If your write path is "user-facing → must commit synchronously", you're tied to the DB's write speed. Decouple it:

client → app → Kafka // fast accept; durable ↓ Consumer pool (auto-scales) ↓ DB.batchInsert() // processed at DB's pace

The user-facing API becomes "we accepted your event"; the actual DB write is async. Used for: click events, audit logs, view counts, analytics.

6Write-Back Caches

Cache absorbs writes; flushes to DB lazily. Extremely high write throughput (Redis can handle 1 M ops/s) but you accept data loss on crash. Use for: view counters, like counts, leaderboard scores. Never for money or auth.

See the Caching page §1 for full mechanics.

7Denormalisation to Remove Writes Entirely

Sometimes the cheapest write is the one you don't make. If you can compute the result at write-time and store it pre-formatted, your reads become free and your "writes" are just appends.

  • Twitter timeline fanout-on-write: when user posts, write into every follower's pre-computed timeline. Read = O(1) ZRANGE; no compute.
  • Materialised views: store the JOIN result as a separate table; refresh on the source table's CDC stream.
  • Trade-off: write amplification scales with consumer count (200M Bieber followers = 200M writes/post). Use hybrid push-pull at that scale.

8Hot Key / Hot Partition Handling

One key receives 10× the traffic of others → that node melts while others are idle. Mitigations:

  • Add a random suffix to the key (key#0 through key#9). Distributes writes across 10 keys. Reads must read all 10 and aggregate.
  • Sharded counter: instead of one row "page_views = 1M", maintain N rows; sum on read.
  • Local in-process write batching: each app server batches updates for the hot key, flushes every 100 ms.
  • Detect & route: count-min sketch identifies hot keys; dynamically reroute their writes to a dedicated shard.
🔑 The Mental Model

Pick the smallest knob that works. If batching gets you there, don't shard. If sharding gets you there, don't switch DB engines. If a single Postgres handles it, your "scaling writes" plan is "do nothing."

Pattern: Handling Large Blobs

Images, videos, files, backups. Three rules to remember: never proxy through app servers, store metadata separately from blob, deliver via CDN.

1The Cardinal Rule: Never Proxy Blobs Through Your App Server

If a 100 MB video upload goes client → app → S3, your app server eats:

  • 100 MB of inbound network
  • 100 MB of memory (or temp-file disk)
  • 100 MB of outbound to S3
  • ~30 s of one worker process held captive

At 100 concurrent uploads = your fleet is dead. Solution: presigned URLs let the client upload directly to S3 — your app server only generates a short-lived signed URL.

Bad (proxied): client → 100MB → app server → 100MB → S3 (eats memory, network, workers) Good (direct): 1. client → POST /uploads → app server 2. app generates presigned S3 URL, returns to client 3. client → 100MB → S3 directly 4. S3 fires "upload-complete" webhook → app updates metadata

2Resumable Upload (TUS / S3 Multipart)

For uploads > 5 MB or flaky mobile networks, use a resumable protocol. Two industry standards:

  • S3 Multipart Upload: client splits file into ~5 MB chunks; each PUT-uploads independently with a part-number; finally CompleteMultipartUpload stitches them. Failed chunks just re-upload.
  • TUS protocol: open standard, supports any HTTP server. POST /upload creates an upload; client PATCHes chunks; server tracks the byte offset. Survives network drops.

Used by: YouTube, Instagram, Dropbox, every serious video / file platform.

3Chunked Download (HTTP Range Requests)

For large downloads (videos, big files), use HTTP Range headers so clients can:

  • Resume a download after a network drop (Range: bytes=5000000-).
  • Seek into a video without downloading the prefix (Range: bytes=2000000-3000000).
  • Parallelise downloads across multiple connections.

S3, every CDN, and all major HTTP servers support range requests natively.

4Metadata in DB, Blob in Storage

Always split: a small row in your relational DB pointing at the blob URL. The DB row is queryable, indexable, joinable; the blob is unindexed bytes.

CREATE TABLE videos ( video_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, user_id UUID, title VARCHAR(255), duration_s INT, s3_key TEXT, -- e.g. "videos/2026/05/abc.mp4" size_bytes BIGINT, uploaded_at TIMESTAMPTZ ); -- The blob lives in S3; the DB knows where.

5Content-Hash Deduplication

Before uploading, compute SHA-256 of the file. If the hash already exists in your blob_refs table, point the new upload at the existing blob. Saves storage when many users upload the same content (memes, shared documents).

6S3 Lifecycle Tiering (Cost Optimisation)

S3 charges per GB-month. Tier old data automatically:

TierCost / TB-moUse for
S3 Standard~$23Hot — accessed weekly
S3 Standard-IA~$13Warm — accessed monthly
S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval~$4Cold — quarterly access
S3 Glacier Deep Archive~$1Archive — yearly access; minutes to retrieve

Lifecycle rule: "objects in this prefix > 30 days → IA; > 1 yr → Glacier." Saves 70%+ on storage with zero code changes.

7CDN for Delivery

Once the blob is in S3, deliver it through CloudFront / Akamai / Fastly. The CDN caches at edge POPs, dramatically lowering latency and offloading 95%+ of traffic from S3. See the Scaling Reads page for CDN latency math.

8Pre-signed URLs for Secure Delivery

Don't make blobs public. Generate short-lived (e.g. 1-hour) signed URLs per request. The user clicks, gets a CDN URL with a signature; CDN validates and serves. Expires automatically; no orphaned public links.

9The Standard Pipeline (every modern platform)

Upload: client → presigned URL → S3 (multipart) ↓ S3 webhook → metadata Svc → DB ↓ (optional) Transcode workers → S3 variants ↓ (optional) ContentID / virus scan Download: client → app → returns signed CDN URL client → CDN edge POP (cache hit) → bytes or CDN miss → S3 origin → CDN caches → bytes

Pattern: Managing Long-Running Tasks

Some tasks (video transcoding, ML inference, batch reports, large data exports) take minutes to hours. They can't return synchronously over HTTP — load balancers and proxies time out at 30–60s. The standard async pattern.

1The Standard Pattern: 202 Accepted + Status Endpoint

POST /v1/exports Body: { dataset: "all_users", format: "csv" } Response 202 Accepted: { "job_id": "job_abc123", "status_url": "/v1/jobs/job_abc123", "estimated_completion": "5-10 minutes" } GET /v1/jobs/job_abc123 Response 200: { "job_id": "job_abc123", "status": "RUNNING", // QUEUED | RUNNING | COMPLETED | FAILED "progress_percent": 47, "result_url": null // populated when COMPLETED }

Three states the client cares about:

  1. Submit → 202 + job_id (don't wait).
  2. Poll → status updates (or webhook).
  3. Done → fetch result via signed URL.

2Job Queue Choices

ChoiceWhen to use
KafkaHigh volume (> 10k jobs/s), need replay, multiple consumer types
SQS / managed queueWant fully managed; throughput modest; per-message visibility timeout
Redis StreamsAlready running Redis; simple consumer groups; ~50 k msg/s
Postgres + SKIP LOCKEDAlready running Postgres; throughput < ~5 k/s; want SQL queryability of jobs
Sidekiq / BullMQ / CeleryOff-the-shelf job lib; Redis-backed; rich features (retries, dashboards)

3Polling vs Webhooks

PollingWebhook
Client repeatedly calls GET /jobs/{id}Server POSTs to client's pre-registered URL on completion
Simple to implementRequires client to host an HTTPS endpoint
Wastes calls if jobs are slowPush only; very efficient
Default for browser appsDefault for server-to-server (Stripe, Twilio, etc.)

Most platforms offer both: poll if you can't host webhooks, otherwise use webhooks for efficiency.

4Retry & Dead-Letter Queues

Long jobs fail. The job runner needs:

  • Idempotency: re-running a job can't double-charge / double-email / double-write.
  • Exponential backoff with jitter: backoff = min(MAX, BASE × 2^attempt × (0.5 + random())).
  • Max retries: typically 3–5; after that move to dead-letter queue (DLQ).
  • DLQ: a separate queue holding poison messages for human review. Must be alertable.

5Watchdog / Lease Timeouts

What if a worker dies mid-job? The job is stuck in RUNNING forever. Two safeguards:

  • Lease / visibility timeout: the worker holds a lease (e.g. 5 minutes); if it dies, the lease expires and another worker can take over. SQS has this built-in.
  • Heartbeat: long-running workers periodically extend their lease. If heartbeats stop, watchdog re-queues.

See P16 Job Scheduler for the full Postgres + SKIP LOCKED + Watchdog pattern.

6Durable Execution (Temporal / Cadence / Step Functions)

For workflows that span multiple services and last hours/days, durable-execution engines persist every step's input/output. Worker crashes? It resumes exactly where it left off. Code looks synchronous; the engine handles all the persistence/retry magic.

  • Temporal / Cadence: code-as-workflow.
  • AWS Step Functions: state-machine-as-workflow.
  • Airflow: DAG-as-workflow (batch-leaning).

7Streaming Progress

For UX, send incremental updates instead of just QUEUED → COMPLETED:

  • Polling: include progress_percent in status response.
  • SSE / WebSocket: push live progress events. Used for AI streaming responses, batch progress bars.

8Result Delivery

Where does the output go?

  • Inline in status response: small results (a few KB).
  • Signed URL to S3: large results (CSV exports, video files). The job uploads to S3; status response returns a presigned download URL.
  • Push to user's email / cloud drive: very large outputs or scheduled reports.

Time-Series Databases

Specialised stores for "many writes per second of (time, value, tags)" workloads — metrics, IoT, financial ticks, sensor data. They beat a general-purpose DB by orders of magnitude on storage and query speed.

1What Makes Time-Series Workloads Special

  • Append-mostly: writes are nearly always "now"; updates and deletes are rare.
  • Highly compressible: consecutive samples differ by tiny amounts; timestamps grow linearly.
  • Range queries dominate: "the last hour", "the last week", "Mondays in May".
  • Tiered access: most queries hit recent data; old data is cold but voluminous.
  • Down-sampling: 1-second data old → store only 1-minute averages → 60× space saving.

2Why Postgres Eventually Falls Over

Naively storing metrics in Postgres works until ~10 M rows; after that, indexes bloat, B-tree depth hurts, and time-range queries scan multiple GB. Specialised TSDBs solve this with:

  • Time-bucketed storage (one segment per hour/day; drop entire old segments).
  • Columnar layout within a segment.
  • Specialised compression (Gorilla, delta-of-delta).
  • Pre-computed down-samples (continuous aggregates / continuous queries).

Result: 10–100× smaller storage, 10–100× faster range queries.

3Gorilla Compression (the magic)

Facebook's Gorilla paper. Two key tricks:

  • Delta-of-delta encoding for timestamps: usually a fixed sample rate → most deltas-of-deltas are 0 → store with just a few bits.
  • XOR encoding for float values: consecutive floats often share most bits → XOR previous, store only the differing middle.

Achieves ~1.4 bytes per sample for typical metrics — vs 16+ bytes raw. ~10× compression in practice.

4The Standard Data Model — Metric Name + Labels

http_request_duration_seconds{ service="orders", method="POST", status="200", region="us-east-1" } 0.124 @timestamp=1715000000

Each unique combination of metric name + labels is one time series. Beware cardinality explosion — adding a label like user_id creates one series per user (millions). Restrict label values to small enumerations.

5The Major Choices

SystemStyleBest for
PrometheusPull-based; in-memory + local TSDB; PromQLInfra/service metrics; the de-facto monitoring standard
InfluxDBPush-based; line protocol; Flux/InfluxQLIoT, app metrics, time-stamped business events
TimescaleDBPostgres extension; SQLYou want SQL + joins + Postgres ops; medium scale
M3 / Cortex / Mimir / VictoriaMetricsPrometheus-compatible, horizontally scalableLong-term metrics storage at fleet scale
ClickHouseColumnar OLAPHeavy ad-hoc analytics on time-stamped events; not just metrics
InfluxDB IOx (3.x) / Apache IoTDBColumnar / Parquet-styleIoT and large-scale sensor data; SQL on time-series

6InfluxDB — Deep Dive

InfluxDB is the most-installed dedicated TSDB. Three major eras you may encounter:

VersionEngineQuery languageNotes
InfluxDB 1.xTSM (Time-Structured Merge Tree)InfluxQL (SQL-like)Stable; widely deployed; single-node OSS
InfluxDB 2.xTSM + TSI (Time Series Index)Flux (functional, pipeline)Tasks + dashboards + alerts bundled in one binary
InfluxDB 3.x (IOx)Apache Arrow + Parquet on object storageSQL (via DataFusion)2023 rewrite in Rust; SQL-native; cloud-friendly

Data model — measurements, tags, fields

measurement: cpu_usage
tags:        { host="server-1", region="us-east", env="prod" }   ← indexed
fields:      { usage_percent=42.3, load_avg=1.7 }                ← not indexed
timestamp:   1715000000000000000  (nanoseconds)
  • Measurement ≈ table name (e.g. cpu_usage).
  • Tags = indexed string labels you filter or group by. Each unique combination of tag values = one series.
  • Fields = the actual numeric values you store (not indexed; cheap to add).
  • Timestamp = nanosecond-precision.

The cardinality lesson: a tag like host with thousands of values is fine; a tag like request_id with millions creates millions of series → cardinality explosion → write/query collapse. Tags should be low-cardinality enums; high-cardinality identifiers belong in fields.

The line protocol — push ingest format

cpu_usage,host=server-1,region=us-east usage_percent=42.3,load_avg=1.7 1715000000000000000

format: <measurement>,<tag1=val1>,<tag2=val2> <field1=val1>,<field2=val2> <timestamp_ns>

Compact, line-oriented, batch-friendly. Clients (Telegraf, vanilla HTTP, language SDKs) POST batches of these lines to /api/v2/write. ~1 M lines / s on a single InfluxDB node with modest hardware.

TSM engine — how InfluxDB 1.x/2.x stores data

  • WAL — every write appended to a write-ahead log first (durability).
  • Cache — recent writes buffered in memory, sorted by series + time.
  • TSM files — periodically flushed from cache; compressed, time-sorted, immutable.
  • Compaction — background process merges TSM files; encodes timestamps via delta-of-delta and values via type-specific compression (RLE, simple8b, double-delta).
  • TSI (Time Series Index) — disk-backed index of series → location, so the working set doesn't have to fit in RAM (older 1.x kept the whole index in memory and OOMed on high cardinality).

Compression: typically ~2–3 bytes per (timestamp, value) pair after compaction. Comparable to Gorilla in spirit, different in algorithm.

InfluxDB 3.x (IOx) — the columnar rewrite

The current direction. Stores data as Parquet on object storage (S3, GCS); query layer uses Apache Arrow + DataFusion for SQL execution. Wins:

  • SQL — direct SQL queries (you can BI-tool against it; previously needed Flux or InfluxQL).
  • Unbounded cardinality — columnar storage handles high-cardinality tags gracefully (the old TSM/TSI ceiling is gone).
  • Object-storage native — separate compute and storage; scale them independently.
  • Cheap long retention — Parquet on S3 is ~$0.023/GB-month; petabyte-scale histories are economically viable.
  • Open formats — your data lives as Parquet + Arrow, queryable from anywhere (Spark, DuckDB, Athena), not locked to InfluxDB.

Retention policies + continuous queries

InfluxDB has first-class support for the down-sampling pattern:

-- Retention policies (how long raw / rolled-up data is kept)
CREATE RETENTION POLICY "raw_7d"   ON metrics DURATION 7d   REPLICATION 1 DEFAULT
CREATE RETENTION POLICY "rolled_90d" ON metrics DURATION 90d REPLICATION 1
CREATE RETENTION POLICY "long_5y"  ON metrics DURATION 1825d REPLICATION 1

-- Continuous Query: every 1m, compute 1-min averages into the 90d bucket
CREATE CONTINUOUS QUERY "cq_1m" ON metrics
BEGIN
  SELECT mean(usage_percent) INTO "rolled_90d"."cpu_usage_1m"
  FROM "raw_7d"."cpu_usage"
  GROUP BY time(1m), host, region
END

In 2.x/3.x the equivalent is "Tasks" (Flux scripts) or SQL materialised views. The principle is identical: raw resolution kept short, aggregated resolution kept long.

When to pick InfluxDB

  • IoT / device telemetry — line protocol fits sensor SDKs perfectly; push from edge devices straight to Influx.
  • Application metrics where push fits — short-lived processes (batch jobs, serverless) can push and disconnect; Prometheus can't scrape them.
  • You want the bundled experience — DB + dashboards + alerts + downsampling tasks in one package (2.x onwards).
  • You want SQL on time-series — InfluxDB 3.x (IOx) is purpose-built; one query language across all your data.
  • You expect high cardinality — 3.x columnar engine handles what 1.x/2.x cannot.

When NOT to pick InfluxDB

  • Service-mesh metrics with Kubernetes auto-discovery → Prometheus is the standard; ecosystem (Grafana, Alertmanager, exporters) is richer.
  • You need joins across time-series + relational tables → TimescaleDB (Postgres extension) is more natural.
  • Heavy ad-hoc OLAP queries → ClickHouse outperforms.
  • Multi-tenant SaaS at hyperscale → Mimir / Cortex / VictoriaMetrics are designed for it.

7Pull vs Push (Prometheus vs InfluxDB)

  • Pull (Prometheus): Prometheus scrapes /metrics on each target every 15 s. Survives client crashes; auto-discovers via Kubernetes/Consul; standard for service monitoring.
  • Push (InfluxDB, Datadog agent): clients push samples to the TSDB. Better when targets are short-lived (batch jobs), behind NAT, or hard to discover.

8Down-Sampling and Retention

Tier 1 (raw): 1-second samples → retained 7 days Tier 2 (rolled-up): 1-minute aggregates → retained 90 days Tier 3 (cold): 1-hour aggregates → retained 5 years

Continuous queries / continuous aggregates compute these on the fly. Querier picks the appropriate tier based on the time range.

9When Columnar OLAP (ClickHouse) Beats a TSDB

If you need rich analytical SQL on time-stamped events — joins, sub-queries, GROUP BY many dimensions — ClickHouse / Druid / Pinot beat dedicated TSDBs. Use a TSDB for metrics monitoring; ClickHouse for ad-hoc analytics; both are fine for ad-click aggregation depending on flexibility needed.

10Interview Defaults

  • "Real-time service metrics" → Prometheus.
  • "Long-term metrics retention" → Prometheus + Thanos / Mimir / VictoriaMetrics.
  • "IoT sensor data, billions of points / day" → InfluxDB or ClickHouse.
  • "Ad-click aggregator with rich analytical queries" → ClickHouse.
  • "I want to keep using Postgres" → TimescaleDB.

Data Structures for Big Data

Probabilistic and compact data structures that let you answer "is X in the set?", "how many uniques?", "what are the top K?" in tiny memory and constant time. The interview-essential ones.

1Bloom Filters — Probabilistic Set Membership

A Bloom filter answers: "Is this element maybe in the set, or definitely not in the set?" Zero false negatives. ~1% false positives. Storage: ~10 bits per element.

How it works: bit array of M bits, all initialised to 0. K hash functions. To add element X: hash with K functions, set the corresponding K bits to 1. To check: hash with K functions, see if all K bits are 1. If any is 0 → definitely not in set. If all are 1 → maybe in set (verify another way).

Use cases:

  • Malicious URL detection: 500M URLs in 600 MB instead of 25 GB.
  • Cassandra: checks if a row exists in an SSTable before reading from disk.
  • Google Bigtable: same purpose.
  • Web crawler dedup: have we seen this URL?
  • CDN cache admission: "is this URL worth caching?"

Sizing: for 10M elements at 0.01% false-positive rate: m ≈ 1.44 × n × log2(1/p) ≈ 192M bits ≈ 24 MB, with k=10 hash functions.

2HyperLogLog — Unique Count in Tiny Memory

Estimates the number of distinct elements in a multiset using ~1.5 KB regardless of the input size. Standard error ~2%. Mergeable across machines.

The intuition: hash each element to a uniform random number; track the longest run of leading zeros seen. The probability of seeing K leading zeros at random is 2^(-K), so seeing K leading zeros suggests ~2^K distinct elements.

Use cases:

  • Daily / monthly active users (DAU / MAU) at scale.
  • Unique IP counts in an analytics pipeline.
  • Unique-visitor counts on Google Analytics, Cloudflare, etc.
  • Redis: PFADD, PFCOUNT, PFMERGE.

3Count-Min Sketch — Frequency & Top-K

Estimates the count of any individual key from a stream using a 2D array of counters. Returns approximate frequencies; biases toward over-counting (never under-counts). Sub-linear memory in stream size.

Use cases:

  • Trending hashtags (top-K with a heap on top of CMS).
  • Heavy hitter detection (DDoS, hot keys).
  • Cassandra's row hot-spot detection.
  • Elements of W-TinyLFU's admission policy (Caffeine library).

4t-digest / HDR Histogram — Approximate Quantiles

Both compute approximate quantile statistics (P50, P95, P99, P99.9) over a stream in tiny memory. t-digest is mergeable across machines, making it ideal for distributed metrics.

Use cases: latency monitoring, SLA reporting, A/B test analysis. Used by Datadog, Splunk, Prometheus (HDR), and many APM tools.

5SimHash & MinHash + LSH — Near-Duplicate Detection

  • SimHash: 64-bit fingerprint where similar documents have similar fingerprints (Hamming distance ≤ 3 means "near-duplicate"). Used by Google for web crawl dedup.
  • MinHash + LSH (Locality-Sensitive Hashing): approximate Jaccard similarity. Used for plagiarism detection, document clustering, recommendation similarity.

6Snowflake IDs — Time-Ordered Unique IDs

Snowflake = 64 bits = 41 timestamp + 10 machine ID + 12 sequence. Generated per-machine without coordination.

  • Time-ordered: newer = larger. Sortable. Great for cursor-based pagination ("give me items older than this ID").
  • Compact: 8 bytes vs UUID's 16 bytes. Better B-Tree index performance.
  • Insertion order: sequential IDs cluster at the right side of B-Tree. UUIDs are random, causing page splits.
  • 2^41 ms ≈ 69 years from epoch; 2^10 = 1024 machines; 2^12 × 1000 ≈ 4M IDs/sec per machine.
  • Trade-off: requires machine_id allocation (Zookeeper, manual) and clock-skew handling.

7Memory-vs-Error Quick Reference

StructureMemoryError
Bloom filter~10 bits per element~1% false positives, 0% false negatives
HyperLogLog~1.5 KB total~2% standard error on cardinality
Count-Min Sketch~10 KBbiased high; tunable accuracy
t-digest~1 KB~1% error on quantiles
HDR Histogram~10 KBconfigurable precision
SimHash8 bytes per doctunable via Hamming threshold

Vector Databases

Stores and queries high-dimensional float vectors (embeddings) by similarity. The retrieval layer behind RAG, semantic search, recommendations, and image/audio search.

1What Is an Embedding?

An ML model (BERT/Sentence-Transformer for text, CLIP for images, Whisper for audio) maps an input to a fixed-length float vector — typically 384, 768, 1536 dimensions. Semantically similar inputs land near each other in the vector space.

  • "king" and "queen" → vectors with cosine similarity ~0.85.
  • A photo of a sunset and a poem about sunsets (via CLIP) → similar.

Storage size: a 768-dim float32 vector = 768 × 4 = 3 072 bytes. 100 M embeddings = ~300 GB.

2The Core Operation — k-NN Similarity Search

Given query vector q and a corpus, find the top-K most similar vectors by:

  • Cosine similarity: (q · v) / (|q| × |v|). Most common for text.
  • Euclidean (L2): ‖q − v‖.
  • Dot product: just q · v; faster when vectors are normalised.

3Why Brute Force Doesn't Scale

Computing similarity against 100 M vectors of 768 dim per query = ~76 GFLOPs per query. At any meaningful QPS this is infeasible. We use Approximate Nearest Neighbour (ANN) — accept ~99% recall in exchange for sub-millisecond retrieval.

4The ANN Algorithms

AlgorithmIdeaTrade-offs
HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World)Multi-layer graph; greedy traversal from sparse top to dense bottomBest recall+latency; high memory; slow build
IVF (Inverted File / k-means)Cluster vectors into N centroids; query searches a few nearest clustersLower memory; tunable speed/recall via probe count
IVF-PQ (Product Quantization)IVF + lossy compression of vectors (8 bytes per vector!)Big memory savings; slight recall loss; FAISS default
ScaNN (Google)Anisotropic quantization + smart partitioningState-of-the-art at billion-scale; complex
DiskANNHNSW-like graph optimised for SSDsLets you index 1 B+ vectors that don't fit in RAM

5The Major Vector DB Choices

ChoiceTypeBest for
pgvectorPostgres extensionYou already have Postgres; small/medium scale; SQL joins on metadata
PineconeManaged SaaSZero ops; easy to start; pricey at very high scale
Weaviate / Qdrant / MilvusSelf-hostable open-sourceFull control, large scale, hybrid search built-in
OpenSearch / Elasticsearch (k-NN)Existing search index + k-NNNative hybrid (BM25 + vector); already running ES
FAISSLibrary, not a DBEmbed in your own service; full algorithmic control

6Hybrid Search (BM25 + Vector)

Vectors are great at meaning ("payment failure" matches "transaction declined"), bad at exact tokens ("v2.3.1"). Real systems combine:

  • BM25 score for keyword matching.
  • Vector similarity for semantic matching.
  • Final score = α × BM25 + (1−α) × vector, with α tuned via offline eval.

Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) is a popular combiner; OpenSearch and Weaviate ship this natively.

7The RAG Pipeline (LLM Retrieval-Augmented Generation)

Document ingestion (offline): docs → chunker (~500 tokens) → embedding model → store (vector + chunk text + metadata) Query (online): user question → embedding model → vector DB top-K ↓ LLM prompt = system + context (top-K chunks) + question ↓ answer (with citations to chunks)

8Sharding and Scaling

  • Vector indexes are sharded by hashing the document ID; queries fan out to all shards (small N is fine).
  • Replicas for availability and read throughput.
  • Index build is offline; query is online — keep them on separate fleets.
  • ~1B vectors per shard is feasible with DiskANN; smaller shards (~10 M) for in-memory HNSW.

9Pitfalls to Mention in Interviews

  • Embedding model upgrades require full re-embedding of the corpus — plan for it.
  • Quality is bounded by chunking strategy and embedding model — the DB itself isn't the differentiator.
  • Watch metadata cardinality (per-tenant filters) — pre-filter then ANN, or post-filter then re-rank.
  • Vector DBs are not your source of truth — keep the original docs in your normal store.
Hard Storage / Sync Chunking Dedup Conflict Resolution CDC-like Sync

Problem 27: Designing Dropbox / File Sync

A cloud file-sync service: edit on laptop, see the change on phone within seconds, never lose data, work offline, share with teammates. The classic "metadata + blobs + change feed" problem at exabyte scale.
