1Context — Sync vs Upload

Dropbox/iCloud/OneDrive are not just file upload — the hard part is keeping N devices and M users in sync without bandwidth waste or data loss.

  • A 1 GB file edited in one place must not re-upload 1 GB — only the changed chunks.
  • Two users editing the same file offline must both be reconciled when they reconnect.
  • A team folder shared across 50 people must see every change within seconds.
  • Selective sync — laptops can't pull 2 TB of team data; they pull metadata + lazy-load files.

2Requirements Gathering

Functional

  • Upload / download files, with progress and resume.
  • Real-time sync across all devices of a user.
  • Share a file or folder with another user (read or read-write).
  • Version history (last 30 days).
  • Conflict handling — if two devices edit while offline, both versions are kept.
  • Selective sync — choose which folders are downloaded locally.
  • Search by filename, optionally by content.
  • Web access (browser file manager + viewer).

Non-Functional

  • Users: 500M; DAU: ~100M.
  • Avg user storage: ~10 GB; tail users (Pro) up to 5 TB.
  • Total stored: ~5 EB (with dedup, ~2 EB physical).
  • Sync latency: P95 < 5 s laptop → other devices.
  • Durability: 11 nines (S3-grade).
  • Availability: 99.99% reads, 99.95% writes.

Clarifying Questions

  • "Web only, or with native desktop / mobile clients?" — native clients enable delta sync and offline.
  • "Is end-to-end encryption required?" — if yes, server can't help with content dedup or content search.
  • "Average file size?" — many small (docs) vs few large (videos) drives chunking strategy.
  • "Multi-region or single region?" — global users need regional storage + sync hubs.

3Capacity Estimation

1 day = 100 k seconds.

MetricCalcValue
DAU—100 M
Avg file changes/user/day—~10
File change events/day100M × 10~1 B/day
Avg event QPS1B / 100k~10 k QPS
Peak event QPS5× avg~50 k QPS
Avg upload size after deltamost changes are small docs~200 KB / event
Avg upload bandwidth10 k × 200 KB~2 GB/s sustained ingress
Peak upload bandwidth50 k × 200 KB~10 GB/s peak
Stored bytes/day1B × 200 KB~200 TB/day
Cumulative total5 yrs of growth~5 EB logical, ~2 EB physical after dedup
Open WebSocket connections~30% of DAU online~30 M
🔑 From Numbers to Architecture
  • ~50 k peak event QPS → need a metadata DB that handles this; sharded Postgres or Cassandra.
  • 10 GB/s peak upload → never proxy through app server; direct-to-S3 with presigned URLs.
  • ~2 EB physical → 60% saved by content-hash dedup; tiered to S3 IA / Glacier for cold data.
  • 30 M persistent WebSocket connections → dedicated push-notification fleet, sharded by user_id.
  • ~200 TB/day → CDC stream feeds the change log, replayable for offline clients catching up.

4API Design

// Initialise upload — server returns chunked upload plan POST /files Body: { path: "/proj/spec.docx", size: 1048576, sha256: "..." } → 200 { file_id, chunks: [{ index, sha256, presigned_put_url }] } // Upload chunks directly to S3 via presigned URL PUT <presigned_url> // client direct-to-S3 per chunk // Finalise after all chunks uploaded POST /files/{file_id}/complete → 201 { revision: 42, server_modified_at: "..." } // List changes since cursor (used by sync clients) GET /changes?cursor=eyJyZXYiOjQwfQ → 200 { changes: [{ type:"upsert", path, file_id, revision, sha256 }, { type:"delete", path }], cursor: "...next..." } // Download specific revision GET /files/{file_id}?revision=42 → 302 redirect to presigned S3 URL // Share POST /shares Body: { path, target_user_id|email, permission: "read"|"edit" }

5Data Model

files (sharded by user_id) file_id PK, user_id, path, current_revision, size, sha256, mime, created_at, updated_at, deleted_at file_revisions (sharded by file_id) file_id, revision, sha256_of_file, size, created_at, device_id blob_refs (the dedup table — content-addressed) sha256 PK, size, s3_key, refcount, last_referenced_at chunks (the dedup unit) chunk_sha256 PK, size, s3_key, refcount file_chunks (composes a file out of chunks) file_id, revision, chunk_index, chunk_sha256 shares share_id, owner_user_id, target_user_id, path, permission, created_at change_log (the per-user sync feed; partitioned by user_id) user_id, revision, op_type, path, file_id, sha256, ts

Notice: the same chunk can be referenced by many file_revisions across many users — that's the dedup win.

6High-Level Architecture

Desktop / Mobile / Web client │ ▼ ┌────────────────────────────┐ │ API Gateway │ ← auth, rate-limit, TLS └────────────┬────────────────┘ │ ┌────────────┴───────────────┬──────────────────┐ ▼ ▼ ▼ Metadata Svc Upload Svc Sync Svc (WebSocket) │ │ │ ▼ ▼ ▼ Sharded Postgres Presigned URL Kafka change_log topic (files, revisions) ↓ │ │ S3 chunk store │ │ (content-addressed) │ ▼ ▼ CDC → Kafka → Sync Svc fanout to subscribed clients │ ▼ Search index (ES) for filename / content search

Why each component (the numbers justify it)

  • Sharded Postgres for metadata — 50k QPS is comfortably within sharded Postgres; we need joins (files ↔ revisions ↔ chunks) so ACID matters.
  • S3 with content-addressed keys — keys are sha256[:2]/sha256[2:]/full_sha256 so identical chunks merge automatically. Refcount tracked separately.
  • Kafka for change_log — replayable per-user feed; clients reconnect with cursor and catch up; ~50k events/s well within Kafka.
  • WebSocket Sync Svc — pushes change events to online clients in < 1 s; sharded by user_id; falls back to polling for clients that can't hold WS.
  • Elasticsearch — filename + (optionally) content-extracted text; built async via CDC of the metadata.

7Deep Dive 1: Chunking & Content-Addressed Dedup

The win is enormous: studies show ~60% of bytes uploaded to a sync service are already present somewhere in the system.

  • Chunk size: ~4 MB is the sweet spot. Bigger → less dedup hit rate. Smaller → too many metadata rows.
  • Rolling hash for boundary detection (Rabin fingerprint): instead of fixed 4MB boundaries, slide a window and cut on hash patterns. Inserting one byte at the start of a file no longer shifts all subsequent boundaries — dedup survives small edits.
  • Per-chunk SHA-256: chunk's content hash is its key. Upload protocol: client computes hashes locally, sends list, server replies "I have these, send only the missing ones."
  • Refcount maintenance: every revision references its chunks. Decrement on revision deletion. GC chunks at refcount=0 with a 30-day grace period (matches version history retention).

8Deep Dive 2: The Sync Protocol

Each user has a monotonically-increasing revision number per file. Each client stores its last-seen cursor (last applied revision).

Initial sync (cold start): 1. Client → GET /changes?cursor=0 (server returns up to 1000 changes) 2. For each change, client downloads file (or chunks it needs) 3. Client commits cursor 4. Repeat until cursor catches up Steady state (online): 1. Client opens WebSocket; subscribes user_id 2. Sync Svc pushes change events as they happen 3. Client applies; persists cursor Reconnect after offline: 1. Client → GET /changes?cursor=<last> to catch up 2. Once empty, reconnect WebSocket

Crucially, the change log is durable and per-user — the client can always replay from any cursor.

9Deep Dive 3: Conflict Resolution

Two devices edit the same file offline; both reconnect. Three strategies, in escalating sophistication:

  1. Last-Writer-Wins: only the later revision survives. Simple but loses data.
  2. Dropbox's "Conflicted Copy": the loser is renamed spec (User-A's conflicted copy).docx. Both versions persist; the user resolves. This is the default for general files.
  3. CRDT / OT merge: for structured files (Google Docs–style), the server reconciles operationally. Different problem (see P19); Dropbox does not do this for general files.

Detection: each file revision carries a parent revision. If a new write claims parent R10 but the server is now at R12, it's a conflict. The client is notified and the file is renamed locally.

10Deep Dive 4: Sharing & Permissions

  • Per-file vs per-folder share: stored in shares table; the change_log fans out to all subscribers — both owner and recipients see the same events.
  • Permission model: owner, editor, viewer, plus link-share with optional password & expiry.
  • Link-share: signed URL with embedded permission claims; resolves to S3 via presigned URL.
  • Selective sync: clients tell server which sub-paths to subscribe to; change_log fanout is filtered server-side to avoid wasting bandwidth on unsubscribed paths.

11Deep Dive 5: Storage Tiering & Cost

At 5 EB logical / 2 EB physical, storage cost dominates. The tiering plan:

TierWhatNotes
S3 StandardLast 30 days of activity per chunkFast retrieval; high cost
S3 Standard-IA30 days – 1 year~40% cheaper; ~ms retrieval
S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval1 year – 3 years~80% cheaper; ms retrieval
S3 Glacier Deep Archive3 years +~95% cheaper; minutes retrieval; only for deleted-but-retained data

Combined with 60% dedup, tiering brings the storage bill down by ~70% vs naive S3 Standard.

12Failure Modes & Recovery

  • S3 region outage → reads fail. Mitigate with cross-region replication (CRR) for hot chunks; failover the metadata DB via replica.
  • Sync Svc node crash → clients reconnect to another node via the load balancer; resume from cursor.
  • Metadata DB shard failure → automatic failover to standby; brief write unavailability for that user shard.
  • Corrupted upload → client recomputes file SHA-256 after assembly; if mismatch, retries from chunk list.
  • Lost chunk in S3 (effectively never, but theoretically) → metadata DB marks file unreadable; alert; client may have a local copy.

13Scaling Path

  • 0 → 1 M users: single Postgres + S3 + WebSocket fleet on one region.
  • 1 M → 100 M users: shard metadata DB by user_id (64 shards); Kafka for change_log; multi-AZ S3.
  • 100 M → 1 B users: regional storage; user pinned to home region; cross-region replication for sharing.
  • Specialised: cold storage migrated to Glacier; rolling-hash chunking for max dedup.

14Cross-Questions and Pushbacks

  • "Why not store the whole file, no chunking?" A 1-byte edit to a 1 GB file would re-upload 1 GB. With 4 MB chunks + rolling hash, you re-upload one chunk (4 MB).
  • "How do you do client-side encryption?" Per-file random data-key, encrypted with user master key, stored alongside metadata. Server can't read content — but loses content dedup and content search.
  • "How does file-name search work without indexing the content?" Filenames + paths are indexed in Elasticsearch via CDC from metadata DB. Content search is opt-in and indexes server-side text extraction (PDFs, docs).
  • "How does the desktop client detect changes?" Native filesystem watchers (inotify on Linux, FSEvents on Mac, ReadDirectoryChangesW on Windows). Periodic scan as fallback.
  • "What if I'm offline for a month and come back?" Client cursor is old; /changes endpoint returns paginated history. Server retains change_log per user for at least 90 days (matches version history retention).
  • "How do you handle very large shared folders?" Selective sync at the path level; clients subscribe only to paths they have locally pulled down. Server filters the fanout.

End of Problem 27.

Medium Web / Indexing BFS Politeness Dedup (SimHash) Distributed Frontier

Problem 28: Designing a Web Crawler

A standalone web crawler that fetches pages of the open web — feeding a search index, an archive (like Common Crawl), or an LLM training corpus. Different from the crawler inside P7 Google Search: here we focus on the crawl machinery itself, not the index.

Article Contents
  1. Context — What "Crawl the Web" Actually Means
  2. Requirements Gathering
  3. Capacity Estimation
  4. API Design (Internal)
  5. Data Model
  6. High-Level Architecture
  7. Deep Dive 1: The URL Frontier
  8. Deep Dive 2: Politeness & robots.txt
  9. Deep Dive 3: URL & Content Deduplication
  10. Deep Dive 4: Freshness — When to Recrawl
  11. Deep Dive 5: Spider Traps & Adversarial Sites
  12. Failure Modes & Recovery
  13. Scaling Path
  14. Cross-Questions and Pushbacks

1Context — What "Crawl the Web" Actually Means

A web crawler does breadth-first search starting from seed URLs:

  1. Pull a URL from the frontier.
  2. Resolve DNS, fetch the HTML.
  3. Parse, extract outgoing links.
  4. Add new links to the frontier (after dedup).
  5. Store the page (full HTML + extracted text).
  6. Schedule a recrawl based on the page's change rate.

The interesting parts are not the fetch itself — they're keeping the frontier balanced, polite to each host, and free of duplicates and traps, at billions-of-URLs scale.

2Requirements Gathering

Functional

  • Crawl the open web starting from a seed list.
  • Discover new URLs from links in fetched pages.
  • Respect robots.txt per host.
  • Avoid hammering any single host (per-host rate limit).
  • De-duplicate URLs and (near-)duplicate content.
  • Recrawl popular / fast-changing pages more often.
  • Persist raw HTML + extracted text + link graph.

Non-Functional

  • Target throughput: ~1 B pages/day = ~10 k pages/sec sustained.
  • Coverage: ~50 B URLs in frontier; ~10 B unique pages stored.
  • Storage: average page ~50 KB compressed → ~500 PB total.
  • Politeness: ≤ 1 request/sec per host by default; honour Crawl-Delay.
  • Freshness: tier-1 pages (news, top sites) recrawled hourly; tier-2 daily; tier-3 weekly+.

Out of Scope

  • Search indexing / ranking (P7).
  • Rendering JavaScript SPAs (mention as a worker-pool extension).
  • Crawling auth-walled / paywalled content.

Clarifying Questions

  • "Are we Google-scale or Common-Crawl-scale?" — drives infra by 10×.
  • "Do we render JS, or only static HTML?" — JS adds a headless-browser fleet that's ~20× more expensive than fetch.
  • "Do we crawl the whole web or only English-language seeds?" — affects DNS / locality strategy.

3Capacity Estimation

1 day = 100 k seconds.

MetricCalcValue
Pages/day target—1 B
Avg fetch QPS1B / 100k~10 k pages/sec
Peak fetch QPS3× avg~30 k pages/sec
Avg page raw size—~150 KB
Avg page compressed3:1 gzip~50 KB
Network in (avg)10k × 150 KB~1.5 GB/s = ~12 Gbps
New URLs discovered/page—~50 (avg ~5 unique after dedup)
Frontier writes/sec10k × 5 unique~50 k QPS
Storage/day1B × 50 KB~50 TB/day
Total store (unique pages, 10 B)10B × 50 KB~500 PB
URL-seen Bloom filter (50 B URLs, 0.01% FP)~10 bits/URL~60 GB shared
🔑 From Numbers to Architecture
  • ~30k peak fetch QPS → fetcher fleet of ~3 k workers (~10 fetches/s/worker including DNS + I/O).
  • 50k frontier-write QPS + 50 B URLs → distributed Kafka-backed frontier; URL-seen filter in Bloom + Cassandra.
  • 50 TB/day raw HTML → S3 (cheap object storage); not a hot DB.
  • Per-host politeness → frontier sharded by host so all URLs of a host land on one fetcher (avoids cross-coordination).
  • ~50 B URLs in Bloom filter (60 GB) → distributed Bloom filters per shard; only definite-not-seen go to the main DB.

4API Design (Internal)

// Add seeds (admin) POST /admin/seeds Body: { urls: [...] } // Inspect frontier state GET /admin/frontier/stats → { size, by_host_top: [...], oldest_enqueued } // Submit a page (fetcher → parser → indexer pipeline) POST /pages Body: { url, fetched_at, http_status, content_sha1, body_s3_key } // Internal: outbound links extracted by parser POST /links Body: { src_url, link_urls: [...] }

The user-facing API is minimal; this is mostly an internal pipeline.

5Data Model

// Frontier (queue) — Kafka topics partitioned by host_hash // key = host_hash, value = { url, priority, enqueued_at, parent_url } // URL metadata (Cassandra, partition by host) url_meta host PK, url SK, first_seen, last_fetched_at, http_status, content_sha1, simhash, fetch_count, change_count, change_rate // Page store (S3 by content_sha1 prefix; immutable) // key = sha1[:2]/sha1[2:4]/full_sha1.html.gz // Link graph (Cassandra) links src_host PK, src_url SK, dst_url // sharded by source so per-page link extraction is single-partition // robots cache (Redis with TTL) robots:<host> → { allowed: regex|patterns, crawl_delay_s, expires_at } // URL-seen Bloom filter (per-shard, in Redis or in-memory) bloom:<shard> → bit array

6High-Level Architecture

Seed URLs ──┐ ▼ ┌──────────────────────────────┐ │ Frontier (Kafka, sharded by │ ←──── New URLs (after dedup) │ host_hash → 1 partition/host)│ └──────────────┬───────────────┘ │ ▼ ┌──────────────────────────────┐ │ Fetcher fleet (3k workers) │ ← consumes its assigned host partitions │ - DNS cache │ ← honours per-host rate limit │ - robots.txt cache │ └────────┬───────────────┬─────┘ │ │ raw HTML │ │ HTTP errors → retry topic ▼ S3 (page store, content-hashed key) │ ▼ ┌──────────────────────────────┐ │ Parser (extract links, │ │ compute SimHash, language) │ └────────┬───────────────┬─────┘ │ │ │ ▼ │ url_meta + link graph (Cassandra) │ ▼ URL-Seen filter (Bloom) ──→ if new: enqueue to Frontier if seen: drop

Why each component

  • Kafka frontier sharded by host_hash — each fetcher worker owns a set of host partitions. All URLs of a host land on one worker → trivial per-host rate-limit, no cross-worker coordination.
  • Fetcher fleet — IO-bound. ~3k workers at 10 fetches/s each handle peak 30k QPS.
  • S3 for raw pages — cheap, durable, immutable. No DB needed; key is content-hash.
  • Cassandra for url_meta + links — partition-keyed by host; high write QPS; no joins required.
  • Redis robots cache — millions of distinct hosts; per-host TTL ~24h; lookup on every fetch.
  • Bloom filter for URL-seen — 60 GB total; partitioned across shards; ~10 ns lookup. False positives drop possibly-new URLs (acceptable for a crawler).

7Deep Dive 1: The URL Frontier

The frontier has three competing requirements:

  1. Politeness: never two simultaneous fetches to the same host.
  2. Priority: high-PageRank / popular hosts get more crawl budget.
  3. Distributedness: scale to billions of URLs without one giant queue.

The classic Mercator design (and what we recommend):

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Front queues (priority bands): │ │ q1 = high priority q2 = medium q3 = low │ └────────────┬────────────────────────────────┘ ▼ (proportional pull) ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Back queues — one per host │ │ host_a: [u1, u2, ...] │ │ host_b: [u3, u4, ...] │ └────────────┬────────────────────────────────┘ ▼ (round-robin with politeness gate) Fetcher

Implementation: each fetcher consumes Kafka partitions assigned to its host hashes. A small in-process scheduler picks the next eligible host (politeness timer expired) and dequeues one URL.

8Deep Dive 2: Politeness & robots.txt

  • Before the first fetch to a new host, fetch https://<host>/robots.txt; cache for 24h.
  • Honour Crawl-Delay directive (Bing/Yandex respect it; Google ignores it but uses its own model).
  • Default rate: ≤ 1 request/sec per host. For tiny sites, even 1 req/sec is too aggressive — apply adaptive throttling on 4xx/5xx.
  • Identify the crawler in User-Agent; expose contact info for webmasters.
  • Adaptive: if a host returns 503 or slow responses, halve the rate; on success, slowly recover.

9Deep Dive 3: URL & Content Deduplication

URL canonicalisation

  • Lower-case scheme + host.
  • Strip default ports (:80 for http, :443 for https).
  • Sort query params; drop tracking params (utm_*, fbclid, ...).
  • Resolve %xx escapes consistently.
  • Drop fragment (#).

URL-seen check (Bloom)

Hash canonical URL → check Bloom filter shard for that host. If "definitely not seen," enqueue + add to Bloom + write to Cassandra. If "maybe seen," double-check Cassandra (rare path).

Content dedup (SimHash near-duplicate)

Many distinct URLs serve identical or near-identical content (mirror sites, syndicated articles, parameterised URLs). Compute SimHash (64-bit hash with Hamming-distance similarity) on the page text. Two pages within Hamming distance ~3 are near-duplicates → store only one canonical copy; link the others as aliases.

See the Big-Data Data Structures Advanced Topics page for SimHash mechanics.

10Deep Dive 4: Freshness — When to Recrawl

A static page recrawled hourly is wasted budget; a news site recrawled weekly is stale. Adaptive scheduling:

  • Track change_rate per page = #(content changes) / #(fetches) over last 30 days.
  • Tier-1 (high-change rate, popular): recrawl every ~hour.
  • Tier-2 (medium): every ~day.
  • Tier-3 (rarely changes): every ~week or longer.
  • Use HTTP If-Modified-Since / ETag conditional GETs — server returns 304 with no body when unchanged. Saves ~70% of recrawl bandwidth.
  • News / sitemap-based discovery: subscribe to sitemap pings + RSS feeds for hot sites.

11Deep Dive 5: Spider Traps & Adversarial Sites

  • Calendar trap: /calendar/2026/05/19/2026/05/20/... generates infinite URLs. Defence: per-host depth limit + pattern detection (URLs with monotonically growing date paths are flagged).
  • Session-id loops: every link contains a new session id. Defence: canonicalisation strips known session params; URL-seen check based on stripped form.
  • Soft 404 pages: server returns 200 for non-existent URLs. Defence: detect identical body across many different URLs (same SimHash) → flag the host.
  • Cloaking: server detects crawler UA and returns different content. Defence: occasional random sampling with a regular-browser UA.
  • Honeypot links: hidden display:none links lead to "crawler-detection" pages. Defence: respect nofollow; render-aware crawler can detect hidden links.

12Failure Modes & Recovery

  • Fetcher worker dies mid-fetch → Kafka offset not committed; partition reassigned to peer; URL re-attempted.
  • DNS resolver overloaded → in-process LRU DNS cache (TTL 1h) + multiple resolvers; failures backed off.
  • Single host unreachable → exponential backoff per host; eventually mark host as dead and stop scheduling.
  • Cassandra hot partition (a host with millions of URLs) → composite partition key (host, hash_bucket) to bucket within a host.
  • Frontier drift (some hosts dominate; others starve) → priority bands ensure tier-1 always gets bandwidth.

13Scaling Path

  • 0 → 100M pages: single-machine crawler with SQLite frontier; 1 fetcher process.
  • 100M → 1B pages: distributed Kafka frontier; ~50 fetcher workers; Cassandra for metadata.
  • 1B → 100B pages: regional crawl fleets (NA, EU, APAC) for DNS / network locality; per-region Cassandra clusters; cross-region link reconciliation.
  • JS rendering: separate headless-browser fleet, ~20× cost per page; limited to "JS-required" hosts.

14Cross-Questions and Pushbacks

  • "Why Kafka and not Redis Lists?" Kafka is durable + replayable; on a 50 B-URL frontier you can't afford to lose any state. Redis Lists are RAM-only; capacity caps before frontier size.
  • "Why Cassandra and not Postgres for url_meta?" Write QPS is ~50k sustained; reads are partition-keyed; no joins. Cassandra is the right shape.
  • "What if a popular site is also a giant?" A single host like youtube.com has billions of URLs. We bucket within a host ((host, bucket_id)) so its URLs distribute across partitions; politeness still enforced via a single fetcher per (host, bucket_id) pair.
  • "How does this differ from Google's crawler?" Google's crawler integrates with their PageRank and serving — recrawl is governed by query-time importance signals. We're approximating with offline change-rate stats.
  • "How do you handle 10 PB of HTML?" S3 with content-hashed keys; lifecycle to Glacier for old crawls; we typically only keep the latest crawl + last 1–2 historical for delta analysis.
  • "What about JS-rendered SPAs?" Headless Chrome/Puppeteer fleet for opt-in hosts; ~10× the latency, ~20× the cost. Detect JS-required pages by initial HTML being ~empty.

End of Problem 28.

Hard Real-time / Analytics Kafka Flink ClickHouse Exactly-Once

Problem 29: Designing an Ad Click Aggregator

Real-time aggregation of ad-click events. Billions per day. Advertisers see updated counts within ~1 minute. The classic streaming problem — and a perfect showcase for Kafka + Flink + ClickHouse.

Article Contents
  1. Context — Why "Just Increment a Counter" Doesn't Work
  2. Requirements Gathering
  3. Capacity Estimation
  4. API Design
  5. Data Model
  6. High-Level Architecture
  7. Deep Dive 1: The Streaming Pipeline (Kafka → Flink)
  8. Deep Dive 2: Exactly-Once Aggregation
  9. Deep Dive 3: Late Events & Watermarks
  10. Deep Dive 4: Click Fraud Detection
  11. Deep Dive 5: Billing-Grade Counts
  12. Failure Modes & Recovery
  13. Scaling Path
  14. Cross-Questions and Pushbacks

1Context — Why "Just Increment a Counter" Doesn't Work

"Click happens → INCR Redis counter" looks fine until you ask:

  • How do I get clicks-per-minute over the last 24 hours, broken down by ad / campaign / country / device?
  • The user reloaded; the SDK fired the event twice — how do I dedup?
  • A mobile user came back from a tunnel; their event arrives 30 minutes late. Which minute does it count toward?
  • Advertisers are billed per click — undercounting loses money, overcounting is illegal.

The real system has to be event-time correct, exactly-once, billing-grade, fraud-resistant, and live within ~1 minute of the click.

2Requirements Gathering

Functional

  • Ingest click events from billions of users.
  • Aggregate by minute / hour / day across many dimensions: ad_id, campaign_id, advertiser_id, country, device_type.
  • Live advertiser-facing dashboards: P95 query < 1 s.
  • Generate billable totals (per-day) by midnight UTC + 1 hour.
  • Deduplicate (the same click counted once even with retries).
  • Detect & filter fraud (bots, click farms, accidental double-taps).

Non-Functional

  • Click events/day: ~10 B = ~100 k events/sec avg, ~500 k peak.
  • Reporting freshness: aggregates visible within 1 min of the event.
  • Accuracy: billing-grade — exactly-once.
  • Retention: raw events 30 days; minute aggregates 90 days; hour 1 year; day forever.
  • Availability: 99.99% — losing data is loss of revenue.

Clarifying Questions

  • "Are we serving the ads ourselves or only counting?" — we focus on counting; ad-serving is a separate system.
  • "Click vs impression vs conversion?" — same pipeline, different topics; we focus on clicks.
  • "What's the worst-case lateness we'll tolerate?" — 5 min for live dashboards; up to 1 hour for billing.

3Capacity Estimation

1 day = 100 k seconds.

MetricCalcValue
Click events/day—10 B
Avg ingest QPS10B / 100k~100 k events/sec
Peak ingest QPS5× avg~500 k events/sec
Per event size—~500 B
Network in (avg)100k × 500 B~50 MB/s = 400 Mbps
Raw events/day stored (S3 + Kafka)10B × 500 B~5 TB/day
Distinct (ad × minute) cells/day1M ads × 1.4k minutes~1 B
Aggregate rows/day in OLAPafter rollup~100 M/day (~10 GB/day in ClickHouse)
Dashboard QPS~500 advertisers polling~5 k QPS
🔑 From Numbers to Architecture
  • ~500 k peak events/sec → Kafka (single broker handles 1 M+; we run a small cluster, partition by ad_id).
  • Real-time per-minute aggregations + exactly-once → Flink with checkpointing (its sweet spot).
  • ~5 k dashboard QPS over multi-dimensional aggregates → ClickHouse (columnar, sub-second on billions of rows).
  • Billing-grade exactness → idempotent click_id at the SDK; Flink dedup state; daily reconciliation against raw events in S3.
  • Late events up to ~1 hour → Flink watermark allowance + ClickHouse upsert via ReplacingMergeTree.

4API Design

// Click ingest (from ad SDK / browser) POST /v1/clicks Body: { click_id: "uuid-from-sdk", // idempotency key ad_id, campaign_id, advertiser_id, user_id_hash, ip, user_agent, device_type, country, ts_iso } Response: 202 Accepted (always; cheap path) // Advertiser dashboard query GET /v1/reports ?advertiser_id=...&from=2026-05-01&to=2026-05-19 &groupBy=ad_id,country&granularity=hour Response: rows of aggregates

Ingest endpoint always 202s — push the event to Kafka and return. Heavy lifting is in the streaming pipeline.

5Data Model

// Kafka topic: clicks_raw, partitioned by ad_id, retention 30 days // { click_id, ad_id, campaign_id, advertiser_id, ts, ip, ... } // Flink state (RocksDB on each TM, checkpointed to S3): // per (ad_id, minute_bucket): { count, unique_user_estimate (HLL), // click_ids seen (set, TTL 1h for dedup) } // Sink: ClickHouse table CREATE TABLE clicks_per_minute ( minute_bucket DateTime, ad_id UInt64, campaign_id UInt64, advertiser_id UInt64, country FixedString(2), device String, count UInt64, unique_users UInt64, insert_ts DateTime ) ENGINE = ReplacingMergeTree(insert_ts) PARTITION BY toYYYYMMDD(minute_bucket) ORDER BY (advertiser_id, ad_id, minute_bucket); // Materialized view aggregates clicks_per_minute → clicks_per_hour, _per_day // Raw events archived to S3 (parquet, partitioned by date) for replay / audit

6High-Level Architecture

Ad SDK / browser │ ▼ POST /v1/clicks (with click_id) ┌──────────────────────┐ │ Ingest API (stateless)│ → Kafka clicks_raw (partitioned by ad_id) └──────────────────────┘ │ │ ├─── S3 archive (parquet, daily partitions) │ ▼ ┌─────────────────┐ │ Flink job │ │ - dedup (click_id)│ │ - fraud filter │ │ - tumbling 1-min│ │ - watermark 5min│ └────┬─────────┬───┘ │ │ ▼ ▼ ClickHouse Redis (hot keys (per-min agg) for sub-second current-minute reads) │ ▼ Dashboard / Reports API

Why each component

  • Ingest API — stateless, 202s; pushes to Kafka. Auto-scales horizontally; ~10 cheap nodes for 500 k/s peak.
  • Kafka clicks_raw — partitioned by ad_id so Flink can keyBy locally; replication factor 3.
  • S3 archive — every event also persisted as parquet; lets us replay / re-aggregate; required for billing audit.
  • Flink — tumbling 1-min windows keyed by (ad_id, minute); RocksDB state; checkpointed every 60 s to S3 → exactly-once with Kafka source's offsets.
  • ClickHouse — columnar; receives Flink's per-minute aggregates; materialized views roll up to hour and day; sub-second multi-dimensional queries on billions of rows.
  • Redis hot cache — for "current minute, top ads" widget on the dashboard; updated by Flink as the window emits.

7Deep Dive 1: The Streaming Pipeline (Kafka → Flink)

The Flink job topology:

source(Kafka clicks_raw) → filter(fraud_score < THRESHOLD) → keyBy(click_id) → keyedProcessFunction with TTL state for dedup (1h window) → keyBy(ad_id) → window(TumblingEventTimeWindows.of(1 min)) → aggregate({ count, HLL_for_unique_users }) → sink(ClickHouse, Redis)

Why both keyBys: dedup needs click_id-keyed state; aggregation needs ad_id-keyed state. Two different shuffles in the dataflow.

8Deep Dive 2: Exactly-Once Aggregation

Three layers of exactly-once protection:

  1. SDK-side click_id — random UUID generated on the device; same retried HTTP call carries the same id.
  2. Flink dedup state — keyed-state set of click_ids seen in last 1 hour; duplicates dropped.
  3. ClickHouse ReplacingMergeTree — same (window-key, insert_ts) row replaces previous on merge; even if Flink emits a window twice (after a recovery), the latest insert_ts wins.

Flink's checkpoint coordinates Kafka source offsets + RocksDB state + ClickHouse sink barrier → end-to-end exactly-once.

9Deep Dive 3: Late Events & Watermarks

Mobile user goes through a tunnel; their event arrives 10 minutes late.

  • Watermark policy: declare watermark = max_observed_event_time − 5 min. Window for minute M closes 5 min after M+1.
  • Allowed lateness: 1 hour. Events arriving within 1 hour past window close trigger an additional emit (an UPDATE row in ClickHouse).
  • Side output for very-late events: events > 1 hour late go to a side topic; reconciled in the next-day batch job from S3.
  • Trade-off: longer watermark = more late events captured but slower close. 5 min is the industry sweet spot for ad-tech.

10Deep Dive 4: Click Fraud Detection

Before counting, filter:

  • Bot signatures: known data-centre IP ranges, headless-browser fingerprints.
  • Rate-based: same user_id_hash > 10 clicks/min on the same ad_id → flag.
  • Pattern-based: clicks from one IP /24 with too-uniform inter-arrival times → flag.
  • ML re-scoring: an offline model assigns fraud probability; high-probability clicks are excluded from billable totals (kept in raw for audit).

The fraud filter runs in Flink as the first stage. False positives lose advertisers' attribution; false negatives cost them money. Tuned with constant offline eval.

11Deep Dive 5: Billing-Grade Counts

The dashboard shows live numbers (eventually consistent within seconds). The billable total is computed by a daily batch job:

  1. At midnight UTC + 1 hour, run a batch job over S3 raw events for the previous day.
  2. Compute "ground truth" per-ad day total with full dedup + fraud rules (which can use a more expensive ML model than streaming).
  3. Compare to ClickHouse's day rollup; flag deltas > 0.1% for review.
  4. Charge advertisers from the batch number, not the stream number.

Stream is for dashboards; batch is for money. The two converge but billing always trusts batch.

12Failure Modes & Recovery

  • Flink TM crash → state restored from latest S3 checkpoint; Kafka resumes from checkpointed offset; window may re-emit same minute (ReplacingMergeTree handles).
  • ClickHouse node down → distributed query hits replicas; writes buffer in Flink sink with retry.
  • Kafka topic loss → S3 archive is the durable backstop; replay job reconstructs.
  • Late event flood (an entire region disconnect ends) → Flink sees a spike; watermark advances slowly; dashboards show "data settling" badge until normal.
  • Bug in fraud filter → discovered weeks later; replay raw events from S3 with corrected filter; rebuild aggregates.

13Scaling Path

  • ~10k events/s: single Kafka broker + small Flink job + Postgres for aggregates.
  • ~100k–500k events/s (this design): 5-broker Kafka, ~50 Flink TM cores, ClickHouse cluster.
  • 10×: shard ClickHouse, increase Kafka partitions, scale Flink TM count linearly.
  • Global multi-region: ingest in each region; replicate to a single analytics region (DC traffic = 1 click event ~500 B is cheap).

14Cross-Questions and Pushbacks

  • "Why Flink and not Spark Streaming?" Spark micro-batches at ~10s; we need 1-min freshness with event-time semantics. Flink is true streaming.
  • "Why ClickHouse and not Druid / BigQuery?" All work; ClickHouse is open-source, low-cost, very fast on this exact pattern (single-table aggregates with high-cardinality dimensions). Druid is heavier ops; BigQuery is great if you're already on GCP.
  • "How would you do impressions instead of clicks?" Same pipeline, separate topic; volume is ~100× higher (every ad render). May need sampling or sketch-based unique-user counting (HLL).
  • "How do you compute unique users in real time?" HyperLogLog state in Flink — ~16 KB per (ad, window); 2% accuracy; mergeable. Final exact counts come from batch.
  • "What if the SDK can't generate click_id?" Server generates from (user_id, ad_id, ts truncated to second). Less perfect but good enough for retry-window dedup.
  • "How would advertisers query their data?" Reports API issues a parameterised SQL to ClickHouse; cache popular queries in Redis (TTL 30 s); rate-limit per advertiser.

End of Problem 29.

Medium Geo / Search Geohash / H3 / S2 Elasticsearch Read-Heavy CDN

Problem 30: Designing Yelp / Geo-Search

"Show me restaurants within 2 km of my current location, open now, rated 4+, sorted by distance." A read-heavy geo-search system at city / global scale. Different from Uber (P5) — here the points-of-interest are static; the user is mobile.

1Context — Why Geo-Search Is Hard

A naive solution: SELECT * FROM places WHERE distance(point, $loc) < 2000. That's a full-table scan over millions of rows. Even with a B-tree on (lat, lng), B-trees are 1-D — they can't efficiently answer 2-D range queries.

The trick is to map 2-D space to a 1-D key with locality preservation: nearby places get nearby keys → range scan on the 1-D index returns nearby places. Geohash, H3, S2, and quadtrees are all variants of this idea.

Then layer non-geo filters (open-now, ratings, cuisine, price) and ranking on top.

2Requirements Gathering

Functional

  • Search places by location + radius + filters (cuisine, rating, price, open-now).
  • View place details (photos, hours, menu, reviews, map).
  • Browse popular places per neighbourhood.
  • Submit a review (rating + text + photos).
  • Owner-side: claim listing, update info, respond to reviews.

Non-Functional

  • Listings (places): ~100 M globally.
  • Users: ~500 M; DAU: ~50 M.
  • Search QPS: ~10 k avg / 50 k peak.
  • Reviews / day: ~1 M.
  • Photos / day: ~10 M.
  • Latency: P95 search < 200 ms; place page < 100 ms (cached).
  • Read:Write: ~1000:1 (browse-heavy).
  • Availability: 99.99%.

Clarifying Questions

  • "Cell-phone GPS only or also IP-based location?" — affects accuracy assumptions.
  • "Is owner-side dashboard in scope?" — affects auth + write paths.
  • "Booking / ordering integrations?" — out of scope here; design accommodates additions.

3Capacity Estimation

1 day = 100 k seconds.

MetricCalcValue
Listings—100 M
DAU—50 M
Searches/day50M × ~20 actions × 10% are searches~1 B/day
Avg search QPS1B / 100k~10 k
Peak search QPS5× avg (Friday evening)~50 k
Place-page reads/day50M × ~5~250 M/day
Photos/day10M × 500 KB~5 TB/day raw → ~7 TB/day with variants
Reviews/day write QPS1M / 100k~10 QPS (laughably small)
Listings storage100M × 5 KB metadata~500 GB
Photo storage cumulative5 yrs growth, dedup~20 PB
🔑 From Numbers to Architecture
  • ~50 k peak search QPS with rich filters → Elasticsearch (geo + filter + ranking in one query).
  • ~1000:1 read:write → aggressive caching (Redis for place pages, CDN for photos).
  • Listings (~500 GB metadata) → single Postgres handles writes (10 QPS for reviews is trivial).
  • Photos (~20 PB cumulative) → S3 + CloudFront; never proxy through app server.
  • Heavy read on tiny write → Postgres → CDC → ES; CDC keeps ES eventually consistent within seconds.

4API Design

// Search GET /v1/search ?lat=37.77&lng=-122.41&radius_m=2000 &q=ramen&cuisine=japanese&price=2,3 &open_at=2026-05-19T19:30Z &rating_gte=4&sort=distance &cursor=... → 200 { results: [{ place_id, name, distance_m, rating, photo_url, ... }], next_cursor } // Place details GET /v1/places/{place_id} → 200 { ...full details with photos, hours, recent reviews } // Reviews GET /v1/places/{place_id}/reviews?cursor=... POST /v1/places/{place_id}/reviews { rating, text, photo_ids: [...] } // Photo upload (presigned) POST /v1/photos { place_id, content_type } → { photo_id, presigned_put_url } PUT <presigned_url> // direct-to-S3

5Data Model

// Postgres (source of truth) places (place_id PK, name, lat, lng, address, hours_json, cuisine_tags[], price_tier, owner_id, status, created_at, updated_at, rating_cached NUMERIC(2,1), review_count_cached INT) reviews (review_id PK, place_id FK, user_id, rating, text, photo_ids[], created_at) photos (photo_id PK, place_id, user_id, s3_key, w, h, created_at) // Elasticsearch index "places" { place_id, name, name_ngram, location: { lat, lng }, // geo_point cuisine_tags: [...], price_tier, rating, popularity_score, hours: [...], // for open_at filter is_open_now (denormalised; recomputed periodically), ... } // Redis caches "place:{id}" → place page JSON (TTL 5 min) "search:{hash}" → search result JSON (TTL 30 s)

6High-Level Architecture

Client (mobile / web) │ ▼ ┌──────────────────────┐ │ CDN (CloudFront) │ ← serves photos + cached static └─────────┬────────────┘ ▼ ┌──────────────────────┐ │ API Gateway │ └─────────┬────────────┘ │ ┌────────┼────────────────┬────────────────┐ ▼ ▼ ▼ ▼ Place Search Svc Reviews Svc Photo Svc Svc │ │ │ ┌┴────────────┐ ▼ │ ▼ ▼ S3 │ Elasticsearch Redis │ │ (geo + filter) (search cache) ▼ ▼ CDN Postgres (places + reviews + photos meta) │ ▼ CDC → Kafka → ES indexer (keeps ES in sync) → analytics warehouse (offline)

Why each component

  • Elasticsearch handles geo_point + multi-field filter + ranking + pagination in a single query — no DB can match this combination.
  • Postgres is the source of truth (ACID, joins for owner dashboards).
  • Redis caches place pages and the popular search queries; ~95% hit rate for place pages.
  • CDN for photos + static assets — millions of photo views without touching origin.
  • CDC pipeline keeps ES eventually consistent with Postgres in seconds; review submissions show up in search shortly after.

7Deep Dive 1: Geo Indexing — Geohash vs H3 vs S2 vs Quadtree

GeohashH3 (Uber)S2 (Google)Quadtree
Cell shaperectangle (lat/lng grid)hexagonsquare (sphere-projected)square (recursive split)
Levels1–12 (each level halves)0–150–30arbitrary
Key formbase32 string64-bit int64-bit inttree path
Locality preservationGood (Z-order)Excellent (uniform neighbours)Excellent (Hilbert curve)OK
Edge effectsBad at antimeridian/polesGoodGoodBad at poles
Best forsimple proximity, easy DB indexUber-like dispatch, ride-sharingGoogle Maps-grade large coveragegame maps, R-tree alternatives

For Yelp specifically, Elasticsearch's geo_point + geo_distance filter handles this natively — under the hood ES uses BKD trees (essentially a 2-D k-d-tree variant) which is excellent for geo range queries.

If we built our own index, we'd use H3 level 9 cells (~150 m hex side); search query is "all hexes overlapping the radius circle" → up to ~7 hex IDs → fetch their listings → filter by exact distance.

8Deep Dive 2: Combined Geo + Filter Search

The Elasticsearch query for "ramen, 2 km from here, open now, rated 4+":

{ "query": { "bool": { "must": [ { "match": { "name_ngram": "ramen" }}, { "term": { "cuisine_tags": "japanese" }} ], "filter": [ { "geo_distance": { "distance": "2km", "location": { "lat":..., "lon":... }}}, { "range": { "rating": { "gte": 4 }}}, { "term": { "is_open_now": true }} ] } }, "sort": [ { "_geo_distance": { "location":..., "order":"asc" }} ], "size": 20 }

Filters are bitset-cached and ANDed; the geo_distance + sort uses ES's BKD-tree spatial index. Sub-100 ms on a corpus of 100 M docs.

The "open-now" trick

Computing "is this place open right now" per query is expensive (timezones, holidays, hours-json eval). Solution: a periodic job (every 5 min) flips the is_open_now boolean on each ES doc. Filter is then a simple term query.

9Deep Dive 3: Ranking — Distance, Rating, Popularity

Pure distance sort feels mechanical ("the closest place might be terrible"). Yelp blends:

  • Relevance (BM25 on text query if present).
  • Distance (decay function — score drops as distance grows).
  • Rating × log(review_count) — popularity-weighted rating.
  • Personalisation (if signed in: cuisine affinity, past visits).
  • Recency boost (newer reviews favoured slightly).

ES function_score query expresses this in JSON; weights tuned offline against click logs.

10Deep Dive 4: Photo Pipeline (Heavy Read Side)

Photos dominate user-perceived performance.

  • Upload: presigned URL → direct to S3.
  • Variants: an async worker (triggered by S3 ObjectCreated event) generates thumbnails (200×200, 400×400, 800×800) and AVIF/WebP encodings; stored alongside the original.
  • Delivery: CloudFront with origin S3; cache-key includes variant; immutable URL → high CDN hit rate.
  • Metadata: photos row in Postgres; photo_ids referenced from listings + reviews.
  • Moderation: NSFW classifier on upload; flagged photos held for review.

11Deep Dive 5: Reviews — Tiny Writes, Massive Reads

~10 review writes/sec is laughable for any DB. The challenge is read-side:

  • Place page must show top reviews — pre-sorted by helpfulness (votes / freshness).
  • Cache the place page (which embeds top-N reviews) in Redis with TTL 5 min.
  • "Helpful" votes update review row + invalidate cache (or just rely on TTL).
  • Pagination uses cursor on (helpful_votes desc, created_at desc).

Aggregate metrics (rating, review_count) are denormalised on the place row; updated via DB trigger or Kafka consumer on review writes.

12Failure Modes & Recovery

  • ES down → fallback to Postgres geo query (PostGIS) — slower but functional; cache hit rate masks most of it for popular queries.
  • Postgres primary fail → standby promoted; brief write outage; reads continue from replicas.
  • S3 region outage → photos fail to load; CDN serves still-cached variants; uploads buffered locally with retry.
  • CDC pipeline lag → ES becomes stale; place pages updated within minutes; alert on lag > 60 s.
  • Hot place (a viral restaurant) → place page Redis cache key sees 100k QPS; soft TTL + request coalescing prevents stampede.

13Scaling Path

  • Single city: Postgres + ES + Redis on small fleet; handle 10 k DAU comfortably.
  • Country scale (millions DAU): horizontal scale ES (5+ nodes), Redis cluster.
  • Global (this design): regional ES indexes (US / EU / APAC) sharded by region; users routed by IP-geo; cross-region only for owner dashboards.
  • Photo cost dominant → tier S3 to IA after 30 days, Glacier after 1 year.

14Cross-Questions and Pushbacks

  • "Why ES and not pure Postgres + PostGIS?" Postgres can do geo well — but combining geo + multi-field filter + ranking + pagination at 50k QPS taxes a relational DB. ES is purpose-built for this.
  • "Why not Redis GEO commands?" Redis GEO is great for pure proximity (Uber-style "nearest driver"). It doesn't combine with multi-field filters or ranking — wrong shape for this problem.
  • "How do you handle a viral place at 100k QPS?" Place page is the hot key; Redis cached + request coalescing; CDN can also cache the API response by URL with short TTL.
  • "How fresh is search data?" Eventual consistency — CDC pipeline lag is < 30 s typically. Reviews and ratings show up in search within seconds.
  • "Multi-language search?" ES analysers per language; queries detect language client-side or via header; index has name_en, name_ja, etc.
  • "How do you compute 'open now' across timezones?" Periodic job (every 5 min) flips a denormalised boolean on each ES doc per local time + holidays. Filter is then trivial.

End of Problem 30.

Problem 31: Designing a Metrics Monitoring System

Prometheus / Datadog / Mimir scale. Ingest tens of millions of points/sec, store cheaply, query at sub-second latency, alert on rules. The canonical "build-your-own time-series DB" interview.

1Context — Why Metrics ≠ Logs ≠ Events

Three observability data types people often conflate:

MetricsLogsTraces
Shapenumeric time seriesstructured textspans of work with parent/child links
Volumehigh (every 15 s × N series)highestmedium
Compressionexcellent (~1.4 B/sample)moderatemoderate
Usedashboards, alertsdebugging, auditdistributed-system perf
Storagespecialised TSDBElasticsearch / Loki / S3Tempo / Jaeger

This problem is purely the metrics system. Specialised because the workload (high-throughput numeric, time-stamped, label-multidimensional) is wildly compressible and queryable in ways general DBs aren't.

2Requirements Gathering

Functional

  • Collect metrics from thousands of services and hosts.
  • Multi-dimensional labels: http_request_duration{service, method, status, region}.
  • Real-time dashboards (last 1 min – last 30 days, all granularities).
  • Long retention (1–5 years) for capacity planning.
  • Alerting on PromQL-like rules.
  • Multi-tenant: per-team isolation, quotas.

Non-Functional

  • Series count: ~10 M active time series.
  • Sample rate: every 15 s → ~700 k samples/sec average ingest, ~2 M peak.
  • Query QPS: ~5 k from dashboards + alerts.
  • Query latency: P95 < 1 s for last-hour queries; < 5 s for 30-day queries.
  • Retention: raw 15 s for 7 days; 1-min rollups for 90 days; 1-hour rollups for 5 years.
  • Availability: 99.99% — outages mean blind to incidents.

Clarifying Questions

  • "Single tenant or SaaS multi-tenant?" — multi-tenant adds quota + isolation complexity.
  • "Pull (Prometheus-style) or push (Datadog-style)?" — affects collector design.
  • "Are we storing logs / traces too?" — out of scope here.

3Capacity Estimation

1 day = 100 k seconds.

MetricCalcValue
Active series—~10 M
Sample rate1 every 15 s~700 k samples/sec
Peak ingest—~2 M samples/sec
Bytes per sample (Gorilla)—~1.4 B
Storage/day raw700k × 86400 × 1.4 B~85 GB/day raw (compressed)
Raw retention 7d85 × 7~600 GB
1-min rollup retention 90d÷ 4 (1-min vs 15-s) × 90 d~2 TB
1-hour rollup retention 5y÷ 240 × 1825 d~1.6 TB
Total long-term storage—~5 TB
Query QPS—~5 k
🔑 From Numbers to Architecture
  • ~2 M samples/sec ingest → Kafka (or a write-buffer) → ingester fleet sharded by series_id.
  • ~5 TB total → cheap storage; S3 for long-term + local SSD for hot 24h.
  • ~1.4 B/sample with Gorilla → 12× cheaper than naïve storage; the killer feature.
  • 5 k query QPS with multi-dim filter + range scan → query engine fan-out across shards; gRPC merges results.
  • Retention tiers (raw / 1-min / 1-hour) → continuous-aggregate compactor; query router picks correct tier by time-range.

4API Design

// Push ingest (push-based mode) POST /api/v1/write Body: protobuf-encoded list of (series_id, timestamp, value) Response: 204 // Pull (Prometheus model): system scrapes targets' /metrics endpoints GET http://target/metrics → text-format metrics // Query GET /api/v1/query ?query=sum(rate(http_requests_total[5m]))%20by%20(service) &time=2026-05-19T10:00Z GET /api/v1/query_range ?query=...&start=...&end=...&step=15s // Series metadata (UI for dashboard builders) GET /api/v1/series ?match[]=http_request_duration{service="orders"} GET /api/v1/labels GET /api/v1/label/{name}/values // Alerts POST /api/v1/rules { group, rule: { alert, expr, for, labels, annotations }} GET /api/v1/alerts → currently firing

5Data Model — Metric + Labels

A "time series" is uniquely identified by its (metric_name, labels) tuple: http_request_duration_seconds{ service="orders", method="POST", status="200", region="us-east-1", pod="orders-7f4b9c-2" } Each series has a stream of (timestamp, value) samples. Inverted index maps label → series_ids: service="orders" → { sid_1, sid_5, sid_42, ... } status="200" → { sid_1, sid_2, sid_5, ... } A query "service=orders AND status=200" intersects the two postings lists.

6High-Level Architecture

┌──────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ │ Targets │ /metrics scraped (pull) │ Service-side │ │ (services, │ ─────────────────────────────► │ /metrics │ │ exporters) │ └──────────────┘ └──────────────┘ │ (or) ▼ ┌──────────────┐ │ Collectors │ ← scrape OR receive push └──────┬───────┘ │ ▼ ┌──────────────────────────────┐ │ Ingester fleet (sharded by │ → Kafka WAL (durable buffer) │ hash(series_id)) │ └──────┬─────────────┬──────────┘ │ │ ▼ ▼ In-memory Inverted-label block (last 2h) index per shard │ │ ▼ │ Periodic flush │ to S3 (Parquet │ blocks, immutable) │ │ │ ▼ ▼ ┌──────────────────────────────┐ │ Compactor: 15s → 1-min │ │ 1-min → 1-hour │ └──────────────────────────────┘ Query path: Client → Query Router → routes by time-range to right tier fans out to ingesters (recent) + S3-backed queriers (historical) merges results → returns JSON Alert engine: periodically evaluates rules via Query path → fires alerts → Notification Service

Why each component

  • Collectors — language-agnostic; scrape mode for service mesh, push mode for batch jobs / NAT-ed targets.
  • Ingester fleet — owns hot 2h of data in memory + RocksDB-style local store; replicates to peers (factor 2).
  • Kafka WAL — durable buffer; ingester crash recovery replays from offset.
  • S3 blocks — Parquet-style immutable blocks; cheap; queried via lazy fetch on cold paths.
  • Compactor — produces tiered rollups; deletes raw samples after 7 days.
  • Query Router — picks the appropriate tier per time-range; fans out queries to shards by label-set.
  • Alert engine — runs each rule on a schedule (default every 1 min) via the Query path.

7Deep Dive 1: Pull vs Push Collection

Pull (Prometheus)Push (StatsD / Datadog agent)
Discoveryvia Kubernetes / Consul / static configclient knows endpoint
NAT / firewalled targetsDoesn't reachWorks
Ephemeral jobs (cron)job ends before scrapeperfect (push at exit)
Liveness signalscrape success = upneed separate heartbeat
Backpressurescraper-controlledcan DDoS the ingester

Modern systems support both. Default to pull for steady services, push for batch jobs and serverless. Internally both feed the same ingester fleet.

8Deep Dive 2: Storage — Gorilla Compression & Tiered Retention

Gorilla compression

Two tricks (Facebook 2015 paper):

  • Delta-of-delta timestamps: regular sample rates → most deltas-of-deltas are 0; encode in 1 bit.
  • XOR-encoded floats: consecutive values share most bits; XOR with previous, store only the differing middle bits.

Achieves ~1.4 bytes/sample for typical metrics. 12× compression vs naïve 16-byte (timestamp + double).

Block layout (per series, per 2-hour chunk)

chunk_header   { series_id, t_start, t_end, sample_count }
gorilla_bytes  { compressed deltas + values }
checksum

Tiered retention

Compactor runs continuously:

  • 2h chunks → daily blocks at original 15 s resolution; kept 7 days.
  • Rolled up to 1-min aggregates (avg, min, max, count); kept 90 days.
  • Rolled up to 1-hour aggregates; kept 5 years.

Query router picks the appropriate tier per requested resolution.

9Deep Dive 3: Query Engine (PromQL-style)

PromQL operations:

  • Selectors: http_requests_total{service="orders"} → look up label index → list of series.
  • Range vector: [5m] → samples within last 5 min for those series.
  • Functions: rate(), increase(), histogram_quantile(), avg_over_time().
  • Aggregations: sum by (service), topk(5, ...).

Execution: parse → AST → planner picks the right tier(s) by time-range → fans out to ingester / querier shards by series_id → results streamed back and merged → aggregations applied.

Cache plan results in Redis (TTL 30 s) — same dashboard, same rule fires every minute and hits cache for < 30 s old data.

10Deep Dive 4: Alerting Engine

Alerting is a scheduled query evaluator with state:

  • Each rule defines: expr (PromQL), for (must be true for X minutes), labels, annotations.
  • Evaluator runs every interval (default 1 min); evaluates expr; if non-empty result, that's a "pending" alert.
  • Alert flips to "firing" once "pending" duration ≥ for. Avoids transient flaps.
  • Firing alerts pushed to a notification service (PagerDuty / Slack / Webhooks) — deduped + grouped + silenced based on labels.
  • Alert state stored locally + replicated for HA; gossip-based syncing across alertmanager replicas.

11Deep Dive 5: Cardinality Control

Cardinality = number of unique (metric_name, label_values) tuples. The single biggest scaling killer.

  • Bad pattern: http_requests{user_id="42"} → one series per user → millions of series.
  • Defence: per-tenant series limit (e.g. 100 k); reject ingest beyond the limit; alert the team.
  • Per-label limits: cap distinct values per label name (e.g. status_code has ~10 values; reject if 1000+ values appear).
  • Cardinality dashboards: show the top-10 highest-cardinality metrics per tenant.
  • Recording rules: pre-aggregate high-cardinality combinations into lower-cardinality series (service:http_requests:rate5m).

12Failure Modes & Recovery

  • Ingester crash → in-memory data lost; replay from Kafka WAL; replicas (factor 2) cover continuity.
  • Compactor lag → query router falls back to scanning raw blocks; alert if lag > 1 hour.
  • S3 unavailable → cold queries fail; recent data served from ingesters; alert.
  • Cardinality explosion (a buggy deployment emits a label with timestamps) → ingester refuses new series; alert pages on-call.
  • Network partition between collector and ingester → collector buffers locally; replays after reconnection (push mode).

13Scaling Path

  • Single team / 100 k series: vanilla Prometheus on one box. ~30 min ops.
  • Single org / 10 M series (this design): clustered Prometheus + Mimir/Cortex/Thanos for long-term + S3 for blocks.
  • Multi-tenant SaaS: hash-shard tenants across ingester groups; quota enforcement; per-tenant query budget.
  • Hyperscale (Datadog scale, ~10 B series): regional ingest, central query plane, per-tenant DBs.

14Cross-Questions and Pushbacks

  • "Why not Postgres / TimescaleDB?" Ingest at 2 M samples/sec sustained breaks Postgres. TimescaleDB scales further but specialised TSDBs achieve 5–10× better compression and 10× faster range queries.
  • "Why not InfluxDB?" Equally valid choice; InfluxDB pushed; Prometheus pulled. Modern InfluxDB (IOx) and the Prometheus ecosystem are converging on Parquet + Datafusion-style backends.
  • "Why not ClickHouse?" ClickHouse is an excellent fit for ad-click events / log analytics; for metrics you lose the per-series compression and label-index optimisations. Specialised TSDB wins on metrics.
  • "What if I want both metrics + logs in one query?" That's an "observability platform" (Grafana, Datadog). They join across systems at query time; the underlying stores are still specialised.
  • "How do you handle high-cardinality counters from microservices?" Recording rules pre-aggregate; per-tenant series quotas; PR review of new label dimensions.
  • "How does PromQL execute distributed queries?" Query router parses → fans out by series_id ranges to shard-owning queriers → they evaluate the leaf selectors locally → router combines via the operator tree (sum, avg, topk).

End of Problem 31.
